specializations.title: Sensitive Data Detection and Redaction
description:
Guardrails are safety controls placed between users, tools, and generative AI models to evaluate prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, and agent actions before they are accepted, executed, or shown to a user. They can help block, modify, or route unwanted content such as malicious code, malicious instructions, sensitive data, unsupported claims, policy-violating responses, or unsafe tool requests.

Guardrails can be implemented using rule-based controls such as filters, allowlists, blocklists, regular expressions, schema validation, policy rules, and permission checks, or using AI-based techniques such as classifiers, LLM reviewers/judges, named entity recognition, groundedness checks, and task-adherence checks. They may be applied at multiple stages of a generative AI workflow, including input handling, prompt construction, retrieval, tool execution, model output review, and post-deployment monitoring.

Examples of specific guardrail implementations include:[[owasp-llm-top10]]  [[datadog-llm-guardrails]] [[azure-ai-content-safety]] [[nvidia-nemo-guardrails]]
- Input moderation: Screen user prompts for harmful content, prompt injection attempts, jailbreak attempts, sensitive data, off-topic requests, or inputs that exceed expected length or format.
- Output moderation: Scan model responses before sending them to users for harmful content, PII, secrets, policy violations, unsupported claims, or unsafe code using classical scanners, classifiers, or a dedicated reviewer model .
- System prompt and policy enforcement: Enforce system instructions, user roles, domain boundaries, response formats, and refusal policies before the model responds (See [Generative AI Guidelines](/mitigations/AML.M0021)).
- Tool and action guardrails: Validate tool calls, tool arguments, permissions, and tool outputs before execution or before results are returned to the model. Require human approval for high-impact, irreversible, privileged, or externally visible actions (See [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029), [Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components](/mitigations/AML.M0033)).
- Retrieval guardrails: Filter and validate retrieved documents before they are added to model context, including checks for untrusted sources, malicious instructions, irrelevant context, or sensitive data.
- Groundedness and factuality checks: Compare model responses against trusted source material or approved knowledge bases to detect unsupported or hallucinated claims.
- Sensitive data and secret protection: Detect, redact, or block personal information, credentials, tokens, proprietary data, system prompts, and other confidential information in prompts, retrieved context, tool outputs, and model responses.
- Structured output validation: Enforce schemas, type checks, allowed values, and safe formats before model outputs are consumed by downstream systems

Guardrails should be continuously evaluated, red-teamed, and updated as adversarial techniques evolve. Guardrail decisions should be logged (See [AI Telemetry Logging](/mitigations/AML.M0021)) and observed failures should be systematically incorporated into updated policies, evaluation datasets, detection logic, prompts, and [Generative AI Model Alignment](/mitigations/AML.M0022).

Content or claims that fail are excluded from context or held for review rather than executed.

mitigations.title: Generative AI Guardrails
description:
Guardrails are safety controls placed between users, tools, and generative AI models to evaluate prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, and agent actions before they are accepted, executed, or shown to a user. They can help block, modify, or route unwanted content such as malicious code, malicious instructions, sensitive data, unsupported claims, policy-violating responses, or unsafe tool requests.

Guardrails can be implemented using rule-based controls such as filters, allowlists, blocklists, regular expressions, schema validation, policy rules, and permission checks, or using AI-based techniques such as classifiers, LLM reviewers/judges, named entity recognition, groundedness checks, and task-adherence checks. They may be applied at multiple stages of a generative AI workflow, including input handling, prompt construction, retrieval, tool execution, model output review, and post-deployment monitoring.

Examples of specific guardrail implementations include:[[owasp-llm-top10]]  [[datadog-llm-guardrails]] [[azure-ai-content-safety]] [[nvidia-nemo-guardrails]]
- Input moderation: Screen user prompts for harmful content, prompt injection attempts, jailbreak attempts, sensitive data, off-topic requests, or inputs that exceed expected length or format.
- Output moderation: Scan model responses before sending them to users for harmful content, PII, secrets, policy violations, unsupported claims, or unsafe code using classical scanners, classifiers, or a dedicated reviewer model .
- System prompt and policy enforcement: Enforce system instructions, user roles, domain boundaries, response formats, and refusal policies before the model responds (See [Generative AI Guidelines](/mitigations/AML.M0021)).
- Tool and action guardrails: Validate tool calls, tool arguments, permissions, and tool outputs before execution or before results are returned to the model. Require human approval for high-impact, irreversible, privileged, or externally visible actions (See [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029), [Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components](/mitigations/AML.M0033)).
- Retrieval guardrails: Filter and validate retrieved documents before they are added to model context, including checks for untrusted sources, malicious instructions, irrelevant context, or sensitive data.
- Groundedness and factuality checks: Compare model responses against trusted source material or approved knowledge bases to detect unsupported or hallucinated claims.
- Sensitive data and secret protection: Detect, redact, or block personal information, credentials, tokens, proprietary data, system prompts, and other confidential information in prompts, retrieved context, tool outputs, and model responses.
- Structured output validation: Enforce schemas, type checks, allowed values, and safe formats before model outputs are consumed by downstream systems

Guardrails should be continuously evaluated, red-teamed, and updated as adversarial techniques evolve. Guardrail decisions should be logged (See [AI Telemetry Logging](/mitigations/AML.M0021)) and observed failures should be systematically incorporated into updated policies, evaluation datasets, detection logic, prompts, and [Generative AI Model Alignment](/mitigations/AML.M0022).

Validation includes enforcing a common data format, schema validation, checks for sensitive or prohibited information leakage, and data sanitization to remove potential injections or unsafe code. Input and output validation can help prevent compromises from spreading in AI-enabled systems and can help secure the workflow when multiple components are chained together. Validation should be performed external to the AI agent.

mitigations.title: Generative AI Model Alignment
description:
Generative AI Model Alignment is the process of training or fine-tuning a generative model to guide its output toward a set of human values, goals, or ethical principles. Desired principles can be in alignment with safety, security, content policies, and legal requirements, with goals such as removing harmful content or hallucinations, reducing biases, increasing predictability, and ensuring models do not have adverse societal consequences. In the context of agentic AI, alignment is about producing models that make decisions in support of the goals of the organization and individual users, with actions that remain in scope of the designated task, and designing agents that follow security standards, exhibit transparency in decision making, and operate within organizational boundaries.

Common methods for aligning a generative model during training or fine-tuning include[[ibm-llm-alignment]][[meta-llama]]:
- Reinforcement Learning from Human or AI Feedback (RLHF or RLAIF)
- Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
- Targeted Safety Context Distillation
- Instruction Tuning
- Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
- Constitutional AI
- Incoulation Prompting

For agentic systems, alignment depends on the purpose of the agent, the tools available to the agent, and the levels of privileges and risks associated with tool calls. Standard alignment methods for LLMs can often be used in conjunction with domain-specific fine-tuning data, reward signals with examples of correct tool calls, or reinforcement learning based on interactions with a realistic environment. Examples of alignment methods specific to agentic AI are:
- Trajectory Preference Optimization[[tpmm-dpo]]
- Environment-Driven Reinforcement Learning[[envrl]]
- Reinforcement Learning with Execution Feedback (RLEF)[[rlef]]
- Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)[[nvidia-mastering-agentic]]

Generative AI Model Alignment should be used in combination with [Generative AI Guardrails](mitigations/AML.M0020) and [Generative AI Guidelines](mitigations/AML.M0021). Models should be continually evaluated for alignment and retrained or fine-tuned systematically to incorporate observed failure modes or updated policies. It is important to also consider that fine-tuning a model can remove previously learned alignments and should be undertaken with care and a comprehensive plan for testing the updated model for safety and security.

mitigations.title: Generative AI Guidelines
description:
Guidelines are instructions, policies, and behavioral constraints provided to a generative AI model to direct it toward desired outputs and away from unsafe, unreliable, or policy-violating behavior. Guidelines can help reduce risks related to organization policy violations, brand damage, private data leakage, false or unsupported information, unsafe advice, and misuse of tools or external content.

Guidelines can be implemented as system prompts, prompt templates, policy text appended to user prompts, or task-specific instructions included during prompt construction. They can define the system's goals, role, tone, allowed and disallowed behavior, domain boundaries, citation requirements, data-handling expectations, escalation criteria, and safety or security rules.

Common prompt elements include:
- Instructions to cite sources or identify when an answer is not supported by available context.
- Instructions to treat external, retrieved, or user-provided content as untrusted data rather than authoritative sources.
- Instructions to avoid revealing system prompts, hidden policies, credentials, private data, or other sensitive information.
- Instructions to stay within the application's approved domain and refuse requests outside that scope.
- Instructions to follow organization-specific policies, brand requirements, and regulated-domain restrictions.
- Instructions to request human approval before proceeding with potentially unsafe, privileged, irreversible, or externally visible actions when untrusted content is in context (See [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029)).

Guidelines should be tested, red-teamed, and updated as observed failures, prompt injection techniques, policy requirements, and application capabilities evolve. Guidelines are most effective when paired with [Generative AI Guardrails](/mitigations/AML.M0020) that validate inputs, outputs, retrieved context, and tool use.

mitigations.title: AI Telemetry Logging
description:
Implement logging of inputs and outputs of deployed AI models. When deploying AI agents, implement logging of the intermediate steps of agentic actions and decisions, data access and tool use, installation commands, and identity of the agent. Monitoring logs can help to detect security threats and mitigate impacts.

Additionally, having logging enabled can discourage adversaries who want to remain undetected from utilizing AI resources.

mitigations.title: AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls
description:
Limit an AI agent's ability to autonomously acquire, assume, or otherwise obtain additional authorities that expand its effective permissions during execution. The maximum authority available to the agent should be explicitly granted prior to runtime. Additional resources, identities, services, and targets discovered during execution should be treated as outside the authorized boundary unless they are independently validated and added to scope. All authority expansion controls should be implemented outside the AI agent and should not rely solely on system prompts, model alignment, or the agent recognizing that an action is out of scope. Implementations of these controls may be achieved through enforcement mechanisms such as: 

- Policy engines
- Target allowlists
- Protocol and destination restrictions
- Approval gates
- Preventing the agent from using credentials that were not approved for the task
- Monitoring and auditing changes in the agent's effective authority over time

Authority expansion controls include placing restrictions on the number, scope, duration, and concurrent use of authentication and/or authorization tokens available during execution. Tokens may include API access tokens, OAuth tokens, cloud IAM session credentials, service account tokens, Git tokens, or other short-lived authentication artifacts. When policy limits are reached or exceeded, organizations may revoke access, prevent additional token acquisition, require human approval, or terminate the agent's execution.

Propagate the original authority constraints to sub-agents and delegated tasks. A delegated agent may receive narrower restrictions but should not expand the parent agent's scope, authority, targets, or permitted actions.

Authority expansion controls should be implemented alongside permissions configurations for AI agents and tools (See [Privileged AI Agent Permissions Configuration](/mitigations/AML.M0026), [Single-User AI Agent Permissions Configuration](/mitigations/AML.M0027), [AI Agent Tools Permissions Configuration](/mitigations/AML.M0028)). Attempted changes in scope should be accompanied with [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029). Log new resource discovery, denials, exceptions, approvals, and scope changes using [AI Telemetry Logging](/mitigations/AML.M0024).

mitigations.title: Restrict AI Agent Tool Invocation on Untrusted Data
description:
Untrusted data can contain prompt injections that invoke an AI agent's tools, potentially causing confidentiality, integrity or availability violations. It is recommended that tool invocation be restricted or limited when untrusted data enters the LLM's context.

The degree to which tool invocation is restricted may depend on the potential consequences of the action. Consider blocking the automatic invocation of tools or requiring user confirmation once untrusted data enters the LLM's context. For high consequence actions, consider always requiring user confirmation.

mitigations.title: Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions
description:
Systems should require the user or another human stakeholder to approve AI agent actions before the agent takes them. The human approver may be technical staff or business unit SMEs depending on the use case. Separate tools, such as dedicated audit agents, may assist human approval, but final adjudication should be conducted by a human decision-maker. 

The security benefits from Human In-the-Loop policies may be at odds with operational overhead costs of additional approvals. To ease this, Human In-the-Loop policies should follow the degree of consequence of the task at hand. Minor, repetitive tasks performed by agents accessing basic tools may only require minimal human oversight, while agents employed in systems with significant consequences may necessitate approval from multiple stakeholders diversified across multiple organizations.

mitigations.title: Memory Hardening
description:
Memory Hardening protects persistent state used by AI agents, including saved preferences, episodic or semantic memories, conversation summaries, stored chat history, and agent-managed experience stores. Unlike guardrails that evaluate content during an interaction, memory hardening controls how durable agent state is created, modified, isolated, audited, and recovered.

Apply the following controls throughout the memory lifecycle, from creation and use through deletion and recovery:
- Enforce memory access controls: Authenticate memory operations and authorize them within the appropriate user, tenant, agent, and session scope.
- Set strong memory security policies: Enforce limits on memory size and update frequency, validate memory integrity, and define retention and deletion policies.
- Preserve memory provenance: Record the source of all memory updates and preserve a history with known good versions. Quarantine or roll-back suspicious records.
- Audit and monitor memory operations: Audit security relevant reads and writes. Monitor for unusual update frequency and repeated self-authored updates.

Content filtering and protections against malicious prompts may be provided by [Generative AI Guardrails](/mitigations/AML.M0020), but does not replace memory access control, isolation, provenance, integrity, or recovery.

Open-source tools that implement memory hardening controls include OWASP Agent Memory Guard[[owasp-agent-memory-guard-project]] and Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit[[microsoft-agent-governance-toolkit]]. Memory management and persistence tooling such as Mem0[[mem0-entity-partitioning]], and LangGraph Persistence[[langgraph-persistence]] can also support aspects of memory hardening.

mitigations.title: AI Agent Scope Drift Detection
description:
Continuously evaluate whether an AI Agent's planned actions remain consistent with its current authorized objective throughout execution. As autonomous agents interact within a dynamic environment, they may discover or generate intermediate objectives or adapt their strategy based on environment feedback. While limited adaption may be necessary to complete legitimate tasks, substantial deviations from the original objective may indicate unintended behavior, excessive autonomy, or attempts to pursue objectives outside the authorized scope. 

Implementation of scope drift detection can vary through runtime policy engines, planning monitors, orchestration frameworks, or additional supervisory AI Agents. Indicators to monitor may include:

- Significant changes in planned objectives or task hierarchy.
- Generation of new long-term goals unrelated to the assigned objective.
- Tool usage inconsistent with the original mission.
- Attempts to access systems or resources outside the authorized scope.
- Repeated adaptation toward objectives requiring progressively broader authority.
- Planning sequences that introduce persistence, privilege escalation, or unrelated lateral movement.

When scope drift is detected, pause execution, restrict tool access, require external approval, return the agent to a known authorized plan, or terminate the task.

mitigations.title: Limit AI Service Query Volume and Rate
description:
Limit the number and rate of requests that users can submit to an AI service. Apply limits by user, API key, tenant, device, or other authenticated identity. Use short-term rate, burst, and concurrency limits together with longer-term usage quotas.

Query limits can increase the time and cost required to extract model information, optimize adversarial inputs, discover system behavior, verify attacks, or overwhelm a service. Monitor for attempts to evade limits through distributed requests, account rotation, or stolen credentials. Query limits may not protect against attacks that require few requests or are performed against an offline model.

mitigations.title: Limit AI Workload Resource Consumption
description:
Limit the resources that an AI request, inference job, or agent workflow can consume. Set bounds on input size, batch size, execution time, memory, compute, and output size. Generative AI services should also limit context and output tokens. Agentic AI systems should limit iterations, retries, tool calls, parallel tasks, delegation depth, and downstream spending.

Apply resource limits across the complete workflow because one request may initiate multiple model calls or external actions. Use timeouts, cost ceilings, circuit breakers, and safe termination conditions to prevent individual workloads from exhausting shared resources. These controls complement query-rate limits, which address large numbers of otherwise inexpensive requests.

mitigations.title: AI Red Team
description:
Establish an AI red team responsible for conducting recurring, authorized, and threat-informed red-teaming exercises to identify and remediate vulnerabilities in AI-enabled systems before deployment and throughout operation. AI red-teaming simulates realistic adversary behavior to evaluate how attacks could affect the confidentiality, integrity, availability, safety, privacy, and mission performance of an AI-enabled system.

Red-teaming exercises should consider the complete AI-enabled system, including models and data, agents (including memory and tools), data flows, decision processes, application logic, retrieval systems, identities and permissions, software dependencies, non-AI system components, infrastructure, user interfaces, and human workflows.

An AI red team exercise can be organized into three phases: planning and scoping the exercise, executing the selected exercises, and assessing the results to guide reporting and remediation.

1. **Plan and Scope**
    - Document the system's intended use, deployment environment, users, sensitive data, connected resources, and potential consequences of failure or misuse. Diagram the system's components, trust boundaries, data flows, external services, human decision points, and training- and inference-time access points.
    - Establish rules of engagement covering authorized systems, accounts, data, techniques, test windows, resource limits, escalation procedures, evidence handling, and stop conditions. Plan destructive, privacy-invasive, or high-cost tests for isolated environments with appropriate safeguards.
    - Develop a threat model based on the system's operating environment and relevant adversary behavior. Define the adversary's objectives, access, knowledge, capabilities, resources, and constraints, and account for digital and physical attack paths and the role of human oversight.
    - Use ATLAS tactics, techniques, and procedures to identify relevant adversary behaviors and construct threat vectors. Prioritize them according to likelihood and severity of impact to the system.
    - Define success criteria and stopping conditions. Identify task-level metrics for effects on the AI capability and operational metrics for measuring impact to the overall system.

2. **Execute**
    - Conduct the selected exercises using manual and automated methods as appropriate. Automation can generate input variations, replay attack sequences, and evaluate responses at scale. Human testers can develop system-specific attacks, adapt to observed defenses, and investigate unexpected behavior.
    - Follow the rules of engagement and record attack activity, system responses, control behavior, deviations from the test plan, and evidence needed to evaluate the results.
    - Stop or escalate testing when predefined conditions are reached. After testing, remove test accounts, modified data, installed software, persistent instructions, and other exercise artifacts.

3. **Assess, Report, and Improve**
    - Evaluate the results against the defined task and operational metrics. Document successful and unsuccessful attacks, their consequences, observed control behavior, deviations from the test plan, and gaps in the threat model.
    - Report findings to the appropriate developers, defenders, operational teams, risk owners, and other stakeholders.
    - Assign findings to responsible owners, track remediation, and retest corrected systems.
    - Use demonstrated attacks to improve preventive controls, detection, incident response, and recovery. Where appropriate, convert confirmed failures into regression tests, evaluation datasets, detection logic, monitoring requirements, or deployment criteria.

Red-teaming is a continuous process and should be repeated as the threat landscape evolves and when changes are made to the system, its components, intended use, or deployment environment. New threat intelligence, vulnerabilities, and test results should inform the scope and priorities of future exercises.

mitigations.title: Input Screening Guardrails
description:
Guardrails are safety controls placed between users, tools, and generative AI models to evaluate prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, and agent actions before they are accepted, executed, or shown to a user. They can help block, modify, or route unwanted content such as malicious code, malicious instructions, sensitive data, unsupported claims, policy-violating responses, or unsafe tool requests.

Guardrails can be implemented using rule-based controls such as filters, allowlists, blocklists, regular expressions, schema validation, policy rules, and permission checks, or using AI-based techniques such as classifiers, LLM reviewers/judges, named entity recognition, groundedness checks, and task-adherence checks. They may be applied at multiple stages of a generative AI workflow, including input handling, prompt construction, retrieval, tool execution, model output review, and post-deployment monitoring.

Examples of specific guardrail implementations include:[[owasp-llm-top10]]  [[datadog-llm-guardrails]] [[azure-ai-content-safety]] [[nvidia-nemo-guardrails]]
- Input moderation: Screen user prompts for harmful content, prompt injection attempts, jailbreak attempts, sensitive data, off-topic requests, or inputs that exceed expected length or format.
- Output moderation: Scan model responses before sending them to users for harmful content, PII, secrets, policy violations, unsupported claims, or unsafe code using classical scanners, classifiers, or a dedicated reviewer model .
- System prompt and policy enforcement: Enforce system instructions, user roles, domain boundaries, response formats, and refusal policies before the model responds (See [Generative AI Guidelines](/mitigations/AML.M0021)).
- Tool and action guardrails: Validate tool calls, tool arguments, permissions, and tool outputs before execution or before results are returned to the model. Require human approval for high-impact, irreversible, privileged, or externally visible actions (See [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029), [Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components](/mitigations/AML.M0033)).
- Retrieval guardrails: Filter and validate retrieved documents before they are added to model context, including checks for untrusted sources, malicious instructions, irrelevant context, or sensitive data.
- Groundedness and factuality checks: Compare model responses against trusted source material or approved knowledge bases to detect unsupported or hallucinated claims.
- Sensitive data and secret protection: Detect, redact, or block personal information, credentials, tokens, proprietary data, system prompts, and other confidential information in prompts, retrieved context, tool outputs, and model responses.
- Structured output validation: Enforce schemas, type checks, allowed values, and safe formats before model outputs are consumed by downstream systems

Guardrails should be continuously evaluated, red-teamed, and updated as adversarial techniques evolve. Guardrail decisions should be logged (See [AI Telemetry Logging](/mitigations/AML.M0021)) and observed failures should be systematically incorporated into updated policies, evaluation datasets, detection logic, prompts, and [Generative AI Model Alignment](/mitigations/AML.M0022).

mitigations.implementation: Evaluate model inputs and outputs against harm categories, denied topics, blocked terms and organisation-specific policy classifiers, server-side at the inference gateway or the application's output-handling stage rather than inside the model. A pass returns the content unchanged; a fail blocks the turn, substitutes a refusal or annotates the response for the consuming application to act on.

mitigationsAttribution: Canonical mitigation identifiers, names and definitions come directly from MITRE D3FEND 1.6.0 and MITRE ATLAS 2026.09. This repository authors only the selection, implementation guidance, deployment scope and supporting CoSAI mappings. No custom mitigation identifiers are added. A mapping does not establish control fulfillment or MITRE endorsement.

mitigationGaps.missing: No sufficiently explicit capability for differential privacy, secure aggregation, privacy-preserving federated training, or evaluated anonymization/synthetic-data privacy. Ordinary encryption and access control do not establish these guarantees.

Guardrails cover sensitive-data detection and redaction. Secure multiparty inference, homomorphic computation and privacy-preserving query mechanisms are not explicitly represented. Message/file encryption does not imply encrypted computation.

Hardware process isolation is represented. Confidential-memory guarantees, workload attestation, measurement-bound key release and side-channel protections require explicit implementation evidence beyond that technique.

Guardrails, inventory, access mediation and memory hardening cover constituent functions. End-to-end consent and purpose enforcement, user-data retention/deletion across all stores and provider copies, and proving those commitments remain outside these mappings. ATLAS Memory Hardening does include retention/deletion for agent memory.

Dataset provenance and sanitization contribute, but provenance does not establish legal authorization, consent or permitted purpose for training/evaluation data. Data-use approval and provenance interpretation remain explicit implementation and governance requirements.

User-facing AI disclosures, consent choices and data-use controls have no sufficiently matching capability in this technical profile. Content filtering, authentication and human approval of agent actions are not substitutes for those experiences.

Policy publication and user education remain people/process obligations. ATLAS AML.M0018 User Training is available as a nontechnical mitigation, but is deliberately excluded from the technology-capability catalogue.
Internal policy authoring, publication and employee education remain people/process obligations. ATLAS AML.M0018 User Training is related but is not a technical capability.

Model validation and operational risk assessment support governance. Ownership, policy approvals, supplier assurance, release authorization and accountable decisions are not implemented merely by deploying those capabilities.

Operational Risk Assessment provides a standardized concept. Residual-risk acceptance, supplier evidence evaluation and ongoing governance workflows still need organizational processes and evidence; a tool does not fulfill them automatically.

AI telemetry and system-file tampering analysis are represented. Immutable retention, non-repudiation and complete audit-chain guarantees need separate implementation evidence. Observable execution events do not reveal complete internal model reasoning.

Code/artifact signing, verification and integrity monitoring are represented. Signed-media provenance interoperability (for example C2PA), watermark semantics and authenticity of generated media are not fully specified by these capabilities. Authenticity is not truth.

Configuration permissions and integrity monitoring support route protection. Signed route manifests, binding responses to the chosen model, and end-to-end route/provenance checks must be verified as application-specific implementations.

archetypes.title: Single agent workflow
summary: A single agent operating a business process end to end — reading a request, deciding, and writing to systems of record in seconds, with no human between the decision and the effect. The architecture where the design question is reversibility rather than accuracy.
description:
Everything structural here follows from one fact: the agent writes. A retrieval assistant that is wrong produces a wrong sentence; this produces a refund, a provisioned account, a cancelled order. The controls that matter are the ones that bound what can be done and make it undoable, not the ones that improve the odds of being right.
The tool services are the primary control, and here they should be a deterministic action catalogue. The model chooses among named, parameter-validated actions rather than composing arbitrary calls, and each action declares its own blast radius and its own compensating transaction. An agent that can call an arbitrary API is not an agent with a policy problem; it is an agent with no policy surface at all.
The attacker is typically an authenticated customer. The request text is supplied by the person who benefits from the outcome, and it reaches the same context window as the system instruction — indirect prompt injection with a very short path to money. The second injection path arrives through retrieval: record content written months earlier, by requesters and by staff, re-enters the loop as context. That is why the approval threshold is tied to consequence rather than confidence, and why it must be rare — a gate on every action is a queue nobody reads, while below the threshold the compensating path, reversal rather than review, is what keeps a wrong action survivable.
The agent needs an identity of its own. Actions taken as a shared service account are neither attributable nor separately revocable, which turns every incident into a full-service outage when the response is to disable the credential. And its network calls leave through an AI gateway — brokered credentials, budget limits and the audit tap — the same crossing the durable multi-agent workflow draws, at single-agent scale. The in-process tool set is the drawn exception, and the reason it is drawn.
distinguishedBy:
Against the chat agent with tools: same loop, but there a human sits in the thread and approves as part of the conversation. Here the trigger is a queue or a timer, nobody is between the decision and the effect, and the catalogue, the threshold and the compensating transaction carry the weight the human carried there.
Against the durable multi-agent workflow: that one is a durable, multi-agent process surviving crashes and replay across days. This is one agent on one fast path, deciding in seconds — no supervisor, no journal, no replay — and still consequential, which is why the catalogue, the threshold and the compensating transaction carry the weight instead of durability machinery. The relationship is nesting, not contrast: each of that architecture's subagents is this diagram one level down.

zones.note: Nobody, most of the time. The operator appears only when a proposal escalates — reached through a work queue, never waiting on a socket — and is absent for the rest of it.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: Everything we operate: the queues, webhooks and timers that start the loop, the loop itself, its state, the crossing every call leaves through, and our own tool servers and systems of record.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Outside the company — the model provider, third-party tool servers, and the services an action lands on.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band. With no human in the loop, this band is the whole of the oversight — there is no in-thread approval to fall back on.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Triggers & schedules
blocks.note: Queue messages, file drops, webhooks and timers that start the loop with no human in the room — and the approval that resumes a parked proposal. There is no front end: this is the only way in, which is the fact that reorganises this architecture's whole control set. Whose authority a run carries is bound here, before the loop starts.

items.label: Schedules & events
items.note: The timer or queue message that starts a run nobody asked for interactively, and the approval event that resumes one. Each carries the grant the run acts on — a service principal with its own named scope, or an on-behalf-of grant attached to the message.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The tools compiled into the application itself, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop: decorated functions running in the loop's own process, under its identity, with its egress and its secrets, and the sandbox the loop's generated code runs in. This is the default way a tool gets attached, and the reason it is drawn: the in-process tool set is invisible to any gateway. What these tools reach is drawn — memory and retrieval through their handlers, and the package mirror through the sandbox's package manager.

items.label: Tool handlers
items.note: Functions in the application, holding whatever the application holds — including the outbound calls it makes itself, with no broker in front, and the retrieval and state reads the loop treats as context.

items.label: Sandboxed tools
items.note: Code execution in an isolated runtime inside the harness's own tool surface — the loop writes code, only the sandbox runs it, and what it installs comes from the mirror and nowhere else. Bash is where the package manager lives.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: Chooses the next action from the catalogue, given the request and what it has read. Runs under its own workload identity, distinct from both the requester and the service.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Reads context, calls the model, proposes an action. The full cycle completes in seconds.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the instruction, the memory and the tool results into one prompt.

items.label: MCP client
items.note: The harness's own MCP client — the party that connects out, through the gateway's MCP brokerage, to remote servers.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: The business policy, the customer's history and the working state of this case. Record content is the second injection path — written by requesters and staff, re-entering as context.

items.label: Vector index
items.note: Reads scoped to the account under discussion, not to what the service can reach.

items.label: Case state
items.note: Scoped to one case. Cross-case memory would let one requester's text influence another's outcome.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The one crossing every network-brokered model and tool call leaves through — the in-process tool set is the drawn exception. The agent tier holds no standing credentials; the gateway brokers them per call, meters spend and writes the audit trail as a tap on the crossing. Its items are the traffic classes it brokers — the checks it runs are the numbered pins on this block and its edges, and the call-outs beneath.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own action surface, and this architecture's primary control. Whatever the transport, what is admitted here should form a deterministic catalogue — named, parameter-validated actions with a declared blast radius and a compensating transaction — rather than arbitrary calls. With no human in the loop, this is what stands in for approval.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface. What runs behind it is the provider's and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Returns the chosen action and its parameters — content the catalogue validates rather than trusts.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems where effects land, and where reversal either exists or does not — and the source the tool surface reads back into context on the same hop. Record content written by requesters and staff is this architecture's second injection path, and it arrives by the same edge the writes leave on.

items.label: Org data
items.note: Orders, accounts and entitlements — the authoritative state the agent changes.

items.label: File storage
items.note: Case documents and attachments, read back into context on a later run.

blocks.title: Tool services

items.label: A2A peer agents
items.note: Cross-org delegation over the A2A protocol. A peer's output enters the loop as input.

blocks.note: Third-party servers, connectors and peer agents, out where nobody we contracted with operates them. Admitted by assessment at the crossing, or refused there.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: Where an action lands outside the company — mail sent, tickets moved, calendar entries written on the requester's behalf — and where the untrusted content that returns enters the next model call.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: Where the mirror gets what it serves: the public package registries and the skill and extension hubs it proxies and admits from. Nothing here is ours, which is why admission happens at the mirror and not at the tool that asked.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and their kind — mirrored, never reached by a tool directly in the target state.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Community catalogues of skills, extensions and images, admitted through the same door.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Issues the agent's workload identity and the requester's, and keeps them distinct. The loop runs as itself and acts on the requester's grant — conflating the two is how an unattended agent quietly acquires standing authority.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Short-lived credentials minted per call, so a loop running with nobody watching holds no standing keys.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: The bounds the tool surface enforces per invocation, authored and changed outside the loop — because the loop is the thing that may be misbehaving.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Which actions exist at all — admission, not discovery — the behavioural checks in front of every model, prompt or catalogue change, and the versioned ownership of the system instruction itself.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: The decision audit and the stop, plus the approval threshold — keyed to irreversibility and value rather than model confidence, and rare enough that somebody actually reads it.

blocks.title: Operator
blocks.note: The approver for actions above the threshold — an operator work queue, never the customer who benefits, because the beneficiary approving their own remedy is no gate at all. Reached by a tool call and answering with an event; present only when a proposal escalates, and the loop runs without them the rest of the time.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The organisation's package registry: public packages mirrored and admitted, and the organisation's own builds published by its CI pipelines. It serves whatever the sandbox installs — a dependency the agent's generated code needs, a tool package a step pulls in — pinned by digest. Pulling and publishing are separate grants: agents pull, build pipelines publish, and the registry's own proxying of upstream sources is bounded to what admission allows.

edges.label: trigger
edges.note: A timer, queue message, file drop or webhook starts a run with nobody in the room. In many deployments this is the common path and the request surface is the exception.

edges.label: escalation
edges.note: The reach-back: a proposal above the threshold is written to an approval channel — a work queue, a ticket, a chat — as an ordinary tool call, bound to the exact action, arguments and case, with an expiry. Nobody is on a socket waiting for it.

edges.label: approval / instruction
edges.note: The human's answer arrives the way everything arrives here: as an event. It is validated against the parked proposal before anything executes — a blanket "yes" approves nothing in particular.

edges.label: read & write / context
edges.note: Business policy, the customer's history and the working state of this case, read back as context through the retrieval and state handlers, and written forward by them.

edges.label: inference, MCP & skills
edges.note: Every network call out of the loop crosses here on a brokered credential. The agent tier holds no standing keys of its own.

edges.label: pinned installs
edges.note: What the harness's sandbox installs — a package manager running as a shell command — is pulled straight from the mirror, pinned by digest, never from a public registry. The gateway is the other doorway into the harness, for inference, MCP, skills and APIs; it is not on this path.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: Inference on the brokered credential. The completion names the action and its parameters — content the tool surface validates rather than trusts.

edges.label: internal tool calls
edges.note: The proposed action, admitted against the catalogue and narrowed to a scoped grant before anything executes.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Where the effect lands and where reversal either exists or does not — and where record content written by requesters and staff is read back into a later run as context.

edges.label: brokered external calls
edges.note: Third-party servers and peer agents, reached only through the crossing that admitted them.

edges.label: action / returned content
edges.note: Actions landing outside the company, and the untrusted content that returns into the next model call with nobody reading it first.

edges.label: mirrored & admitted
edges.note: The mirror's own supply chain: public packages proxied in, scanned, pinned and admitted before anything inside can pull them. Build pipelines publish the organisation's own artifacts beside them.

risks.note: The payload that starts a run — a ticket, a queue message, a webhook body — is authored by the party who benefits from the outcome, and it reaches the same context window as the system instruction.
Record content is the harder injection path — written months earlier, by someone handling a different case, re-entering as context now.
Untrusted request text, a model choosing among real transactions, and a write path into records compound here.
The completion names an action and its parameters, and it is unauthenticated content.
The agent acts on a requester's behalf using authority broader than theirs. Keeping the requester's context alive through the loop is what closes the gap.
Reads not scoped to the account under discussion pull other customers' records into context.
A loop that retries and re-plans in seconds can spend and act faster than anyone notices.
Case memory keyed loosely enough to collide across cases lets one requester's text steer another's outcome — memory poisoning by its OWASP name, pinned as prompt injection per the recorded deviation.
The search index grounds every case decision; content planted there by whoever can write to the indexed sources returns as trusted context.
Handlers compiled into the loop's process hold whatever the process holds and cross no chokepoint — a vulnerable or malicious in-process tool is invisible to every drawn control.
Content returning from actions outside the company was authored by somebody else and re-enters the next model call as context.
The catalogue is the policy surface; whoever can edit it programs the agent.
Per-token inference behind an open trigger surface makes unbounded requests a spend problem.

What the sandbox installs is code the agent chose, on a name it read in a task or a tool result; the mirror decides which build answers to that name, and whoever can write to the mirror programs every sandbox that pulls from it.

mitigations.note: Whose authority a run carries, established at ingress before the loop runs — a service principal with its own named scope, or the on-behalf-of grant attached to the message. It is the identity every downstream action is taken on behalf of, and the thing that bounds the reachable set.
Actions exist because the catalogue admitted them, not because a model named them. Admission is a change-time decision made here; the gateway enforces the resulting catalogue per call.

Behavioural checks in front of every model, prompt or catalogue change — the system instruction versioned, reviewed and owned like the catalogue it governs — because with nobody watching a run there is no later opportunity to notice the change was wrong.
Named, parameter-validated actions with declared blast radius and a compensating transaction each — the deterministic surface everything else assumes.

An approval gate keyed to irreversibility and value, rare enough to be read; below it, reversal rather than review. The approver is the operator on the drawing, reached over the front end — never the requester, because the beneficiary approving their own remedy is no gate at all. The escalation scenario walks the round trip.
A per-invocation policy decision — this action, this record, this value, now — rather than a session-time grant.
A distinct, revocable workload identity per agent, so actions are attributable and separately revocable.
Entitlement-filtered retrieval scoped to the account under discussion, enforced before fetching.
Classify the payload before the loop; whoever authored it cannot be trusted about their own request.
Case-scoped memory with hard boundaries — no cross-case reads, ever.
Brokered, per-workload, expiring model credentials; the agent tier holds no standing key.
Quotas and cost ceilings on the crossing, before token spend and action volume are committed.

The sandbox's network policy: the only routes out are the AI gateway and the package mirror. Shell commands, fetches and anything else a tool emits are bounded here — not at the gateway, which brokers model, MCP and API calls and sees nothing else.
Returned record and external content is classified at the crossing before it re-enters the loop's context — the harder injection path gets the same treatment the request text does.
Effective authority is the intersection of the requester's grant, the agent's identity, the action policy and the target record — never the union, which is what a confused deputy runs on.
Every action with reasoning, inputs and identity, written where the agent can append and cannot amend.
A halt that also revokes the agent's identity, and does not require a deploy.
Ingest trust on what enters the case index and per-tenant isolation inside it — the answer to a poisoned index, distinct from scoping what a read may return.
Admission is change-time; the rug-pull is a tool whose definition changes after admission. Content-hash pinning of admitted tool descriptions is what catches it.

Admission scanning at the mirror: digest and signature verification, malware and typosquat checks on everything proxied in from a public source, before anything inside can pull it. The registered embodiment of artifact scanning, on the one edge where it applies.

walkthrough.title: A refund request lands on the queue
walkthrough.moves: A queue message in, the agent's chosen action out, and the record it changed.

steps.label: refund request (queue message)
steps.note: A refund request arrives as a queue message — written by a customer through some upstream system, bound to an account and carrying the grant the run will act on. Nobody is waiting on a socket for the answer.

steps.label: policy & history lookup
steps.note: Policy and the customer's history are requested through the retrieval handler, scoped to this account.

steps.label: case context
steps.note: They come back into the context window.

steps.label: context on brokered credential
steps.note: The context leaves the loop through the gateway, on a brokered credential.

steps.label: inference
steps.note: The model proposes an action and parameters from the catalogue.

steps.label: proposed action
steps.note: The proposal comes back across the crossing — unauthenticated content, now the plan.

steps.label: validated action
steps.note: The proposal is validated — well-formed, in policy, under the value threshold.

steps.label: refund executes
steps.note: The refund executes, with its compensating transaction on file.

steps.label: record confirmed
steps.note: The record confirms the change.

steps.label: result, logged
steps.note: The result crosses back, logged against the call that caused it.

steps.label: outcome posted back
steps.note: The loop closes its plan with the outcome and posts it back on the channel the request came from — within seconds, and the audit holds the reasoning.

scenarios.title: The payload is the attack

steps.label: poisoned ticket text
steps.note: The ticket text instructs the agent to ignore policy and refund in full; whatever survives classification enters the same context window as the system instruction, as the task.

steps.label: context with injected text
steps.note: Whatever survived classification rides out with the context.

steps.label: inference
steps.note: A steered model proposes the most generous action available.

steps.label: steered proposal
steps.note: The steered proposal comes back as the plan.

steps.label: catalogue bounds it
steps.note: The catalogue does not care what steered the model — parameters and policy bounds hold.

steps.label: compensable below threshold
steps.note: Below the threshold the action is compensable; above it the approval gate fires.

scenarios.title: A timer fires with nobody in the room

steps.label: schedule fires
steps.note: A schedule starts the run — no request, no payload authored by anyone, and nobody to return an outcome to.

steps.label: unattended context
steps.note: The unattended run crosses on the same brokered credential an attended one would.

steps.label: inference, nobody watching
steps.note: The model proposes an action with nobody watching the proposal.

steps.label: proposal, nobody reading
steps.note: The proposal comes back with nobody to read it.

steps.label: outbound action
steps.note: The action reaches outward, admitted by the same catalogue and egress allowlist.

steps.label: effect lands outside
steps.note: The effect lands outside the company, and what returns re-enters the next call as somebody else's content. With no human anywhere on this path, the catalogue, the threshold and the compensating transaction are the whole of the control set.

scenarios.title: The injection was written months ago

steps.label: lookup for a record
steps.note: The loop needs a customer record — and crosses first, because nothing on the agent tier reaches a tool surface directly.

steps.label: admitted lookup
steps.note: The lookup is admitted against the catalogue and narrowed to this case.

steps.label: record read
steps.note: The record is read like any other.

steps.label: note from another case
steps.note: A note written into it long ago, in someone else's case, comes back with the content.

steps.label: tool result
steps.note: It crosses back as an ordinary tool result.

steps.label: lands in context
steps.note: And lands in context beside the system instruction.

steps.label: context with injected note
steps.note: The assembled context — injected note included — leaves for the model.

steps.label: inference
steps.note: The model reads it with nothing marking it apart.

steps.label: attacker's proposal
steps.note: The proposal it produces is the attacker's, in the model's voice.

steps.label: catalogue & policy hold
steps.note: The catalogue and the per-call policy are the controls that were built for exactly this turn.

scenarios.title: A refund above the threshold escalates

steps.label: refund above threshold
steps.note: The loop proposes a refund well above the compensable threshold.

steps.label: threshold trips
steps.note: The per-call policy trips the threshold; the catalogue refuses to execute and returns a suspension.

steps.label: suspension
steps.note: The suspension comes back as the call's result.

steps.label: proposal parked
steps.note: The loop parks the proposal rather than retrying it.

steps.label: approval-channel call
steps.note: The loop reaches back — a call to the approval channel, admitted like any tool.

steps.label: approval channel (tool)
steps.note: The approval channel is a tool: a work queue, a ticket, a chat.

steps.label: queue item for operator
steps.note: An operator, never the customer, finds the proposal in the queue — the action, the amount, the case, an expiry. Nothing is waiting on a socket for them.

steps.label: approval event
steps.note: Approved — this action, these arguments; a blanket "yes" approves nothing in particular. The answer arrives as an event, like everything else here.

steps.label: validated against proposal
steps.note: The approval is validated against the parked proposal before anything moves.

steps.label: action leaves again
steps.note: Only then does the action leave again.

steps.label: admitted with approval
steps.note: Admitted now, carrying the approval it lacked before.

steps.label: refund executes
steps.note: The refund executes, attributable to both the loop and the approver.

scenarios.title: A dependency arrives with the task

steps.label: package install (pinned)
steps.note: A sandboxed step needs a package its generated code imports; the package manager runs as a shell command inside the harness's own tool surface and pulls from the mirror — the one destination the sandbox's network policy allows.

steps.label: admitted build
steps.note: The admitted build comes back, pinned by digest — the hop a poisoned package actually arrives on, which is why admission and pinning are the controls that live here.

deviations.subject: The gateway's Skills catalogue item has no drawn supply path
deviations.reason: The aiGatewayTraffic pack is byte-identical across the catalogue, and this drawing keeps it whole because the tier brokers skills traffic in deployments that use skills. The supply chain behind the item — a private package registry and its signing pipeline — is deliberately outside this runtime drawing's scope; the endpoint personal agent draws the pull path.

deviations.subject: The trigger ingress absorbs inbound classification
deviations.reason: Input screening (cap-input-guardrails) is embodied by the AI gateway, but a payload is classified where it arrives — the trigger ingress absorbs the duty in this simple deployment shape, mirroring the chat sibling's recorded absorption of the service edge.

deviations.subject: Memory poisoning is pinned as prompt injection
deviations.reason: OWASP's agentic taxonomy names memory poisoning as a distinct threat; CoSAI's risk set has no equivalent, so the cross-case memory risk is pinned as prompt injection — the nearest true statement, recorded rather than papered over, matching the multi-agent sibling.
