archetypes.title: Coding & desktop session managed agent runtime
summary: The vendor's coding or desktop agent run on the vendor's compute instead of the developer's machine: one hosted harness in a per-session sandbox, reachable through several doors — a hand-off from the local harness, the vendor's web, mobile and chat surfaces, a source-control event or a schedule, and an API. The session clones a repository through a credential proxy, works on a branch, and hands back a draft pull request that a person merges. The doors are concurrent, not variants; the runtime behind them is one thing.
description:
Every vendor built the same product: the engine from the endpoint drawings, hosted. What changes is custody. On the endpoint the loop runs on a machine that also holds the user's SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions, and the person is present to approve what matters. Here the loop runs in a vendor microVM or container that is created for the session and reclaimed after it, the repository credential never enters that sandbox — a proxy substitutes a scoped placeholder — and nobody is watching. The human's approval point moves from each tool call to the merge gate, and every control on this drawing is about making that gate real and keeping the sandbox from reaching anything the gate does not cover.
The ingress is the repository host. Issue text, pull-request comments, review threads and the instruction files committed beside the code all enter the session as instruction, and most of them are writable by people with no commit access. Every 2026 incident in this class arrived that way: a comment drove a hosted CI agent into exfiltrating its keys, an issue title poisoned a triage workflow's cache and a release token walked out through it, an App that should never have been able to trigger a run did. The trigger authorisation — a verified human with write access — and the classification of what a session reads are therefore pinned where the events originate, not inside a loop we cannot see.
The egress is the same host, plus whatever the sandbox's network policy allows. The agent may push to its own branch and nothing else; it cannot mark a pull request ready, approve it or merge it, and its own initiator's approval does not count. Workflows a pull request would fire wait for a person to approve and run them, because a run that fires on an agent's reply is a run an attacker who can make the agent reply controls. The sandbox's egress is an allowlist the vendor enforces and we author — with two facts to carry: some traffic bypasses it in every product (the vendor's connectors, the git proxy, the inference API), and the hosts every allowlist permits — the repository host, the package registries — are write-capable, so they are exfiltration channels unless methods are restricted too.
Inference is the vendor's. No product in this class lets the hosted loop's model calls route through a customer gateway, including the variants that execute on workers we run; the AI gateway on this drawing is on the tool path only — and that path is the one place external compute reaches back into our systems, so it carries the drawing's strictest pins: the vendor's connector service arrives through an outbound-only tunnel we run and meets one aggregate MCP endpoint, on a per-user grant our authorization server issued, evaluated per call and scoped to a named server list. Everything the gateway does for inference elsewhere in the catalogue has to be re-obtained as tenant configuration — server-managed settings, shared environments, an org-level switch for the hosted mode — and as exported audit, whose coverage differs by product and by plan.
Identity is three different things, and the drawing carries all three because the products do. A session acts as the user who started it (their commits, their pull requests, their replies on the thread), as a bot or App with the user as co-author, or as a shared service identity for sessions raised from a channel or a schedule. Which one a product uses decides whose grant is exercised and what "revoke this agent" means, and it is the first thing to establish per product before any other control is assessed.
distinguishedBy:
Against the third-party coding & desktop agents: the same engine and the same vendor control plane, with the loop moved off the machine. There the human is present and the machine holds the credentials; here the human is absent, the sandbox holds a scoped placeholder, and the merge gate is the approval. The endpoint drawing keeps this runtime as an item on its Vendor service block and draws the hand-off toward it; this drawing is where that item lands.
Against the API/SDK managed agent runtime: the same hosted harness, driven from different doors. There our own application invokes the session, binds the user to it, executes custom tools and receives the stream; the definition is authored by an engineer and deployed. Here the vendor's own surfaces start the session, the definition is repository content plus an admin-owned environment, and the result is a pull request. The blocks that appear and disappear between the two are the reason they are two drawings.

exemplars.name: Claude Code on the web and Claude Cowork in the cloud
exemplars.note: Sessions on Anthropic-managed VMs started from claude.ai/code, the mobile app, the Desktop app, "claude --cloud", routines and Claude Tag; a git proxy keeps the credential outside the VM; network access is an allowlist per environment ("Trusted" by default) that the git proxy, MCP connectors and the inference API bypass. Acts as the user on GitHub. Self-hosted environments move execution to runners we operate while orchestration and inference stay with Anthropic and cannot be routed through a gateway. Org switches: allow_remote_sessions, Routines, Remote Control; ZDR organisations cannot use any of it.

exemplars.name: Cursor Cloud Agents
exemplars.note: One Firecracker microVM per agent in a dedicated AWS account, started from the desktop, the CLI, the web, iOS, Slack, GitHub, Linear, an API or Automations. Internet is on by default and lockable to allowlist-only by Enterprise; runtime secrets are redacted from transcripts and commits; commits are signed by an HSM key and pull requests stay drafts. Team automations run as a shared service identity, private ones as the user.

exemplars.name: OpenAI Codex cloud
exemplars.note: OpenAI-hosted containers with a two-phase runtime: the setup script has internet, the agent phase does not unless an environment allows it (None / Common dependencies / All, with GET-only method restriction). Secrets are removed before the agent phase. Started from the web, the CLI, the IDE's "Delegate", GitHub, Slack, Linear or a schedule; the managed configuration that governs local clients does not govern the cloud.

exemplars.name: GitHub Copilot cloud agent and Agent HQ
exemplars.note: An ephemeral GitHub Actions job with a firewall on by default, a token that reaches one branch, no ability to mark ready, approve or merge, and "approve and run workflows" on anything the pull request would trigger. Started from the agents panel, an issue, a PR comment, VS Code's cloud session target (Copilot, Claude or Codex), the CLI's /delegate, mobile or chat. Third-party agents run under the same policies.

zones.note: The developer at the keyboard for the hand-off and the review, and the same person — or, on a chat surface, not necessarily the same person — steering from a phone, a browser or a channel while the session runs.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The local harness is only a door on this drawing: it pushes a branch and a conversation summary up, and pulls the cloud branch back on teleport. Nothing on the machine executes on the session's behalf.
zones.title: Managed endpoint

zones.note: The repository host the session reads and writes, the tunnel the vendor's connector service arrives through, our gateway where it is admitted to our tool servers, and the systems behind them. The host is drawn here whether we run it or rent it: its policy is ours either way.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Two blocks for one vendor, because a session is admitted by one and executed by the other: the control plane — settings, environments, the relay and the scheduler — and the runtime that holds the loop, the model and the sandbox. What they operate inside either is assured, not drawn.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: What the sandbox reaches under its egress policy: package registries in the setup phase, the web in the agent phase, and the third-party tool services our gateway brokers.
zones.title: External

zones.note: On a runtime we do not operate, this band is where the vendor's exports are fused with our record — and where "stop this agent" has to be defined with its delay, because revoking an App or a seat does not stop a running session.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Developer
blocks.note: Present at the start and at the end — the hand-off and the merge — and absent for the run in between. The merge gate is the approval this archetype has; every control on the drawing exists to make it a real one.

blocks.title: Remote device
blocks.note: The doors that start and steer a session with nobody at the machine: the vendor's web and mobile apps, and an @-mention in a chat channel. Admission is the vendor's account binding for the first and whoever the channel admits for the second — the widest admission decision on the drawing.

items.label: Phone & web apps
items.note: The owner's own surfaces, signed into the vendor account the session is bound to.

items.label: Chat channels
items.note: A session raised from Slack, Teams or Linear runs on the vendor's cloud under a shared channel identity on most products — not as the person who typed.

blocks.title: Local applications
blocks.note: The vendor's application on the machine — CLI, editor extension or desktop app — drawn only as far as this drawing uses it: the loop that hands off. "Continue in the cloud", a prefix on the prompt or a delegate command pushes the working branch and a summary of the conversation up and starts a session from it; teleport brings the cloud branch and its history back. The full anatomy — native tools, memory, the local model path — is the endpoint drawing's, and nothing of it executes on this drawing's path.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: The conversation that becomes the hosted session's opening context.

blocks.title: Source control
blocks.note: The one tier that is ingress, egress, definition and gate at once. Issue text, comments and review threads enter the session as instruction; a branch and a draft pull request come back out; the instruction files, setup scripts and environment configuration committed beside the code are the session's definition; review, merge and "approve and run workflows" are the gate. Drawn in our band whether we host it or rent it, because the policy that matters — App installation scope, branch protection, CODEOWNERS on the agent's own configuration, who may trigger a run — is ours either way.

items.label: Repositories & instruction files
items.note: The code, and CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, setup scripts, hooks and MCP configuration — content that executes as instruction and is versioned like code because it is code.

items.label: Issues & PR threads
items.note: Writable by anyone the repository admits, read by the session as instruction. Hidden characters and HTML comments carry payloads the human reviewer never sees.

items.label: Pull requests & CI
items.note: The draft the session opens, the review a person gives, the workflows the pull request would fire — and the single branch the session may write.

blocks.title: Managed runtime
blocks.note: The vendor's own coding agent, hosted: the loop, context assembly and compaction, the model, session state and one sandbox per session, on compute the vendor operates. What we configure about it — the environment, the network policy, the credentials it may draw — is drawn as pins on this block and on the sandbox nested inside it; the execution behind them is assured, not inspected. Product-specific caveats — retention, session sharing, snapshot lifetimes, which plans get proxied credentials — belong on the exemplars and the tool records, not here.

items.label: Agent harness
items.note: Their harness running the repository's instructions — the loop, context assembly, compaction and retries, theirs to operate — with the built-in tools nested beneath.

items.label: Model inference
items.note: Their model, called inside their boundary. It never crosses our AI gateway, and no product in this class lets it — including the variants that execute on our workers.

items.label: Memory store
items.note: Agent-written memory and session transcripts the vendor holds: persisted after the browser closes, shareable on some plans, and merged into later sessions on the products that ship auto-memory.

items.label: Credential vault
items.note: The git proxy that substitutes a scoped credential so the sandbox never holds the repository token, the environment secrets that exist only in the setup phase, and the runtime secrets redacted from transcripts — each a different product's answer to the same requirement, and the plan-gated gaps recorded per product.

items.label: MCP client
items.note: The harness's own MCP client. On most products it reaches servers through the vendor's connector service, outside the environment's network policy — which is why the path to our servers is drawn from the control plane to our gateway, and why the connector allowlist is a control-plane setting rather than a sandbox one.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The sandbox: a microVM or container created for the session and reclaimed after it, holding the file tools, the shell, the skills the repository names and the hosted browser where the product offers one. Two phases where the product has them — setup with network for dependencies, then the agent phase under the environment's allowlist. Drawn because what it may reach is ours to author; where a product moves execution to a worker we run, this block is what moves.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Read, write, edit, glob and grep across the cloned repository.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Command execution inside the session sandbox — and the place a hook, a task file or a virtual-environment interpreter written now is executed later by a tool nobody sandboxed.

items.label: Installed skills
items.note: Packaged instructions the repository or the environment names, downloaded at session start — content that executes as instruction.

items.label: Computer use
items.note: The hosted browser and remote desktop, where offered: the widest reach a session can be given, and the one whose content returns unclassified.

blocks.title: Vendor service
blocks.note: The published surfaces of the vendor's control plane: the settings that reach a hosted session (server-managed, never the device's), the shared environments an owner defines, the org-level switch for the hosted mode, the relay behind the phone and the channel, the scheduler behind routines and automations, and the connector service that calls MCP servers on the session's behalf. This is the tier a hosted session is admitted by; the runtime above is the tier it executes in.

items.label: Managed settings
items.note: Server-managed settings and organisation-shared environments — network access level, environment variables, setup script — plus the toggles that enable hosted mode at all.

items.label: Connector broker
items.note: The vendor's MCP and connector service, calling our gateway and third-party servers from the vendor's side, outside the sandbox's egress policy, on tokens the vendor holds.

items.label: Session audit export
items.note: Session logs, agentic audit events and compliance exports — whose coverage of the hosted surface differs by product and plan, and is verified rather than assumed.

items.label: Remote & scheduled sessions
items.note: The relay that admits a phone or a channel to a running session, and the scheduler that starts one with nobody present at all.

blocks.title: Tunnel connector
blocks.note: Vendor-supplied software we run inside our own network so the vendor's connector service can reach our gateway without an inbound rule: it dials out, holds the connection open and carries the vendor's MCP requests in. Transport only — it does not authenticate to the upstream, and the payloads still traverse the vendor's cloud — so it hands to the AI gateway, never to a server or the data. The tunnel token and the TLS key on this host are the load-bearing secrets. Both first-party vendors ship one for their connectors (OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel for ChatGPT and Codex; Anthropic's MCP tunnels, an Enterprise research preview, for claude.ai connectors); where a product has none, the reach-back is an internet-facing gateway endpoint, recorded as a deviation.

items.label: Outbound connector
items.note: Dials out to the vendor's edge; opens nothing inbound.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The customer-operated crossing where the vendor's connector service is admitted to our MCP servers: the one component on the reach-back path where the grant is ours to scope and revoke and the call is recorded on our terms. Not on the inference path — nothing in this class routes the hosted loop's model calls through us.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: Which of our servers a hosted session may reach, and on whose grants.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own MCP servers and connectors — ticketing, documentation, systems of record — that a hosted session is adopted in order to reach beyond the repository.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record behind those servers, reached on grants we scope per session.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: What the setup phase installs from, straight from the public index under the environment's allowlist — the path a mirror would close, and the write-capable host every allowlist permits.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and the rest — pulled from directly, under the environment's allowlist.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Skills and plugins the repository or the environment names, fetched at session start.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: The web the sandbox fetches from in the agent phase, where the environment allows it, and where the actions our gateway brokers land.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Third-party servers and connectors our gateway brokers outward — the same component as the internal surface, out where nobody we contracted with operates it.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Who may start a session and as whom it runs: federated login and trusted devices at the vendor's account layer, write access as the trigger condition at the repository host, and an inventory of the App installations, service identities and user-bound sessions a product acts through — with an owner and an expiry on each.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: The repository credential the proxy substitutes, the environment secrets that exist only in the setup phase, and the tunnel token and TLS key on the host we run for the reach-back — with the plan-gated gaps recorded per product rather than assumed of the class.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: One branch, no merge, a human reviewer who is not the initiator, workflows that wait for approval, a network allowlist an administrator locks, a connector allowlist the session cannot widen — and a session budget, because an unattended loop bills by the minute.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Routines, automations, environments and connector registrations inventoried like agents, each with an owner; the platform assessed on a clock because its defaults move.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: The vendor's session logs and agentic audit events exported and fused with the repository host's record and our gateway's — one trail per session, from trigger to merge — and a stop whose delay is known: disabling the App or the seat prevents the next session, not the one that is running.

edges.label: local session
edges.note: The person at the keyboard, in the CLI, the editor or the desktop app — the same pattern as the endpoint drawings, used here only as far as the hand-off.

edges.label: away from the machine
edges.note: The same person on a phone or in a browser — or, on a chat surface, whoever the channel admits.

edges.label: hand-off / teleport
edges.note: The local conversation and the working branch become a hosted session; the cloud branch and its history come back the same way. Asymmetric on most products: a terminal session cannot be pushed up mid-task, but the desktop app can, and a finished cloud session can be pulled down.

edges.label: start & steer session
edges.note: The phone, the browser or the channel talks to the vendor's relay directly. Nothing we operate is on this path — a personal device on a cell network has no reason to traverse our egress — so admission is the vendor's account binding and whatever the managed settings allow, and on a channel it is whoever the channel admits.

edges.label: settings, environment & schedules
edges.note: The control plane admitting a session to the runtime: which environment it runs in, what the server-managed settings permit, which connectors it may call, and — from the scheduler — sessions that start with nobody present at all.

edges.label: events in, branch & PR out
edges.note: Both directions of the repository host. Inward: an issue assigned, a comment, a CI failure or a review starts or steers a session, and the instruction files and threads enter its context. Outward: the clone through the git proxy on a scoped credential, the push to the session's own branch, and the draft pull request — the only write the runtime is permitted.

edges.label: review & merge
edges.note: The gate. A person reviews the draft, approves the workflows it would fire, and merges — or does not. The initiator's approval does not count on the products that enforce it, and the agent cannot approve, mark ready or merge on any of them.

edges.label: outbound-only tunnel
edges.note: The reach-back path, and the crossing this drawing exists to govern: compute we do not operate calling back into our systems for data connectors. The vendor's connector service sends its MCP requests down a connection our side opened, so nothing is exposed inbound. The public-endpoint form — the connector service calling an internet-facing gateway URL, admitted at our edge by the vendor's IP ranges — is recorded as a deviation rather than drawn as a second path.

edges.label: tool call / result
edges.note: The tunnel hands to our gateway's aggregate MCP endpoint, never to a server or the data: admitted on audience-bound tokens and per-user grants our own authorization server issued, per-call policy evaluated at the gateway, the servers and tools scoped to a named list, and every call recorded against the grant. The vendor's identity and IP ranges admit the caller; they authorise nothing.

edges.label: brokered tool calls
edges.note: Which of our servers a hosted session may call, on short-lived grants we issue.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: The records and systems the session was adopted to reach beyond the repository.

edges.label: brokered external calls
edges.note: Third-party servers and connectors reached through the crossing that admitted them — egress and returned-content classification enforced at our boundary. The connectors the vendor calls from its own side never meet this list; that path is recorded as a deviation.

edges.label: action / returned content
edges.note: Actions landing outside, and the content they return.

edges.label: setup installs
edges.note: The setup phase pulling dependencies from the public index under the environment's allowlist — a phase that has network before the agent does, runs whatever the setup script says, and caches its result for the next user of the environment. The registry is also a write-capable host every allowlist permits, which is what makes it an exfiltration channel.

edges.label: web fetch under egress policy
edges.note: The sandbox's own reach to the web in the agent phase, where the environment allows it — closed by default on some products, open by default on others — and the content that comes back as instruction.

risks.note: Issue text, comments, review threads and instruction files enter the session as instruction, and most are writable by people with no commit access. The dominant ingress of the archetype, and the one every 2026 incident used.
A fetched page enters a loop nobody is watching. On the products where the agent phase has internet by default this is the unclassified ingress the environment policy exists to close.

The hosts every allowlist permits are write-capable: a gist, a package publish, a pages site. Stolen tokens left through the repository host itself in the 2025 supply chain worm, and through a public index in the vendor's own 2026 evaluation incidents.

The repository, the transcript, tool output and environment variables all live on their side under their retention terms; sessions persist after the browser closes, snapshots outlive the run, and on some plans a session can be shared publicly with private-repository content inside it.

A push, a pull request, a reply on the thread — from a loop that reads its own thread. An agent's reply can fire comment-triggered automation, and an automation configured to approve low-risk pull requests removes the gate this drawing rests on.

The session exercises the user's grant, an App installation's, or a shared service identity's — whichever the product uses — and the repository host cannot tell an injected instruction from an intended one. What bounds it is the token's scope: one repository, one branch, no merge.
Dependencies and skills pulled from a public index in a phase that has network and runs as root in the sandbox — admitted by the environment's allowlist and vetted by nobody on the path.

Instruction files arrive with the clone. A CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md shipped inside a dependency, a hook committed by a worm, a setup script edited by anyone with access to the environment: content that executes as instruction, delivered through the supply chain.
A channel raises sessions for whoever it admits, a schedule runs them for an owner who may have left, and none of it appears in any inventory we keep unless the vendor's export is queried.

Automations that re-run on CI failure and review comments, and sessions that reply to their own threads, make a loop with no natural end — billed by the minute and bounded only by the budget the tenant sets.

A session bound to a user's account keeps that grant after the person has gone; an App installation keeps its scope after the team that installed it has moved on; a shared automation identity outlives every owner it had. Nothing on the vendor's side ties any of them to a lifecycle we run.

The grant the vendor's connector service presents to our gateway is the load-bearing secret on the reach-back path, and it is held on the vendor's side: a connector grant attached to an environment rather than a person, an environment variable visible to everyone who shares the environment, a setup cache kept for hours, a tunnel token on a host we run — each a way one session's authority becomes another's, on infrastructure nobody of ours watches.

Their infrastructure exercising our authority, steered by whatever the session read. The grant is the only thing bounding it, and the grant is issued at our gateway — which is the entire argument for drawing one and for never letting the vendor's tunnel or allowlisted IP range reach past it.

mitigations.note: Hosted mode is an organisation decision: enabled per role or group behind federated login and trusted-device enrolment, the relay bound to the owner's account, and the switches that widen it — personal-token setup, self-hosted runners, remote control — off until someone owns them. Zone-2 configuration, because nothing we operate is on the remote path.

The environment an administrator owns and locks: the connector and MCP allowlist the session cannot widen, the network access level, the built-in tools enabled and the permission mode, with bypass modes removed. Unattended runs have no prompt to answer, so these settings are the whole of the in-session control.
Session budgets, usage ceilings and automation caps in the tenant, because an unattended loop that re-triggers itself bills by the minute and nobody is watching the meter.

Only a verified human with write access may start or steer a session from the repository host; Apps, bots and non-collaborators may not. The condition the 2026 trigger-bypass fix restored, and the one setting that decides whether a public issue is an attack surface.

Hidden-character and HTML-comment filtering on what the session reads, the agent's own configuration directories under CODEOWNERS and required review, and content from non-collaborators treated as untrusted input rather than instruction.

Every App installation, service identity and user-bound session inventoried as a non-human identity with an owner and an expiry — because the products act through three different kinds of principal and "revoke this agent" means a different operation for each.

The repository credential and the secrets stay out of the sandbox: a git proxy substitutes a scoped credential for a placeholder, setup-phase secrets are removed before the agent runs, runtime secrets are redacted from transcripts and commits, and environment variables are treated as visible to the model and to everyone who shares the environment. Where a product does not proxy, the credential is in the sandbox and the finding says so.

What persists and who can read it: agent-written memory merged into later sessions, transcripts that can be shared, snapshots that outlive the run — each a setting whose default is wider than most adopters assume, set deliberately.

Their isolation, retention and tenancy assured by assessment rather than drawn — the only representation a vendor-internal control gets — and re-assessed on a clock, because the defaults move: egress on or off, self-approving automations, which plan gets proxied credentials, whether the audit export covers this surface.

One microVM or container per session around the built-in tools, created for the run and reclaimed after it, with no shared filesystem between sessions — the provider's boundary, or ours where execution moves to a worker we run.

The environment's network policy, authored by us and enforced by the vendor around the sandbox: an allowlist, locked by an administrator, with the setup phase separated from the agent phase and write methods restricted on the hosts the list must permit. What bypasses it in every product — the git proxy, the connector service, the inference API — is bounded elsewhere.

A token that reaches one repository and one branch, cannot push the default branch, mark ready, approve or merge; protected scopes and repository blocklists on the products that have them; a session that can reach only repositories its trigger could already reach.

The gate: a draft pull request a person reviews and merges, an initiator whose approval does not count, workflows that wait for "approve and run", and the agent's own configuration — instruction files, hooks, setup scripts, MCP config — under CODEOWNERS. It approves the output, not the actions taken to produce it: a session's tool calls and network effects have already happened when the reviewer arrives, which is why the sandbox and egress pins exist.

The tunnel token and TLS private key on this host are the load-bearing secrets on the path — issued scoped, rotated like a service credential, and revocable without redeploying the host. The tunnel carries traffic on them but never authenticates to our server; that is the gateway's job.

Which servers and tools a hosted session may reach, on whose grant — a per-user, audience-bound grant our authorization server issued, never the vendor's service identity: one aggregate endpoint fronting a named list per vendor, read-mostly unless a write has a named owner. A marketplace that admits every server to every caller is the failure this pin exists to name.
Returned tool and connector content classified at our crossing before it goes back to a loop we cannot see.
Routines, automations, scheduled tasks, shared environments and App installations inventoried like agents, with an owner each — the population a hosted runtime makes cheap enough to sprawl.

The vendor's session logs — every commit linking to the session that made it — exported to our side and fused with the repository host's audit events and our gateway's record, so one session has one trail from trigger to merge. The export's coverage of the hosted surface is a per-product fact to verify.

Disable hosted mode in the tenant, uninstall the App, revoke the seat — and know the delay: none of it stops a session that is already running, so the stop for that is the vendor's cancel, and the finding names how long it takes.

walkthrough.title: A task handed to the cloud comes back as a pull request
walkthrough.moves: A developer's conversation becomes a hosted session, the session works on the repository and reaches our systems through our gateway, and a person merges what it made.

steps.label: local session
steps.note: The task starts at the keyboard, in the CLI, the editor or the desktop app.

steps.label: hand-off
steps.note: The working branch and a summary of the conversation go up; a session starts from them on the vendor's compute.

steps.label: environment applied
steps.note: The control plane admits the session to a shared environment: network access level, setup script, connectors, permission mode — the settings that reach a hosted session, none of which came from the device.

steps.label: clone via git proxy
steps.note: The sandbox clones through the proxy on a scoped credential it never sees.

steps.label: instructions & threads in context
steps.note: The instruction files, the issue and the review thread enter the session as instruction — classified on the way in, because most of them were not written by us.

steps.label: setup installs
steps.note: The setup phase pulls dependencies under the allowlist and caches the result; then the network closes and the agent phase begins.

steps.label: tool call down the tunnel
steps.note: The session needs a record our systems hold. The vendor's connector service calls back into us — the one crossing on the drawing where external compute reaches our systems — down the outbound-only connection our tunnel holds open.

steps.label: to our gateway
steps.note: The tunnel hands the request to our gateway's aggregate MCP endpoint: admitted on a per-user grant we issued, evaluated per call, scoped to a named server list, recorded against the grant.

steps.label: per-session grant
steps.note: Admitted to a named server on a short-lived grant scoped to this session.

steps.label: read on our side
steps.note: The read happens on our side, which is the only reason it is bounded.

steps.label: record
steps.note: The record comes back.

steps.label: recorded
steps.note: Through the crossing, where the call is recorded against the grant.

steps.label: into the tunnel
steps.note: Classified at the gateway, then back into the connector.

steps.label: tool result
steps.note: And back to the vendor's side, where the loop reads it.

steps.label: push branch, open draft PR
steps.note: The session pushes to its own branch and opens a draft — the only write the token allows. Commits are signed and link back to the session.

steps.label: review & merge
steps.note: A person reviews the draft, approves the workflows it would fire, and merges. The gate approves the output; everything the session did to produce it already happened.

scenarios.title: A comment becomes a command

steps.label: hostile issue in context
steps.note: Someone with no commit access files an issue whose hidden text is an instruction. A session starts on it — or reads it while working on something else.

steps.label: attacker page fetched
steps.note: The instruction sends the sandbox to a page the attacker controls, where the second stage waits — on a product where the agent phase has internet, or an environment where someone opened it.

steps.label: exfiltration via an allowed host
steps.note: What the sandbox holds — environment variables, the clone, whatever the setup phase left behind — leaves through a host the allowlist permits: a gist, a package publish. The list said where the sandbox may talk, not what it may say.

steps.label: hook committed, PR opened
steps.note: The session commits a hook, a task file or a workflow change into its branch and opens the draft. The payload is now in the repository, waiting for a tool nobody sandboxed to execute it.

steps.label: the gate holds — or not
steps.note: A person is the last check: CODEOWNERS on the agent's configuration directories, required review, and workflows that wait for approval are what stand between the branch and the default branch.

scenarios.title: Nobody at the machine: a channel and a schedule

steps.label: from a phone or a channel
steps.note: The owner on a phone — or, in a shared channel, anyone the channel admits.

steps.label: session raised on the relay
steps.note: The relay admits whoever the account binding or the channel allows; a session raised from a channel runs under a shared identity on most products.

steps.label: scheduled & re-triggered runs
steps.note: A routine fires on a schedule; an automation re-runs the session on every CI failure and review comment. The loop has no natural end and no person in it.

steps.label: replies that trigger automation
steps.note: The session's own replies on the thread fire comment-triggered automation — and an automation configured to approve low-risk pull requests approves its own.

scenarios.title: Execution moves to a worker we run

steps.label: same hand-off
steps.note: The session starts the same way, but the environment names a self-hosted runner: orchestration and inference stay with the vendor, the sandbox is ours.

steps.label: clone on our credentials
steps.note: The proxy is no longer on the path; our deployment supplies the git credential and our firewall is the egress policy — with the isolation now our responsibility.

steps.label: installs from our mirror
steps.note: Setup pulls through our registry under our policy. Tool inputs and outputs still cross to a loop we cannot see, and inference still cannot be routed through our gateway.

deviations.subject: The local harness is drawn as Local applications, a door rather than an anatomy
deviations.reason: The endpoint drawings carry the full Agent harness — Native tools, Memory & state, the local model path — and the registered data-chain pattern rightly requires any drawing with that block to reach our data through the gateway. Here nothing on the machine executes on the session's behalf: the local application appears because the hand-off pushes a branch and a conversation up and teleport pulls the cloud branch back, which is a real data crossing. It is drawn under the registered Local applications title with the loop item only, so a reader flipping between the drawings sees that the engine moved rather than that the endpoint lost something, and the pattern is not asserted of a block that does not carry it.

deviations.subject: Source control is drawn in our band whether we host it or rent it
deviations.reason: Bands measure who operates the environment, and a rented code host is operated by another vendor. It is drawn as ours because the policy on the data path — App installation scope, branch protection, CODEOWNERS on agent configuration, who may trigger a run, "approve and run workflows" — is ours whether the host is on our network or on theirs, and because drawing a second vendor in the vendor band would conflate two agreements. The endpoint drawings keep the repository as an Enterprise data item because there it is a working copy on a disk; here the host itself is the ingress, the egress and the gate.

deviations.subject: Two vendor blocks for one vendor
deviations.reason: The three-zone rule draws a vendor as one block. This drawing has two because a session is admitted by one tier and executed by another, and the controls sit on different ones: the control plane carries the settings, the relay, the scheduler and the connector service, all of which we configure; the runtime carries the loop, the model and the sandbox, of which we configure only the sandbox's reach. The endpoint drawing has the first, the API/SDK drawing the second; this one needs both.

deviations.subject: The vendor's own connector path to third parties is recorded, not drawn
deviations.reason: The API/SDK sibling draws the runtime's MCP client calling third-party servers from the vendor's side. The same path exists here — the connector service reaches Slack, Linear and the rest without touching our network — and it is recorded on the Connector broker item and pinned as tool-permission scoping on the control plane rather than drawn as a second edge into the external band, so the drawing keeps one brokered external path and matches the endpoint twin these products also appear on. The finding is unchanged: content those connectors return enters the loop unclassified by anything we run.

deviations.subject: The tunnel is drawn; the public-endpoint reach-back is recorded
deviations.reason: The target state is the API/SDK sibling's: the vendor reaches our gateway through an outbound-only tunnel, so no MCP endpoint of ours faces the internet. Where a product has no tunnel, the vendor's connector service calls an internet-facing gateway URL instead, admitted at our edge by the vendor's published IP ranges — the same crossing with a weaker admission, because an inbound listener now exists. Either way the gateway, not the transport, is the control. Products whose tool calls leave from compute we run — a self-hosted runner or a privately networked one — reach the gateway from inside our network and need neither. Source control is not on this path: a rented code host is reached by the vendor over the internet, and a self-hosted one over the vendor's private connectivity where it offers any.

deviations.subject: The self-hosted execution variant is recorded as a scenario, not drawn
deviations.reason: Every product now offers execution on workers we run — self-hosted environments, team pools, self-hosted runners — with orchestration and inference staying with the vendor. It would move the nested Native tools block into our cloud band and remove the git proxy from the path. It is a scenario here until an organisation adopts it, because a drawing that shows both at once implies a choice nobody has made; the scenario names the two facts to carry into that drawing when it comes — the credential proxy is gone, and the inference path still cannot be ours.

deviations.subject: Identity binding is absorbed into the vendor's account layer
deviations.reason: Access policy (D3-APA) is embodied by an identity provider, an authorization server or an Identity binding item elsewhere in the catalogue. On this drawing the binding is the vendor's account layer for the remote path and the repository host's write-access check for the event path; neither is a tier we run, so the capability is pinned on the control plane and on the event edge and the embodiment is absorbed into them.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway carries tool traffic only
deviations.reason: The vendor calls its own model inside its own runtime — drawn as the Model inference item on the Managed runtime block, with no Model provider block on this drawing — and no product in this class lets the hosted loop's inference route through us. The gateway is drawn with its one real traffic class rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack, following the SaaS siblings: the honest signal that a gateway is not on the model path is its own contents.

deviations.subject: Native tools nest inside the Managed runtime, the fused-runtime exception
deviations.reason: The same exception the API/SDK sibling records (2026-09-09): the built-in tools are the vendor's coding-agent tool surface, bounded by an environment egress policy we author, and in the self-hosted variant they execute on a worker we run. What we configure, we draw. Unlike the sibling, edges do leave the nested block here — setup installs and web fetch — because the products' default policies open them and the drawing shows what ships.

archetypes.title: UI/low-code managed agent runtime
summary: A vendor platform where non-engineers assemble agents from prompts, connectors and triggers. The agents are real, the authors are not engineers, and there is no code review between an afternoon's work and something that acts on production data.
description:
The builder is a self-service surface, and that is both the product and the problem. A business user can create an agent, grant it connectors, give it a trigger and publish it to colleagues without any of the checkpoints a software delivery pipeline would impose — no pull request, no staged rollout, no security sign-off unless the platform enforces one. The result is a population problem rather than an instance problem: individual agents are simple; the risk is four hundred of them, each with connector grants, each authored by someone who has left — and, until somebody actually queries the platform's inventory, no list of which reach customer data. The unmanaged default has no list; the target state queries one.
Credential inheritance is the specific technical trap. A low-code agent typically runs on connections authorised by its author, so a published agent lends its author's access to every colleague who uses it. A user who could not read a table directly can often read it through an agent someone else built, and neither party intended that. Whether the platform supports per-invoker authorisation rather than author-credential execution is the single question worth asking during evaluation.
The authoring surface is also an injection surface: instructions, knowledge sources and connector descriptions are assembled by someone who is not thinking about untrusted input, and a shared agent's knowledge source is frequently a folder anyone can write to. Because no sandbox or runtime enforcement can be inserted into a vendor's execution, every control on the vendor side is a population control — inventory, publication gating, connector policy, and audit that can retire what nobody uses; the runtime controls that survive are the ones on the crossing we run.
distinguishedBy:
Against the API/SDK managed agent runtime: same hosting model, different author. There engineers define agents in code and the delivery pipeline still applies; here the builder UI replaces that pipeline with a publish button, and the unit of concern moves from the definition of one agent to the governance of a population.
Against an internal AI platform you operate: same intent — a paved road for many builders — with the paving done by a vendor. You inherit their guardrails and their environment model, and you cannot add a deployment gate they did not build.

exemplars.name: Microsoft Copilot Studio
exemplars.note: Low-code agent authoring bundled with the productivity suite, available to licensed users by default — verify per tenant which credential mode connectors default to and what the publish gate actually blocks.

exemplars.name: Salesforce Agentforce
exemplars.note: The CRM-embedded builder: agents assembled over platform connectors with the Einstein trust layer as the vendor-side guardrail surface — the zone-2 configuration this page pins.

exemplars.name: Zapier Agents
exemplars.note: The standalone end of the class: a connector marketplace measured in thousands, maker credentials as the natural default, and publication to anyone with the link — the population problem in its purest form.

zones.note: Two populations, and the distinction is the archetype: the colleagues who build agents without being engineers, and the colleagues who then use what they published.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The platform, and effectively the whole system. Authoring, the orchestrator, the model calls, the sandbox and the connector runtime all execute here — there is no customer-hosted agent runtime on offer. Drawn before our own band because a maker reaches the platform first and the platform reaches back into us second.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: The narrow strip that is still ours: the tunnel the platform reaches us through, the gateway a published agent is admitted at, and our own tool servers and data behind it.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: The model the vendor calls on our behalf, and the third-party services their connectors reach.
zones.title: External

zones.note: On a self-service platform this band is population management rather than change review. There is no deployment pipeline to hook into — which is precisely why the platform's own policy engine matters more here than anywhere else in the catalogue.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Citizen builder
blocks.note: Someone who is not an engineer, shipping software. No pull request, no pipeline, no review — which is not a gap in their discipline but the product working as designed.

blocks.title: Agent consumers
blocks.note: Colleagues who run what a maker published, usually without knowing who built it or whose access it acts on.

blocks.title: Agent builder platform
blocks.note: One block, because from our side it is one thing: the authoring surface, the orchestrator, the harness, the sandbox and the connector runtime all run in the vendor's cloud. The only part of it we operate is policy configuration, and that is the whole of our leverage.

items.label: Authoring surface
items.note: Where an agent is built and published, by someone who does not think of it as shipping.

items.label: Agent runtime
items.note: Their harness executing the maker's agent, with the model calls theirs to make.

items.label: Connector framework
items.note: Hundreds of prebuilt connectors, executing in their cloud on credentials that are the crux of this page.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: Where a published agent is admitted into our systems, and the policy point on that path. It carries no inference here — the vendor calls its own model — so this is purely about tools and data, which is the useful distinction from every other gateway in the catalogue.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: Which of our servers a published agent may reach, and on whose grants.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own MCP servers and connectors. The platform's MCP path is not a policy bypass — the same data policies that regulate its connectors regulate its MCP tools — reached through the tunnel and our gateway, never exposed to the platform directly.

blocks.title: Tunnel connector
blocks.note: The platform's on-premises data gateway, or its private-network equivalent: vendor-supplied software on a host we run that dials out, so nothing is opened inbound, and relays the platform's connector and MCP calls to our gateway — the same component, and the same chain, as on every SaaS sibling. It does not run agents and does not authenticate for us, and its hard payload limits make it a query path rather than a bulk one. The connection credentials it caches sit on this host, which is why the secrets pin lands here.

items.label: Outbound connector
items.note: Polls outward; no inbound firewall rule, and a small ceiling on what any one call may carry.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record a maker attached as grounding or as an action target — often without anyone asking whether the agent's audience should reach them.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The vendor's model, called by the vendor — for the platforms whose model is their own it sits under the same agreement, and this band is external only for the bring-your-own-provider variant. We neither broker it nor hold the key, which is why our own gateway carries no inference on this page. Two variants worth noting in assessment: some platforms run the model entirely inside their own boundary (then this block collapses into the platform and is assured, not drawn), and some let the customer bring a model key — zone-2 configuration that changes whose terms the grounding content leaves under.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Third-party services the platform's connectors reach, on whichever credential the maker chose.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Whose credentials a published agent runs on, which on this platform is a configuration choice with four answers. End-user credentials are the default and the safe one. Maker credentials are the ambient-authority case: every consumer of that agent transitively inherits the maker's access to the backend. The platform's own inventory records which mode each connector uses, and that field is the single most useful thing an administrator can query here.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: The tunnel host's cached connection credentials — issued, rotated and revoked from here, because they sit on a host we run and nowhere our gateway can see.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: The platform's data policies classify every connector and forbid mixing groups across the boundary — and unusually for this catalogue, they have teeth: a violation greys out the publish button outright. Exemptions were removed, so every agent is subject to them.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: The inventory and the publication gate. On a platform where anyone can build, an agent nobody registered is an agent nobody can revoke — and that is the normal case rather than the exception.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Run history, and the population view: which agents exist, who built them, which have outlived their author. The unit of observation here is the population, not a deployment.

edges.label: authors & publishes
edges.note: Built and shipped inside the vendor's surface. No pipeline is involved, so there is no place to insert a review that the platform does not itself provide.

edges.label: uses a published agent
edges.note: Colleagues run what a maker published, on whichever credential the maker configured.

edges.label: their model
edges.note: The vendor calls its own model provider. We are not on this path and hold no key for it, which is why our gateway carries tools and data only.

edges.label: brokered tool calls
edges.note: Which of our servers a published agent may call, on grants we scope rather than the maker's standing access.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Grounding content and action targets, reached on our terms.

edges.label: outbound-only tunnel
edges.note: Their cloud reaching back into us through software we run. Outbound-only, so nothing is opened inbound; the public-endpoint form most platforms default to is recorded as a deviation.

edges.label: connector calls into our systems
edges.note: The tunnel hands to our gateway rather than to a server or the data. A vendor-hosted agent reaching our data crosses here or it does not reach it at all.

edges.label: third-party connectors
edges.note: Connectors reaching services outside both environments. This path never touches our network, so the connector policy in their tenant is the only control on it.

risks.note: The defining risk of the archetype, and it materializes in the platform's connection store: a maker attaches a connector on their own credentials and publishes to a team; every consumer then transitively holds the maker's access to that backend. Nobody granted it, nobody sees it in an access review — and most of it plays out on paths our gateway never touches.

An agent is a form away, and the unregistered population accumulates in the platform — not in any one builder. Without the inventory queried, the population is unbounded, and agents outlive the people who built them.
Writes into systems of record from an agent nobody reviewed.

A maker attaches a folder as grounding and the platform indexes it. Whoever can write to that folder can write to the index, and every agent grounded on it reads what they left — the poisoning is of the retrieval source, not of the model.
Grounding content and connector results re-enter the agent as instruction. A document dropped in a shared folder is an instruction channel on this platform.
The tunnel reaches into systems that were never meant to be internet-adjacent, and the credentials it caches sit on a host somebody has to patch.
Grounding content leaves for a model we do not broker and hold no key for.
Publish to a public channel with authentication off and the audience is the internet: the agent's grounding and connectors answer anyone with the URL — found by the thousands by recon tooling.
A document in a grounding folder anyone can write to comes back as a tool result and enters their runtime as instruction — the path the shared-drive scenario walks.
Bulk knowledge upload — folders pushed into the platform as grounding by someone not thinking of it as data movement.

mitigations.note: Classification before knowledge is attached: a maker uploads whole folders as grounding, and this is the only point where what leaves can still be read.

Whose credentials a published agent runs on, and who may run it at all: end-user credentials by default, maker credentials as a deliberate, reviewed exception, and authentication on for every channel an agent is published to — an agent published with authentication off answers anyone with the URL.

A directory principal minted per published agent, so conditional access, revocation and ownership transfer attach to one agent — the grants live in the platform's connection store, and our gateway sees only the slice it issued.
The platform's own inventory, queried rather than assumed — including which connectors use maker credentials, which is the field that finds the ambient-authority agents.

The publication gate: review between an author and an audience, a limited audience first, versioned agents and unpublish as rollback. Frequently off by default, and the nearest thing this platform has to code review.
The platform's own grounding and connector-output classification, configured as zone 2 — theirs to implement, ours to switch on and verify, because nothing of ours sits on the connector paths.

Their runtime, their sandbox, their model — assured by assessment rather than drawn, because none of it is ours to inspect, and re-assessed on a clock: connector defaults, publication channels and authentication toggles drift as the vendor ships.

Connector policy authored centrally in the tenant: every connector classified, a confidential source never paired with a path that sends data out, unclassified connectors blocked — and enforced, so a violating agent cannot be published. The only control on a path that never touches our network.

The cached connection credentials on the tunnel host — issued scoped and short-lived, rotated, and revocable without redeploying the host. Absorbed here per the recorded deviation, because this is where the secret actually sits.
Which of our servers a published agent may reach, decided at our tier rather than by the maker.
Grounding read through our gateway is classified before it goes back to their runtime — the one return leg we can inspect.

What a maker may attach as grounding: sources with governed write access only, classified before they are attachable, and every read scoped to the invoker's entitlement. The default connector set is the real policy, and a permissive default is a decision nobody remembers making.

Run history per agent and per consumer, and maker activity, exported where we can query it rather than left in their console — the baseline that shows which agent's connector mix or run pattern moved.
Disable the app in the tenant and revoke every connector grant — the SaaS form of the stop, and the response the departed-author and public-link scenarios actually invoke.

walkthrough.title: An agent is built, published, and used
walkthrough.moves: A colleague assembles an agent from prompts and connectors; another colleague runs it, and the answer comes back.

steps.label: build & publish
steps.note: Built and published inside the vendor's surface by someone who is not an engineer. No pipeline is involved, so the platform's own publish gate is the only review there is — and governance here is population management rather than change review.

steps.label: colleague runs it
steps.note: A colleague runs what was published — on their own credentials if the maker chose end-user auth, and on the maker's if they did not.

steps.label: vendor's model call
steps.note: Now the model is called — the vendor's own, on its own key, for the running turn. We are not on this path, which is why our gateway carries tools and data only.

steps.label: completion
steps.note: The completion comes back into their runtime as the turn's plan.

steps.label: down the tunnel
steps.note: Their cloud reaches back into us through the connection our tunnel holds open.

steps.label: reach into our data
steps.note: Handed to our gateway. A published agent reaching our data crosses here or not at all.

steps.label: scoped grant
steps.note: Scoped to grants we decided, rather than to the maker's standing access.

steps.label: records
steps.note: The records the agent was built to reach.

steps.label: records
steps.note: The records come back.

steps.label: recorded
steps.note: Through our crossing, where the call is recorded.

steps.label: into the tunnel
steps.note: Classified at the gateway, then back into the connector.

steps.label: tool result
steps.note: And up the tunnel to their runtime as a tool result.

steps.label: reply
steps.note: The reply returns to the colleague who ran it, grounded on everything the walk touched.

scenarios.title: A maker attaches a connector on their own credentials

steps.label: publish with connectors
steps.note: Prompt written, connectors attached, agent published to a team.

steps.label: run; inherit maker's access
steps.note: Colleagues run it — and inherit the maker's access to whatever it was attached to. The gap between who built an agent and whose access it uses is where this archetype's incidents live.

steps.label: back into us
steps.note: The agent reaches back into our systems through the tunnel.

steps.label: reach bounded at our tier
steps.note: Which is only bounded at all because the reach into our systems crosses a tier we run.

scenarios.title: A shared drive becomes an instruction channel

steps.label: folder as grounding
steps.note: A running agent asks for a folder somebody uses as grounding.

steps.label: to our gateway
steps.note: The request comes up the tunnel to our gateway.

steps.label: admitted read
steps.note: Admitted like any other read.

steps.label: folder read
steps.note: The folder is read.

steps.label: document with instruction
steps.note: A document written by anyone with access to that folder comes back with the rest.

steps.label: tool result
steps.note: It crosses back as an ordinary tool result.

steps.label: into the tunnel
steps.note: Classified at the gateway, which cannot tell it apart from any other record.

steps.label: model input
steps.note: And enters their runtime as model input.

steps.label: acts with maker's authority
steps.note: The agent acts on it with the maker's authority — on connectors that never touch our network, so nothing of ours can intervene past this point.

scenarios.title: The author leaves

steps.label: agent outlives maker
steps.note: An agent outlives the person who built it, still holding their connector grants.

steps.label: third-party grants keep flowing
steps.note: The maker's third-party grants keep flowing — these never touch our network, so only the platform's connection-ownership transfer or revocation can cut them. That inventory operation is the primary response.

steps.label: grants into us
steps.note: The departed maker's grants into our systems still arrive through the tunnel.

steps.label: our slice cut
steps.note: Our gateway cuts the slice it issued — the grants into our own systems — which is real, and is not most of what the departed maker left behind.

scenarios.title: Published to anyone with the link

steps.label: stranger's question
steps.note: A maker publishes to a public channel and leaves authentication off; the "consumer" is now anyone who finds the URL, and recon tooling finds them by the thousands.

steps.label: down the tunnel
steps.note: The stranger's question comes back into us through the tunnel.

steps.label: agent's own grants
steps.note: It reaches our crossing on the agent's own grants.

steps.label: admitted like any run
steps.note: Admitted like any run of this agent — the catalogue does not know who is asking.

steps.label: grounding for a stranger
steps.note: The grounding answers a stranger. Inventory and publication gating are what would have caught it.

deviations.subject: The vendor band is drawn before our cloud band
deviations.reason: Band order is left-to-right by convention; here the vendor sits first because a maker reaches the platform first and the platform reaches back into us second. The same break, for the same reason, as the enterprise chat sibling; the API/SDK runtime, reached through our own front end, keeps the conventional order.

deviations.subject: The tunnel absorbs secrets
deviations.reason: Credential hardening (D3-CH) is embodied by the AI gateway, but the load-bearing secrets on this path are the connection credentials cached on the tunnel host — the pin sits where they live, and the issuance story in the governance call-out.

deviations.subject: The tunnel is drawn; the public endpoint and the direct data path are recorded
deviations.reason: The target state is the SaaS siblings': the platform reaches our gateway through an outbound-only tunnel on a host we run, so none of our endpoints faces the internet. Most platforms in this class default instead to calling an internet-facing endpoint of ours, admitted at our edge by their published IP ranges — the same crossing with a weaker admission — and some offer private networking in place of a relay. The on-premises data gateway can also carry the platform's standard data connectors straight to an on-premises source, bypassing our gateway; where that path is used, the connector's data-policy classification and the relay's scoped credentials are the only controls on it, and it is recorded here rather than drawn as a second chain.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway does not reach a model provider
deviations.reason: Everywhere else in the catalogue the gateway is the model path, and the registered pattern says so. Here it is not: the vendor calls its own model, on its own key, and our gateway exists only to admit a published agent to our tools and data. Drawing an inference leg out of our gateway would assert a broker we do not operate. The model edge is therefore vendor to provider — a property this drawing shares with its two SaaS siblings and the MCP publisher, each recording it the same way. It is drawn with its own items rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack for the same reason: no model proxy, because there is no model traffic to proxy.

deviations.subject: The vendor platform is a single block despite containing an orchestrator, a harness and a sandbox
deviations.reason: The three-zone responsibility rule forbids drawing vendor internals we cannot inspect. On a platform with no customer-hosted runtime option, everything but policy configuration is theirs, so the honest drawing is one block assured by assessment rather than four boxes implying visibility we do not have.
