tools.name: Claude Managed Agents

variants.name: Managed Agents API (agents, environments, sessions, vaults) on api.anthropic.com
Self-hosted sandboxes (your worker polls the environment work queue)
variants.note: Control plane stays with Anthropic; sandbox image, egress, service-key custody and session-content retention are yours. Environment-variable vault credentials are not yet supported here.

summary: Anthropic's hosted agent harness (beta, enabled by default for API accounts; Managed Agents endpoints take the managed-agents-2026-04-01 beta header, memory store endpoints agent-memory-2026-07-22): you define an agent (model, system prompt, toolset, MCP servers, skills), an environment (Anthropic cloud sandbox — an isolated Ubuntu container, up to 8 GB / 10 GB — or a self-hosted sandbox), then run sessions that stream events over SSE. The sandbox runs bash, file tools and code; web_search and web_fetch run on Anthropic's servers. Sessions are stateful: event history persists until you delete the session and sandbox state is checkpointed for 30 days, so Managed Agents is not ZDR- or HIPAA-BAA-eligible.

Governance is API-native and workspace-scoped: permission_policy always_allow / always_ask per toolset or per tool (MCP toolsets default to always_ask), tool enable flags, per-tool allowed_domains / blocked_domains, environment networking unrestricted / limited with allowed_hosts, vault credentials injected at egress so the agent never sees the secret, hard dollar session budgets, versioned agent definitions, memory stores with immutable version history and redaction, signed webhooks and a persisted event stream. Also available on Claude Platform on AWS with differences.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Any Claude API organisation (beta, on by default); MCP tunnels and dreaming are a limited research preview. Billed per model token, $10 per 1,000 web searches and $0.08 per session hour at list rates.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Anthropic API only (plus Claude Platform on AWS); model pinned per agent with optional inference_geo "us" or "global", validated against the workspace's allowed_inference_geos when the agent is saved, when a session is created and on every turn.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Everything runs on Anthropic infrastructure: conversation, tool inputs/outputs, files and sandbox state; self-hosted sandboxes keep tool execution and files on your side while the transcript still passes through Anthropic.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: Commercial terms (no training). Session transcripts persist until you delete the session; sandbox checkpoints 30 days; memory versions retained 30 days (recent versions longer); not eligible for ZDR or HIPAA BAA.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents (overview through reference)

riskNotes.note: Vaults and credentials are workspace-scoped: any API key with workspace access can reference them at session creation, and the docs recommend separate workspaces and environments per trust boundary for self-hosted sandboxes.

Memory stores attach read_write by default and the docs warn a successful injection can write content later sessions read as trusted; use read_only for reference stores and limited networking with allowed_hosts for production.

The built-in agent toolset defaults to always_allow, including bash with unrestricted egress on API-created environments; production guidance is limited networking and always_ask on bash or MCP tools that write.

MCP servers are declared by URL with no allowlist beyond the agent definition; MCP toolsets default to always_ask so newly added server tools do not run unapproved, and per-tool enabled flags can pin the set.

Custom tool results, uploaded files and outputs are stored server-side until deleted; OAuth exchanges performed inside the sandbox return tokens unredacted, so perform exchanges outside and store the result in the vault.

controls.mechanism: Require SSO for Console (Authentication section of Identity and access at platform.claude.com/settings/identity) sends every interactive Console login to the IdP, whose MFA policy supplies the second factor for the people who can change agents, environments, vaults, keys, tunnels and federation rules; API key expirations and Workload Identity Federation narrow the non-interactive path around that login

steps.title: Require SSO for the Console
body: After verifying your domain on Identity and access (platform.claude.com/settings/identity), turn on Require SSO for Console in the Authentication section and enforce MFA on the Claude app in your IdP.

steps.title: Shrink the key path around the login
body: Create API keys linked to a service account with a short expiration (an organisation maximum expiration policy removes Never), and move production callers to Workload Identity Federation, because a key acts without any interactive login.

controls.note: Partial on the MFA rule applied to every vendor (as on toolClaudeCode): the Console has no second factor of its own — login is Google, an emailed link or SSO, and no Console password exists (support article 13371040) — so MFA is the IdP's, reached only through Require SSO for Console, and that page appears only after SSO is enabled through Sales or an organisation merge. Paths around it: personal, service-account, legacy workspace and Admin API keys, and federated tokens, act without an interactive login, and any Workspace Developer or Limited Developer can create a key, so a key holder changes agents, vaults and environments with no MFA. End-user MFA at the front end, which decides whom a session runs for, is the deployer's application.

original.mechanism: Claude Console organisation and workspace membership, roles, SSO/SCIM and API-key or workload identity federation credentials gate who can create agents and sessions

steps.title: Scope operators by workspace
body: Create agents, environments and vaults in a dedicated Console workspace and issue keys (or a WIF service account) scoped to it; Console SSO and SCIM govern the humans.

controls.mechanism: No per-agent principal: agent ids and versions identify configuration. The calling application authenticates as a service account (svac_) through Workload Identity Federation or a service-account key; outbound MCP and API calls carry whatever credential the session's vaults map (vault display_name and metadata name the end user); a self-hosted worker holds an environment key and a per-session secret

steps.title: Give each calling application its own service account
body: In Settings → Workload identity run Connect workload to create an issuer, a service account and a federation rule scoped to the agent's workspace, so the application that drives the agent holds short-lived tokens tied to a named non-human identity.

steps.title: Map each vault to one end user
body: Create one vault per end user with metadata external_user_id and pass only that vault in vault_ids at session creation, so the credential an MCP server sees is that user's.

steps.title: Protect self-hosted worker credentials
body: Store ANTHROPIC_ENVIRONMENT_KEY in a secrets manager, pass the per-session secret only into the sandbox serving that session, and revoke the key on suspicion; revocation is validated on every request.

controls.note: Partial by the agent-identity rule: the runtime mints no identity per agent. What authenticates is layered — the application's service account or API key to Anthropic (inventoried under Settings → Service accounts and API keys, revocable apart from people), the vault credential to each MCP server, and the environment key for a self-hosted worker — and none is bound to an agent id, so revoking an agent means archiving it and finding every vault its sessions attached. Any key with workspace access can attach any vault, and in a multiagent session every thread uses the session's vaults. No agent identity is presented to third parties, and the MCP tunnel does not authenticate to the upstream.

original.mechanism: Agent resources with ids and versions; per-session vault identity (display_name and metadata mapping to your user); environment service keys and per-session secrets for self-hosted workers; no cryptographic agent identity presented to third parties

steps.title: Bind each session to an end-user vault
body: Create one vault per end user (metadata external_user_id) and pass vault_ids at session creation so actions on MCP servers are attributable to that user's credentials.

steps.title: Protect the environment key
body: Store ANTHROPIC_ENVIRONMENT_KEY in a secrets manager, pass the per-session secret only into the sandbox serving that session, and revoke on suspicion (validated on every request).

original.note: The agent id and version identify a configuration, not a principal third parties authenticate; vault credentials carry the authority for outbound calls, so the identity a tool sees is whatever credential the vault mapped — inventory those as the non-human identities.

controls.mechanism: Vault credential values are write-only, never returned and stored under Anthropic-managed encryption (outside workspace CMEK), rotated in place with running sessions re-resolving; Workload Identity Federation tokens (token_lifetime_seconds 60 to 86400, default 3600) and API key expirations for the API itself; the MCP tunnel token (Rotate token, archive) and up to two CA certificates (Revoke), provisioned over a workspace:manage_tunnels federation rule

steps.title: Register credentials in a vault and rotate in place
body: Add mcp_oauth (with a refresh block), static_bearer or environment_variable credentials; update the secret to rotate (running sessions re-resolve without a restart) and archive to purge it while keeping the record.

steps.title: Federate the API credential
body: Connect the workload under Settings → Workload identity with a workspace:developer rule and a short token_lifetime_seconds, unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY wherever it runs (it shadows federation), and delete the old key.

steps.title: Provision the tunnel over federation
body: Create the tunnel with programmatic access so the setup component fetches the tunnel token and registers a locally generated CA over a workspace:manage_tunnels rule; the private key never leaves your environment.

steps.title: Rotate and revoke tunnel credentials
body: Use Rotate token on the tunnel's detail page, register a new CA certificate beside the old one and Revoke the old, and archive the tunnel to invalidate its token; every reveal and rotation is recorded in the Compliance API activity log.

controls.note: Native by the credential-hardening rule: an encrypted write-only store for tool credentials, federated short-lived credentials for the API, and a scoped, rotatable, revocable tunnel credential. Boundaries: nothing refuses static API keys — any Workspace Developer can create one and Never is offered unless an organisation maximum expiration policy is set (where that policy is set is not documented); static_bearer credentials live as long as the upstream token; an OAuth exchange run inside the sandbox leaves the returned token there unredacted. Tunnel (research preview, request access): rotating the token does not sever established cloudflared connections, so cutting a compromised host means stopping the stack or archiving the tunnel; the tunnel token and TLS private key sit on the organisation's host and in its secrets manager.

original.mechanism: Vault credentials (mcp_oauth with managed refresh, static_bearer, environment_variable with networking.allowed_hosts and injection_location) substituted at egress; secret values are write-only; rotate via update, archive purges the secret

steps.title: Register credentials in a vault
body: Add mcp_oauth or static_bearer credentials keyed by mcp_server_url, or environment_variable credentials keyed by secret_name with networking type limited and allowed_hosts; the agent sees only an opaque placeholder.

steps.title: Rotate and revoke
body: Update the credential's secret (running sessions re-resolve without restart), archive to purge the secret while keeping the audit record (vaults page), and subscribe to vault_credential.refresh_failed on the webhooks page (platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/webhooks) for the notification.

original.note: Vault substitution keeps values out of the sandbox and the model; it does not scope them per requesting user. A credential in a vault is presented for every session that vault is attached to, so tenant-scoped delegation — one user's authority, not a shared credential's — is the application's to arrange through per-user vaults or mcp_oauth per user. Where no credential matches, the connection is attempted unauthenticated.

controls.mechanism: Agents, environments, vaults, memory stores and deployments are listable workspace resources (id, name, description, metadata, immutable agent version history, archived_at); agent.created / updated / archived webhooks and the Compliance API Activity Feed's platform_agent_created / updated / archived records; the only gate on writing a definition is workspace membership and role

steps.title: Treat the agent resource as the register
body: Create each agent once with owner and approval metadata, list its versions, and archive retired agents so new sessions cannot reference them.

steps.title: Record who changed each definition
body: Turn on the Compliance API (Console Settings > Security) and pull platform_agent_created, platform_agent_updated and platform_agent_archived from the Activity Feed, alongside the agent.* webhooks.

steps.title: Limit who can write definitions
body: Give Workspace Developer only to the authors and the pipeline's service account and Workspace User to everyone else, since any role that can use the API can create, update and override agents.

controls.note: Partial by the registry rule: the inventory, version history and change record exist, but nothing gates a definition before it runs. Any key or token with workspace:developer — the only non-admin scope; finer-grained scopes "per resource, or read versus write" are not available — can create or update an agent (omitting version makes the update unconditional), and a session created with agent_with_overrides replaces model, system, tools, mcp_servers and skills without creating a version, so a session can run a configuration the register never saw. Environments are not versioned. There is no approval state; ownership is metadata the organisation writes, and reconciliation is its pipeline.

original.mechanism: Agents are first-class workspace resources with id, name, description, metadata, version history, archive; environments, vaults, memory stores and deployments likewise; list endpoints and lifecycle webhooks

steps.title: Treat the agent resource as the registry
body: Create agents once with metadata for ownership, list versions, and archive retired agents (new sessions cannot reference them); subscribe to agent.created / updated / archived webhooks.

original.note: A registry of deployed definitions with ids and versions. Ownership lives in metadata the organisation writes, and there is no approval workflow before deploy — the change-gating the architecture pins is the organisation's pipeline.

controls.mechanism: Immutable agent versions (version increments on every change; optimistic concurrency through the version field, 409 on mismatch; full version history); sessions and scheduled deployments pin agent {id, version}; coordinator rosters keep the version pinned when last updated; user.define_outcome runs a grader inside one session

steps.title: Pin sessions to a version
body: Create sessions with agent as an object carrying id and version, so your application decides which version each session runs and rolling back is changing that pinned number.

steps.title: Update with optimistic concurrency
body: Supply version on every update (ant apply does this), list versions to audit, and re-apply an earlier configuration to make it the latest again.

steps.title: Use outcomes as an in-session check
body: Send user.define_outcome with a rubric so a separate grader evaluates each iteration and emits span.outcome_evaluation_end.

controls.note: Partial: versioning and pointer-flip rollback are met — a session pinned to a version object keeps it, and the docs describe pinning to "stage rollouts of new versions independently" — but progressive release is the application's: the runtime has no alias, traffic split or canary percentage, and a session created with the bare agent id gets the latest version the moment it is saved. No evaluation gate sits in the promotion path: define_outcome grades one session's artifact, not a version. Environments are not versioned; agent_with_overrides and mid-session tools updates run configurations no version records; rolling the agent back rolls back neither environments, vaults nor running sessions. Rated partial on the same rule as the other managed runtimes.

original.mechanism: Agent version increments on every change with optimistic concurrency (version field, 409 on mismatch), full version history, coordinator rosters pinned to a version; sessions keep the configuration they started with

steps.title: Roll forward and back by version
body: Update with the version field for safe concurrent edits, list versions to audit, and re-apply an earlier configuration to roll back; environments are not versioned, so keep your own record.

original.note: Immutable versions, full history and re-applying an earlier version are the versioning half; there is no canary alias, percentage exposure or regression gate, environments are not versioned, and rolling back the agent does not roll back credentials or running sessions (they keep the configuration they started with). Rated partial on the same rule as the other hosted runtimes.

original.mechanism: Outcome-driven sessions run a grader that evaluates iterations against a defined outcome; no release-gate eval harness

steps.title: Use outcomes as an in-session check
body: Send user.define_outcome so a grader (without web tools) evaluates each iteration and emits span.outcome_evaluation_end with satisfied / needs_revision / failed.

original.note: The outcome grader evaluates iterations within a session against a defined outcome; it is not a release-gate regression suite with datasets and results across versions. Anthropic's model evaluations are supplier evidence for TPRM.

controls.mechanism: agent_toolset_20260401 default_config / configs with enabled and permission_policy per tool; mcp_toolset default_config.enabled false plus named configs; web_search / web_fetch allowed_domains or blocked_domains; mcp_servers declared by URL on the definition (up to 20); custom tools returned to the application

steps.title: Enable only the tools the agent needs
body: Set default_config.enabled false on agent_toolset_20260401 and enable bash, read, write and the others individually in configs.

steps.title: Switch the vendor's web tools off or bound them
body: Set enabled false on web_search and web_fetch, or put allowed_domains or blocked_domains (1 to 64 each) on their configs entries; environment networking does not govern these tools.

steps.title: Enable only the MCP tools you reviewed
body: Set default_config.enabled false on each mcp_toolset and list the tools to enable, so tools the server operator adds later stay off until reviewed.

steps.title: Leave MCP toolsets on always_ask
body: Keep the always_ask default on MCP toolsets and per-tool configs so new or consequential tools do not run without approval; switch a server to always_allow only after review.

controls.note: Native by the tool-permission rule: per-tool enablement plus a per-tool approval policy, and domain scoping on the web tools, enforced server-side for the built-in and MCP toolsets. Not covered: anything a declared MCP server serves (session creation does not check connectivity or credentials), and scoping by principal beyond the vault attached. Every setting is definition content the next update undoes, with no tenant restriction on definition changes beyond workspace role; a session created with agent_with_overrides replaces tools and mcp_servers wholesale, and an idle session's tools can be updated mid-session. Custom tools are the application's to permit. The gateway half of this pin — which servers, which tools, whose grant — is the organisation's MCP gateway on the tunnel path.

original.mechanism: agent_toolset_20260401 default_config / configs with enabled false per tool, MCP toolset per-tool enabled flags, web_search / web_fetch allowed_domains or blocked_domains, permission_policy per tool

steps.title: Enable only the tools the agent needs
body: Set default_config.enabled false and enable bash, read, write and so on individually; do the same on mcp_toolset entries so server-added tools stay off.

steps.title: Restrict the web tools
body: Put allowed_domains or blocked_domains on the web_search and web_fetch config entries (up to 64 domains each); environment networking does not govern these tools.

original.note: enabled false hides a tool, permission_policy pre-approves or gates it, domain lists limit web tools' arguments. Custom tools are the application's: the runtime returns them to the application without applying toolset policy.

original.mechanism: mcp_servers declared by name and URL on the agent definition (up to 20, every entry referenced by an mcp_toolset); default_config.enabled false plus configs to enable named tools; MCP toolsets default to always_ask

steps.title: Enable only the tools you reviewed
body: Set default_config.enabled false on each mcp_toolset and list the tools to enable, so tools the server operator adds later stay off until reviewed.

steps.title: Leave MCP toolsets on always_ask
body: The always_ask default exists so new tools an MCP server adds do not execute without approval; only switch a server to always_allow after you have reviewed it.

original.note: Rated partial on the hosted-runtime rule: admission is per agent definition by whoever may edit it — there is no workspace-wide allowlist of servers — and the runtime verifies nothing a declared server serves; session creation does not even validate connectivity or credentials. The always_ask default and per-tool enablement are the only guards against a server's tool list changing underneath you. Gate definition changes in your own pipeline.

controls.mechanism: permission_policy always_ask pauses the session (session.status_idle, stop_reason requires_action with the blocking event_ids) until a user.tool_confirmation naming that tool_use_id with result allow or deny (optional deny_message); a confirmation for a call not at ask is rejected with 400; subagent requests are cross-posted to the primary thread; webhook session.status_idled

steps.title: Require confirmation for consequential tools
body: Set permission_policy always_ask on the agent toolset or on bash alone via configs, and keep it on MCP toolsets (their default).

steps.title: Put each paused call in front of a person
body: On requires_action (or the session.status_idled webhook) show the agent.tool_use or agent.mcp_tool_use input to the approver in your front end, then send user.tool_confirmation with its tool_use_id; match session_thread_id for subagent calls.

controls.note: Native by the approval rule: the runtime pauses on the configured tool and runs it only on a confirmation bound to that call's event id, whose input is fixed; the model cannot send it and the session waits indefinitely. Boundaries: the runtime cannot tell a person's confirmation from the application's — any holder of a workspace key can send one — so that a human decides is the front end's to guarantee; auto is not a human checkpoint ("the call runs before anyone sees it"); custom tools are never paused by policy and are the application's to gate; the policy is definition content that an update or a session override can loosen. On this drawing the organisation's gateway owns the gate and this is the second, configured layer.

original.mechanism: permission_policy always_ask pauses the session (session.status_idle with requires_action) until a user.tool_confirmation allow/deny event; custom tools always return to your application; webhooks notify on session.status_idled

steps.title: Require confirmation for risky tools
body: Set permission_policy type always_ask on the agent toolset (or on bash alone via configs) and on MCP toolsets (the default); answer with user.tool_confirmation including a deny_message.

controls.mechanism: Nothing in the runtime: no configurable classifier or hook over user messages, tool results, MCP results or fetched pages; Inference hooks exclude Claude Platform organisations. Integration points are the MCP server URL on the definition (the gateway's tunnel hostname) and the application's own user.message and custom tool results

evidence.title: Inference hooks, current limitations (Platform organizations out of scope)
Permission policies (auto assesses tool results but takes no instructions from them)
MCP connector (servers declared by URL on the agent)

controls.note: External on the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolGrokBot): nothing in Managed Agents classifies content before it enters context, and there is no hook to attach a classifier. Inference hooks, which screen tool results on Claude Enterprise surfaces, list "Platform organizations (API access through the Claude Platform)" as out of scope. The organisation's MCP gateway classifies returns when each server is declared as its hostname behind the tunnel, and the application screens user.message content and custom tool results before posting them. web_search and web_fetch results and bash output from allowed hosts reach the model unscreened, so disable the web tools and keep networking limited. auto reads tool results without taking instructions from them; that is action policy, not screening, and containment (limited networking, read_only memory, always_ask) is credited on those rows.

original.mechanism: Model-side safeguards plus structural limits: limited networking, read_only memory stores, always_ask policies and domain lists; no configurable injection classifier

steps.title: Contain the blast radius
body: Use networking type limited with allowed_hosts, attach reference memory stores as read_only, and keep MCP toolsets on always_ask when the agent processes untrusted input.

original.note: Containment, not detection: networking limits, read-only memory and always_ask bound what an injected instruction can do; nothing classifies tool results or retrieved content for injection.

controls.mechanism: Anthropic Trust Center artifacts, the API data-retention eligibility table and the CMEK scope feed the organisation's TPRM platform

evidence.title: Anthropic Trust Center (compliance table and Request access)
API and data retention (feature eligibility: Managed Agents, MCP tunnels)
Customer-managed encryption keys (Managed Agents data in scope, vault values excluded)
MCP tunnels overview (research preview, Cloudflare as subprocessor)

controls.note: External: the assessment, its evidence expiry and the reassessment trigger live in the organisation's TPRM platform. The Trust Center lists SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, CSA STAR, HIPAA and NIST 800-171 for Claude via Anthropic's API, with reports and questionnaires behind Request access. Product-specific findings to record: Managed Agents (every sub-feature, self-hosted sandboxes included) and MCP tunnels are not eligible for ZDR or a HIPAA BAA; transcripts persist until the session is deleted; workspace CMEK covers agent configurations, environments, sessions and events, memory stores and dreams but not vault credential values; MCP tunnels are an as-is research preview carried by Cloudflare; inference can be pinned with inference_geo "us". The configuration the API reads back is input for posture checks the organisation writes, not an assessment.

original.mechanism: Anthropic Trust Center artifacts and the API data-retention page feed the buyer's TPRM platform

steps.title: Record the retention posture
body: Managed Agents is stateful and not ZDR- or HIPAA-eligible; capture this from the retention page in the vendor assessment.

original.mechanism: Every configuration is readable through the API (agents, environments, vaults minus secrets, memory stores, deployments) for posture checks

steps.title: Check posture from the API
body: Enumerate environments for networking type unrestricted, agents for always_allow bash or missing domain lists, and sessions without budgets; treat these as findings.

original.note: Every configuration is readable through the API, which is the input an SSPM product needs; the checks listed in the step are ones the customer writes, not ones the product runs.

controls.mechanism: Persisted session event history (agent.tool_use / tool_result and agent.mcp_tool_use / mcp_tool_result with inputs and results, agent.custom_tool_use, agent.message, span.model_request_start / end with model_usage, thread and compaction events, session.error, session.usage) streamed over SSE and listable in full per session and per thread; lifecycle webhooks; Compliance API Activity Feed session and agent lifecycle records

steps.title: Stream and archive every session's events
body: Open the stream before sending, list the full history (GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/events, and each thread's in multiagent sessions) to reconcile, and store events in your own system keyed by id and processed_at.

steps.title: Do not treat webhooks as the log
body: Webhooks make three attempts and then drop the event with no signal; reconcile by listing session events, and export memory versions before their 30-day window.

steps.title: Correlate with the lifecycle record
body: Enable the Compliance API and pull platform_agent_session_created, platform_agent_session_deleted and platform_agent_updated activities (retained six years) to tie sessions to definition changes and their actors.

controls.note: Native by the tracing rule: every persisted event — tool calls with inputs and results, MCP calls, model requests with usage, thread handoffs, compaction and errors — is retrievable by API for export to the organisation's store, and memory reads and writes appear as ordinary tool events. Not included: thinking content (agent.thinking is a progress signal) and event deltas. There is no OTLP export or log sink: the stream is pulled, and any workspace key can delete a session and its history, so tamper resistance is the organisation's archive. Detection runs in the consumer.

original.mechanism: Persisted session event stream (agent.tool_use / tool_result / mcp_tool_use / message, span.model_request_start/end with usage, session.error, thread events) over SSE and list endpoints; session.usage snapshots

steps.title: Consume and archive the event stream
body: Stream events per session (open the stream before sending), and list past events by type for reconstruction; every persisted event has an id and processed_at.

original.note: Events cover tool use, model requests with usage, errors and thread events, correlated by session; there is no model chain-of-thought and no OTLP export — the stream is pulled through the API. Observability is not detection; that logic runs in the consumer.

original.mechanism: Full event history persisted with the session until deletion; memory version history attributed to sessions; vault archive keeps records after purging secrets; signed webhooks (webhook-signature, 5-minute freshness)

steps.title: Keep an off-platform copy
body: Webhooks are not a durable log (three attempts, then dropped); reconcile by listing session events and export memory versions before the 30-day window expires.

original.note: The event history is customer-deletable and not tamper-evident in the Five Eyes sense; your archive is the record.

controls.mechanism: Memory stores (agent-memory-2026-07-22) are workspace-scoped and absent unless attached in a session's resources at creation (up to 8), with access read_write (default) or read_only enforced at the filesystem; every write is an immutable version attributed to the session, listable and redactable, retained 30 days (recent versions of a live memory longer); memories and stores editable, archivable and deletable by API; session history deleted with the session

steps.title: Scope stores and attach them deliberately
body: Use one store per end user, team or project and attach shared reference stores with access read_only; nothing is shared unless your application attaches it.

steps.title: Audit, roll back and scrub memory
body: List memory versions, restore by writing an earlier version's content back with memories.update, redact versions that captured secrets or PII, and export versions you need beyond 30 days.

steps.title: Delete conversation state you no longer need
body: Delete sessions to remove their event history and sandbox; transcripts otherwise persist.

controls.note: Native on this drawing's memory rule: scope is set per attachment and writes are controllable (read_only, delete and redact by API, a version per write). Content validation, the rule's other write control, is absent: nothing checks what a read_write session writes, and the docs warn an injection can plant content later sessions read as trusted. Separation between users is the application's attachment choice, since any workspace key can attach any store. On self-hosted sandboxes read_only protects the store from upload, not the local copy, which bash, custom tools and sandbox MCP servers can still change. Sandbox state lasts 30 days from creation.

original.mechanism: Memory stores are workspace-scoped resources attached per session with access read_write or read_only, capped at 8 per session; every write creates an immutable version; versions can be redacted; stores can be archived or deleted

steps.title: Segment and scope stores
body: Use one store per user, team or project, attach shared reference stores read_only, and pass instructions per attachment.

steps.title: Audit and roll back memory
body: List memory versions, restore prior content by writing it back, and redact versions that captured secrets or PII while keeping the audit trail.

original.note: Integrity and recovery are real here: read_only stops sessions writing, every write is an immutable version, and recovery is re-pointing to an earlier version. What can still write: any session attached read_write, and the API. Writes are trusted as the session's — nothing scans content for poisoning before it is versioned.

controls.mechanism: user.interrupt per session or thread, then session archive or delete; agent archive (read-only, no new sessions, its scheduled deployments archived); vault and credential archive or delete, propagated at periodic re-resolution; deployment pause (future runs only); environment key revocation for self-hosted workers; tunnel archive

steps.title: Interrupt the agent's running sessions
body: List sessions with agent_id and status running, send user.interrupt without session_thread_id to stop every thread, then archive or delete each session once it is idle.

steps.title: Archive the agent
body: Archive the agent so no new session can reference it; existing sessions keep running until you stop them.

steps.title: Revoke its credentials
body: Archive the vaults or credentials its sessions used (secrets purged, records kept) or delete them; running sessions pick the change up at their next re-resolution.

steps.title: Cut self-hosted workers
body: Revoke ANTHROPIC_ENVIRONMENT_KEY and generate a replacement; revocation takes effect on the worker's next call.

controls.note: Partial by the kill-switch rule: all three actions exist, but the delays are not documented. user.interrupt stops a model response immediately but "can take longer to apply while tool calls are running", and a running session can be neither archived nor deleted until it applies (delay not documented). Archiving the agent leaves existing sessions running. Vault revocation reaches running sessions at a periodic re-resolution whose interval is not documented. There is no single per-agent stop: it is a loop over the agent's sessions, which any holder of a workspace key can run.

original.mechanism: user.interrupt, session archive and delete (removes events and sandbox), agent archive (blocks new sessions), vault or credential archive/delete (purges secrets, propagates to running sessions), environment key revocation, deployment pause

steps.title: Stop and decommission
body: Send user.interrupt, then archive or delete the session; archive the agent so no new sessions start; archive vault credentials to revoke access (running sessions re-resolve credentials periodically).

original.note: user.interrupt stops the active session; archiving credentials propagates at the sessions' next periodic re-resolution, so that interval is the revocation delay for delegated work.

controls.mechanism: One isolated Linux container per session on Anthropic infrastructure (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, up to 8 GB memory and 10 GB disk), never shared between sessions even when they share an environment; checkpointed while idle, kept 30 days from creation and removed when the session is deleted; self-hosted sandboxes run on a worker you operate

steps.title: Use cloud environments for the vendor's isolation
body: Every session gets its own container even when sessions share an environment; sessions do not share filesystem state.

steps.title: Harden self-hosted sandboxes yourself
body: Anthropic does not inspect your image: drop capabilities, run as a non-root user, use a read-only root filesystem, and give each trust boundary its own workspace and environment.

steps.title: Run one self-hosted sandbox per session
body: Build a per-session image around the worker and have the poller's spawn script start a fresh sandbox for each claimed work item, rather than one handler running every item on one host.

controls.note: Native by the isolation rule: a per-session container is documented and deleting the session removes it. Inside: bash, the file tools, installed packages and memory mounts. Outside: the loop, inference, web_search and web_fetch (Anthropic's servers) and the MCP connector, which connects from Anthropic's side. The container technology and its escape testing are not documented beyond "isolated Linux containers". In a multiagent session every agent shares the one sandbox and filesystem. A self-hosted sandbox moves the boundary to the deployer, including how tools are isolated from each other inside it.

original.mechanism: Isolated Linux container per session on Anthropic infrastructure (Ubuntu 24.04, no filesystem shared between sessions); self-hosted sandboxes run on a worker you operate

steps.title: Use cloud environments for the vendor's isolation
body: Every session gets its own container even when sessions share an environment; the sandbox holds the languages, databases and tools listed on the reference page and nothing persists between sessions.

steps.title: Harden self-hosted sandboxes yourself
body: Anthropic does not inspect your image: drop capabilities, run as a non-root user, use a read-only root filesystem, and isolate untrusted workloads into separate workspaces and environments so each service key covers one trust boundary.

original.note: Inside the boundary: bash, file tools, packages and any custom tool served from the sandbox. Outside: the loop, inference, web_search and web_fetch (which run on Anthropic's servers) and the MCP client. Anthropic's boundary stops at the sandbox — how tools are isolated from each other inside it, and everything about a self-hosted worker, is yours.

controls.mechanism: Environment networking type limited with allowed_hosts (bare hostnames or wildcard patterns), allow_mcp_servers and allow_package_managers (an Anthropic-maintained registry list), enforced around the cloud sandbox; unrestricted (a general safety blocklist only) is the default; web_search / web_fetch bounded separately by allowed_domains or blocked_domains on the tool

steps.title: Set limited networking with an explicit host list
body: Create environments with networking type limited and allowed_hosts naming only the hosts the agent needs; leave allow_package_managers false unless the environment installs packages, and allow_mcp_servers false unless code in the sandbox must reach the agent's MCP endpoints.

steps.title: Bound the vendor's web tools separately
body: The networking policy does not touch web_search or web_fetch, which run on Anthropic's servers; set allowed_domains or blocked_domains on those tool entries, or disable them.

steps.title: Firewall self-hosted workers yourself
body: Restrict the worker's VPC or firewall egress to the endpoints its tools require; a self-hosted sandbox's network reach is your policy, not the environment's.

controls.note: Native by the egress rule, for the cloud sandbox's own traffic. Access is per host, not per operation: an allowed host accepts uploads, git push and package publishing, and allow_package_managers opens a list Anthropic can change. Paths it does not see: web_search and web_fetch (their own lists), the MCP connector, which connects from Anthropic's side, and inference. Environments start unrestricted, are not versioned, and can be updated by any workspace key, so the least-privilege posture is set and re-checked deliberately.

original.mechanism: Environment networking type limited with allowed_hosts, allow_mcp_servers and allow_package_managers; unrestricted (a general safety blocklist only) is the default for API-created environments; web_search / web_fetch bounded separately by allowed_domains or blocked_domains on the tool

steps.title: Set limited networking with an explicit host list
body: Create environments with networking type limited and allowed_hosts naming only the hosts the agent needs; set allow_mcp_servers true only if the agent's declared MCP endpoints must be reachable from the sandbox, and allow_package_managers true only when packages are installed.

steps.title: Bound the vendor's web tools separately
body: The networking policy does not touch web_search or web_fetch, which run on Anthropic's servers; set allowed_domains or blocked_domains on those tool entries in the agent toolset, or disable them.

original.note: Covers the sandbox's outbound traffic only. The web tools take their own path under their own lists, the MCP client's connections are opened by allow_mcp_servers, and a self-hosted sandbox's egress is your VPC and firewall. API-created environments start unrestricted, so the least-privilege posture must be set deliberately.

controls.mechanism: permission_policy (always_allow, always_ask, auto) per toolset in default_config and per tool in configs, evaluated server-side before each built-in or MCP tool call; enabled false removes a tool; auto is a server-side model evaluation; evaluated_permission and evaluation recorded on every agent.tool_use and agent.mcp_tool_use event

steps.title: Gate consequential tools with always_ask
body: Set permission_policy always_ask on bash (a configs entry) and keep it on every mcp_toolset (the default), so each call pauses with requires_action until your application answers.

steps.title: Keep the evaluation in your audit record
body: Store evaluated_permission and the evaluation object (policy type, reason_code) from each agent.tool_use and agent.mcp_tool_use event; a call denied under auto carries reason_code high_risk and cannot be re-allowed.

steps.title: Decide custom tools in your application
body: Evaluate each agent.custom_tool_use in your handler before returning user.custom_tool_result; permission policies do not govern custom tools.

controls.note: Partial by the rule: per-tool allow / ask / auto in the definition, set by whoever can edit the agent. There is no declarative policy over arguments or target resources beyond the web tools' domain lists, and no workspace or organisation floor a builder cannot lower (the Console's organisation-level web settings apply to the Messages API only). auto is a model's judgement, not a deterministic decision point: it reads user.message content as intent, so relayed end-user input can get a call allowed. Any workspace key can loosen a policy for one session with agent_with_overrides, or for an idle running session with a tools update; agent updates reach only sessions created afterwards. Custom tools return to the application unevaluated.

original.mechanism: permission_policy per toolset and per tool (always_allow, always_ask, auto) evaluated by the server before a built-in or MCP tool runs; auto denials cannot be overridden by the client; evaluated_permission recorded on every tool event

steps.title: Gate the tools a person must see with always_ask
body: Set permission_policy always_ask on bash and on every MCP toolset (their default) so the session pauses with requires_action until a user.tool_confirmation arrives; always_ask is the deterministic gate, auto is the server's own reviewer.

steps.title: Keep the evaluation in your audit record
body: Store evaluated_permission and the evaluation object (policy type, reason_code) from each agent.tool_use and agent.mcp_tool_use event; a call denied under auto carries reason_code high_risk and cannot be re-allowed.

original.note: Custom tools are not governed: the runtime returns agent.custom_tool_use to your application unevaluated, so the same decision must exist there. Policy changes apply to sessions created afterwards, not running ones. Under auto, what you post in user.message counts as your intent — relayed end-user input can get a call allowed, so keep always_ask on anything that user must not run unreviewed.

original.mechanism: Anthropic's model safety systems (content blocks can be redacted by model policy); web tool domain lists; no organisation-level content filter applies to Managed Agents sessions

steps.title: Note what the Console settings do not cover
body: Organisation-level web search and fetch settings in the Console apply to the Messages API only; configure allowed_domains / blocked_domains on the toolset instead.

original.note: Vendor-operated safeguard, not an organisation-configured policy: Anthropic's model safety systems act on every session, and the domain lists bound web tools, but no denied-topic, blocked-term or output filter is configurable. Rated partial on the same rule as Claude Code on the web, Copilot cloud and Codex cloud.

controls.mechanism: Vault credentials substituted at egress: mcp_oauth and static_bearer keyed to an mcp_server_url (normalised exact match), environment_variable keyed by secret_name with networking.allowed_hosts and injection_location header / body; values are write-only and the sandbox holds an opaque placeholder; vault_ids chosen per session, one vault per end user

steps.title: Hold one user's credentials in one vault
body: Create a vault per end user, add mcp_oauth (with refresh) or static_bearer credentials keyed by mcp_server_url, and pass only that user's vault in vault_ids when you create the session.

steps.title: Bind environment secrets to named hosts and headers
body: Create environment_variable credentials with networking type limited, the exact allowed_hosts, and injection_location {"header": true}, so the secret is substituted only into request headers to those hosts.

steps.title: Run token exchanges outside the sandbox
body: Perform OAuth client-credentials and other exchange flows in your application and store the resulting token in the vault, because a token returned into the sandbox arrives unredacted.

controls.note: Native by the credential-scoping rule: credentials stay out of the sandbox and the model's context and are presented only to the destination they are keyed to, and per-user vaults are the documented model ("the collection of credentials associated with an end user"). Boundaries: vaults are workspace-scoped, so which user's vault a session gets is the application's binding — any key with workspace access can attach any vault; in a multiagent session the vaults apply to every thread whose definition declares the matching server; the first matching vault wins; with no match the connection is attempted unauthenticated; an environment_variable credential set to unrestricted is substituted for any host, and that type is not supported on self-hosted sandboxes. The tunnel carries traffic without authenticating to the upstream.

original.mechanism: Vault credentials substituted at egress (the sandbox holds a placeholder; values are write-only); per-session secret for self-hosted workers; the environment service key scoped to one environment's work queue

steps.title: Attach credentials through vaults, never the environment
body: Register mcp_oauth, static_bearer or environment_variable credentials in a vault and pass vault_ids at session creation; the agent sees only an opaque placeholder and the proxy substitutes the value for matching hosts.

steps.title: Scope self-hosted credentials per session
body: Pass the per-session secret only into the sandbox serving that session, keep the environment key in a secrets manager and out of images, and give each trust boundary its own workspace and environment.

original.note: A vault credential is presented for every session the vault is attached to, so tenant- scoped delegation — one user's authority rather than a shared credential — is your arrangement through per-user vaults or per-user mcp_oauth, not the runtime's default. Where no credential matches a server, the connection is attempted unauthenticated.

summary: Claude Tag is Anthropic's organisation-managed @Claude for Slack (public beta on Team and Enterprise, first-party service only, not for ZDR or CMEK organisations). In channels Claude acts under its own service accounts that an Owner provisions, not as the person who tagged it; each thread runs in an ephemeral sandbox on the same infrastructure as Claude Code on the web (or in a self-hosted environment, where Access bundles don't apply yet), and in an Anthropic-hosted environment every outbound request crosses Agent Proxy, which injects credentials from a write-only store and blocks hosts no allow layer covers. Direct messages instead run on the sender's own claude.ai account with their personal connectors.

Admin control lives at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-tag (Owner role): pairing workspaces, Access bundles of credentials, repository grants, domains, plugins and instructions attached per scope (organisation, workspace or channel), the "Enable Claude Tag for your organization" toggle, per-scope version Off, member and guest restrictions, blocked channel patterns, DM toggle, auto-mode allow rules, and spend limits at claude.ai/admin-settings/usage/claude-tag. Channel work bills to the organisation's usage balance. Session transcripts, channel and workspace memory, routines and artifacts are stored by Anthropic with no automatic retention period during the beta and are not yet in the Compliance API session endpoints.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Team and Enterprise only; not on Free, Pro, Max, third-party deployments, or ZDR or CMEK organisations; not covered by Anthropic's BAA. Routines must be enabled at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-code. Slack Connect (externally shared) channels are never served.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Anthropic first-party API from Anthropic-managed sandboxes; self-hosted environments run the sandbox on your runners but still call api.anthropic.com.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Slack messages Claude is shown (including other people's and guests'), attached files, Slack search results, data retrieved from connected tools and everything Claude did are held as session transcripts on Anthropic's side; web search runs on Anthropic's servers outside Agent Proxy rules.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: No automatic retention period during the beta; custom organisation retention does not apply to transcripts or memory (it does to artifacts); deletion is by disconnecting a workspace, removing a channel scope, deleting memory files or routines, or uninstalling the app. Commercial terms (no training).

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: claude.com/docs/claude-tag (concepts, admins, users)

riskNotes.note: Anyone in a channel under a bundle's scope can make Claude act with that bundle's credentials; the docs say to connect a dedicated service account per tool, attach narrow bundles to private channels, and never a personal login.

Claude reads whole threads and can respond without being tagged; guests' and other members' messages become instructions and transcript content. Auto-mode allow rules pre-approve actions per scope, and there is no per-thread deny list.

Public-channel memory is shared workspace-wide and survives a channel going private; Claude can keyword-search public channels without being added to them; artifacts are readable by anyone with access to the source channel.

On an Enterprise Grid paired to several Claude organisations, one organisation's access settings govern the whole grid; bundle isolation comes from where a bundle is attached, not from the bundle itself.
Routines and channel watches run unattended with the channel's credentials and are created by any channel member; the Audit page's Scheduled work tab is the inventory.

controls.mechanism: "Enable Claude Tag for your organization" toggle (top of claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-tag, turns off DMs too), per-scope Claude Tag version Off or the Team Enable Claude Tag switch, bundle Delete (revokes its credentials everywhere, running sessions included), federated connection removal, Scheduled work Pause/Delete, spend limits, workspace Disconnect or app uninstall

steps.title: Turn Claude Tag off for the organisation
body: Turn off Enable Claude Tag for your organization at the top of claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-tag; it stops channels and direct messages.

steps.title: Revoke the credentials in bulk
body: Delete each Access bundle, which revokes its credentials in every scope it was attached to, and remove federated connections under Federated cloud access.

steps.title: Stop unattended work
body: Pause or delete routines on the Scheduled work tab at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-tag/audit.

steps.title: Decommission a workspace
body: Select Disconnect on the workspace in Connected workspaces to delete its sessions, memory, routines, artifacts, scopes and account links.

controls.note: Native by the rule: an Owner can disable the product organisation-wide, revoke every credential a bundle holds in one action per bundle, and the docs say running sessions lose a revoked credential after "a short window" (no bound published) and that a removed federated gateway stops at once and a removed cloud role or authorisation server within about a minute, with tokens already issued valid up to 10 minutes (exchanged AWS credentials up to an hour). Not documented: whether the organisation toggle or version Off ends a thread already running, so work that needs no credential may continue until it finishes (delay not documented). Members removed from the organisation lose access within minutes; personal connectors are revoked per member (Home tab Disconnect) or with the workspace disconnect; the Claude GitHub App is uninstalled at GitHub.

original.mechanism: Enable Claude Tag for your organization toggle, per-scope Claude Tag version Off, Allow direct messages off, /remove @Claude, bundle deletion (revokes credentials everywhere), workspace disconnect, app uninstall, spend limit reached

steps.title: Stop responding and revoke credentials
body: Set the scope's version to Off (or the org toggle), then delete the bundle to revoke its credentials; running sessions may hold a revoked credential briefly.

steps.title: Decommission the data
body: Disconnect the workspace at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-tag to delete its sessions, memory, routines, artifacts and account links.

original.note: Setting a scope Off stops new sessions; a running session may hold a revoked credential briefly, and the docs give no bound for that window — measure it.
