items.title: VS Code device policies and the Copilot managed-settings plane
body: VS Code's ADMX/plist/policy.json set carries the agent lockdown: ChatAgentMode, ChatToolsAutoApprove, ChatToolsTerminalEnableAutoApprove, ChatAgentSandbox*, ChatAgentNetworkFilter with allowed/denied domains, ChatMCP / ChatAllowedMcpServers / ChatDeniedMcpServers / ChatAllowManagedMcpServersOnly, McpGalleryServiceUrl, ChatPlugins* and ChatStrictMarketplaces, ChatHooks / ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly, Claude3PIntegration / Codex3PIntegration, ChatApprovedAccountOrganizations and the CopilotOtel* export keys. Developer: Policy Diagnostics shows which source won.

The same keys arrive through GitHub's managed-settings.json (permissions deny/ask/allow, disableBypassPermissionsMode, allowedMcpServers, enabledPlugins, telemetry). Precedence in VS Code 1.128+: MDM-delivered managed settings, then server-managed, then the local file — and a Copilot managed setting outranks the equivalent VS Code policy.

links.title: VS Code AI settings for enterprises

riskNotes.note: Three of the four 2025–26 CVEs on this surface are prompt injection turned into code execution (settings-file rewrite in VS Code, shell metacharacters in the JetBrains plugin, consent-prompt bypass in the extension host). The vendor mitigations are approval prompts and the sandbox; the enterprise controls that survive a successful injection are ChatToolsAutoApprove=false, ChatAgentSandboxEnabled and the network filter.

The registry-based restriction matches on server name only and is bypassable by editing mcp.json; only the managed-settings allowlist (name, URL, stdio command) is a real boundary. Starting a server straight from mcp.json also skips the trust prompt.

Content exclusion is not honoured by edit and agent modes, and the IDE can still surface semantic information from excluded files. Local BYOK moves prompts off GitHub's ZDR contracts onto whatever the developer's provider retains.

Agent Host sessions can run Claude Agent SDK and Codex runtimes inside VS Code; unless Claude3PIntegration / Codex3PIntegration are set to false, a "Copilot" seat is also a third-party agent seat, with its own model and data path.

controls.mechanism: GitHub's own second-factor requirement (Enterprise > Settings > Authentication security > "Require two-factor authentication for the enterprise and all of its organizations", optionally "Only allow secure two-factor methods") plus client pinning in VS Code (ChatApprovedAccountOrganizations) and Visual Studio (ADMX Copilot Settings); the JetBrains, Xcode, Eclipse and Vim plugins cannot be pinned

steps.title: Require two-factor authentication for every organization
body: Enterprise > Settings > Authentication security: select "Require two-factor authentication for the enterprise and all of its organizations" and "Only allow secure two-factor methods"; members without 2FA cannot reach organization resources until they enable it. The policy is not available to Enterprise Managed Users, whose second factor is the IdP's.

steps.title: Pin VS Code to your organizations
body: Set the ChatApprovedAccountOrganizations policy to your organization logins; chat, agents and inline suggestions stay disabled (the policy is fail-closed) until the signed-in GitHub account belongs to one of them and its account-side policy has resolved.

steps.title: Block personal Copilot plans in Visual Studio
body: Deploy the Visual Studio ADMX templates and under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Visual Studio > Copilot Settings disable Copilot for individual accounts (17.10+) and Copilot Free (17.13+).

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor. GitHub's identity layer can require a second factor for every organization member, but this entity can pin its client to the organization account only in VS Code (ChatApprovedAccountOrganizations, fail-closed) and Visual Studio (ADMX blocks individual and Copilot Free plans); the JetBrains, Xcode, Eclipse and Vim plugins document no account pin, so a personal account works there. VS Code alone meets the native definition. With Enterprise Managed Users the 2FA policy is unavailable: MFA is configured in the IdP and, per GitHub, enforced only at IdP sign-in. Paths that skip the second factor once issued: the OAuth token each editor keeps (lifetime not documented) and fine-grained PATs (Enterprise > Policies > Personal access tokens can cap lifetime and require approval for organization resources; whether that governs the Copilot Requests account permission is not documented). In VS Code, Codex sessions can run on a ChatGPT sign-in (chat.agentHost.allowSignedOutWhenUsable); Codex3PIntegration=false closes that path.

original.mechanism: Enterprise licensing (seat assignment, enterprise teams synced from the IdP) plus the VS Code ChatApprovedAccountOrganizations device policy and Visual Studio ADMX

steps.title: Assign seats through enterprise teams or organisations
body: Enterprise > Billing and licensing > Licensing > Copilot > Manage: assign licences to users or enterprise teams; with Enterprise Managed Users, sync the team to an IdP group so access follows the IdP.

steps.title: Gate VS Code chat to approved GitHub organisations
body: Set the ChatApprovedAccountOrganizations policy to the list of organisation logins; chat, agents and inline suggestions stay off until the signed-in account belongs to one, which forces the organisation's policies to apply before any AI feature works.

steps.title: Block personal Copilot accounts in Visual Studio
body: Deploy the Visual Studio ADMX templates and use Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Visual Studio > Copilot Settings to disable Copilot for individual accounts or Copilot Free.

controls.mechanism: Managed permissions.deny / ask / allow (Shell, Read, Edit, Domain selectors) and machine-wide Copilot Policy Hooks (preToolUse deny) in VS Code Copilot sessions on Agent Host only; Local-harness sessions have ChatToolsEligibleForAutoApproval and Preview PreToolUse hooks (ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly)

steps.title: Pin deny / ask / allow rules in the managed file
body: In copilot/managed-settings.json set permissions.deny, permissions.ask and permissions.allow with Shell(...), Read(...), Edit(...) and Domain(...) selectors; deny from any source wins and a managed ask cannot be satisfied by bypass mode, auto-approval, a hook or a saved grant. VS Code applies these rules only to Copilot sessions that use Agent Host.

steps.title: Deploy a machine-wide policy hook
body: Install a root-owned hook file in /etc/github-copilot/policy.d/ (Windows C:\ProgramData\GitHub\Copilot\policy.d\ or HKLM\Software\Policies\GitHub\Copilot) whose preToolUse hook calls your policy service and returns permissionDecision "deny"; policy hooks load first and disableAllHooks cannot switch them off.

steps.title: Move editor chat onto the harness that runs them
body: Set ChatEditorPreferCopilotHarness=true (VS Code 1.134+) so new editor-chat sessions use the Copilot SDK harness, which loads Policy Hooks, and ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly=true so Local-harness hooks come only from managed sources and policy-enabled plugins.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the rules cover only some sessions. Inside: VS Code Copilot sessions on Agent Host, where managed deny/ask/allow govern shell, file and domain operations and a Policy Hook can deny any tool, MCP included (command hooks fail closed on error but open on timeout; HTTP preToolUse hooks fail open). Outside: Local-harness sessions (ChatToolsEligibleForAutoApproval only forces a prompt, a false terminal rule "does not block the command", and Local PreToolUse hooks are Preview), Claude and Codex harness sessions (their own permission models), JetBrains (honours only permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode among the permission keys) and Visual Studio, Xcode and Eclipse (no rule engine; Visual Studio can only disable agent mode). Managed selectors do not name MCP tools; only a hook does. VS Code's AI-settings page still warns that the granular permissions are "supported only in GitHub Copilot CLI" while GitHub's reference and the 2026-09-09 changelog list VS Code Agent Host sessions — test before relying on them.

original.mechanism: managed-settings.json permissions.deny / ask / allow (Shell, Read, Edit, Domain selectors; GA 2026-09-09) for VS Code Agent Host sessions, plus PreToolUse hooks

steps.title: Pin deny / ask / allow rules in the managed file
body: Write permissions.deny, permissions.ask and permissions.allow with Shell(...), Read(...), Edit(...) and Domain(...) selectors. Deny wins from any source, ask forces a fresh approval that bypass mode cannot satisfy, and the effective allow list is the intersection of all sources.

steps.title: Confirm the client honours managed permissions
body: Managed permissions are enforced in VS Code sessions that use Agent Host, the Copilot app and the CLI; the reference matrix shows JetBrains honouring only permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode, so JetBrains lockdown relies on that key and the sandbox.

steps.title: Add a PreToolUse hook as a second gate
body: VS Code runs .github/hooks/*.json and ~/.copilot/hooks; a PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision allow / deny / ask. Set ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly so only enterprise-managed hooks and policy-enabled plugins can register.

original.note: Component-specific: managed permissions and PreToolUse hooks apply to VS Code Agent Host sessions (enterprise-managed settings page); the VS Code enterprise AI settings page governs editor policies and auto-approval, a different scope. JetBrains, Visual Studio and the other plugins have no runtime rule engine. Where the two pages appear to conflict, the enterprise-managed settings reference is the narrower and authoritative one.

controls.mechanism: No vendor feature; the organisation's TPRM platform assesses GitHub and each model provider from the GitHub Copilot Trust Center and the model-hosting page

evidence.title: GitHub Copilot Trust Center (compliance reports; most documents behind Request access)
Hosting of models for GitHub Copilot (providers and retention terms)

controls.note: External: the organisation's TPRM platform owns the assessment. Rendered in a browser on 2026-09-25 the trust center lists SOC 1, SOC 2 and SOC 3 (SOC 1 Type 2 and SOC 2 Type 2 reports), ISO 27001:2013, ISO/IEC 42001:2023, CSA STAR Level 2, TISAX, a 2026 CAIQ, a PCI DSS AOC and bug-bounty letters, most behind Request access; no penetration-test summary is listed. Treat GitHub plus each model provider as the subprocessor set: OpenAI on Azure, Anthropic models on AWS, Anthropic and Google Cloud (Claude Fable 5 / 5.1 retain prompts and outputs by default outside the ZDR agreement; a ZDR exemption can be requested through end-2026), Google, xAI, and Moonshot models on Azure AI Foundry and Fireworks. The hosting page changes with each model launch; local BYOK moves prompts to whatever provider the developer configures.

original.mechanism: No vendor feature; the assessment inputs are the model-hosting page (providers, ZDR terms) and the Copilot Trust Center
original.note: Treat GitHub plus each model provider (OpenAI on Azure, Anthropic on AWS/GCP/Anthropic, Google, xAI, Moonshot on Foundry/Fireworks) as the subprocessor set; the hosting page is the only first-party list and it changes with every model launch. The trust centre page did not render for automated fetch on 2026-09-10.

steps.title: Record the model-provider set and their retention terms
body: Use the hosting page to enumerate where each model runs and which retain data (Claude Fable 5 / 5.1 retain by default; request the ZDR exemption).

controls.mechanism: No built-in detector; Copilot Policy Hooks in VS Code Copilot sessions on Agent Host can rewrite or deny prompt and tool traffic (userPromptTransformed, preToolUse modifiedArgs, postToolUse modifiedResult); content exclusion as data minimisation

steps.title: Hand prompt and tool traffic to your inspector
body: In a root-owned /etc/github-copilot/policy.d/*.json policy hook, return modifiedTransformedPrompt from userPromptTransformed with secrets masked, and have preToolUse and postToolUse call your DLP service and deny or return modifiedArgs / modifiedResult.

steps.title: Route editor chat through the harness that runs the hooks
body: Set ChatEditorPreferCopilotHarness=true; Local-harness sessions do not load Policy Hooks.

steps.title: Exclude secret-bearing paths
body: Enterprise > AI controls > Copilot > Content exclusion (or the organization's Copilot > Content exclusion): add fnmatch entries such as "*": ["**/.env"]; changes can take up to 30 minutes to reach IDEs that already loaded the settings.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: no Copilot editor detects secrets or PII itself; the Agent Host Copilot harness exposes inline hooks that can block or rewrite prompt and tool content, an attach point that works only once the organisation attaches a detector (userPromptSubmitted config-file hooks cannot change the prompt; userPromptTransformed can). Content exclusion is path filtering, credited as data minimisation: VS Code honours it in chat but not in Edit or Agent mode, Xcode and Eclipse chat do not honour it, symlinks and remote filesystems are exempt, and IDE-provided type information from excluded files can still reach the model. Local-harness, Claude and Codex sessions and the other editors have no such hook; endpoint DLP or an SSE / AI gateway covers them. telemetry.captureContent=false with lockCaptureContent keeps prompts out of the OTel export — data minimisation of telemetry, not redaction.

original.mechanism: Content exclusion (repository / organisation / enterprise) plus telemetry.captureContent=false with lockCaptureContent
original.note: Content exclusion is a context filter, not DLP: it does not apply to edit and agent modes, symlinks or remote filesystems, and IDE-provided type information can still leak. Inline inspection of the prompt stream needs an SSE or endpoint DLP product.

steps.title: Exclude secret-bearing paths at enterprise scope
body: Enterprise > AI controls > Copilot > Content exclusion (or Organization Settings > Copilot > Content exclusion): add fnmatch entries such as "*": ["**/.env"] and per-repository paths; changes propagate within 30 minutes.

steps.title: Keep prompt content out of the telemetry export
body: In managed-settings.json set telemetry.captureContent to false and telemetry.lockCaptureContent to true so users cannot turn content capture on.

controls.mechanism: No classifier; a Copilot Policy Hook's postToolUse can replace a tool result before the model sees it (VS Code Copilot sessions on Agent Host); URL response review and Workspace Trust are human review and admission

steps.title: Screen tool results with a post-tool hook
body: In a policy hook, have postToolUse send each result to your classifier and return modifiedResult (a replacement textResultForLlm) or a failure when it flags injected instructions.

steps.title: Keep fetched content under review
body: Leave chat.tools.urls.autoApprove without approveResponse: true entries so fetched pages are shown for review before they are added to the chat context.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: GitHub ships no injection classifier for tool results, fetched pages or repository files in any editor. The post-tool hook is an attach point in VS Code Copilot sessions on Agent Host only; URL response approval is a person reading content, and Workspace Trust and MCP server trust are admission decisions, not screening. For Local-harness, Claude and Codex sessions and the other editors the answer is external: an AI or MCP gateway classifier on the brokered path. Prompt injection produced code execution on this surface (CVE-2025-53773, CVE-2026-21516).

original.mechanism: VS Code two-step URL approval, Workspace Trust restricted mode, edit review flow; no configurable injection classifier
original.note: Defences are structural (approvals, trust boundaries, sandbox), not detection. Prompt injection has produced RCE on this surface twice (CVE-2025-53773, CVE-2026-21516), so pair these with tool scoping and egress control rather than relying on them.

steps.title: Keep the structural defences on
body: Leave URL fetching on the two-step trust-domain-then-review flow, keep Workspace Trust so untrusted folders open in restricted mode with agents disabled, and require edit review before commits.

controls.mechanism: VS Code policies ChatToolsAutoApprove, ChatToolsEligibleForAutoApproval, ChatAgentExtensionTools, BrowserChatTools, ChatMCP and ChatAgentMode (per tool class); argument-scoped managed permissions in Agent Host Copilot sessions only; Visual Studio "Disable Agent Mode"

steps.title: Remove global auto-approval and pin approval-only tools
body: Set ChatToolsAutoApprove to false and ChatToolsEligibleForAutoApproval to entries such as {"runTask": false, "fetch": false, "runInTerminal": false} so those tools always need a manual approval users cannot switch off.

steps.title: Cut tool classes you do not need
body: ChatAgentExtensionTools=false blocks extension-contributed tools, BrowserChatTools=false removes the integrated-browser tools, ChatMCP=registry or none limits MCP sources, and ChatAgentMode=false removes agents entirely.

steps.title: Scope arguments in Agent Host sessions
body: Use permissions.deny / ask / allow with Shell(git push *), Read(~/.ssh/**), Edit(//etc/**) and Domain(...) selectors; they apply to VS Code Copilot sessions that use Agent Host.

steps.title: Disable agent mode in Visual Studio where needed
body: Visual Studio 17.14.16+ honours Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Visual Studio > Copilot Settings > Disable Agent Mode.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: outside Agent Host the admin controls are per tool class (on/off or approval-required), with no argument or path scoping; the managed Shell/Read/Edit/Domain selectors reach only VS Code Copilot sessions on Agent Host and do not name MCP tools. Bypass is not fully removable: Agents-window worktree sessions always run with Allow all ("can't be changed"), and the Claude harness has a user setting, github.copilot.chat.claudeAgent.allowDangerouslySkipPermissions, that bypasses every check (Claude3PIntegration=false removes the harness). JetBrains honours only permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode; Xcode and Eclipse have no tool policy.

original.mechanism: VS Code policies ChatToolsAutoApprove, ChatToolsEligibleForAutoApproval, ChatAgentExtensionTools, BrowserChatTools, ChatAgentMode; Visual Studio "Disable Agent Mode"; managed permissions

steps.title: Remove global auto-approval and pick eligible tools
body: Set ChatToolsAutoApprove to false (it "disables manual approval completely for all tools in all workspaces") and use ChatToolsEligibleForAutoApproval to name the tools that may ever skip approval.

steps.title: Cut extension and browser tools
body: ChatAgentExtensionTools=false blocks tools contributed by third-party extensions; BrowserChatTools=false removes the integrated browser tool; ChatAgentMode=false removes agent mode entirely.

steps.title: Disable agent mode in Visual Studio where needed
body: Visual Studio 17.14.16+ honours Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Visual Studio > Copilot Settings > Disable Agent Mode.

original.note: VS Code policies hide tool classes and control auto-approval; managed permissions limit arguments for Agent Host sessions; Visual Studio can only disable agent mode. Other editors have no tool-level policy.

controls.mechanism: VS Code ChatAgentSandboxEnabled with ChatAgentSandboxAllowUnsandboxedCommands and ChatAgentSandboxAllowNetwork (terminal commands; macOS, Linux, WSL2 Preview); Agent Host SDK-shell sandbox (chat.agentHost.sdkSandbox.enabled, Experimental); JetBrains enterprise-managed sandbox (preview); per-server stdio MCP sandbox in mcp.json

steps.title: Require the VS Code terminal sandbox and close its exits
body: Set ChatAgentSandboxEnabled=on, ChatAgentSandboxAllowUnsandboxedCommands=false and ChatAgentSandboxAllowNetwork=false so agent terminal commands run sandboxed and cannot leave the sandbox after a confirmation.

steps.title: Check Agent Host sessions and Windows
body: Copilot sessions on Agent Host use the Copilot SDK built-in shell, whose sandbox is Experimental and enabled by chat.agentHost.sdkSandbox.enabled; Windows uses chat.agent.sandbox.enabledWindows (Experimental). Run /sandbox-policy in a session to see the effective policy.

steps.title: Push the JetBrains sandbox policy from managed settings
body: The JetBrains plugin reads the enterprise-managed sandbox policy (enablement, filesystem and network access, proxy, developer-tool and macOS Keychain access) and locks it under GitHub Copilot > Sandbox — public preview.

steps.title: Sandbox local stdio MCP servers
body: In a server entry set "sandboxEnabled": true with sandbox allowWrite paths and allowedDomains (macOS and Linux); this is a user or workspace mcp.json setting, not a policy.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the sandbox exists but is platform-limited and only partly admin-requirable. VS Code can require it by policy for Local sessions and the Agent Host custom terminal tool on macOS, Linux and WSL2 (Preview), disables the session toggle when a managed setting requires it without a bypass, and does not fall back unsandboxed when its dependencies are missing; the Agent Host's default SDK shell and Windows sandboxes are Experimental, enabled by settings the policy reference does not list. The boundary is terminal commands only: built-in file tools, extension tools, remote MCP servers, the extension host and the Agent Host process run outside it, and chat.agent.sandbox.retryWithAllowNetworkRequests (no policy) lets a user retry a blocked command with open network. Copilot's managed sandbox key is not supported in VS Code, and GitHub's managed-settings reference marks it unsupported in JetBrains too, while the 2026-09-08 changelog announces a JetBrains managed sandbox in preview. Visual Studio, Xcode and Eclipse have no sandbox; a dev container or VM supplies one.

original.mechanism: VS Code ChatAgentSandboxEnabled / AllowNetwork / AllowAutoApprove / AllowUnsandboxedCommands (macOS, Linux, WSL2; preview); JetBrains enterprise-managed sandbox (preview 2026-09-08); per-server MCP sandbox
original.note: Rated partial because the entity spans editors with different support: VS Code (macOS, Linux, WSL2; preview) and JetBrains (preview 2026-09-08) can be required to sandbox, while Visual Studio and the Xcode, Eclipse and Vim plugins have no sandbox at all. Inside the boundary: terminal commands and per-server local MCP; outside: remote MCP servers, the editor's own tools and the model endpoint. The VS Code setting chat.agent.sandbox.retryWithAllowNetworkRequests has no policy, so a sandboxed command can be retried with network unless allowNetwork is also false.

steps.title: Force the VS Code sandbox on and close its exits
body: Set ChatAgentSandboxEnabled=true, ChatAgentSandboxAllowNetwork=false and ChatAgentSandboxAllowUnsandboxedCommands=false; keep ChatAgentSandboxAllowAutoApprove false unless sandboxed commands may run unattended.

steps.title: Sandbox stdio MCP servers
body: In the server entry set sandboxEnabled: true with allowWrite paths and allowedDomains; sandboxed servers can only touch the paths and domains listed.

steps.title: Push the JetBrains sandbox policy from managed settings
body: The JetBrains plugin reads the managed sandbox policy (enablement, filesystem and network access, proxy, dev-tool and Keychain access) under GitHub Copilot > Sandbox — public preview.

controls.mechanism: VS Code terminal sandbox (ChatAgentSandboxEnabled) keeps sensitive home-directory locations away from sandboxed commands by default, with extra denyRead rules in chat.agent.sandbox.fileSystem.mac / .linux; managed Read(...) denies in Agent Host sessions; otherwise the agent holds the developer's credentials

steps.title: Require the sandbox so credential paths stay unreadable
body: Set ChatAgentSandboxEnabled=on and ChatAgentSandboxAllowUnsandboxedCommands=false so terminal commands cannot leave the sandbox after a confirmation.

steps.title: Deny credential directories explicitly
body: Add denyRead entries for the SSH, cloud-CLI and browser-profile directories to chat.agent.sandbox.fileSystem.mac and chat.agent.sandbox.fileSystem.linux; these are user settings with no enterprise policy.

steps.title: Deny credential reads in Agent Host sessions
body: Put Read(~/.ssh/**) and similar selectors under permissions.deny in the managed file; VS Code applies them to Copilot sessions that use Agent Host.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor. VS Code's sandbox makes "sensitive locations in your home directory" unreadable to sandboxed terminal commands by default and can be required by policy on macOS, Linux and WSL2 (Preview), but the path rules are user settings, the Agent Host's default SDK shell sandbox and the Windows sandbox are Experimental, and built-in file tools, MCP servers and extensions sit outside the terminal sandbox. Not documented: whether environment variables, the ssh-agent socket or the git credential helper reach sandboxed commands. Tool calls carry the signed-in user's GitHub authority with no on-behalf-of exchange. JetBrains' managed sandbox (preview) adds Keychain and developer-tool access switches; Visual Studio, Xcode and Eclipse run with the developer's full credential set, where a dev container or VM is the external fix.

original.mechanism: The agent acts with the developer's own GitHub session; org OAuth-app access policy and PAT policies bound what the GitHub MCP server can reach
original.note: There is no on-behalf-of exchange: tool calls carry the signed-in user's authority. The usable boundaries are the organisation's OAuth app access restrictions, fine-grained PAT approval and SSO enforcement on the GitHub MCP server, and the sandbox for local commands.

steps.title: Bound the GitHub MCP server with org access policies
body: Enforce the OAuth app access policy for third-party hosts, require approval of fine-grained PATs and keep SSO enforcement on so tokens must map to a recent SSO login.

controls.mechanism: ChatStrictPluginOnlyCustomization and ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly lock instruction and hook sources; CopilotSessionSync and the "Store local sessions in the Cloud" policy govern session sync; VS Code's local memory tool has no documented policy; Copilot Memory does not apply to IDEs

steps.title: Lock customization sources to managed plugins
body: Set ChatStrictPluginOnlyCustomization=true to block standalone user and workspace skills, agents, hooks, instructions and MCP servers, and ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly=true so hooks come only from managed sources (VS Code 1.132+).

steps.title: Decide whether sessions leave the device
body: Set the CopilotSessionSync policy (chat.sessionSync.enabled) to false to keep session history local.

steps.title: Review and clear local agent memory
body: VS Code's memory tool writes /memories/ (user, auto-loaded into every session up to 200 lines), /memories/repo/ and /memories/session/ locally; use Chat: Show Memory Files and Chat: Clear All Memory Files to inspect and remove them.

steps.title: Confirm Copilot Memory is out of scope for IDEs
body: The supported-surfaces table marks the Copilot Memory policy as not applying to IDEs (it applies to the cloud agent, third-party agents, the CLI and code review).

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: an administrator can lock instruction and hook sources in VS Code (ChatStrictPluginOnlyCustomization, ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly) and keep sessions local, but VS Code's own memory tool writes notes that are loaded into later sessions with no documented policy to disable it and no validation or review of what it stores. Organization instructions and agents are applied only when the developer leaves github.copilot.chat.organizationInstructions.enabled and showOrganizationAndEnterpriseAgents on — user settings, not policy. Repository instruction files are read as trusted context and writable by anyone with push access (the CVE-2025-53773 pattern); nothing version-pins them. Other editors expose no memory or instruction-source control.

original.mechanism: CopilotSessionSync policy (VS Code) and the "Store local sessions in the Cloud" policy; Copilot Memory does not apply to IDEs
original.note: IDE sessions have no persistent agent memory of their own; the exposure is session history synced to github.com and repository custom-instruction files, which the agent reads as trusted context.

steps.title: Decide whether IDE sessions sync to GitHub
body: Set the CopilotSessionSync policy (chat.sessionSync.enabled) to false to keep session history local; at the organisation level the "Store local sessions in the Cloud" policy controls the same sync for Copilot clients.

steps.title: Confirm Memory is out of scope for IDEs
body: The supported-surfaces table lists Copilot Memory as not supported in IDEs, the CLI and the app; the memory policy therefore governs github.com, the cloud agent and code review only.

original.mechanism: Organisation and enterprise custom instructions and custom agents, ChatStrictPluginOnlyCustomization, ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly
original.note: Repository .github instruction files are read as trusted context and are writable by anyone with push access — CVE-2025-53773 exploited exactly that pattern against settings files. The enterprise can force its own instructions but cannot version-pin repository ones.

steps.title: Apply organisation instructions and managed agents
body: Enable github.copilot.chat.organizationInstructions.enabled and showOrganizationAndEnterpriseAgents so organisation-level instructions and custom agents are applied and offered by default.

steps.title: Block user and workspace overrides
body: ChatStrictPluginOnlyCustomization removes standalone user and workspace instructions, agents, skills and hooks; ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly keeps hooks to managed sources.

controls.mechanism: VS Code's secure credential store for MCP server inputs; GitHub PAT policies (maximum lifetime, restrict access); edit approval for secret files (chat.tools.edits.autoApprove); nothing forbids the static keys a developer brings (local BYOK, API keys in MCP env files)

steps.title: Keep MCP secrets out of configuration files
body: Supply MCP API keys as sensitive input parameters rather than literals in mcp.json; VS Code stores sensitive MCP input parameters in its secure credentials store.

steps.title: Cap personal access token lifetime
body: Enterprise > Policies > Personal access tokens: set "Set maximum lifetimes for personal access tokens", require approval of fine-grained tokens, and restrict classic tokens from organization resources.

steps.title: Require approval for edits to secret files
body: Set chat.tools.edits.autoApprove with patterns such as "**/.env": false so those edits need explicit approval (a user setting).

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: MCP inputs sit in an encrypted store and PAT lifetime can be capped, but the editors issue no short-lived credentials to tools, the GitHub sign-in token's lifetime is not documented, and no admin control forbids static keys (local BYOK provider keys, API keys in MCP env files) — the BYOK concept page says local BYOK in IDEs can be disabled by an enterprise or organization policy without naming it. McpEnterpriseManagedAuthIdp (OAuth/OIDC IdP for enterprise-managed MCP authentication) is listed in the VS Code policy reference with a one-line description only. Keeping secrets out of model context relies on content exclusion (not honoured in VS Code Edit or Agent mode) and edit approval; agents read whatever the developer's environment holds.

original.mechanism: chat.tools.edits.autoApprove glob patterns, content exclusion for secret files, GitHub sign-in through the editor's account provider
original.note: No vault integration: agents read whatever the developer's environment holds. The vendor lever is to keep secret files out of context and out of auto-approved edits.

steps.title: Require manual review for edits to secret files
body: Set chat.tools.edits.autoApprove with patterns such as "**/.env": false so those files always need explicit approval.

steps.title: Exclude secret files from context
body: Add **/.env and credential paths to organisation or enterprise content exclusion.

controls.mechanism: managed-settings.json allowedMcpServers / deniedMcpServers (serverName, serverUrl with wildcards, exact serverCommand) with ChatAllowManagedMcpServersOnly; the registry restriction (MCP Registry URL, Registry only; McpGalleryServiceUrl in VS Code) matches names only and is what Visual Studio 2026, Eclipse and Xcode enforce

steps.title: Publish the enterprise MCP allowlist
body: In .github-private copilot/managed-settings.json set allowedMcpServers entries with serverUrl or serverCommand (pin package versions inside serverCommand, e.g. an exact npx package@version) and deniedMcpServers for hard blocks; keep "MCP servers in Copilot" enabled and set "Restrict MCP access to registry servers" to Allow all.

steps.title: Make VS Code ignore user and workspace allowlists
body: Set ChatAllowManagedMcpServersOnly (managed key allowManagedMcpServersOnly, VS Code 1.132+) to true so only the enterprise-managed allowlist can grant access.

steps.title: Treat the registry restriction as discovery
body: "Registry only" enforcement matches server name/ID and "can be bypassed by editing configuration files"; the cloud agent ignores it.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: an allowlist admits servers but pins nothing they serve. Nothing hashes or re-verifies tool definitions: VS Code re-shows its trust dialog when a non-workspace server's configuration changes (workspace servers inherit Workspace Trust even after their configuration changes), not when its tools change. Exact serverCommand matching that includes a pinned package version is version pinning for stdio servers only; remote (serverUrl) servers stay unpinned, and first-party servers such as the built-in GitHub MCP server are exempt from deny rules. The managed allowlist reaches VS Code and JetBrains; Visual Studio, Eclipse and Xcode enforce only the name-matched registry restriction. An MCP gateway supplies definition scanning and pinning.

original.mechanism: managed-settings.json allowedMcpServers / deniedMcpServers (name, URL wildcard, stdio command), ChatAllowManagedMcpServersOnly, McpGalleryServiceUrl registry, Visual Studio 2026 allowlist

steps.title: Publish the enterprise MCP allowlist
body: In .github-private/copilot/managed-settings.json set allowedMcpServers entries with serverName, serverUrl (wildcards allowed) or serverCommand arrays and deniedMcpServers for hard blocks; prerequisite is MCP servers in Copilot enabled and Restrict MCP access to registry servers set to Allow all.

steps.title: Make VS Code ignore user and workspace allowlists
body: Set ChatAllowManagedMcpServersOnly (managed key allowManagedMcpServersOnly) to true and ChatMCP to registry or none; point McpGalleryServiceUrl at a private registry if one exists.

steps.title: Treat the registry restriction as advisory
body: Registry-only enforcement matches on server name/ID and "can be bypassed by editing configuration files"; the cloud agent ignores it. Use it for discovery, not control.

original.note: Admission by identity: allowedMcpServers and deniedMcpServers with ChatAllowManagedMcpServersOnly. Admission is not integrity — nothing pins the tool descriptions a server returns or detects a changed implementation.

controls.mechanism: permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode and permissions.ask in managed settings (ask only in Agent Host Copilot sessions); VS Code ChatToolsAutoApprove, ChatToolsEligibleForAutoApproval, ChatToolsTerminalEnableAutoApprove and ChatAgentSandboxAllowAutoApprove

steps.title: Remove bypass and Autopilot
body: Set permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode to "disable": VS Code turns off chat.tools.global.autoApprove and it cannot be re-enabled; JetBrains honours the same key.

steps.title: Force approval on the operations that matter
body: Put Shell(git push *), Edit(/.github/workflows/**) and similar selectors under permissions.ask; a managed ask needs a fresh approval every time and cannot be satisfied by bypass, auto-approval, hooks or saved grants (Agent Host Copilot sessions).

steps.title: Remove the auto-approval paths in Local sessions
body: Set ChatToolsTerminalEnableAutoApprove=false and name tools under ChatToolsEligibleForAutoApproval so they always prompt.

steps.title: Stop sandboxed commands from auto-approving

summary: The Copilot SDK embeds the agent runtime behind Copilot CLI in a customer-hosted application: the SDK talks JSON-RPC to a Copilot CLI process (bundled, local, or a persistent --headless server) that plans, calls tools, edits files and streams turns. The customer owns request routing, user authentication, session ownership, tool registration, secrets and scaling; GitHub supplies the model access and the permission model the CLI already enforces.

Inference goes to the Copilot API using a GitHub OAuth token, a fine-grained PAT, a server-to-server installation token, or — under BYOK — straight to OpenAI, Azure, Anthropic or a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint, bypassing GitHub entirely. Session state lives on the host under COPILOT_HOME/session-state/{sessionId} (or an application-provided sessionFs); cloud sessions run on GitHub compute and appear in the agents panel.

The controls are code: onPermissionRequest (requests are not approved without it), onPreToolUse allow / deny / ask / modify, mode "empty" with an explicit availableTools list, per-session gitHubToken or a rotating gitHubTokenProvider, sessionLimits, and an OpenTelemetry TelemetryConfig with W3C trace propagation. The SDK's own enterprise-permissions layer — enableManagedSettings (v1.0.7: the runtime self-fetches the enterprise's managed policy with the session's token) and a host-injected managedSettings option (v1.0.13: deny / ask / allow rules, re-supplied on every resume) — composes with device-managed (MDM) policy on the runtime host, but the enterprise managed-settings client matrix does not list the SDK, so server-managed policy reaches an SDK session only when the application opts in.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Any Copilot subscriber including Free; non-Copilot users via BYOK. Sessions bill AI credits to the token's owner; usage is exposed as assistant.usage and session.usage.getMetrics (nano-AI units).

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Copilot API with the session's GitHub token, or BYOK ProviderConfig (type openai / azure / anthropic, baseUrl, apiKey, wireApi) with prompts sent directly to the provider; Azure managed identity can supply bearer tokens instead of keys.

facts.label: Data leaving the host
facts.value: Prompts, tool results and file context to the Copilot API or the BYOK provider; OTLP traces only where configured; cloud sessions publish to github.com/copilot/tasks/{sessionId}; the CLI's telemetry stays on unless COPILOT_OFFLINE=true.

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Session state persists on the host filesystem (or a shared volume) until deleted — there is no idle timeout by default (set sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds or --session-idle-timeout); GitHub-hosted models follow the Copilot ZDR terms (Claude Fable 5 / 5.1 retain by default); BYOK providers apply their own retention.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: Copilot SDK how-tos: setup, authentication, features, hooks, integrations, observability, troubleshooting.

items.title: Multi-user server mode — the isolation checklist
body: Set gitHubToken per session so content exclusion, model routing and quota follow the requesting user; use mode: "empty" and an explicit availableTools list (custom:*, mcp:tool) so ambient OS tools are off; encode tenant and user in session IDs and check ownership before resume or delete; set sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds; use baseDirectory and sessionFs to isolate runtime state. The docs list the pitfalls plainly: default mode copilot-cli exposes the host filesystem, one shared GitHub token loses per-user authorisation, client-provided session IDs cannot be trusted.

Deployment patterns: an isolated CLI per user (strongest; SOC 2 / HIPAA), a shared CLI with per-session isolation, or shared collaborative sessions that need application locking. The backend guide says there is no built-in auth between SDK and CLI; the Node.js README documents a connectionToken shared secret for the runtime link (generated automatically when the SDK spawns a TCP runtime) — set one and still bind --headless to loopback or a private network.

links.title: Copilot SDK for Node.js — README (connection options)

items.title: Hooks as the policy layer
body: onPermissionRequest decides every file write, shell command and URL fetch; without it nothing is approved (the compatibility guide calls this deny-by-default, the Node.js README says requests stay pending until resolved). onPreToolUse returns permissionDecision allow / deny / ask with modifiedArgs, additionalContext and suppressOutput; onPostToolUse can redact secrets and audit; onUserPromptSubmitted / onUserPromptTransformed filter or replace prompts; onSessionStart / End and onErrorOccurred carry sessionId for correlation. All run inline in the turn.

riskNotes.note: The documented anti-pattern is one service token for every user; with it, content exclusion and quotas collapse to the service account's view. Per-session gitHubToken and backend ownership checks on session IDs are the vendor's answer.

The SDK–CLI JSON-RPC link is authenticated only by an optional connectionToken shared secret; a headless CLI bound to 0.0.0.0 without one is an open agent runtime with whatever token it was started with, and anyone holding the secret can drive every session on it.
The only built-in ceiling is a soft per-session AI-credit cap (sessionLimits.maxAiCredits); there is no rate limiting or session cap, so the application must enforce limits and evict idle sessions.
MCP servers and custom tools are registered by the application; nothing verifies them, and the default tool mode inherits the CLI's host tools.

controls.mechanism: Per-session state under COPILOT_HOME/session-state/{sessionId} or a per-session sessionFs provider; baseDirectory per runtime; memory { enabled } and enableSessionStore (both off by default in mode "empty"); "memory" permission requests through onPermissionRequest; sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds and deleteSession

steps.title: Namespace state per tenant and run
body: Encode tenant and user in sessionId, check stored ownership before resumeSession or deleteSession, give each runtime its own baseDirectory (COPILOT_HOME) and route state through a per-session sessionFs provider when it must live in your own store.

steps.title: Keep shared memory out of multi-tenant sessions
body: Start the client in mode "empty", or pass memory: { enabled: false } and enableSessionStore: false on createSession and resumeSession, so neither Copilot Memory nor the cross-session store is read or written.

steps.title: Gate every memory write
body: In onPermissionRequest, inspect requests of kind "memory" (subject, fact, citations) and reject any fact your own validator does not accept.

steps.title: Expire and delete state
body: Set sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds (no default; sessions with running commands or background agents are never idle-cleaned) and call deleteSession when a workflow ends to remove its history, planning state and artifacts from disk.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing, as on the Claude Agent SDK: state is namespaced per session by configuration and can be expired and deleted, but the only write control on memory is the host's own permission handler (an attach point), and nothing validates on read what a step wrote — custom agents and fleet-mode workers share the parent session's state. Enabled, Copilot Memory is repository-scoped and shared by every user with access to that repository; GitHub checks repository facts against their citations before use and deletes entries unused for 28 days, which is vendor-side hygiene, not tenant separation. Enforcing actor: the runtime for storage paths, the application for ownership checks and the memory decision.

original.mechanism: Per-session runtime state under COPILOT_HOME/session-state/{sessionId}, sessionFs to route state into application storage, sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds, application-enforced ownership checks

steps.title: Isolate and expire session state
body: Encode tenant and user in session IDs, verify ownership before resume or delete, set sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds (15–30 minutes for chat) and use baseDirectory / sessionFs to keep state per process or in your own store.

original.note: Isolation and retention are the application's: sessionFs decides where state lives, ownership checks decide who reads it, and idle timeouts bound retention. Nothing validates or restores memory.

body: Configure mcpServers on each customAgents entry with that agent's own credential in headers (remote) or env (local), and list only its tools, so its MCP calls authenticate as a distinct principal.

steps.title: Attribute the application
body: Set clientInfo (applicationName, applicationVersion, integration fields) on the client and GITHUB_COPILOT_INTEGRATION_ID on the runtime process so runtime telemetry and Mission Control requests name your integration.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: credentials can be configured per custom agent for the MCP servers it uses, but every agent and sub-agent in a session shares the session's GitHub identity for model calls and GitHub access, and none is authenticated or revocable as its own principal. agentId and the agent-<id> message source are correlation labels the application derives, not authentication. The runtime's own credential — a GitHub App installation token or a user's OAuth token — authenticates the deployment, not an agent.

original.mechanism: Server-to-server installation access tokens (short-lived) and GITHUB_COPILOT_INTEGRATION_ID stamping requests with the product identity
original.note: The agent's identity is the token's identity; there is no agent-specific credential or registry. Rotate installation tokens and stamp the integration ID for attribution.

steps.title: Stamp the integration identity
body: Set GITHUB_COPILOT_INTEGRATION_ID on the runtime so requests are attributed and routed by product.

controls.mechanism: gitHubTokenProvider (rotating session-scoped GitHub tokens with expiresIn, no fallback to ambient auth); BYOK bearerTokenProvider (e.g. Azure managed identity); GitHub App installation tokens (one hour); MCP OAuth tokens held in memory by default (mcpOAuthTokenStorage); storage in the deployer's secret manager

steps.title: Broker GitHub credentials per session
body: Set gitHubTokenProvider on createSession instead of a static gitHubToken and return { kind: "token", accessToken, expiresIn } from your broker; the runtime calls it for initial and refresh acquisition and rejects the operation rather than falling back to ambient authentication.

steps.title: Replace static provider keys
body: For BYOK set bearerTokenProvider so the runtime asks your identity library for a bearer token before outbound provider requests instead of holding an apiKey.

steps.title: Use short-lived app tokens for services
body: Mint GitHub App installation access tokens with the Copilot Requests permission (they expire after one hour) and restart or reconnect the runtime before expiry instead of a long-lived COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN.

steps.title: Keep secrets in a manager
body: The scaling guide's production checklist names Vault or Kubernetes Secrets for credentials and persistent volumes for session state.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: short-lived credentials are brokered only through callbacks the deployer implements (helper hooks), per session rather than per step, and a secret manager or workload identity supplies them. The runtime process holds whatever it receives and every tool in the session acts with it; a static gitHubToken, apiKey or COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN on a headless server is long-lived. MCP OAuth tokens are discarded at session end unless mcpOAuthTokenStorage is "persistent" (OS keychain, shared across sessions). The repository README's FAQ still says BYOK is key-based only; the BYOK and Azure managed identity guides document bearerTokenProvider — prefer the guides.

original.mechanism: Provider keys via ProviderConfig.apiKey or Azure managed-identity bearer callbacks; platform secret managers recommended; no vault integration in the SDK

steps.title: Prefer managed identity over static keys
body: Use the Azure managed identity setup so the SDK obtains bearer tokens through callbacks instead of storing apiKey values.

steps.title: Keep keys in a secret manager
body: The scaling guide's production checklist names Vault or Kubernetes Secrets for credentials and persistent volumes for session state.

original.note: Storage and issuance are the application's: managed-identity callbacks give ephemeral provider tokens, a static apiKey does not. Whatever the application passes the CLI process is readable by the tools that process runs.

controls.mechanism: Host-injected managedSettings.permissions (deny / ask / allow with Shell(), Read(), Edit(), Domain() selectors; disableBypassPermissionsMode) on session create and resume; enableManagedSettings to self-fetch the enterprise's managed policy; onPreToolUse deny / modifiedArgs; onPermissionRequest

steps.title: Inject the permission rules on every session
body: Pass managedSettings: { permissions: { disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable", deny: [...], ask: [...], allow: [...] } } on createSession and on every resumeSession (omitting it on resume clears the layer); rules use the managed-policy vocabulary such as Shell(git push *) and Read(**), and need Copilot CLI 1.0.79-5 or later.

steps.title: Apply the enterprise's own policy
body: Set enableManagedSettings: true with a per-session gitHubToken so the runtime self-fetches the enterprise's managed policy at bootstrap (session creation fails without the token); approveAll then throws, so ship a real handler.

steps.title: Gate MCP and custom tools in onPreToolUse
body: Return { permissionDecision: "deny", permissionDecisionReason } for disallowed tools or arguments and constrain modifiedArgs; the managed selectors do not name MCP tools.

controls.note: Native by the rule applied to every vendor (Claude Agent SDK deny rules, Copilot CLI managed permissions): a declarative deny / ask / allow engine over shell commands, file paths and network domains, evaluated by the runtime before each call and composed restrictively with server-managed and device-managed (MDM) layers. Boundary: the layer is startup-only and not persisted, so a resume without it drops it; an older runtime may ignore the field (pin the CLI version); MCP and custom tools are reachable only through the pre-tool hook, an attach point whose logic the deployer writes, and tools registered with skipPermission skip the confirmation step. Sub-agent tool calls fire the same hooks (fleet-mode guide). managedSettings and enableManagedSettings are documented in the SDK repository, not on docs.github.com, and the enterprise managed-settings client matrix does not list the SDK.

original.mechanism: onPermissionRequest (deny-by-default) and onPreToolUse returning permissionDecision allow / deny / ask with modifiedArgs; SDK-native enableManagedSettings / managedSettings enterprise-permissions layer added post-GA

steps.title: Implement the permission handler
body: Without an onPermissionRequest handler every file write, shell command and URL fetch is denied; implement it as a policy decision, not approve_all.

steps.title: Gate every tool call in onPreToolUse
body: Return { permissionDecision: "deny", permissionDecisionReason } for disallowed tools or arguments, constrain modifiedArgs (timeouts, allowed directories) and always return an explicit decision.

steps.title: Check whether managed permissions reach your sessions
body: The SDK's own enableManagedSettings flag and managedSettings option on session.create / session.resume are the SDK's enterprise-permissions layer, not the org-wide managed-settings.json feature; the enterprise managed-settings client matrix still does not name the SDK, so wire enableManagedSettings or managedSettings explicitly rather than assuming central policy reaches SDK sessions.

original.note: The hooks are an integration point; the deny-by-default onPermissionRequest is real only when the application implements it. managedSettings brings enterprise permissions into the SDK, but the application must enable it.

controls.mechanism: Per-session gitHubToken / gitHubTokenProvider makes GitHub retrieval and content exclusion run as the requesting user; per-server MCP headers or OAuth for other sources; enableSessionStore and skipEmbeddingRetrieval against cross-session leakage

steps.title: Never retrieve as a shared principal
body: Set gitHubToken or gitHubTokenProvider per session so the runtime resolves the requesting user's identity for content exclusion, model routing and quota; for custom tools pass the user's identity into the tool handler rather than a service credential.

steps.title: Carry the user's grant to MCP data sources
body: Put the requesting user's token in each remote MCP server's headers (or answer the server's OAuth challenge with it) when the session is created, not a service credential.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: identity passthrough is built in only for GitHub sources, when the application passes a per-user token; a shared token makes retrieval service-owned. Every other source gets the user's grant only if the application wires it into the MCP server's headers, OAuth answer or tool handler — a per-call credential attach point. The runtime's cross-session store and shared embedding cache can surface one session's content in another unless disabled (see the retrieval row). Oversharing analysis of the repositories themselves is GitHub's and the data owners'.

original.mechanism: Per-session gitHubToken makes GitHub retrieval and content exclusion run as the requesting user; other data sources are the application's tools

steps.title: Never retrieve as a shared principal
body: Set gitHubToken per session; for custom tools, pass the user's identity into the tool handler rather than a service credential.

original.note: Delegated for GitHub sources when the application passes a per-user token; a shared token makes retrieval service-owned. Every other source is the application's tool, enforcing whatever it enforces.

controls.mechanism: mode "empty" plus availableTools / excludedTools (custom:*, mcp:name, builtin:*); per-agent tools and mcpServers on customAgents and defaultAgent.excludedTools; per-server MCP tools lists; managedSettings.permissions argument and path selectors

steps.title: Start from no tools
body: Set mode: "empty" so CLI defaults and ambient OS tools are disabled, then list availableTools explicitly and use excludedTools for exceptions; avoid builtin:* without review.

steps.title: Narrow every custom agent
body: Give each customAgents entry an explicit tools list and only the mcpServers it needs (tools omitted or null inherits every session tool), and use defaultAgent.excludedTools to keep delegated tools away from the main agent.

steps.title: Scope arguments and paths
body: Put Shell(...), Read(...), Edit(...) and Domain(...) selectors under managedSettings.permissions deny and ask, with disableBypassPermissionsMode "disable".

steps.title: List tools per MCP server
body: Set tools on each mcpServers entry to the named tools the session needs ([] for none) rather than ["*"].

controls.note: Partial on the rule applied to all three SDKs on this drawing (as toolClaudeAgentSdk): each delegation hop should carry a narrower grant, and here a sub-agent narrows only by tool name — allowlists exist per session, per custom agent and per MCP server, but the argument- and path-scoped deny / ask / allow rules are session-wide, not per sub-agent. A custom agent without a tools list inherits every session tool; MCP tools are scoped by name only; nothing is enforced unless the application sets these on each create and resume.

original.mechanism: mode "empty" plus an explicit availableTools allowlist (custom:*, mcp:name, builtin:*); MCP servers chosen per session

steps.title: Start from no tools
body: Set mode: "empty" so CLI defaults and ambient OS tools are disabled, then list availableTools explicitly; avoid builtin:* without review.

original.note: Application integration required: mode empty plus availableTools hides everything not listed, and hooks are the only argument limits. Nothing is enforced unless the application sets these per session.

controls.mechanism: Per-session gitHubToken / gitHubTokenProvider per user; per-server MCP headers or env and per-agent mcpServers; sandboxConfig.auth.git / auth.gh (default false) keeping GitHub credentials out of sandboxed commands; no on-behalf-of exchange

steps.title: Scope GitHub auth to the requesting user
body: Set gitHubToken or gitHubTokenProvider per session; the docs warn that sharing one token across users breaks content exclusion and quota attribution.

steps.title: Scope tool credentials per server and agent
body: Put each MCP server's credential in its own headers or env and attach servers only to the customAgents entries that need them.

steps.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of agent-run commands
body: When enabling the runtime sandbox through session.rpc.options.update({ sandboxConfig }), leave auth.git and auth.gh false (the default) so no Git credential header or GH_TOKEN is injected into sandboxed commands.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: credentials can be scoped per MCP server and, through per-agent mcpServers, per custom agent, but every agent in a session shares its GitHub token and model credential, and without the runtime sandbox (experimental and off by default in the SDK) shell commands inherit the runtime process's environment. Rated below Copilot CLI's native because that rating rests on an admin-required managed sandbox floor that no SDK guide documents for SDK sessions. No on-behalf-of exchange: a sub-agent acts with the parent session's authority, and the per-session token crosses the SDK–runtime link, which is unauthenticated unless a connectionToken is set.

steps.title: Scope GitHub auth to the requesting user
body: Set gitHubToken per session; the docs warn that sharing one token across users breaks content exclusion and quota attribution.

steps.title: Protect the SDK–CLI link
body: There is no built-in auth between SDK and CLI; keep copilot --headless on loopback or inside a private network.

original.note: Rated partial on the same rule as the Claude Agent SDK: a per-session token, per-session BYOK keys and loopback binding are design choices the application makes, not isolation the SDK enforces, and the token the session holds is readable by every tool in it. No on-behalf-of exchange — the token's authority is the session's authority.

controls.mechanism: sessionLimits.maxAiCredits soft per-session AI-credit cap with the exhausted-budget decision (session_limits_exhausted.requested); per-server MCP timeout; sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds for idle sessions only; experimental Node.js Agent Factories limits for factory sub-agents; account.getQuota

steps.title: Set a per-session credit cap
body: Pass sessionLimits: { maxAiCredits } on createSession and resumeSession, and answer session_limits_exhausted.requested with "cancel" unless an operator raises the cap.

steps.title: Time-box tool servers
body: Set timeout (milliseconds) on each mcpServers entry so a hung server cannot hold a turn open.

steps.title: Cap and evict sessions
body: Limit concurrent active sessions per runtime (the guide's pool uses 50), evict the oldest idle ones, set sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds and delete completed sessions.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: the only built-in ceiling on the stable surface is a soft credit budget per session — usage is checked after each model call returns, so one response can overrun it, and at the cap the session asks the host for a decision instead of ending. No turn, iteration or wall-clock limit ships for sessions; idle cleanup never touches a session with running commands or background agents; fleet-mode fan-out has no configured bound, and whether sub-agent spend counts toward the session cap is not stated. The experimental Node.js Agent Factories API declares concurrency, total, time and (soft) credit ceilings for factory sub-agents and their descendants — the only documented child bound, in one language. Account-wide spend is Copilot billing's.

original.mechanism: sessionLimits.maxAiCredits per-session soft cap (SDK 1.0.5+), sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds, 30-minute idle cleanup, recommended concurrent-session cap and eviction, account.getQuota; no account-wide or concurrent-session rate limiting
original.note: maxAiCredits is a soft cap checked after each model call, so one response can exceed it before the next call is blocked; quota beyond that is visible, not enforced, so the application must still cap concurrent sessions and total spend.

steps.title: Set a per-session credit cap
body: Pass sessionLimits: { maxAiCredits } when creating or resuming a session; the SDK forwards it to the CLI, which triggers the exhausted-budget flow when the cap is hit.

steps.title: Cap and evict sessions
body: Limit concurrent active sessions (the guide suggests 50), evict the oldest idle ones, set sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds and delete expired sessions.

steps.title: Watch quota
body: Poll account.getQuota for remaining entitlement and reset dates, and meter assistant.usage per turn.

controls.mechanism: onUserPromptSubmitted (modifiedPrompt, additionalContext) and onUserPromptTransformed on the way in, onPostToolUse modifiedResult on tool results, onPreToolUse deny on the resulting calls; no built-in classifier

steps.title: Screen prompts and tool results in hooks
body: Call your classifier in onUserPromptSubmitted and replace a flagged prompt with modifiedPrompt, and in onPostToolUse replace a flagged tool result with modifiedResult before the model reads it.

steps.title: Deny the calls a flagged turn proposes
body: Return permissionDecision "deny" from onPreToolUse for tool calls that follow flagged content.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: the hooks are attach points that can transform both the initiator's request and returned tool content before it enters context, but nothing is classified until the deployer attaches a detector, and the prompt hook "cannot reject a prompt or enforce policy" on its own — only replace it. Typed message sources (user, system, agent-<id>) let the runtime tell agent input from human authorisation; that is labelling, not screening.

original.mechanism: onUserPromptSubmitted / onUserPromptTransformed hooks to filter or rewrite prompts and onPreToolUse to gate resulting tool calls; no built-in classifier

steps.title: Screen prompts and tool outputs in hooks
body: Filter or annotate prompts in onUserPromptSubmitted, inspect model-facing content in onUserPromptTransformed, and deny suspicious tool calls in onPreToolUse.

original.note: The hooks are an attach point, not a detector: nothing is classified until the application supplies the logic.

controls.mechanism: onPostToolUse modifiedResult and onUserPromptSubmitted modifiedPrompt as redaction attach points; TelemetryConfig captureContent off; per-user token so content exclusion applies; no vendor inspection of the prompt stream

steps.title: Redact in hooks
body: Run your detector in onPostToolUse and return modifiedResult with secrets masked before the model sees them, and replace prompts that carry credentials in onUserPromptSubmitted.

steps.title: Keep content out of traces
body: Leave TelemetryConfig captureContent off in production so exported traces carry no prompts, tool arguments or results.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the hooks can mask a span inline, but the SDK ships no scanner, so content is inspected only where the deployer attaches one; captureContent=false and content exclusion are minimisation, not detection. Model responses and what the runtime journals under session-state are not covered by any hook.

original.mechanism: onPostToolUse redaction, captureContent=false in telemetry, per-user token so content exclusion applies; no inspection of the prompt stream by the vendor

steps.title: Redact in onPostToolUse and keep content out of traces
body: Use onPostToolUse to redact secrets from tool results before they reach the model; leave TelemetryConfig captureContent off in production.

original.note: Redaction in onPostToolUse is code the application writes; the SDK ships no scanner, so content inspection exists only where the application attaches one.

controls.mechanism: Runtime cross-session store (enableSessionStore, on by default in "copilot-cli" mode) and embedding-based retrieval with a shared cache (skipEmbeddingRetrieval, embeddingCacheStorage); no ingest screening or grounding verification

steps.title: Keep retrieval inside the run
body: Use mode "empty" or pass enableSessionStore: false so session content is neither written to nor read from the cross-session store.

steps.title: Stop cross-session leakage through embeddings
body: In multi-tenant deployments set skipEmbeddingRetrieval: true, or embeddingCacheStorage: "in-memory" so the embedding cache is discarded when the session ends.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: the runtime has retrieval of its own — a cross-session store for search across sessions and an embedding cache shared across sessions and restarts unless configured otherwise — and both can be scoped to the run. Nothing screens what enters those stores, trust-tiers sources or checks a response against retrieved content (enableCitations only asks supported models to cite). A corpus behind the application's own tools or MCP servers is that application's control. Both switches are documented only in the SDK repository.

controls.mechanism: permission.requested with requestId, toolCallId and the exact action (fullCommandText, fileName and diff, MCP args, url) answered through onPermissionRequest or the pending-permission RPC; managed ask rules mark requests managedApprovalRequired; onPreToolUse "ask"

steps.title: Route each request to a person
body: Handle permission.requested: show the operator the exact command, diff or arguments and answer that requestId with approve-once or reject; the call waits until it is answered.

steps.title: Make approval mandatory for risky operations
body: Put Shell(...), Edit(...) and Domain(...) selectors under managedSettings.permissions.ask on every create and resume so matching calls always need an explicit decision.

steps.title: Send managed asks to a person
body: In onPermissionRequest, route requests flagged managedApprovalRequired to your confirmation UI instead of approving them automatically; approveAll leaves them pending.

steps.title: Escalate from policy code
body: Return permissionDecision "ask" from onPreToolUse for calls your rules cannot decide.

controls.note: Native by the rule for this drawing, as the Claude Agent SDK's canUseTool: the runtime suspends the call and resumes only on a decision for that requestId, which carries the tool call id and the exact arguments; the deployer supplies the UI and the approver. Boundary: the SDK cannot tell whether a person or code answered — approveAll, setApproveAll, skipPermission tools, approve-for-session / location / permanently scopes and a model-backed handler all satisfy it, and an AI reviewer never counts as human approval; only managed ask rules (managedApprovalRequired, which approveAll refuses) force a fresh decision per call. Without a handler nothing is approved (deny-by-default per the compatibility guide; pending until resolved per the Node.js README); fail closed on timeout in the host.

steps.title: Route privileged actions to a human
body: Return permissionDecision "ask" (interactive) or hold the onPermissionRequest promise until an operator approves for shell, write and network operations.

original.note: The SDK routes the decision to the application; the application must implement an authenticated human approver and fail closed on timeout, so the control is complete only in the deployed application.
