summary: GitHub's own MCP server: tools, resources and prompts over repositories, issues, pull requests, Actions, code security, projects and more, grouped into toolsets. One open-source Go codebase (MIT, v1.12.2 on 2026-09-16) ships as a local stdio binary and container, a self-hosted Streamable HTTP server, and — bound into GitHub's infrastructure from an internal repository — the hosted remote server at https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/, which adds remote-only toolsets (Copilot Spaces, support-docs search, handing work to the Copilot cloud agent).

No model runs in it. Every tool call becomes a GitHub REST or GraphQL call made with the caller's own GitHub credential — OAuth user token, fine-grained or classic PAT, or GitHub App installation token — so the caller can reach nothing it could not reach through the API; results and the tool descriptions land in the consuming agent's model context. The remote server is stateless since the 2026-07 protocol revision and supports GHE.com (data residency); GitHub Enterprise Server is local-only.

Governance sits in GitHub, not in the server: the "MCP servers in Copilot" policy for Copilot hosts, OAuth app and GitHub App approval for third-party hosts, PAT policies for tokens, SAML SSO as an overlay. GitHub states there is no single toggle for all GitHub MCP server traffic and that MCP calls appear in the audit log only as ordinary API calls. Callers choose toolsets, read-only and lockdown mode by header or URL (remote) or flag (local).

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Available to all GitHub users regardless of plan; each tool inherits its feature's licence (cloud agent tools need a paid Copilot licence). Members of Copilot Business or Enterprise organizations need the "MCP servers in Copilot" policy enabled to use it from Copilot.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: None in the server. Tool calls are executed as GitHub API calls with the caller's token against api.github.com (or the --gh-host GHES / ghe.com host); the consuming agent's own model reads the results.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Local: GitHub API traffic from the host to the configured GitHub host only. Remote: MCP requests and results transit api.githubcopilot.com, which reads method and tool headers "for logging and secret scanning"; repository content returned becomes part of the caller's model context at that agent's vendor.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: Not stated for the server on the pages fetched. The remote server keeps no protocol session state since the 2026-07 stateless change (no session database writes or reads); the underlying API activity is in the organization's GitHub audit log.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: github/github-mcp-server README and docs/ (remote server, server configuration, policies and governance, scope filtering, OAuth login, GitHub App auth, Streamable HTTP, host integration); docs.github.com "About Model Context Protocol".

facts.label: Endpoints
facts.value: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ with /readonly, /insiders, /x/all and /x/{toolset} path variants; https://copilot-api.<subdomain>.ghe.com/mcp for GHE.com; GHES "does not support remote MCP server hosting".

facts.label: Releases
facts.value: Tagged releases on GitHub (v1.12.2, 2026-09-16), container ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server signed with cosign, binaries with build-provenance attestations; listed in the MCP registry as io.github.github/github-mcp-server.

facts.label: Secret push protection
facts.value: For public repositories and private repositories covered by GitHub Advanced Security, push protection blocks secrets in AI-generated tool inputs and actions taken through the server.

items.title: Authentication paths and the policy that governs each
body: Remote server: OAuth through the host's registered OAuth App or GitHub App (OAuth app access restrictions, or GitHub App installation), a PAT in the Authorization header (PAT policies), or a GitHub App installation token. The server "does not provide Authentication services" and accepts any valid GitHub access token; dynamic client registration is not supported. SAML SSO applies to OAuth tokens and PATs, not installation tokens.

Local server: OAuth login with the baked-in app on github.com (token in memory only; bring your own app for GHES and ghe.com), GitHub App installation auth (--app-id, --app-installation-id, --app-private-key-path), or GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN, which takes precedence. With Enterprise Managed Users, PAT use is disabled by default unless an enterprise administrator enables it.

links.title: Policies & governance for the GitHub MCP server
Host integration guide (any valid access token; no dynamic client registration)

items.title: Tool exposure — toolsets, tools, read-only, lockdown
body: Remote: X-MCP-Toolsets, X-MCP-Tools, X-MCP-Exclude-Tools, X-MCP-Readonly, X-MCP-Lockdown and X-MCP-Insiders headers, or /x/{toolset}/readonly style URLs. Local: --toolsets, --tools, --exclude-tools, --read-only, --lockdown-mode, --insiders (GITHUB_* environment equivalents). Default toolsets: context, issues, pull_requests, repos, users. Read-only overrides everything; exclude-tools overrides toolsets and tools.

Lockdown mode surfaces public-repository content only from users with push access (github-actions[bot] and copilot always trusted); GitHub calls it "a best-effort content filter, not a security boundary". In HTTP mode the operator's --lockdown-mode is an upper bound the header cannot relax.

links.title: Remote server — toolsets, headers and URL paths

riskNotes.note: Issues, pull requests, comments and commits in public repositories are attacker-writable text the server returns into the caller's context. Invariant Labs (May 2025) showed a public issue steering an agent to copy private-repository data into a public pull request through this server — a token with both public and private reach is the whole exploit. Lockdown mode filters authors without push access but is best-effort by GitHub's own statement.

The remote server's tools change as GitHub redeploys, with no version a consumer can pin; renamed tools resolve silently through deprecation aliases; on a local server anyone who can write github-mcp-server-config.json beside the binary or set GITHUB_MCP_TOOL_*_DESCRIPTION variables rewrites the descriptions the model reads.

The caller's GitHub token is relayed to GitHub's API and any valid GitHub token is accepted, so a token minted for one host app works through the server for every tool its scopes allow; the delegation is the full user's, bounded only by token scope, SSO authorization and organization approvals.

CVE-2026-48529: in self-hosted HTTP mode with lockdown on, the repository-access cache was a process-wide singleton holding the first user's GraphQL client, so later users' access checks ran on that user's credentials (fixed 1.1.2). A multi-user HTTP deployment is exactly where per-caller isolation lives in code.

Quotas are GitHub's per-identity API limits, shared by every app and token acting for the same user, so one looping agent drains the person's budget; CVE-2026-47427 let an unauthenticated malformed completion/complete request crash a self-hosted server (fixed 1.1.0).

The self-hosted `http` command serves plain HTTP and binds every interface unless --listen-host is set, with CORS open to any origin by design; the delete_repository confirmation is carried as client-held state sealed with GITHUB_MCP_SERVER_MRTR_STATE_KEY, which must stay secret and identical across replicas.

Anyone with a PAT can run the local server or point any host at the remote one; GitHub lists "Real-time list of active MCP connections" among governance features not yet available, so long-lived PATs and approved host apps are the grants to inventory.
Classic PATs carry no expiry unless a lifetime policy is set, and revoking an SSO authorization or a fine-grained PAT's organization access leaves the token valid on public and personal resources.

controls.mechanism: Accepts any valid GitHub access token (OAuth App or GitHub App user tokens, fine-grained and classic PATs, GitHub App installation tokens) with no audience binding to the MCP endpoint and relays it to GitHub's API; transmission is scoped by the token itself (fine-grained PAT resource owner and repositories, installation repositories), SAML SSO authorization per organization, and the organization's PAT policies

steps.title: Admit only approved, resource-scoped tokens
body: Enterprise > Policies > Personal access tokens: require administrator approval of fine-grained tokens, restrict Tokens (classic) from organization resources and set maximum lifetimes, so the tokens hosts present to the server are organization-approved and bound to one resource owner.

steps.title: Keep SSO authorization per organization
body: Enforce SAML SSO so every PAT must be authorized for each SSO-protected organization and every OAuth or GitHub App sign-in needs an active SSO session before its token can reach that organization.

steps.title: Name the resource in self-hosted metadata
body: Run `github-mcp-server http --base-url https://mcp.example.com --base-path /mcp` so the Protected Resource Metadata `resource` is this server's canonical URL, and leave --trust-proxy-headers off unless a trusted proxy sets X-Forwarded-Host.

controls.note: Partial by the D3-CTS rule on this drawing (scoped OAuth/PAT without audience binding): the remote server "does not provide Authentication services" and hosts "may also supply any valid access token", so a GitHub token minted for any OAuth App, GitHub App or PAT is accepted and no resource-indicator or audience check is documented; the same token is valid at api.github.com and every other GitHub endpoint. The server forwards the caller's token to GitHub's API — same issuer and resource owner, so not a cross-vendor passthrough, but not a downstream-audience exchange either. What narrows transmission is the token: fine-grained PATs to one resource owner and selected repositories, installation tokens to the installation's repositories, SSO authorization per organization (not for installation tokens). Self-hosted HTTP mode advertises github.com/login/oauth (or --authorization-server) and ignores X-Forwarded-* headers by default, so a client cannot rewrite the metadata that names the authorization server.

controls.mechanism: Inherited GitHub API primary and secondary rate limits per user, OAuth/GitHub App and installation; no MCP-specific per-client or per-tool quota documented for the remote server or settable in the binary; GHES Management Console "Enable HTTP API Rate Limiting" when the local server targets GHES

steps.title: Give unattended callers their own rate budget
body: GitHub allows 5,000 REST requests per hour per user (shared by every PAT and app acting for that user), 15,000 for apps and installations on an Enterprise Cloud organization, and secondary limits of 100 concurrent requests and 80 content-creating requests per minute; run agents on a GitHub App installation so a looping agent exhausts its own budget, not a person's.

steps.title: Set API limits on GitHub Enterprise Server
body: Site admin > Management Console > Rate Limiting: select Enable HTTP API Rate Limiting and set the limits the local server's calls will meet.

controls.note: Partial by the AML.M0004 rule on this drawing (inherited platform API rate limits only): the server is "subject to GitHub API rate limits based on authentication method" and documents nothing of its own. The limits are per identity, not per MCP client, host or tool, and higher-limit apps draw down the same user's budget, so one agent can starve the person's other tools; secondary limits "are subject to change without notice". Remote-side throttling of the MCP endpoint itself is not documented. Per-client and per-tool quotas in front of a self-hosted HTTP deployment are an MCP or API gateway's job.

controls.mechanism: HTTPS to api.githubcopilot.com/mcp; --gh-host / GITHUB_HOST must carry an https:// scheme (non-HTTPS refused except loopback); bearer token on every request; no Origin validation (cross-origin protection deliberately off, CORS *); self-hosted `http` command serves plain HTTP on :8082 on all interfaces unless --listen-host

steps.title: Set the GitHub host with an explicit https:// scheme
body: Set GITHUB_HOST / --gh-host to https://<GHES host> or https://<subdomain>.ghe.com; the README says non-HTTPS hosts are refused, while docs.github.com says an unprefixed host "defaults to http://", so always write the scheme.

steps.title: Bind the HTTP server to loopback or behind a TLS proxy
body: Start `github-mcp-server http --listen-host 127.0.0.1` (empty binds all interfaces) and terminate TLS at a reverse proxy, advertising the HTTPS URL with --base-url.

steps.title: Publish the container's OAuth callback to loopback only
body: Run the container with -p 127.0.0.1:8085:8085 and GITHUB_OAUTH_CALLBACK_PORT=8085, never -p 8085:8085, which would expose the authorization code to the network.

controls.note: Partial by the D3-MAN rule on this drawing (HTTPS without Origin validation): the remote endpoint is HTTPS and each request carries a bearer token GitHub validates, so the sender is authenticated per message; no replay protection beyond token lifetime is documented. The server validates no Origin: the HTTP handler leaves cross-origin protection unset and answers CORS with * on the reasoning that bearer tokens, not cookies, leave nothing ambient for a rebinding page to ride. Local stdio has no listener except the OAuth loopback callback (random port, or a fixed port that must be published to 127.0.0.1). The self-hosted `http` command has no TLS option and binds every interface by default. The GHES scheme conflict between docs.github.com and the README is recorded in the step; current source refuses both scheme-less and http:// hosts.

controls.mechanism: Toolsets, tools, exclude-tools and read-only (GITHUB_TOOLSETS, GITHUB_TOOLS, GITHUB_EXCLUDE_TOOLS, GITHUB_READ_ONLY / flags locally; X-MCP-* headers or /x/{toolset}/readonly URLs remotely); tool list filtered by classic-PAT and --oauth-scopes scopes; per-call OAuth scope challenges (remote; `http --scope-challenge`); every call authorized by GitHub's permission model as the caller

steps.title: Run the server read-only with named toolsets
body: Start the local server with --read-only --toolsets repos,issues (or GITHUB_READ_ONLY=1 and GITHUB_TOOLSETS) and --exclude-tools for anything never wanted; read-only removes write tools even when requested, and exclusions beat toolsets and tools.

steps.title: Point remote clients at a read-only toolset URL
body: Configure hosts with https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/x/{toolset}/readonly, or X-MCP-Toolsets with X-MCP-Readonly: true, instead of the default URL.

steps.title: Narrow the token so the tool list follows it
body: On the local OAuth login set --oauth-scopes (GITHUB_OAUTH_SCOPES), which narrows the grant and hides tools needing other scopes; self-hosted HTTP deployments add --scope-challenge for 403 step-up challenges.

steps.title: Approve the permissions tokens carry
body: Organization Settings > Personal access tokens > Settings: keep "Require administrator approval" for fine-grained tokens and restrict classic tokens, so an owner reviews each token's repositories and permissions before it reaches organization data.

controls.note: Native by the tool-permission rule on this drawing (token-scope filtering plus toolset/read-only configuration): tool exposure is set by toolset, tool and read-only, the list is filtered by the presenting token's scopes, and the remote server answers a call needing more with an OAuth scope challenge whose scope depends on the arguments (workflow only when a workflow file changes; delete_repo never in the default set); GitHub's API then authorizes every call as the caller, outside the model. Boundaries: scope filtering covers classic PATs and local OAuth scopes only — fine-grained PATs, GitHub App and installation tokens list every tool and rely on API errors — and it fails open, showing all tools, if the scope lookup fails; public read tools are always listed. OAuth scopes are coarse (repo is every private repository, read and write), so minimal grants need fine-grained PATs or GitHub Apps. On the remote server toolsets and read-only are headers or URL paths chosen by whoever writes the host's MCP configuration: the consuming organization cannot force them, its enforceable ceiling is the token. Unknown toolset names are silently ignored. Lockdown mode is a content filter, not a permission.

controls.mechanism: Local: tagged releases, cosign-signed container images and build-provenance attestations; tool schemas snapshotted in the repository and diffed on every pull request (MCP Server Diff workflow). Remote: updated continuously from an internal repository with no version pin; deprecation aliases resolve renamed tools silently; descriptions overridable by a local config file or environment variables

steps.title: Pin the local server to a release
body: Run a tagged release binary or ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server at a fixed version, referenced by digest, rather than latest or a build of main, and upgrade deliberately.

steps.title: Verify the image signature before admitting it
body: The publish workflow signs each image digest with cosign (keyless, Sigstore) and the release workflow attaches signed build-provenance attestations to binaries; verify them in the pipeline that admits the server.

steps.title: Lock the description overrides
body: Keep github-mcp-server-config.json beside the binary absent or root-owned and unset GITHUB_MCP_TOOL_*_DESCRIPTION variables, because both replace the tool descriptions the model reads.

controls.note: Partial by the MCP-integrity rule on this drawing (versioned local releases, unannounced remote changes): a pinned, signed local release gives a fixed set of definitions, and GitHub tracks every tool schema in version control (__toolsnaps__) and diffs the tool surface on each change. The remote server is "regularly update[d]" from this code through an internal repository with no version field, deployment log or hash a consumer can pin; insiders mode and feature flags change tools per request; renamed tools resolve silently through deprecation aliases. Descriptions are rewritable by whoever controls the local config file or environment. Hash pinning with alert-on-change stays an MCP-gateway job on the consumer side; Copilot's allowlists and registry admit the server by URL or name only.

controls.mechanism: CodeQL code scanning (Go, JavaScript, Actions) on every push and pull request, lint and end-to-end tests in CI; coordinated disclosure to opensource-security@github.com; repository security advisories with CVEs

steps.title: Track the server's advisories against your version
body: Review github/github-mcp-server Security > Advisories (GHSA-pjp5-fpmr-3349, GHSA-w4q6-qw23-4rg7) against the release each self-hosted deployment runs.

steps.title: Report findings through coordinated disclosure
body: Send vulnerabilities to opensource-security@github.com, not public issues; open-source repositories are outside GitHub's bug bounty scope.

steps.title: Confirm the publisher's code scanning
body: The CodeQL workflow analyses Go, JavaScript and Actions on every push, pull request and manual run of the main repository.

controls.note: Native by the D3-SYSVA rule on this drawing (documented code scanning plus vulnerability disclosure): the handlers — the same code the remote server is built from as a library — are scanned by CodeQL on every change, GitHub runs coordinated disclosure, and two 2026 advisories with GitHub-assigned CVEs were published with affected and patched ranges. Boundaries: the remote server's hosting wrapper lives in an internal repository whose testing is not published; SECURITY.md puts open-source repositories outside the bug bounty and the pages fetched do not say whether api.githubcopilot.com is in scope; no third-party assessment or penetration test of the server is published. A self-hosted deployment's proxy, TLS and key handling are the operator's to assess.

controls.mechanism: Every read and write is a GitHub API call as the presenting principal ("Users and apps cannot use an MCP server to access more resources than they could otherwise access normally via the API"), under repository roles, SAML SSO authorization, OAuth app access restrictions, GitHub App repository selection and fine-grained PAT approval enforced by GitHub server-side; lockdown mode as a best-effort content filter

steps.title: Keep OAuth app access restrictions on
body: Organization Settings > Third-party Access > OAuth app policy: keep restrictions enabled (the default for new organizations) and approve each MCP host's OAuth app individually; unapproved apps get no API access to private organization resources.

steps.title: Install host GitHub Apps on selected repositories
body: Organization Settings > Third-party Access > GitHub Apps > Configure: under Repository access choose Only select repositories and review the permissions granted.

steps.title: Require approval of fine-grained tokens
body: Organization Settings > Personal access tokens > Settings: Require administrator approval, and restrict classic tokens, since classic tokens are never subject to approval.

steps.title: Fix over-broad base permissions before agents surface them
body: Organization Settings > Member privileges > Base permissions: set the lowest level members need; internal repositories stay readable by every enterprise member regardless.

controls.note: Native by the retrieval rule on this drawing: the server holds no data and scopes nothing itself — every read runs with the caller's own GitHub entitlements, and the organization's policies (SSO authorization per organization, OAuth app restrictions, GitHub App repository selection, fine-grained PAT approval) are enforced by GitHub on each call, remote or local. Boundaries: the bound is the caller's whole entitlement, so a token reaching public and private repositories lets an injected agent carry data between them (Invariant Labs, May 2025); lockdown mode hides public content from authors without push access but is "not a security boundary"; privileged OAuth apps bypass OAuth restrictions; SSO does not apply to installation tokens; PATs read public organization resources whatever the policy. GitHub offers no oversharing analysis for what the server can reach, and whether an organization IP allow list sees the user's address or GitHub's for calls through the remote server is not documented.

controls.mechanism: Local: OAuth login token held in memory only; GitHub App private key read from a mounted file (--app-private-key-path; no inline-PEM flag) minting short-lived, auto-refreshed installation tokens; otherwise a PAT in GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN. Remote: stateless, stores no customer credential. The caller's GitHub token is relayed to GitHub's API — no separate per-upstream credential

steps.title: Use OAuth login instead of a PAT on the local server
body: Start `github-mcp-server stdio` with no GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN set, so it runs the PKCE OAuth flow and keeps the token in memory only (bring your own app with --oauth-client-id for GHES and ghe.com).

steps.title: Hold the GitHub App key as a read-only file
body: For unattended use set --app-private-key-path to a read-only mounted PEM (preferred over GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY), restrict access to the server process, and install the app only on the repositories it needs.

steps.title: Cap PAT lifetimes where PATs remain
body: Enterprise > Policies > Personal access tokens: "Set maximum lifetimes for personal access tokens" on both the Fine-grained tokens and Tokens (classic) tabs; GitHub's governance page recommends 90 days at most.

steps.title: Keep the HTTP confirmation key in a secrets manager
body: For self-hosted HTTP set GITHUB_MCP_SERVER_MRTR_STATE_KEY (32 random bytes, Base64) from a secrets manager, identical on every replica; without it delete_repository is not exposed.

controls.note: Partial by the D3-CH rule on this drawing: the pin's shape — one credential per upstream, never the caller's token — does not hold, because the server's only upstream is GitHub (API, uploads, raw and the log-download URLs it returns) and it calls it with the caller's own token; that keeps attribution on the user but is a relay, not an exchange. Custody is well handled on the local OAuth and GitHub App paths (in-memory token, key file off the command line, short-lived installation tokens, the authorization URL kept out of model context by URL elicitation), but the most-documented path is a long-lived PAT in an environment variable or .env file — some hosts need it hard-coded in config — and the baked-in OAuth client secret is public by design (PKCE secures the flow). The remote server stores nothing; token custody is the host's.

controls.mechanism: The server's own outbound calls go only to the configured GitHub host (--gh-host derives the REST, GraphQL, uploads, raw and OAuth endpoints; api.github.com by default) and the job-log download URLs GitHub's API returns; it is a protected resource, not an authorization server, so it fetches no client metadata documents

evidence.title: Streamable HTTP server — protected resource, not the authorization server
Local server OAuth login — endpoints derived from --gh-host
Host integration guide — dynamic client registration not supported

controls.note: Not applicable by the egress rule on this drawing: the server makes no outbound calls beyond GitHub's own endpoints, and its destinations follow from one setting, the GitHub host. There is no discovery-fetch SSRF surface — GitHub's authorization server does the OAuth work and dynamic client registration is not supported. Restricting a self-hosted deployment's network egress to that host is the operator's firewall or egress-proxy job; the remote server's egress is GitHub's. The consuming agent's own egress belongs to that agent's drawing.

controls.mechanism: Calls appear in the GitHub audit log as ordinary API activity attributable to the actor and the OAuth app, GitHub App or token; "Enable API Request Events" streams security-relevant API requests; no MCP tool, parameters or host in customer logs; self-hosted binary --log-file with --enable-command-logging records every request and response locally

steps.title: Stream the audit log
body: Enterprise > Settings > Audit log > Log streaming: configure a destination so API activity from MCP hosts is kept beyond GitHub's own retention.

steps.title: Include API request events
body: Enterprise > Settings > Audit log > Settings > API Requests: select Enable API Request Events (limited to security-relevant endpoints).

steps.title: Log tool calls on a self-hosted server
body: Start the server with --log-file <path> --enable-command-logging to write every MCP request and response to that file, and ship it to the SIEM.

controls.note: Partial by the telemetry rule on this drawing (API request logs without tool-call detail): GitHub states "MCP traffic appears in standard GitHub audit logs as normal API calls" and that granular, action-by-action MCP audit logs, per-tool or per-host dashboards and a list of active connections are not yet available. API request streaming covers only security-relevant endpoints, so most reads leave no customer-visible record. The self-hosted command log (flag help only, not in the docs) captures parameters but is a local file with no tenant or delegation context. The remote server reads MCP headers "for logging and secret scanning" on GitHub's side and exports none of it; Copilot Usage Records Streaming is not documented as covering this server. Capture is not tamper resistance.

controls.mechanism: Revocation that reaches issued tokens: Authentication security > revoke SSO authorizations (per user, per credential type or bulk; Enterprise Managed Users can delete tokens outright); organization Personal access tokens > Active tokens > Revoke; deny a previously approved OAuth app; suspend or uninstall a GitHub App; "MCP servers in Copilot" disabled for Copilot hosts

steps.title: Revoke SSO authorizations or delete credentials
body: Enterprise Settings > Authentication security: revoke SSO authorizations for one member, one credential type (such as classic PATs) or all members; with Enterprise Managed Users, delete keys and tokens outright. Organization owners have the same actions.

steps.title: Revoke a fine-grained token's organization access
body: Organization Settings > Personal access tokens > Active tokens: select the token (filter by owner, repository or permission) and click Revoke.

steps.title: Cut off a host app
body: Suspend or uninstall the host's GitHub App from the organization's installed apps, or deny its previously approved OAuth app in the OAuth app policy.

steps.title: Switch MCP off for Copilot hosts
body: Enterprise > AI controls > MCP: disable "MCP servers in Copilot", which blocks the GitHub MCP server, remote and local, in the Copilot hosts it governs (not third-party hosts).

controls.note: Native by the kill-switch rule on this drawing: revocation reaches tokens already issued — the server is stateless and GitHub authorizes every call, so a revoked SSO authorization, fine-grained PAT, OAuth app approval or GitHub App installation fails the next tool call in every host, remote or local; no time bound is published. Boundaries: GitHub says there is no single toggle for all GitHub MCP server traffic; "MCP servers in Copilot" reaches Copilot hosts only, propagation delay not documented; revoking SSO authorization or a PAT's organization access leaves the token working on public and personal resources, and outside Enterprise Managed Users the token itself is not deleted; bulk actions do not touch GitHub App installation tokens. A call already executing completes, and a local server process runs until its host stops it.

controls.mechanism: Tagged releases; GHSAs with CVEs and affected/patched ranges for the Go module github.com/github/github-mcp-server in the GitHub Advisory Database; weekly Dependabot updates for Go modules (including the MCP go-sdk), the Docker base image and Actions

steps.title: Follow releases and upgrade the pinned version
body: Watch github/github-mcp-server releases (v1.12.2 on 2026-09-16) and move self-hosted deployments to each release that carries a security fix.

steps.title: Match advisories to deployed versions
body: Check each deployment against the Advisory Database entries: CVE-2026-48529 affects 0.22.0 up to 1.1.2, CVE-2026-47427 versions before 1.1.0.

controls.note: Native by the D3-AVE rule on this drawing (releases, advisories and dependency scanning): the self-hosted server has an enumerable patch stream — releases, reviewed GHSAs in the Advisory Database (so Dependabot alerts fire for anything importing the module), and the publisher's own dependencies on weekly Dependabot updates. Boundaries: the remote server is patched by GitHub with no customer-visible version or deployment record; advisories in the MCP go-sdk are that SDK's maintainers' and surface here only as dependency bumps; no SBOM appears on the pages fetched (third-party licence lists do).

controls.mechanism: "MCP servers in Copilot" policy (Enterprise > AI controls > MCP; Copilot hosts only) with the registry restriction and managed-settings allowlists; OAuth app access restrictions and GitHub App installation approval for third-party hosts; PAT approval and classic-token restriction (PATs off by default for Enterprise Managed Users); SAML SSO and, under Enterprise Managed Users with OIDC, the IdP's Conditional Access Policy

steps.title: Decide MCP for Copilot hosts at enterprise level
body: Enterprise > AI controls > MCP: set "MCP servers in Copilot" for the enterprise rather than letting organizations decide; it does not control the GitHub MCP server in third-party hosts.

steps.title: Approve third-party hosts one by one
body: Keep OAuth app access restrictions enabled and approve each host's OAuth app; install host GitHub Apps only where approved, on selected repositories.

steps.title: Gate personal access tokens
body: Organization Settings > Personal access tokens > Settings: Require administrator approval for fine-grained tokens and restrict classic tokens from organization resources.

steps.title: With Enterprise Managed Users, apply the IdP's conditional access
body: Use OIDC SSO so GitHub applies the Entra ID Conditional Access Policy IP conditions to token use, and leave PATs disabled unless needed.

controls.note: Partial by the D3-APA rule on this drawing: GitHub's governance page lists the levers and adds that "GitHub does not provide a single toggle that blocks all GitHub MCP server traffic for every user". Each is enforced server-side, but they decide different things: the MCP policy and the name-matched registry decide whether Copilot hosts may run MCP servers; OAuth app and GitHub App approval decide which host apps reach organization data, for all members rather than per group (privileged OAuth apps bypass); PAT approval decides per token. None expresses "these groups may use this server under these conditions" the way the pin's IdP registry does, and under Enterprise Managed Users GitHub enforces the IdP's IP conditions on token use but MFA only at sign-in. The server itself is open to every GitHub account; the policies govern organization data.

controls.mechanism: GitHub App installation authentication: the local stdio server signs a JWT with the app's private key (--app-id, --app-installation-id, --app-private-key-path / GITHUB_APP_*) and refreshes short-lived installation tokens; the remote server accepts installation tokens ("similar to the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow"); permissions and repositories set per installation and approved by an organization owner

steps.title: Run unattended callers as a GitHub App installation
body: Start `github-mcp-server stdio --app-id <id> --app-installation-id <id> --app-private-key-path /secrets/app.pem` with the key mounted read-only; exactly one of PAT, OAuth or App auth may be set.

steps.title: Limit the installation's reach
body: In the installed app's settings choose Only select repositories and review Permissions, so the workload holds narrower rights than any user.

controls.note: Native by the D3-AA rule on this drawing (GitHub App installation tokens with narrower scopes): an autonomous workload authenticates as its own installation with a key-signed JWT and no user, with permissions and repositories an organization owner approved; installations are listed in organization settings and revoked by suspension or uninstall. Boundaries: installation auth is built into the local stdio server only — the `http` command's clients must bring their own token; SSO enforcement does not apply to installation tokens; the private key "can mint tokens for every repository and permission granted to the installation", so its custody is the operator's; nothing forces agents onto an app rather than a PAT, which GitHub calls "not recommended for production automation".

advisories.title: CVE-2026-48529 — self-hosted HTTP mode with lockdown on ran every user's repository-access checks on the first user's GraphQL client (GitHub-assigned; fixed 1.1.2)
CVE-2026-47427 — nil pointer dereference in the completion/complete handler lets an unauthenticated request crash the server (GitHub-assigned; fixed 1.1.0)
Invariant Labs research (no CVE) — a public-repository issue steers an agent using the GitHub MCP server to leak private-repository data into a public pull request

tools.family: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (Vertex AI Agent Engine)
tools.name: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Agent Runtime (Vertex AI Agent Engine)

variants.name: Agent Runtime (ReasoningEngine resource): our agent code — ADK, LangChain, LangGraph, AG2, LlamaIndex, A2A or any container meeting the runtime contract — with Sessions, Memory Bank and sandboxes
Managed Agents API on Agent Platform (Agents API + Interactions API, Antigravity harness)
variants.note: Pre-GA and not for production or confidential data: a config-only agent (base_agent antigravity-preview-05-2026, global location only) in an isolated Linux sandbox per env_id with network off by default; an interaction's tools and MCP servers replace the agent's for that turn.

summary: Google Cloud's managed agent runtime, renamed on 2026-04-22 from Vertex AI Agent Engine to Agent Runtime on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (the API resource is still ReasoningEngine on aiplatform.googleapis.com). Our own agent code is deployed from source files, a Dockerfile, an Artifact Registry image or a Developer Connect Git link and served as query and streamQuery endpoints: the loop is ours, while the container, scaling (operations up to 7 days), Agent Platform Sessions, Memory Bank, the Code Execution, Shell and Computer Use sandboxes and telemetry are Google's. The Pre-GA Managed Agents API adds a config-only variant on Google's Antigravity harness.

Governance is Google Cloud's own control plane: a SPIFFE agent identity per agent with certificate-bound tokens, IAM allow, deny and Principal Access Boundary policies on it, Agent Registry as the inventory, Agent Gateway as a default-deny enforcement point for IAM Unified Access Policies, Model Armor and Semantic Governance (Preview), an org-policy constraint that pins agents to approved gateways, Model Armor floor settings over Gemini calls, revisions with percentage traffic split (Preview), OpenTelemetry into our project, VPC-SC, a PSC interface and CMEK. Missing: a runtime approval pause, a documented interrupt of a running query, and egress substitution of third-party credentials — the auth manager hands tokens to the agent's own process.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Google Cloud pay-as-you-go: Agent Compute $0.085 per vCPU-hour after 50 free hours a month and Agent Memory $0.009 per GiB-hour after 100 free GiB-hours, one SKU set for all Scale products (Runtime, Sessions, Memory Bank, sandboxes); model tokens are billed separately. The Managed Agents API is Pre-GA.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Whatever the agent's code calls: Gemini and Model Garden models on Agent Platform (locational, jurisdictional multi-region or global endpoints — a global endpoint may process anywhere and gives no residency guarantee) or an external model. Inference is inside Google, not behind our AI gateway; Model Armor floor settings are the tenant-side screen for Gemini calls.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: The agent runs in a Google-managed network in a Google-owned tenant project, so its code, environment variables, session events, memories, sandbox files and telemetry sit with Google; a PSC interface routes its egress into our VPC, and an Agent-to-Anywhere gateway TLS-inspects every outbound call.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: No training or fine-tuning on customer data without permission. Stateful by design: Sessions and Memory Bank keep data until TTL or deletion (see the memory row); for zero data retention, don't use sandbox snapshots, and Gemini calls carry abuse-monitoring prompt logging and 24-hour in-memory caching unless the page's conditions are met.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform (Build, Scale, Govern, Optimize); old Agent Engine URLs redirect to /scale

facts.label: Network requirements
facts.value: Public internet by default; a PSC interface (psc_interface_config with a network attachment on a /28 subnet and DNS peering) routes egress into our VPC; with VPC-SC the perimeter blocks public internet unless our VPC provides a proxy; an Agent Gateway binding sends all egress, platform APIs included, through the gateway.

facts.label: Naming
facts.value: 2026-04-22: Vertex AI became part of Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Agent Engine became Agent Runtime and Agent Builder Sessions became Agent Platform Sessions; SDK 2.0.1 moved vertexai.agent_engines to agentplatform.Client().runtimes.

items.title: Make the gateway a floor, then choose it over revisions
body: A custom org-policy constraint on aiplatform.googleapis.com/ReasoningEngine (CREATE, UPDATE) can require spec.deploymentSpec.agentGatewayConfig.agentToAnywhereConfig.agentGateway to name an approved gateway, and a gateway binding forces identity_type AGENT_IDENTITY. Agent Gateway cannot be attached to agents that use revisions, cannot bind engines created before 2026-04-29, and every agent in a project and region must use the same egress gateway — plan projects around it.

links.title: Route Agent Runtime traffic through Agent Gateway

items.title: Set agent identity at creation and clean up bindings on deletion
body: identity_type AGENT_IDENTITY cannot be patched onto an existing engine. A redeploy creates a new reasoningEngines ID and so a new principal; deleting an agent leaves its IAM bindings as inactive grants. Grant baseline roles to the project principalSet and keep principal:// bindings for sensitive data.

links.title: Use agent identity with Agent Runtime

riskNotes.note: Without agent identity every agent in a project runs as the shared AI Platform Reasoning Engine Service Agent; Unit 42 (2026-03) and XM Cyber (2026-01) showed agent code reading that identity's token from the metadata server to reach buckets, sessions and memories beyond the agent's own.
Deleting an agent leaves every binding to its principal in IAM policies, and a redeployed agent gets a new principal, so delete-and-recreate pipelines leave orphaned grants and silently lose access.
Agent Registry auto-registers Agent Runtime agents only in their own project; agents in other projects need manual registration, and a non-A2A agent registers without endpoint, identity or skills.

Memory Bank writes LLM-extracted memories from conversation events and feeds them into later sessions; the docs name memory poisoning and point to Model Armor, which only screens what passes a gateway or a Gemini call.

Agent Registry does not introspect a manually registered MCP server's tools — tool-level policies match the toolspec.json we upload — and Model Armor passes tools/list unscreened, so a changed tool description is not caught.
The default split, trafficSplitAlwaysLatest, sends all traffic to every new revision the moment it exists; set a manual split before shipping.

CMEK does not cover display names, descriptions, service-account emails, class method names or environment variables, and content capture writes prompts, responses and user.id to Cloud Logging or Cloud Storage.

controls.mechanism: Google Workspace / Cloud Identity 2-Step Verification enforcement (Admin console > Security > Authentication > 2-step verification > Enforcement) on the accounts that can deploy or change agents, gateways, Model Armor floors and IAM; Google Cloud session control reauthentication with a security key; Google Cloud's own 2SV requirement for the console

steps.title: Enforce 2-Step Verification on agent administrators
body: In the Admin console go to Security > Authentication > 2-step verification, select the organizational unit or group holding Agent Platform administrators and deploying identities, check Allow users to turn on 2-Step Verification and set Enforcement to On.

steps.title: Require security-key reauthentication for Google Cloud
body: Admin console > Security > Access and data control > Google Cloud session control: Require reauthentication at 1 to 24 hours with Reauthentication method Security key; it applies to the console and the gcloud CLI.

steps.title: Close the key path
body: Enforce iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation so no one mints long-lived service-account keys that can update a ReasoningEngine without a second factor.

controls.note: Rated native on the MFA rule applied to every vendor (as on toolBedrockAgentcore): Google's own account layer can require a second factor for everyone who can deploy, update or delete an agent or change its IAM, gateway or Model Armor floor. That holds for Google-managed Workspace and Cloud Identity accounts; where the organisation federates to a third-party IdP (SSO or Workforce Identity Federation) the factor is the IdP's, which is partial for that organisation. Google Cloud's own 2SV requirement covers the console only (Cloud Identity accounts from 2026-10-20, federated accounts to be announced); gcloud asks for the factor only once the account has 2SV. Paths around it: service-account keys, federated workload tokens and any CI identity holding aiplatform.reasoningEngines.update. End-user MFA — which of our people a session runs for — is our front end's; Agent Runtime authenticates the calling workload.

controls.mechanism: reasoningEngines list and get (console Deployments page with an Identity column, gcloud ai reasoning-engines describe), runtimeRevisions list, Agent Registry auto-registration of Agent Runtime agents plus registered MCP servers and endpoints; IAM on aiplatform.reasoningEngines.create / update / delete; custom org-policy constraints on aiplatform.googleapis.com/ReasoningEngine for CREATE and UPDATE

steps.title: Inventory from the platform
body: List agents with reasoningEngines.list (console Agent Platform Deployments page) and each agent's revisions with runtimeRevisions.list; put owner and environment in labels at deploy.

steps.title: Register the rest of the estate
body: SDK-deployed Agent Runtime agents register in Agent Registry automatically, same project only; register agents from other projects, MCP servers (with a toolspec.json) and endpoints with gcloud agent-registry services create.

steps.title: Gate who can deploy
body: Grant aiplatform.reasoningEngines.create, update and delete only to the release pipeline's identity — roles/aiplatform.user carries them — so a definition reaches the runtime only through review.

steps.title: Constrain what may be deployed
body: Apply a custom constraint on aiplatform.googleapis.com/ReasoningEngine with method_types CREATE and UPDATE (the documented example requires an approved Agent Gateway) with gcloud org-policies set-custom-constraint and set-policy.

controls.note: Native on the registry rule (as on toolBedrockAgentcore): a listable inventory of agents, revisions and identities, and the tenant gates create and update by IAM and org policy. Not an approval workflow: registration records, it does not approve, and anyone holding roles/aiplatform.user can deploy (XM Cyber's 2026 finding started from aiplatform.reasoningEngines.update). "Unregistered means denied" holds only for egress through an Agent Gateway. Auto-registration is per project, and a non-A2A agent registers without endpoint or skills. In the Managed Agents API an interaction can replace the agent's tools and MCP servers, so a call can run a configuration the registry never saw.

controls.mechanism: runtimeRevisions (an immutable snapshot on every versioned-field change), trafficConfig trafficSplitManual percentages or trafficSplitAlwaysLatest (the default), a per-revision query path; the Evaluation Service and online monitors beside the release (revisions are Preview, v1beta1)

steps.title: Set a manual split before shipping
body: Govern > Deployments > agent > Revisions > Manage traffic > Split mode Manual (trafficConfig trafficSplitManual) so a new revision starts at 0% instead of taking all traffic under Always latest.

steps.title: Evaluate the candidate revision first
body: Query it on runtimeRevisions/REVISION_ID:query, which bypasses the split, with Evaluation Service cases and simulated users, then raise its percentage.

steps.title: Watch and roll back by pointer
body: Run online monitors over the live traces (scored about every 10 minutes) and set the previous revision back to 100% in trafficSplitManual on regression.

controls.note: Partial: versioning, percentage canary and one-step rollback exist (Preview), but the evaluation is not in the promotion path — the Evaluation Service and online monitors score beside the release, nothing holds a split until they pass, and no automated rollback is documented. Rated partial where toolBedrockAgentcore is native because AgentCore's evaluation step sits in its promote flow; here moving traffic is an ordinary update. The default split sends 100% to each new revision, direct revision queries bypass the split, and an agent bound to Agent Gateway cannot use revisions, so an organisation chooses between the gateway's policy and canary releases. IAM grants, gateway policies and Model Armor templates are not versioned with the agent.

controls.mechanism: identity_type AGENT_IDENTITY mints a SPIFFE principal per ReasoningEngine (principal://agents.global.org-ORG_ID.system.id.goog/resources/aiplatform/projects/N/locations/L/reasoningEngines/ID) with an auto-rotated 24-hour X.509 certificate and certificate-bound tokens under a Google-managed Context-Aware Access policy; listed as spec.effectiveIdentity

steps.title: Deploy every agent with its own identity
body: Set identity_type AGENT_IDENTITY in client.runtimes.create (".agent_engine_config.json" for adk deploy, agents-cli deploy --agent-identity, identity_type in google_vertex_ai_reasoning_engine); it cannot be patched onto an existing engine.

steps.title: Grant, deny and bound per principal
body: Bind roles to the agent's principal:// identifier, baseline roles to the project principalSet, and cap it with an IAM deny policy or a Principal Access Boundary (gcloud iam principal-access-boundary-policies bindings create).

steps.title: Inventory the identities
body: Read spec.effectiveIdentity (gcloud ai reasoning-engines describe ID --format "value(spec.effectiveIdentity)") or the Identity column on Deployments, and leave GOOGLE_API_PREVENT_AGENT_TOKEN_SHARING_FOR_GCP_SERVICES at its default so tokens stay bound.

controls.note: Native on the architecture rule: the platform mints, inventories and lets us revoke a principal per agent, separate from users and from the project's service accounts — the layer the pin says to select for. It is opt-in: without identity_type an agent runs as the shared AI Platform Reasoning Engine Service Agent (service-N@gcp-sa-aiplatform-re) or a custom service account, and manage-agent-access still labels agent identity Preview (a gateway binding forces it). Revocation is IAM's: deleting an agent leaves its bindings, and a redeploy gets a new principal. The identity authenticates to Google APIs and through Agent Gateway; a third-party tool sees whatever credential the auth manager issued. The Managed Agents API documents no per-agent principal.

controls.mechanism: Agent Identity auth manager auth providers (3-legged OAuth per end user, 2-legged OAuth, API key) in a Google-managed vault, each gated by IAM on the agent's SPIFFE ID (roles/agentidentity.user on the provider), retrieved by the agent and attached by ADK; certificate-bound Google Cloud tokens (mTLS, DPoP beyond the gateway); Secret Manager references in env_vars

steps.title: Keep third-party credentials in auth providers
body: Create them with gcloud agent-identity auth-providers create (--three-legged-oauth-* for user-delegated access) and grant only this agent's principal roles/agentidentity.user on the provider.

steps.title: Keep Google API tokens bound to the agent
body: Leave the default Context-Aware Access policy on — do not set GOOGLE_API_PREVENT_AGENT_TOKEN_SHARING_FOR_GCP_SERVICES to False — so a token used outside the agent's runtime fails with 401.

controls.note: Partial on the vault rule applied to every vendor (toolBedrockAgentcore is native only on its gateway, which injects outside the agent): scoping is real — per end user (3LO), per agent (IAM on each provider) and, for Google APIs, bound to the agent's certificate — but the auth manager returns the credential to the agent's own process, where ADK sets the header; it is not substituted at egress. Decrypt-at-the-gateway is documented only for Gemini Enterprise connectors behind Agent Gateway. Secret Manager references in env_vars become environment variables of every instance, shared by all its sessions. Model-generated code runs in sandboxes with no ambient credentials; the agent's own function tools run beside the credential.

controls.mechanism: Agent Gateway in Agent-to-Anywhere mode (governedAccessPath AGENT_TO_ANYWHERE) enforcing IAM Unified Access Policies through IAP — default deny, allow and deny rules in CEL over the agent principal, MCP server, tool name and annotations, endpoint host, path and method, iamEnforcementMode DRY_RUN or ENFORCE — plus custom authorization extensions and Semantic Governance (Preview); custom constraint custom.allowlistedEgressAgentGatewaysForAgentEngine; Model Armor floor settings

steps.title: Create an egress gateway that authorises through IAP
body: Console Agent Gateway page > create in Agent-to-Anywhere mode with Access Authorization set to IAP; test with iamEnforcementMode DRY_RUN (denials logged to Cloud Audit Logs), then remove it to enforce.

steps.title: Write per-tool allow and deny rules
body: gcloud iam access-policies create with rules on destination.agent_registry.mcp_server.tool.name and tool.annotations.read_only_hint or destructive_hint, bound with gcloud iam policy-bindings create after turning off constraints/iam.managed.disableAccessPolicyBindings; deny overrides allow.

steps.title: Make the gateway binding mandatory
body: Enforce a custom constraint on aiplatform.googleapis.com/ReasoningEngine requiring agentToAnywhereConfig.agentGateway in an approved list (gcloud org-policies set-policy; up to 15 minutes to take effect).

steps.title: Set the Model Armor floor
body: gcloud model-armor floorsettings update --add-integrated-services=VERTEX_AI and --vertex-ai-enforcement-type=INSPECT_AND_BLOCK on the project; set template-conformance floors at the organisation or folder with the API.

controls.note: Native on the architecture rule: a declarative per-call policy evaluated by the provider at its tool gateway, default-deny, plus tenant floors — the org-policy gateway binding and Model Armor floor settings — that a builder without IAM admin on the gateway project cannot lower. CEL sees principal, destination, MCP method, tool name and annotations, not arguments: argument rules need a custom authorization extension (our service) or Semantic Governance, which is an LLM verdict in Preview, and there is no escalate-to-human outcome. The gateway sees network calls only; on Agent Runtime every tool is our code, so work done inside the agent's process, in sandboxes or by Google-side tools is outside it, and a result our application executes returns unevaluated. Unavailable to engines created before 2026-04-29 and to agents using revisions.

controls.mechanism: Memory Bank scope dictionaries isolating memories per identity; IAM Conditions on aiplatform.googleapis.com/memoryScope and aiplatform.googleapis.com/sessionUserId; memoryViewer / memoryEditor roles and the agent's default agentContextEditor; ttl_config (default_ttl, granular_ttl); memory revisions with rollback and disable_memory_revisions; DeleteMemory; Sessions ttl / expire_time

steps.title: Scope memories and restrict who reads them
body: Generate and retrieve with a per-user scope such as {"user_id": ...} and grant memory roles with a condition on api.getAttribute('aiplatform.googleapis.com/memoryScope', {}); sessions take the same condition on sessionUserId.

steps.title: Make memories expire
body: Set ttl_config.default_ttl (or granular_ttl create_ttl, generate_created_ttl, generate_updated_ttl) on the Memory Bank — without it memories never expire — and a ttl on each session (default 365 days).

steps.title: Audit and roll back
body: Keep revisions on (memory_revision_default_ttl 365 days), list them to see what was extracted, and call client.memory_banks.memories.rollback or delete on poisoned memories.

controls.note: Native on the memory rule: scope, write permission, expiry, rollback and deletion are all settable. Isolation holds only if our application derives scope and user ID from the authenticated user — both are request fields — and the default agentContextEditor role reaches all of that agent's own sessions and memories. Contents are not validated: memories are LLM-extracted and consolidated into later turns, and the docs put memory poisoning on Model Armor, which sees only what a gateway or template routes to it. Sessions and Memory Bank write no Cloud Logging entries of their own; global endpoints may process generation out of region.

controls.mechanism: The organisation's TPRM platform, consuming Google Cloud's compliance reports (Compliance Reports Manager), the services-in-scope and HIPAA covered-products lists, and the Agent Platform ZDR and Access Transparency pages

evidence.title: Google Cloud services in scope by compliance program (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: ISO 27001/27017/27018, SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, penetration testing; last modified 2026-07-16)
HIPAA covered products (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Model Armor listed)
Agent Platform and zero data retention
Access Transparency for Agent Platform (Agent Engine listed)
Google Cloud compliance resource center

controls.note: External: the assessment is the organisation's TPRM process; Google publishes the evidence. The platform is in scope for ISO 27001/27017/27018, SOC 1/2/3 and PCI DSS and on the HIPAA covered-products list, but Agent Runtime, Sessions and Memory Bank are not broken out, so confirm component scope in the reports and the BAA. Access Transparency covers Agent Engine. Pre-GA pieces — the Managed Agents API (no confidential data), revisions, Semantic Governance, agent identity — sit under Pre-GA terms. Re-assess on the platform's cadence: the April 2026 rename moved features between products and SDKs.

controls.mechanism: Agent Runtime containers per deployed agent (min_instances, max_instances, container_concurrency default 9) in a Google-managed network; Agent Platform sandboxes the agent's code creates — Code Execution (no network, state up to 14 days), Shell, Computer Use and custom containers (7 days) — each isolated by container sandboxing; Managed Agents API sandbox per env_id

steps.title: Run generated code in a sandbox, not the runtime
body: Create a Code Execution sandbox (client.sandboxes.create) for model-written code: limited file system, no network, no libraries beyond the preinstalled set.

steps.title: Tie sandbox lifetime to the session
body: Create one sandbox per session with config.ttl and delete it when the session ends (client.sandboxes.delete), pausing idle ones rather than sharing them.

steps.title: Separate trust boundaries by agent and project
body: One instance serves up to container_concurrency sessions at once, so deploy untrusted workloads as separate agents and projects rather than relying on the container between sessions.

controls.note: Partial on the isolation rule (a per-session sandbox, reclaimed after): the sandbox boundary is documented — each isolated from other sandboxes and the host, no ambient credentials — but per-session binding is our code's choice, sandboxes persist 7 to 14 days and can be shared, and the agent's loop and function tools run in runtime containers serving several sessions at once. Rated partial where toolBedrockAgentcore, a microVM per session around the loop, is native. installation_scripts run as root at build. Managed Agents API: one sandbox per env_id, shared by any interaction or agent passing the same env_id, 7-day TTL.

controls.mechanism: Agent Gateway Agent-to-Anywhere binding (agent_gateway_config.agent_to_anywhere_config) routing all agent egress, platform APIs included, through default-deny IAP access policies over registered endpoints or host/path rules; alternatively VPC-SC with PSC interface egress into our VPC; Code Execution without network; Managed Agents API base_environment.network.allowlist (off by default)

steps.title: Bind every agent to an egress gateway
body: Set agent_gateway_config.agent_to_anywhere_config.agent_gateway with identity_type AGENT_IDENTITY at creation (Terraform deployment_spec.agent_gateway_config), after allowlisting the Google API hostnames the agent uses, regional and mTLS variants included, or while policies are DRY_RUN.

steps.title: Allow only named destinations
body: Register endpoints in Agent Registry and grant iap.resources.egressViaIAP per agent principal; avoid base URIs, which admit a whole domain.

steps.title: Or close the perimeter
body: Put aiplatform.googleapis.com in a VPC-SC perimeter and give the agent a psc_interface_config network attachment, so any internet path is our proxy and Cloud NAT.

steps.title: Managed Agents API
body: Leave base_environment.network unset (no network) or list exact domains in network.allowlist; a domain of "*" is unrestricted.

controls.note: Native on the architecture rule: an exact-host (and path) allowlist enforced by Google around the runtime, default-deny, logged, and mandatory by org policy. It covers every outbound call from a bound agent. Not seen: Google-side tools such as Search grounding and url_context, sandboxes (governed by their own template's PSC interface or VPC-SC), and unbound agents — engines created before 2026-04-29 and agents using revisions. Without a gateway or VPC-SC an agent has public internet access. Pages disagree: manage-agent-access says VPC-SC is unsupported with Agent Gateway; the 2026-09-09 release note supports it for gateways created after 2026-09-08 with an ALL_TRAFFIC connectivity template — test before relying on both.

controls.mechanism: IAM Unified Access Policies at Agent Gateway by agent principal, MCP server, tool name and annotations, and endpoint host, path and method; IAM roles, deny policies and Principal Access Boundary on the agent identity for Google Cloud resources; the agent's tool list in its own code

steps.title: Scope tools per agent at the gateway
body: Allow rules naming destination.agent_registry.mcp_server.tool.name for each tool the agent may call (or tool.annotations.read_only_hint == true) and deny rules for destructive tools.

steps.title: Scope Google Cloud resources by the agent's principal
body: Grant roles on specific resources to the principal:// identifier and cap it with a Principal Access Boundary policy.

steps.title: Register MCP servers with their tool specs
body: Upload a toolspec.json when registering a server so tool-level rules have names to match.

controls.note: Native on the permissions rule (as on toolBedrockAgentcore): per-tool enablement and per-principal permission by operation and resource, enforced outside the model at the gateway and in IAM. Arguments are not in the policy language. The policies live in the gateway project and IAM, not in the agent's code, so the next revision cannot widen them — though a redeployed agent gets a new principal and loses per-principal grants. Tools that never leave the agent's process are bounded only by IAM; registration pins nothing a server serves. In the Managed Agents API an interaction's tools list replaces the agent's for that turn.

controls.mechanism: Agent Identity auth manager vault (API keys, OAuth client secrets, user tokens; IAM per auth provider); Secret Manager references for env_vars; auto-rotated 24-hour agent certificates with bound tokens and no service-account keys; iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation; CMEK through encryption_spec; no vendor tunnel — private reach is a PSC interface network attachment

steps.title: Keep tool secrets in the auth manager
body: Register API keys and OAuth clients as auth providers (gcloud agent-identity auth-providers create) and grant use per agent principal, rather than putting values in env_vars.

steps.title: Reference Secret Manager for anything the code reads
body: Pass env_vars as {"secret": SECRET_ID, "version": VERSION} (same project only) and grant secretmanager.versions.access to the Agent Platform Service Agent, which fetches them at deployment.

steps.title: Run on short-lived credentials
body: Use agent identity — 24-hour certificates, bound tokens, no long-lived keys — and enforce iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation for the pipeline and callers.

controls.note: Partial on the vault rule applied to every vendor (as on toolBedrockAgentcore): custody and lifetime are strong — a Google-managed vault gated per agent principal, 24-hour certificates, bound tokens — but the vault is not write-only: retrieveCredentials returns the value to the agent's process, and Secret Manager values become environment variables of every instance, which CMEK does not cover. Tunnel story: Google offers no outbound-only tunnel; a private MCP server is reached through a PSC interface network attachment in our VPC, which carries no token or TLS key to rotate — the control is who may change the attachment. Our application's own credential for the API is ours to federate.

controls.mechanism: No runtime approval pause. ADK tool confirmation (FunctionTool require_confirmation, request_confirmation, an adk_request_confirmation call answered with the same function_call_id) is experimental and not supported with VertexAiSessionService; an Agent Gateway custom authorization extension can hold a call

steps.title: Build the approval into the agent
body: Wrap consequential tools with require_confirmation so the run pauses on adk_request_confirmation and our front end answers with a FunctionResponse carrying the same function_call_id — on a session service that supports it, which Agent Platform Sessions (VertexAiSessionService) does not.

steps.title: Or hold the call at the gateway
body: Import a custom authorization extension (gcloud service-extensions authz-extensions import) whose service refuses a consequential tool call until our approval service has recorded a person's decision.

controls.note: Partial on the approval rule (as on toolBedrockAgentcore and toolOpenaiAgentsApi): the runtime has no approval primitive, so approval is our code on an attach point. ADK's confirmation binds to the exact call but is experimental and unsupported with the managed Sessions Agent Runtime pairs with, so on the managed stack the gate is our own logic or a gateway extension. Semantic Governance is an LLM verdict and Model Armor a classifier — neither is human approval. The Managed Agents API documents no approval step.

controls.mechanism: Model Armor templates on Agent Gateway — egress: MCP tools/call and prompts/get responses and tool execution errors, A2A v1 SendMessage, OpenAI-compatible LLM payloads; ingress: ADK streamQuery — with prompt-injection and jailbreak, malicious-URI and Sensitive Data Protection filters under INSPECT_AND_BLOCK; floor settings over Gemini generateContent (integrated service VERTEX_AI)

steps.title: Turn Model Armor on at the egress gateway
body: Create templates with pi_and_jailbreak_filter_settings ENABLED and enforcement_type INSPECT_AND_BLOCK, switch on Enable Model Armor on the Agent-to-Anywhere gateway, and grant the Service Extensions service agent roles/modelarmor.calloutUser and roles/modelarmor.user.

steps.title: Screen every Gemini call in the project
body: Floor settings with --add-integrated-services=VERTEX_AI and --vertex-ai-enforcement-type INSPECT_AND_BLOCK apply even when a generateContent call omits modelArmorConfig.

controls.note: Native on the guardrail rule (unlike toolBedrockAgentcore, whose documented output checks omit injection): returned tool content is classified at the gateway with a block and a logged verdict. Inspected: MCP tools/call responses and tool errors, A2A v1 SendMessage, OpenAI-compatible completions. Passed unscreened: tools/list, resources/*, notifications, MCP and A2A streaming (SSE), pre-v1 A2A, plain REST responses to function tools, and anything from an agent without a gateway. The floor covers Gemini generateContent only (not file uploads) and fails open when Model Armor is unreachable or errors; ingress screening covers ADK streamQuery only.

controls.mechanism: OpenTelemetry traces (GOOGLE_CLOUD_AGENT_ENGINE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY, OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN, OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT) to Cloud Trace with prompts and responses in Cloud Logging or Cloud Storage in our project; reasoning_engine_stdout / stderr logs; Agent Gateway telemetry; Cloud Audit Logs for sessions and memories; Log Router sinks

steps.title: Turn telemetry and content capture on
body: Set the three env_vars at deploy, or Deployments > Telemetry configuration > Configure: Enable instrumentation of OpenTelemetry traces and logs, and Enable logging of prompt inputs and response outputs.

steps.title: Enable Data Access audit logs
body: Turn on Data Access logs for aiplatform.googleapis.com: sessions.create, sessionEvents.append, memories.retrieve and related calls are DATA_READ / DATA_WRITE and off by default.

steps.title: Ship it off-platform
body: A Log Router sink to Pub/Sub, BigQuery or a Cloud Storage bucket in a separate project keeps a copy the agent's project cannot alter.

controls.note: Native on the tracing rule: spans for model calls and tool executions, grouped by session, land in our own project and can be exported. Instrumentation is opt-in and emitted by the agent's own framework, so a custom or compromised agent's trace is only as complete as its code; gateway telemetry and audit logs are the independent record. Prompts, responses and user.id are captured only with content capture on; Sessions, Memory Bank and Code Execution write no Cloud Logging entries of their own; Model Armor trace spans are Pre-GA. Not tamper-evident in the project: route to another one.

controls.mechanism: reasoningEngines.delete with force=true (console Deployments > Delete agent), removing the agent with its sessions and memories; IAM deny policy or binding removal on the agent's principal; deny rules in the gateway access policy; removing aiplatform.reasoningEngines.query from callers; sandbox delete

steps.title: Cut the agent off
body: Add an IAM deny policy naming the agent's principal (or a deny rule in the gateway's access policy), then remove its allow bindings and revoke callers' aiplatform.reasoningEngines.query.

steps.title: Decommission
body: client.runtimes.delete(name=..., force=True) or DELETE .../reasoningEngines/ID removes the agent and its child sessions and memories; then delete its sandboxes and the now-inactive IAM bindings.

controls.note: Partial on the kill-switch rule (toolBedrockAgentcore is native on StopRuntimeSession): disable and revoke are documented, but no operation interrupts a running query — Agent Runtime supports operations up to 7 days — and whether delete ends in-flight streams is not documented; IAM propagation time is not stated (delay not documented). Deleting the agent leaves its principal's bindings in place, and nothing cancels work handed to A2A subagents. Managed Agents API: DELETE the agent resource; its environment lasts 7 days after the last interaction.

advisories.title: Unit 42 "Double Agents": code in a deployed Agent Engine agent read the Reasoning Engine service agent's credentials from the metadata server and reached consumer buckets and Google-owned Artifact Registry images (no CVE; Google updated its docs and recommends a custom service account)

XM Cyber: a user with aiplatform.reasoningEngines.update deploys a tool that reads the Reasoning Engine service agent token from metadata, reaching memories, sessions, storage and logging (no CVE; Google: working as intended)
