tools.name: MLflow Tracking Server and Model Registry

variants.name: MLflow Tracking Server with Model Registry (`mlflow server`)
variants.note: One process serves the UI, the tracking and registry REST APIs and, by default, proxied artifact access (--serve-artifacts with --artifacts-destination). Metadata goes to --backend-store-uri (SQLite mlflow.db by default, PostgreSQL or MySQL in production); users and grants to a separate auth database. Listens on 127.0.0.1:5000 unless started with --host.

variants.name: MLflow Python client (mlflow, MlflowClient) in the training job and the promotion pipeline
variants.note: The library the job uses to log runs, datasets and models (MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI, MLFLOW_TRACKING_USERNAME / MLFLOW_TRACKING_PASSWORD or MLFLOW_TRACKING_AUTH), and the promoter uses to copy versions and move aliases. Everything it records is what the calling code chose to log.

summary: Open-source (Apache-2.0) experiment tracking server and Model Registry, self-hosted by the organisation; current release 3.16.1 (2026-09-16). It is the registry-and-promotion tier of this drawing: the training job logs runs, input datasets and the candidate model to it, the registry holds numbered versions of each registered model with aliases (champion), tags, descriptions, signatures and the link back to the run, and consumers load `models:/<name>@<alias>`. Model stages (Staging/Production/Archived) are deprecated since 2.9.0 in favour of aliases and tags.

Nothing is trained or served here: inference runs wherever the model is loaded. Metadata stays in the operator's database and artifact bytes in the operator's object store; what leaves is anonymised usage telemetry to mlflow-telemetry.io (on by default since 3.2.0), webhook POSTs the operator configures, and, for PEFT adapters, a base-model download from the Hugging Face hub at load time.

Every control is a server flag, environment variable or basic_auth.ini key the operator sets. Authentication is off by default (`--app-name basic-auth` turns it on), the shipped default_permission is READ for every authenticated user, and there is no approval workflow, signing or audit log in open-source MLflow; creating a model version, moving an alias and transitioning a stage all need the same EDIT grant on the registered model.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Free and open source (Apache-2.0) on PyPI as mlflow (3.16.1, 2026-09-16) and mlflow-skinny. Managed MLflow is sold by Amazon SageMaker AI (MLflow Apps and Tracking Servers, MLflow 3.10 on Apps) and Databricks; those are out of scope here.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: None in this role. Clients call the REST API at MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI; models registered here are loaded and run by whatever consumes them (`mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/<name>@<alias>")`, a serving tier).

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Self-hosted: run metadata to the backend store and artifacts to the artifact store the operator configures. Anonymised usage telemetry (SDK and Python versions, event names, flavors; no parameters, models or usernames) goes to mlflow-telemetry.io by default since 3.2.0; MLFLOW_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true or DO_NOT_TRACK=true on the server disables UI telemetry globally. Webhooks POST registry events to HTTPS endpoints the operator lists.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: The vendor receives no training data or models. Deleted runs keep metadata and artifacts until `mlflow gc` removes them; deleting a registered model or model version is irrevocable for the registry entry, but the run's artifacts are not removed with it.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: mlflow.org/docs/latest (machine-readable index at /docs/latest/llms.txt; every page has a .md variant)

facts.label: Network defaults
facts.value: Binds 127.0.0.1:5000. Since 3.5.0 the uvicorn server's security middleware validates Host (--allowed-hosts / MLFLOW_SERVER_ALLOWED_HOSTS, default localhost and private IPs) and CORS origins (--cors-allowed-origins, default localhost:*) and sets X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN; it does not run under --gunicorn-opts or --waitress-opts. TLS is left to a reverse proxy.

facts.label: Authentication
facts.value: Built-in basic-auth app (username and password, 12-character minimum, no default admin password since the GHSA-gq3w-7jj3-x7gr fix); role-based grants from 3.13.0 (per-resource legacy APIs removed). SSO through the third-party mlflow-oidc-auth plugin or a reverse proxy; custom schemes through authorization_function.

facts.label: Security reporting
facts.value: SECURITY.md: GitHub private vulnerability reporting only; reports through bounty platforms such as huntr are no longer accepted. Only the latest version is supported; backports are at the maintainers' option.

items.title: Baseline for a self-hosted registry server
body: Run 3.15.0 or later (3.16.1 current): 35 GitHub advisories were published for mlflow in 2025–26, nine critical, several of them authentication bypasses on servers with basic-auth enabled.

Start with `--app-name basic-auth`, MLFLOW_FLASK_SERVER_SECRET_KEY set to a stable secret, the admin password from MLFLOW_AUTH_ADMIN_PASSWORD, and a basic_auth.ini (MLFLOW_AUTH_CONFIG_PATH) with default_permission = NO_PERMISSIONS and database_uri on the central database.
Expose it only as `--host 0.0.0.0 --allowed-hosts <fqdn> --cors-allowed-origins <origin>` behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy; never set --disable-security-middleware.

Keep artifact access proxied (--artifacts-destination, no --default-artifact-root) so the storage credential lives only on the server, set MLFLOW_CREATE_MODEL_VERSION_SOURCE_VALIDATION_REGEX to the proxied prefix, set MLFLOW_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true, and leave server job execution (MLFLOW_SERVER_ENABLE_JOB_EXECUTION) off unless it is needed.
On every process that loads registered models set MLFLOW_ALLOW_PICKLE_DESERIALIZATION=false and log scikit-learn and LightGBM models with serialization_format="skops".

links.title: MLflow Tracking Server — Secure Tracking Server, Model Version Source Validation
MLflow — Authentication with username and password

riskNotes.note: Anyone holding EDIT on a registered model can create a version in it, and any authenticated user can create a new registered model and becomes its MANAGE owner, so which adapters are admitted is decided by which registered model consumers load from. A PEFT adapter is logged with source_model_name and source_model_revision (the Hugging Face repo and commit) and the base weights are downloaded on the fly at load; nothing in the registry checks that the base is an approved one.

Many flavors save with pickle or cloudpickle and MLFLOW_ALLOW_PICKLE_DESERIALIZATION defaults to true, so loading a registered model can execute code. The statsmodels flavor ignored the switch until 3.15.0 (GHSA-gqvg-gmmx-x4hm), and CVE-2025-15379 injected shell commands from a model's python_env.yaml when it was served with env_manager=LOCAL (fixed 3.8.1).

The registry server has its own steady CVE stream: 35 GitHub Advisory Database entries published 2025–26, nine critical — a hard-coded default admin password (CVE-2026-2635), unauthenticated directory-traversal RCE in the artifact handler (CVE-2026-2033), FastAPI routes left outside basic-auth (CVE-2026-2652, CVE-2026-0545) and a full-read SSRF through webhook redirects (CVE-2026-64849).

With proxied artifact access the server holds one storage credential that is "an assumed role of access to all artifacts", so anyone who reaches the server with a grant — or the bucket with that credential — reads every candidate; the shipped default_permission is READ. Before 3.11.0rc1 the multipart-upload endpoints skipped per-resource checks entirely (CVE-2026-2651), and S3 presigned download URLs (3.15.0+) work for whoever holds them until they expire.

Evaluation datasets and results are ordinary runs and datasets in an experiment; anyone with EDIT on that experiment can log metrics to it or replace its datasets, so benchmark custody depends on keeping the evaluation experiment out of the trainers' grants.

A model version records a source URI, not a signature; any caller with EDIT can register a version from any source unless MLFLOW_CREATE_MODEL_VERSION_SOURCE_VALIDATION_REGEX restricts it (bypassed with a prompt tag before 3.10.0, CVE-2026-2614), and a PEFT version pulls its base from the hub by commit at every load.

controls.mechanism: Not applicable — MLflow records which dataset a run read (source, digest, schema, profile) but screens and filters nothing; sanitisation belongs to the curation stage

evidence.title: MLflow Dataset Tracking (mlflow.data — source, digest, schema, profile; no screening)
MLflow documentation index (no dataset screening or filtering feature)

controls.note: Not applicable: the objective belongs to the curation & filtering stage — the quality, safety and sensitive-content filter jobs between the content origins and the versioned corpus — which the data platform runs, not the registry. A dataset profile (row and element counts, column statistics) describes a dataset; it detects no poisoned, mislabelled or restricted example, and neither the tracking server nor the registry refuses a run or a version whose inputs were never screened. What MLflow can add downstream is the record: the curation job logs its screened output with mlflow.log_input so runs cite that version (AML.M0025).

controls.mechanism: mlflow.data Dataset objects (source, digest, schema, profile) attached to runs with mlflow.log_input(dataset, context="training" | "validation" | "evaluation"), stored by the tracking server and shown per run; a MetaDataset records source and schema for data MLflow does not hold

steps.title: Log every input dataset on the run
body: In the training job build each input with mlflow.data.from_pandas / from_huggingface / from_spark (or MetaDataset for a remote corpus) and call mlflow.log_input(dataset, context="training"), repeating for "validation" and "evaluation", so the run records the dataset's source, digest, schema and profile.

steps.title: Point the source at an immutable version
body: Pass source= as a versioned address — an object version, a Delta table version, a Hugging Face revision — because mlflow.data.get_source() and a reload read whatever that address serves later.

steps.title: Log the curation output the same way
body: Have the curation job create its own run and log_input the assembled corpus version with context="training", so the corpus version, its source and its digest exist before any training run cites them.

controls.note: Native on this drawing's rule (dataset tracking records source and digest per run). Boundary: dataset-level and per run, written by the job's own client — the server stores what the job reports and requires nothing, so a run with no logged inputs is accepted and can still be registered. Per-example source and licence at ingest (the pin's curation-stage record) stays with the curation pipeline; MLflow holds a pointer and a fingerprint. The digest is identification, not integrity: for pandas and numpy data it is a truncated MD5 over the first 10,000 rows plus shape and column names, and a MetaDataset's covers only name, source and schema (mlflow/data source); CVE-2026-10803 (predictable collisions from deterministic sampling) is fixed in 3.10.1. Cryptographic integrity of the corpus and its modification history belong to the data store's versioning.

controls.mechanism: basic-auth app (`mlflow server --app-name basic-auth`) with role grants (3.13.0+) of READ / USE / EDIT / MANAGE / NO_PERMISSIONS per experiment and registered model, enforced by the server on REST calls and on proxied artifact reads; default_permission in basic_auth.ini sets the floor

steps.title: Turn authentication on
body: Start the server with `--app-name basic-auth`, MLFLOW_FLASK_SERVER_SECRET_KEY set, the admin password in MLFLOW_AUTH_ADMIN_PASSWORD, and database_uri in the file named by MLFLOW_AUTH_CONFIG_PATH pointing at a central database.

steps.title: Deny by default
body: Set default_permission = NO_PERMISSIONS in that basic_auth.ini; the shipped value READ lets every authenticated user read every experiment, run artifact and registered model.

steps.title: Grant reads per experiment and model
body: In /admin → Roles (or AuthServiceClient create_role, add_role_permission, assign_role) grant READ on the specific experiment and registered model to the people and services that need the candidates, never a (experiment, *, READ) wildcard.

steps.title: Keep artifact bytes behind the server
body: Run with --artifacts-destination and proxied access (the default --serve-artifacts, no --default-artifact-root) and give the storage credential only to the server, so every artifact read passes the per-experiment check.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule: server-enforced read scoping per experiment and registered model exists but is off by default, and neither pin sits wholly inside MLflow. Candidate store: with proxied access the basic-auth app checks the experiment id in each /mlflow-artifacts path (list, download, upload, delete, multipart) and model-version artifact downloads against the caller's grant (mlflow/server/auth source); but the server's storage credential is "an assumed role of access to all artifacts", so anyone reaching the bucket directly, or holding an S3 presigned URL (3.15.0+, MLFLOW_PRESIGNED_DOWNLOAD_URL_TTL_SECONDS, default 300), bypasses it, and with --no-serve-artifacts the storage IAM is the only control. Reads are not logged per user (no audit log; AML.M0024), so the "logged" half is the storage access log or a proxy (external). Corpus: MLflow holds dataset metadata, not the corpus, so who may read it is cloud IAM on the corpus store. Identity is MLflow's own user store (or the mlflow-oidc-auth plugin or a reverse proxy) and is not carried through to storage. Authorization gaps fixed recently: CVE-2026-2651 (multipart upload, 3.11.0rc1), CVE-2026-2734 (model-version enumeration, 3.10.0), CVE-2026-8147 (trace endpoints, 3.13.0).

controls.mechanism: A model-file scanner and a scanning package mirror (artifact repository / package firewall) in front of the job; MLflow analyses no file. MLflow's integration points: MLFLOW_CREATE_MODEL_VERSION_SOURCE_VALIDATION_REGEX, the model_version.created webhook, and MLFLOW_ALLOW_PICKLE_DESERIALIZATION=false at loaders

evidence.title: MLflow Tracking Server — Model Version Source Validation (regex on the source URI)
MLflow Webhooks — model_version.created (experimental, SQL backend only)
MLflow — Pickle-free models (MLFLOW_ALLOW_PICKLE_DESERIALIZATION, default true)

controls.note: External: the pin is format and content inspection gating admission of base checkpoints and dependencies to the private mirror, and MLflow is neither the mirror nor a scanner. Integration points: have the scanner write cleared artifacts to one prefix and set MLFLOW_CREATE_MODEL_VERSION_SOURCE_VALIDATION_REGEX on the server so the registry refuses versions sourced elsewhere (a regex on the URI, not a check of the bytes; CVE-2026-2614 bypassed it with a prompt tag before 3.10.0); the model_version.created webhook can start a scan, but it fires after registration and asynchronously, so it can only tag or delete. At load time MLFLOW_ALLOW_PICKLE_DESERIALIZATION=false refuses pickle and cloudpickle models (default true; ignored by the statsmodels flavor before 3.15.0) — a loader format policy, not file analysis. A PEFT version downloads its base weights from the Hugging Face hub at load unless that host is reachable only through the mirror.

controls.mechanism: Separate registered models per environment (dev.<team>.<model>, prod.<team>.<model>) with role grants, so the run's user can create versions only in the candidate model and a different promoter user copies and aliases in the release model; no approval step, and within one registered model creating a version, setting an alias and transitioning a stage all require the same can_update (EDIT)

steps.title: Split candidate and release registered models
body: In /admin → Roles grant the training job's user EDIT on its experiment and on dev.<team>.<model> only, and a promoter group EDIT on prod.<team>.<model>; keep MANAGE on the release model with the registry owners.

steps.title: Promote by copy, as the promoter
body: The promoter runs client.copy_model_version(src_model_uri="models:/dev.<team>.<model>@candidate", dst_name="prod.<team>.<model>") and then set_registered_model_alias on the release model; the copy needs READ on the source and EDIT on the destination.

steps.title: Notify on every release alias
body: Create a webhook for model_version_alias.created and model_version.created with a secret (HMAC X-MLflow-Signature) pointed at the change-management or CI endpoint that records who promoted what.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule: MLflow separates credentials by resource, not by action. On one registered model "Create Model Version", "Set Registered Model Alias" and "Transition Model Version Stage" all require can_update, so a job and its promoter are separated only when release lives in a registered model the job has no grant on — the per-environment pattern the workflow page documents. Whoever holds EDIT on the release model then promotes alone: no second approver, no approval record bound to the version and its evaluation, and nothing stops that user being a CI service account rather than a person. Webhooks fire after the alias is set (asynchronous, retried), so they notify, not gate; admins bypass every grant; any authenticated user can create a new registered model, so consumers must load only from the named release model. The approval itself needs a gate around the promoter credential (a CI job with required reviewers, a change ticket). Managed variant: SageMaker AI IAM separates sagemaker-mlflow:CreateModelVersion from SetRegisteredModelAlias, scoped to the whole tracking server, still without an approval step.

controls.mechanism: OpenSSF Model Signing (`model_signing sign`, sigstore/model-transparency) run by the promotion pipeline under an identity the job never holds, with the signature bundle stored outside the job's reach and referenced from the release version's tags; MLflow signs and verifies nothing

evidence.title: MLflow model format — MLmodel fields (flavors, run_id, signature, input_example; no signature of the artifact)
sigstore/model-transparency — model_signing sign / verify (Sigstore keyless, private key, certificate, PKCS#11)
OpenSSF Model Signing

controls.note: External: open-source MLflow has no artifact signing, no signature field on a model version and no verification when `models:/` URIs are loaded (docs index; the MLmodel "signature" is the input/output schema, not a cryptographic signature). Integration point: after copy_model_version to the release model, the promotion pipeline downloads the version's artifacts, runs `model_signing sign <dir>` with a Sigstore identity, key or PKCS#11 token the training job never holds, stores the bundle (model.sig) where the job cannot write, and records its location and digest with set_model_version_tag. The serving tier must run `model_signing verify` before loading, since MLflow's loaders will not. For a PEFT version the signature covers the adapter only; the base weights fetched by source_model_revision need their own pinning.

controls.mechanism: mlflow.models.evaluate and mlflow.genai.evaluate (built-in and custom scorers, plugin evaluators such as Giskard) logging results to a run, and mlflow.validate_evaluation_results(..., validation_thresholds=...) raising ModelValidationFailedException in the deployer's pipeline; the server never blocks promotion on results

steps.title: Evaluate the candidate in a protected experiment
body: Run mlflow.models.evaluate(model=..., data=..., model_type=...) — or mlflow.genai.evaluate(data=..., predict_fn=..., scorers=[Safety(), Correctness(), Guidelines(...)]) for a tuned LLM — logging to an evaluation experiment on which the trainers hold no EDIT grant.

steps.title: Fail the pipeline on thresholds
body: Call mlflow.validate_evaluation_results(candidate_result=..., baseline_result=..., validation_thresholds={"<metric>": MetricThreshold(threshold=..., greater_is_better=True)}) and run the promotion step only when no ModelValidationFailedException is raised.

steps.title: Add safety judges for tuned LLMs
body: Pass the predefined LLM judges (Safety, Guidelines, Correctness, RetrievalGroundedness) as scorers to mlflow.genai.evaluate; they need a judge model configured.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule: the harness and a threshold check ship, but the check runs in the deployer's pipeline and the registry accepts an alias on a version with no evaluation or a failed one — native would need the server to block promotion on results. Backdoor probing (trigger-phrase hunting) and memorisation or extraction testing are not built-in evaluators; they are custom metrics or scorers, or a plugin, the deployer supplies. The GenAI judges are models grading a model. Benchmark custody depends on RBAC: anyone with EDIT on the evaluation experiment can log metrics or swap its datasets. Validation moved out of mlflow.models.evaluate into validate_evaluation_results in 2.18.0.

controls.mechanism: Storage-side encryption with organisation-held keys (cloud KMS, bucket default encryption) under the artifact store and the backend database; MLflow only passes MLFLOW_S3_UPLOAD_EXTRA_ARGS (for example ServerSideEncryption aws:kms with SSEKMSKeyId) through to S3 uploads

evidence.title: MLflow Artifact Stores — Passing extra arguments to S3 upload (MLFLOW_S3_UPLOAD_EXTRA_ARGS), bucket ownership verification
MLflow Tracking Server — Authentication and Encryption (TLS via reverse proxy)

controls.note: External: MLflow does not encrypt artifacts or metadata at rest and holds no keys. It passes MLFLOW_S3_UPLOAD_EXTRA_ARGS='{"ServerSideEncryption": "aws:kms", "SSEKMSKeyId": "<key>"}' to S3 uploads made by the process that sets it — the server with proxied access, every client without — so enforce it with the bucket's default encryption and a bucket policy that denies other keys; MLFLOW_S3_EXPECTED_BUCKET_OWNER guards against a recreated bucket. Checkpoints the job writes outside MLflow and the backend database (PostgreSQL or MySQL) are encrypted by their own stores. In transit the server speaks plain HTTP and the docs put TLS at a reverse proxy or VPN. Key custody, rotation and revocation are the KMS's.

controls.mechanism: Model version records (run_id, source, logged-model id) plus the run's parameters, tags and input datasets and the MLmodel file (flavors, signature, input_example, mlflow_version, time_created, run_id, with requirements.txt, python_env.yaml and conda.yaml; source_model_name and source_model_revision for transformers and PEFT models), written automatically when the job logs and registers the model

steps.title: Log and register from inside the run
body: Log the candidate with mlflow.<flavor>.log_model(..., registered_model_name="dev.<team>.<model>") in the same run that called log_input, so the version links to the run, its datasets and the MLmodel file.

steps.title: Record the base model for adapters
body: Log PEFT adapters with mlflow.transformers.log_model so MLmodel carries source_model_name and source_model_revision (the Hugging Face repository and commit hash) of the base.

steps.title: Accept versions only from tracked artifacts
body: Set MLFLOW_CREATE_MODEL_VERSION_SOURCE_VALIDATION_REGEX="^mlflow-artifacts:/.*$" on the server so a version cannot be registered from a path outside the tracked artifact store.

steps.title: Walk lineage in both directions
body: From a version read run_id and the run's dataset inputs; from a suspect run set find every version with client.search_model_versions("run_id IN ('<id>', ...)").

controls.note: Native on this drawing's rule (versions linked to runs, datasets, signatures and source). Boundary: this is MLflow's own lineage graph, not an exportable AI BOM — no CycloneDX or SPDX output. Everything in it is what the job's client logged and nothing is signed (AML.M0013): the run's user comes from the client (MLFLOW_TRACKING_USERNAME or the OS user), not the authenticated caller. A signature is optional in open source (only Unity Catalog requires one); datasets hang off the run, not the version; the base of a full fine-tune is recorded only if the job logs it (the transformers flavor records it); and a version can be registered from a model saved outside MLflow unless the source regex forbids it.

controls.mechanism: Run records (parameters, metrics, tags, input datasets, start and end time, client-supplied user) and model version records (creation time, run_id, source) in the backend store; no audit log of user actions in open source — request-level records come from a reverse proxy in front

steps.title: Record the run completely
body: In the job call mlflow.autolog() or log parameters, metrics, the code version tag and every input dataset explicitly, so each run answers which data, which base and which code.

steps.title: Keep the backend store central and durable
body: Start the server with --backend-store-uri on a managed PostgreSQL or MySQL database (not the default SQLite mlflow.db) with its own backup and access logging.

steps.title: Keep deleted runs until reviewed
body: Deleted runs stay restorable until `mlflow gc` purges them; restrict run deletion (can_delete needs MANAGE) and who may run mlflow gc against the backend store.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule (native only with an audit log of user actions): open-source MLflow documents none — not on the basic-auth, RBAC or tracking-server pages, though the last says proxying makes access "easier to secure and audit". "Who ran what" is self-reported: the run's user is sent by the client (MLFLOW_TRACKING_USERNAME or the OS user), not stamped from the authenticated caller; reads, downloads, alias moves and permission changes leave no record beyond the entity's current state; admins and MANAGE holders can delete runs and versions, and the records sit in a database the operator can edit — telemetry is not tamper-resistance. An authenticating reverse proxy's access log shipped to the SIEM supplies the action log (external). Managed variant: SageMaker AI MLflow Tracking Servers log data-plane calls (Mlflow* event names) to CloudTrail with the IAM identity; MLflow Apps log them as CallMlflowApp data events, off by default and without request bodies.

controls.mechanism: Registered-model and model-version descriptions (Markdown), tags (validation_status and the like), aliases, the MLmodel signature and input example, and run lineage per version; no approval state enforced on promotion and no model-card generation

steps.title: Describe the model and each version
body: Set descriptions with client.update_registered_model(name, description=...) and client.update_model_version(name, version, description=...), or edit them in the registry UI.

steps.title: Log a signature and input example with every model
body: Pass signature= or input_example= to mlflow.<flavor>.log_model so MLmodel records the input and output schema that travels in the artifact directory.

steps.title: Record approval state as a version tag
body: Set client.set_model_version_tag(name, version, "validation_status", "approved") from the evaluation pipeline — a label the promoter's pipeline must check, not a gate the server enforces.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule (documentation without a gate). The capability's gate — a version without a current card and an approval record is not eligible for promotion — is not in open-source MLflow: set_registered_model_alias accepts any version whatever its tags, description or signature, and a signature is optional (only Unity Catalog requires it). There is no model-card generator. The MLmodel file travels inside the artifact; descriptions, tags and approval labels live in the registry database and do not follow the bytes when they are copied elsewhere. The gate is the promoter pipeline refusing to call set_registered_model_alias without the tag and a current description; a model_version_alias.created webhook can flag a release that skipped it, after the fact.

controls.mechanism: Not applicable — deny-by-default egress from the training job is the compute platform's network policy; the tracking server is one destination on that allowlist

evidence.title: MLflow Tracking Server — proxied versus direct artifact access (what the job must reach)
MLflow Webhooks — URL validation and SSRF protection (the server's own egress)

controls.note: Not applicable: the pin bounds the training job and is absorbed by the compute platform (the drawing's recorded deviation). MLflow's contribution is shaping the allowlist: with proxied artifact access (the default) the job needs only the tracking server's URL, and with --no-serve-artifacts it also needs the bucket. The server's own outbound traffic — webhooks (HTTPS only, private addresses refused unless MLFLOW_WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS=true; redirect bypass fixed in 3.15.0, CVE-2026-64849) and telemetry to mlflow-telemetry.io (MLFLOW_DISABLE_TELEMETRY) — belongs to the egress policy of wherever the server runs.

controls.mechanism: A dedicated MLflow user per training job (basic-auth, MLFLOW_TRACKING_USERNAME and MLFLOW_TRACKING_PASSWORD in the job) whose role grants reach only its experiment and candidate model; or MLFLOW_TRACKING_AUTH=kubernetes sending the pod's service-account token to a proxy or authorization_function that verifies it

steps.title: Create a user for the job identity
body: Create the job's user in /admin → Users or with POST 2.0/mlflow/users/create, and hand its password to the job as MLFLOW_TRACKING_USERNAME / MLFLOW_TRACKING_PASSWORD from the secret store.

steps.title: Keep it away from the release model
body: Assign that user a role holding only (experiment, <id>, EDIT) and EDIT on the candidate registered model, with no grant on the release model the promoter uses.

steps.title: Use the pod's workload identity instead of a password
body: Set MLFLOW_TRACKING_AUTH=kubernetes in the job so each request carries the pod's service-account token, with the server behind kube-rbac-proxy or a custom authorization_function that validates it.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule: MLflow can hold separate users for run logging and promotion and enforces their grants, but its own identity is a username and static password (12-character minimum; no token issuance or expiry documented), shared by every run of the job unless rotated per run. The Kubernetes provider only attaches the service-account token on the client — validating it (kube-rbac-proxy, a custom authorization_function, the mlflow-oidc-auth plugin) happens outside MLflow. Scoping the run to the dataset version an approved spec names is cloud IAM on the corpus store (external): MLflow does not mediate corpus reads. Admin users bypass every grant. Managed variant: SageMaker AI authenticates callers with IAM roles.

controls.mechanism: Registry withdrawal: set_registered_model_alias back to the last good version, delete_registered_model_alias, or delete_model_version (transition_model_version_stage to Archived is deprecated); consumers resolving models:/<name>@<alias> or models:/<name>/<version> get the replacement or an error on their next load

steps.title: Roll the release alias back
body: Point the alias at the last known-good version with client.set_registered_model_alias("prod.<team>.<model>", "champion", <version>) (needs EDIT on the release model).

steps.title: Withdraw the version outright
body: Remove it with client.delete_registered_model_alias(...) and client.delete_model_version(name, version) — both need MANAGE, and deletion is irrevocable for the registry entry.

steps.title: Find every version a bad run produced
body: List them with client.search_model_versions("run_id IN ('<id>', ...)") before withdrawing, so a poisoned dataset's runs map to every release that came from them.

steps.title: Tell the serving tier to reload
body: Subscribe the deployment system to model_version_alias.deleted and model_version_alias.created webhooks so it restarts or reloads the consumers that resolved the old version.

controls.note: Native on this drawing's rule (the registry's stage transition is the stop, at load time), with the boundary stated: the withdrawal takes effect on each consumer's next resolution of the alias or version, and already-loaded copies keep serving until the serving tier reloads — `mlflow models serve` resolves the URI once at start, and no delay is documented. MLflow pushes nothing but the asynchronous, experimental webhook. Consumers loading by runs:/ or models:/<model_id> URI, a storage path or a cached copy are untouched, because deleting a version removes the registry entry, not the artifacts. "Fails load-time verification everywhere" additionally needs signatures checked by the serving tier (AML.M0013); MLflow verifies nothing and revokes no consumer credentials.

controls.mechanism: Not applicable — RL and agentic rollouts execute model output inside the training job's environment, contained by the compute platform; MLflow runs none of it

evidence.title: MLflow documentation index (tracking, registry and evaluation; no rollout execution)
MLflow — Pickle-free models (the loader-side execution risk, rated under other drawings)

controls.note: Not applicable: the pin bounds the training job's rollouts and is absorbed by the compute platform's execution environment (the drawing's recorded deviation). MLflow's own code-execution surfaces — loading pickle-based flavors, building a serving environment from a model's python_env.yaml (CVE-2025-15379) and the server's optional job execution (MLFLOW_SERVER_ENABLE_JOB_EXECUTION, CVE-2026-0545) — sit with the loaders and the server host, recorded in this entry's risk notes and items, not with this pin.

tools.name: Hermes Agent
summary: An open-source (MIT) personal agent runtime (v0.21.5, 2026-09-24) — a competing product to OpenClaw, not a variant of it, with a one-command migration from it (hermes claw migrate). Its posture centres on per-command approval with dangerous-command detection, DM pairing, fully isolated per-profile state, and sandboxed execution across multiple terminal backends.

The operator model is the single trusted user: whoever runs Hermes is its administrator, so every control below is a key in ~/.hermes/config.yaml or ~/.hermes/.env, a CLI command or an approval policy that user sets — the optional /etc/hermes managed scope only pins values against a non-root user and is advisory against the agent itself.

items.title: Approval-first execution and isolated state
body: Execution goes through command approval with dangerous-command detection — blocked actions return a tool error naming the denied command rather than silently proceeding — and an unknown DM gets a one-time pairing code the owner approves from the CLI (the FAQ still words this as the first DM claiming access). Profiles are fully isolated (own memory store, session database and skills directory), subagents run isolated, and sandboxed execution spans local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Daytona and Vercel Sandbox backends with container hardening and namespace isolation.

The governance trade-off to weigh: Hermes is a self-improving agent that writes its own skills from experience, which is also the feature demanding the most trust — an organisation sanctioning it should decide whether self-modification is acceptable and pin the approval policy accordingly.

links.title: Hermes Agent FAQ (approvals, pairing, profile isolation)
NousResearch/hermes-agent README (seven terminal backends, isolated subagents, migration)

controls.mechanism: Pattern scanners block flagged context files (AGENTS.md, .cursorrules, a profile-distributed SOUL.md), memory entries and hub, URL and project skills, and inbound A2A text is filtered and framed as untrusted; the transform_tool_result and pre_gateway_dispatch plugin hooks are the attach points for tool results and inbound channel messages

steps.title: Keep context-file scanning on and treat its blocks as findings
body: The built-in scanner drops an AGENTS.md, .cursorrules or profile-distributed SOUL.md that carries ignore-prior-instructions text, hidden HTML comments, secret reads, curl exfiltration or invisible Unicode with a '[BLOCKED: ... potential prompt injection]' banner; your own SOUL.md loads with a warning in /context instead, so review any hit you did not write.

steps.title: Screen tool results with a transform_tool_result plugin
body: Register a transform_tool_result callback in a plugin listed under plugins.enabled; it receives tool_name, args and the model-bound result after every call, and the first string it returns replaces the result, so your classifier can quarantine a poisoned web_extract, browser or MCP result before the model reads it.

steps.title: Screen inbound channel messages with pre_gateway_dispatch
body: A pre_gateway_dispatch plugin callback sees every incoming non-internal message before authorization, pairing and dispatch and can return skip or rewrite, which is where an injection classifier for Telegram, Discord, Slack or email traffic plugs in.

controls.note: Partial by the input-screening rule: the shipped scanners are pattern heuristics (the security page calls them "heuristics, not semantic intent detection") on context files, memory writes and skills, and A2A input is labelled untrusted rather than classified. Nothing screens messaging-channel messages or web_extract, browser, MCP and file-read results; those need your own classifier on the transform_tool_result and pre_gateway_dispatch plugin hooks. tirith scans commands before they run, which is action screening and is credited under action policy, not here. CVE-2026-9366 and CVE-2026-10223 were bypasses of the context-file and memory scanners, fixed in 0.15.0.

original.mechanism: Heuristic scanners on project context files, memory writes and inbound A2A text, plus tirith content scanning of shell commands before execution (security.tirith_*); nothing classifies fetched web or tool content

steps.title: Keep context-file scanning on
body: AGENTS.md, .cursorrules and SOUL.md are scanned for ignore-prior-instructions text, hidden HTML comments, secret reads, curl exfiltration and invisible Unicode before entering the system prompt; a hit is dropped with a "[BLOCKED: ... potential prompt injection]" warning, so treat that banner as a finding, not noise.

steps.title: Make tirith fail closed
body: In ~/.hermes/config.yaml set security.tirith_enabled: true and security.tirith_fail_open: false so homograph URLs, pipe-to-interpreter and terminal-injection patterns block a command when the scanner is unavailable instead of letting it through (the default fails open).

steps.title: Gate memory writes as well as scanning them
body: Memory entries are scanned for injection and exfiltration patterns before they are accepted; add memory.write_approval: true so an unprompted background save still needs your approval before it can reach the next session's system prompt.

original.note: The scanners are pattern heuristics on files, memory and commands — web_extract, browser and MCP results are not classified. Rely on approvals.mode manual, an isolated terminal backend and the egress proxy for anything a poisoned page could trigger.

controls.mechanism: No built-in harm, denied-topic or blocked-term classifier; a transform_llm_output plugin hook can replace the final response before delivery, and model.base_url (Custom endpoint) can route inference through an AI gateway that applies policy to requests and responses

steps.title: Attach a response classifier with transform_llm_output
body: Register a transform_llm_output callback in a plugin listed under plugins.enabled; it receives the final response_text before post_llm_call and delivery, and the first non-empty string it returns replaces the response, so a policy classifier can substitute a refusal.

steps.title: Route model traffic through an AI gateway for the request leg
body: Choose Custom endpoint in hermes model (saved in config.yaml as model.base_url) and point it at an OpenAI-compatible AI gateway that classifies requests and responses; route auxiliary.*.provider there too, since compression, vision and smart-approval calls also send conversation content to a model.

controls.note: Partial by the attach-point rule: Hermes ships no content policy of its own (the FAQ says it does not turn its execution controls into a content-refusal layer and that provider controls such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply when configured), and the one hook that can change model output is transform_llm_output on the final response. The request leg has observer hooks only (pre_api_request ignores its return and pre_llm_call can only add context), so blocking a request needs an AI gateway in front of the provider; streamed deltas and interim messages also have observer hooks only.

original.mechanism: No harm-category, denied-topic or blocked-term filtering of prompts or responses ships with the product
original.note: The only content policies are security.redact_secrets on tool output and the website_blocklist on URLs. To add a guardrail, register a pre_llm_call / post_llm_call hook that calls your own classifier, or rely on moderation at the model provider.

evidence.title: Hermes Agent — official site, reviewed; no setting for this control (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: security.redact_secrets (on by default) masks credential-shaped strings in tool output before it enters context and logs; privacy.redact_pii hashes sender IDs and phone numbers in the gateway system prompt; A2A replies and MCP error text are scrubbed; transform_llm_output and pre_tool_call plugin hooks are the attach points for the reply and tool-call legs

steps.title: Keep secret redaction on
body: Leave security.redact_secrets: true in ~/.hermes/config.yaml (the default) so API-key, token and password patterns in tool output are redacted before the model or the logs see them, and reads of .env files, shell rc files and config.yaml return a non-reusable «redacted-secret» marker.

steps.title: Hash sender identifiers on messaging platforms
body: Set privacy.redact_pii: true so WhatsApp, Signal and Telegram user IDs, phone numbers and chat IDs reach the model as user_<sha256> hashes; Discord and Slack are excluded because mentions need the real ID.

steps.title: Inspect replies and tool-call arguments with plugin hooks
body: Register a transform_llm_output callback (replaces the final reply) and a pre_tool_call callback (blocks or modifies the arguments of web_search, browser, MCP and messaging calls) in a plugin listed under plugins.enabled, each calling your own DLP classifier.

steps.title: Redact before sharing history
body: Use hermes sessions export backup.jsonl --redact for anything you hand to others; --redact scrubs API keys, tokens and credentials from the exported content.

controls.note: Partial by the redaction rule: the product detects credential-shaped strings by pattern on the way into the model (tool output) and scrubs A2A replies, but inspects nothing it sends — the reply to a messaging channel and the arguments of outbound tool calls (a web_search query, a browser form, an MCP or email call) carry whatever the model puts there unless your own transform_llm_output or pre_tool_call hook checks them. PII handling is limited to hashing sender identifiers on three platforms; security.website_blocklist and the SSRF guard are destination controls, not detection.

original.mechanism: security.redact_secrets scrubs key-shaped strings from tool output and logs, security.website_blocklist blocks destinations for web and browser tools, A2A replies are credential-redacted and session exports take --redact; no classifier on prompts or uploads

steps.title: Keep secret redaction on
body: security.redact_secrets: true (the default) redacts API-key, token and password patterns in tool output before they enter the conversation context or logs; set it to false only for debugging.

steps.title: Block sensitive destinations
body: Set security.website_blocklist.enabled: true with domains such as "*.internal.company.com" or a shared_files rule list; web_search, web_extract, browser_navigate and every URL-capable tool refuse a match.

steps.title: Redact before sharing history
body: Use hermes sessions export --redact for anything you hand to others; outbound A2A replies are scrubbed of credential-shaped strings automatically.

original.note: Detection is pattern-based and aimed at credentials; personal or business data in prompts to the model provider is not inspected — enforce that at the provider or a proxy in front of it.

controls.mechanism: One ordered authorization check for every messaging adapter — per-platform *_ALLOW_ALL_USERS, the DM-pairing approved list, per-platform *_ALLOWED_USERS, GATEWAY_ALLOWED_USERS, GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS, then default deny — set in ~/.hermes/.env, with unauthorized_dm_behavior in config.yaml and hermes pairing approve / revoke; A2A peers and the API server admit callers by their own tokens

steps.title: Keep every bridge on explicit allowlists
body: Set GATEWAY_ALLOWED_USERS and per-platform lists such as TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS or SLACK_ALLOWED_USERS in ~/.hermes/.env; with no list configured every user is denied, and never set GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS, a per-platform *_ALLOW_ALL_USERS flag or gateway.allow_all_users: true.

steps.title: Admit new senders by pairing, or refuse them
body: Set unauthorized_dm_behavior: pair (or ignore / decline, per platform) in ~/.hermes/config.yaml and approve codes with hermes pairing approve <platform> <code>; codes expire after one hour, and five failed approvals lock the platform for an hour.

steps.title: Re-check the approved list yourself
body: A pairing approval is permanent, so review hermes pairing list on a schedule and remove anyone who should no longer reach the agent with hermes pairing revoke <platform> <user-id>.

steps.title: Name the peers allowed over A2A
body: Give each peer its own token in A2A_PEER_TOKENS, list the identities allowed to send tasks in A2A_TRUSTED_PEERS and leave A2A_ALLOW_ALL_USERS at false.

controls.note: Partial on the D3-APA rule: one default-deny decision function covers every chat bridge, but a paired sender is "permanently approved" — nothing expires or re-checks the approval, so revocation is manual — and identities are platform user IDs, not directory-bound accounts. Per-platform allow-all flags open a bridge wholesale, and the A2A server (A2A_TRUSTED_PEERS, A2A_PEER_TOKENS), the API server (API_SERVER_KEY), webhook platforms and the dashboard each admit callers by a separate mechanism, so there is no single admission decision across every ingress. The FAQ still describes pairing as "first user to message claims access"; the security page's owner-approved code flow is the documented behaviour.

original.mechanism: Gateway user allowlists and DM pairing in ~/.hermes/.env and config.yaml (default deny), username/password auth on a non-loopback dashboard, API_SERVER_KEY bearer on the API server; no MFA or IdP integration

steps.title: Keep the gateway on explicit allowlists
body: Set GATEWAY_ALLOWED_USERS and per-platform lists such as TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS or DISCORD_ALLOWED_USERS in ~/.hermes/.env; with no allowlist configured every user is denied, and the docs say never to set GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS=true on a machine you care about.

steps.title: Approve new senders through DM pairing
body: Leave unauthorized_dm_behavior: pair in config.yaml (or ignore to drop unknown DMs silently), approve codes with hermes pairing approve <platform> <code> and remove access with hermes pairing revoke <platform> <user-id>; codes expire after one hour and five failed approvals lock the platform for an hour.

steps.title: Protect a remotely reachable dashboard
body: A dashboard bound off loopback fails closed unless HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_USERNAME, HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD and HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_SECRET are set in .env; --insecure no longer bypasses the gate.

steps.title: Key the OpenAI-compatible API server
body: Enable it only with API_SERVER_ENABLED=true and a strong API_SERVER_KEY in ~/.hermes/.env; every request must carry it as a bearer token and the server binds 127.0.0.1 by default.

original.note: Identity is platform user IDs plus static shared secrets; there is no phishing-resistant MFA, so put any exposed dashboard or API port behind your own identity-aware proxy.

controls.mechanism: approvals.deny fnmatch globs over normalised terminal commands (checked before --yolo and approvals.mode off, on every backend) and the code-shipped hardline blocklist; HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT and the protected-path list for write_file and patch; security.website_blocklist for URL tools; hooks.pre_tool_call entries that can block, escalate or modify any tool call; all read from ~/.hermes/config.yaml or .env

steps.title: Declare commands that must never run
body: Add quoted fnmatch globs under approvals.deny in ~/.hermes/config.yaml (for example 'git push --force*' or 'dd if=* of=/dev/*'); they match normalised command variants on every terminal backend before --yolo or approvals.mode off is consulted and return a BLOCKED error to the model.

steps.title: Fence file writes to a safe root
body: Set HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT=/path/to/project:/home/you/.hermes so write_file and patch outside those prefixes are hard-blocked with no approval prompt; OS and Hermes credential stores stay blocked even inside the root.

steps.title: Decide every other tool call in a fail-closed pre_tool_call hook
body: Declare hooks.pre_tool_call entries in config.yaml with a matcher regex, a command and fail_closed: true; the script reads the tool name and arguments as JSON and can block the call, send it to approval or rewrite its arguments, and a crash or timeout blocks the call.

steps.title: Pin the rules where the agent cannot write them
body: Put approvals.deny and approvals.mode in a root-owned /etc/hermes/config.yaml, which wins over ~/.hermes/config.yaml for the keys it names, fix HERMES_MANAGED_DIR in the service unit and run the gateway as a non-root user.

controls.note: Partial: every decision is deterministic and taken outside the model, but the rules sit in ~/.hermes/config.yaml, which the agent's own write_file and patch can overwrite (the security page lists config.yaml among control files that are "read-denied but stay writable") and a local-backend terminal can edit, and approval-config edits apply without a restart. The vendor scopes the engine itself: deny rules are "a guardrail against an honest-but-wrong agent", "not a complete shell interpreter or an OS capability sandbox", and managed scope is "a management-convenience boundary against a normal user, not an un-escapable sandbox". Per-call argument rules cover terminal commands, file writes and URLs; MCP, browser and computer_use calls are decided only by a pre_tool_call hook you write. Unattended turns: cron_mode, single_query_mode and unattended_mode deny flagged commands and webhook runs get the read-only hermes-webhook toolset, but command_allowlist entries still run there. tirith (security.tirith_enabled, tirith_fail_open false) adds content scanning of commands, routed to approval.

original.mechanism: approvals.deny glob rules and the code-shipped hardline blocklist run before --yolo or approvals.mode off; HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT hard-blocks writes; pre_tool_call shell and plugin hooks can block or escalate any tool call and fail closed

steps.title: Declare commands that must never run
body: Add quoted fnmatch globs under approvals.deny in ~/.hermes/config.yaml (for example "git push --force*", "dd if=* of=/dev/*"); they are matched against normalised command variants on every backend, return a BLOCKED error to the model and take effect without a restart.

steps.title: Fence file writes to a safe root
body: Set HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT=/path/to/project:/home/you/.hermes in ~/.hermes/.env; write_file and patch outside those prefixes are hard-blocked with no approval prompt, and credential paths such as ~/.ssh and .env stay blocked even inside the root.

steps.title: Add a pre_tool_call policy hook
body: Declare hooks.pre_tool_call entries in config.yaml with a matcher regex, a command and fail_closed: true; the script reads the tool call as JSON on stdin and blocks it by returning {"action": "block", "message": ...} or exiting 2, and a timeout blocks rather than proceeds.

steps.title: Keep the approval mode manual on a work machine
body: Set approvals.mode: manual so every flagged command prompts you instead of the smart mode's auxiliary-LLM auto-approval, and leave approvals.timeout at 300 so an unanswered prompt is denied.

original.note: Deny globs and the hardline blocklist are deterministic; pre_tool_call hooks are an integration point that must be set fail_closed. Delegated subagents inherit approvals; MCP tool calls pass the hooks, a server's own actions do not.

controls.mechanism: hermes dashboard binds 127.0.0.1:9119 behind a DNS-rebinding Host-header guard and, off loopback, refuses to start without a password, OAuth or OIDC provider (dashboard.basic_auth or HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_*), but has no login on loopback; the API server binds 127.0.0.1:8642 and requires API_SERVER_KEY even there; the A2A server binds 127.0.0.1 until a token is set

steps.title: Keep the dashboard on loopback and tunnel to it
body: Run hermes dashboard without --host so it binds 127.0.0.1 and reach it over an SSH tunnel or Tailscale; --insecure is a no-op and no longer disables authentication.

steps.title: Configure an auth provider before any remote bind
body: Set HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_USERNAME, HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH and HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_SECRET (or the OAuth or OIDC provider) before --host 0.0.0.0 or a non-loopback public URL; without one the dashboard fails closed at startup.

steps.title: Key the API server
body: Enable it only with API_SERVER_ENABLED=true and a strong API_SERVER_KEY in ~/.hermes/.env; the key is required on loopback too, and browser access needs a narrow API_SERVER_CORS_ORIGINS list.

steps.title: Authenticate every A2A peer before widening the bind
body: Set A2A_PEER_TOKENS (one token per peer) and A2A_TRUSTED_PEERS, and only then move A2A_HOST off 127.0.0.1; the server refuses a non-loopback bind without a token.

controls.note: Partial on the D3-MAN rule: loopback binding, a Host-header guard and a fail-closed auth gate off loopback are all in place, but the dashboard — which reads and writes .env and config.yaml and can create shell hooks — has "no login required" on 127.0.0.1 (a page-issued session token only), and the gate engages only on a non-loopback bind or public URL, so other processes on the host, including commands the agent runs on the local backend, are trusted. Webhook-mode adapters (WhatsApp Cloud, WeCom, LINE) listen on 0.0.0.0 by default and authenticate with each platform's own secret (TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is mandatory for a Telegram webhook); polling adapters are outbound-only; stdio MCP servers have no transport authentication. CVE-2026-53869 (dashboard WebSocket DNS rebinding) was fixed in 0.16.0.

original.mechanism: HTTPS MCP servers with OAuth 2.1 (auth: oauth) or mutual TLS (client_cert/client_key) per server in mcp_servers; A2A binds loopback until a bearer or per-peer token is set; no protocol-version pinning

steps.title: Use client certificates for internal MCP servers
body: Set mcp_servers.<name>.client_cert (combined PEM or [cert, key] list) and client_key on remote HTTP servers that require mTLS; a missing file raises a server-scoped error rather than an opaque handshake failure.

steps.title: Prefer OAuth over static bearer headers
body: Write auth: oauth on hosted MCP servers so Hermes performs discovery, PKCE and refresh; tokens are cached at ~/.hermes/mcp-tokens/<server>.json with 0600 permissions and hermes mcp login <server> forces re-authentication.

steps.title: Authenticate every A2A peer
body: Give each peer its own credential with A2A_PEER_TOKENS="alice:tok1,bob:tok2", restrict callers with A2A_TRUSTED_PEERS, and only then widen A2A_HOST from 127.0.0.1; inbound text is framed as untrusted and cannot invoke slash commands.

original.note: Stdio MCP servers have no transport authentication at all, and nothing pins MCP or A2A protocol versions or server certificates; typed message contracts are the server's job.

controls.mechanism: memory.memory_enabled and memory.user_profile_enabled switch the built-in stores off; memory.write_approval and skills.write_approval stage agent writes (the background self-improvement review included) for approval; memory entries are injection- and exfiltration-scanned and size-capped; each profile has its own memories, sessions, skills and .env; /memory pending and hermes journey review and edit what was kept

steps.title: Require approval for memory writes, or switch memory off
body: Set memory.write_approval: true in ~/.hermes/config.yaml so every save to MEMORY.md or USER.md — including the unprompted background review — is staged for /memory approve, pinned to the exact entry; set memory_enabled and user_profile_enabled to false to remove the memory tool entirely.

steps.title: Gate the agent's self-written skills the same way
body: Set skills.write_approval: true so create, edit, patch, write_file and delete operations on skills stage for /skills diff and /skills approve, since skills are the other persistent store the agent feeds back into its own prompt.

steps.title: Give every agent its own profile
body: Run hermes profile create <name> for each purpose; a profile is a separate Hermes home with its own config.yaml, .env, SOUL.md, memories, sessions, skills, cron jobs and state database, and the agent never falls back to another profile's memory.

steps.title: Review and correct what the agent remembered
body: Use hermes journey list, hermes journey edit <node> and hermes journey delete <node> to inspect and correct USER.md and MEMORY.md entries and self-written skills; the system prompt takes a frozen snapshot at session start, so a fix lands on the next session.

controls.note: Native on the memory rule: the user can switch the built-in stores off or scope them per profile, and with write_approval every save through the memory tool is scanned for injection and exfiltration patterns and staged for an approval bound to that exact entry. Boundaries: write_approval is off by default; memory is injected into the system prompt as trusted text, not marked untrusted on read; session_search reaches every past session in state.db; external memory provider plugins (Honcho, Mem0 and others) run alongside the built-in stores; ~/.hermes/memories/ is not on the protected-path list, so a local-backend terminal or write_file can edit MEMORY.md outside the gate. CVE-2026-10223 was a bypass of the memory scanner, fixed in 0.15.0.

original.mechanism: memory.write_approval and skills.write_approval gate agent writes, memory entries are injection-scanned and size-capped, and each profile has its own memories, sessions, skills and .env; hermes journey edits entries

steps.title: Require approval for memory writes
body: Set memory.write_approval: true in ~/.hermes/config.yaml so every save to MEMORY.md or USER.md — including the unprompted background review — is staged for your approval; memory_char_limit and user_char_limit keep the stores bounded.

steps.title: Gate the agent's self-written skills the same way
body: Set skills.write_approval: true so create, edit, patch and write_file operations on skills need approval, since skills are the other persistent store the agent feeds back into its own prompt.

steps.title: Give every agent its own profile
body: Run hermes profile create <name> for each purpose; a profile is a separate Hermes home with its own config.yaml, .env, SOUL.md, memories, sessions, skills, cron jobs and state database, so one agent's memory never reaches another.

steps.title: Review and edit what the agent remembered
body: Use hermes journey list and hermes journey edit to inspect and correct USER.md and MEMORY.md entries; the system prompt takes a frozen snapshot at session start, so a fix lands on the next session.

original.note: Write approval and injection scanning are genuine integrity gates; what can still write is an approved agent turn and the user's own edits. Recovery is the checkpoint store, not a versioned memory; per-profile isolation is the tenant boundary.

controls.mechanism: terminal.backend docker / singularity / modal / daytona / vercel_sandbox (or ssh) in config.yaml moves terminal, the file tools and execute_code into a sandbox; Docker containers run --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, pids-limit 256 and size-limited tmpfs, with terminal.docker_network false for --network=none and container_persistent false for a fresh container per session; the default backend is local

steps.title: Move command execution into a container
body: Set terminal.backend: docker with docker_forward_env: [] in ~/.hermes/config.yaml; every terminal, write_file, patch and execute_code call then runs through docker exec in a container started with all capabilities dropped (DAC_OVERRIDE, CHOWN and FOWNER added back), no-new-privileges and a 256-process limit.

steps.title: Give each session its own bounded container
body: Set terminal.container_persistent: false so every chat gets a fresh container that is removed when the session closes, and set container_cpu, container_memory and container_disk; the default (true) shares one long-lived container across sessions and subagents.

steps.title: Air-gap the sandbox when the task allows
body: Set terminal.docker_network: false (env TERMINAL_DOCKER_NETWORK) to start the execution container with --network=none; an existing networked container is replaced by a fresh air-gapped one.

steps.title: Close the routes back to the host
body: Leave computer_use disabled in hermes tools, keep ~/.hermes and other host paths out of terminal.docker_volumes, add nothing to docker_extra_args that weakens the hardening, and review every stdio server under mcp_servers, since those run on the host.

controls.note: Partial on the sandbox rule (core rule 3): the container is a real boundary for terminal, write_file, patch and execute_code, and config.yaml on the host is out of the agent's reach from inside it, but the product keeps host-side paths the agent can use — computer_use drives the host desktop after an approval that can be granted once, per session or always (and /yolo bypasses), stdio MCP servers run on the host, and cron no_agent scripts run on the host from $HERMES_HOME/scripts — while docker_volumes and docker_extra_args can re-expose the host. The default backend is local, with no isolation; dangerous-command approval is skipped inside container backends because the container is treated as the boundary; Docker and Singularity share the host kernel, while Modal, Daytona and Vercel Sandbox run remotely.

original.mechanism: terminal.backend docker / ssh / singularity / modal / daytona / vercel_sandbox in config.yaml; Docker containers run --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, pids-limit 256 and size-limited tmpfs with optional --network=none and ephemeral workspaces

steps.title: Move command execution into a container
body: Set terminal.backend: docker with docker_forward_env: [] in ~/.hermes/config.yaml; every container is started with all capabilities dropped (DAC_OVERRIDE, CHOWN and FOWNER added back), no-new-privileges, a 256-process limit and nosuid tmpfs mounts.

steps.title: Bound and discard the sandbox
body: Set terminal.container_cpu, container_memory and container_disk, and container_persistent: false to keep the workspace on tmpfs so it is lost on cleanup instead of persisting under ~/.hermes/sandboxes/docker/.

steps.title: Air-gap the sandbox when the task allows
body: Set terminal.docker_network: false (env TERMINAL_DOCKER_NETWORK) to run the execution container with --network=none; an existing networked container is replaced by a fresh air-gapped one.

steps.title: Or keep execution off the host entirely
body: Set terminal.backend: ssh and put TERMINAL_SSH_HOST, TERMINAL_SSH_USER and TERMINAL_SSH_KEY in ~/.hermes/.env so commands run on a separate machine while the messaging connections stay on the gateway host.

original.note: The default backend is local with no isolation, and dangerous-command checks are skipped inside container backends because the container is treated as the boundary.

controls.mechanism: hermes tools per-tool toggles per platform (persisted to config.yaml), toolsets per platform, agent.disabled_toolsets and --toolsets per session, mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include / exclude, and argument or path limits from approvals.deny (terminal), HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT (file writes), security.website_blocklist (URL tools) and computer_use.permission_mode bounded with a capability_manifest

steps.title: Trim the tool surface per platform
body: Run hermes tools to switch individual tools on or off for cli, telegram, discord and the other platforms; disabled tools are filtered out even when their toolset is enabled, and the result persists to config.yaml.

steps.title: Remove whole toolsets everywhere or per session
body: List toolsets under agent.disabled_toolsets in ~/.hermes/config.yaml to strip them after the per-platform selection, or start a narrow session with hermes chat --toolsets web,file; opt-in sets such as a2a and x_search stay off until enabled.

steps.title: Whitelist the tools each MCP server may contribute
body: Set mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include (or exclude) with names or globs, or enabled: false on a server; hermes mcp configure <name> writes the same filter from a checklist.

steps.title: Bound computer use to reviewed apps and origins
body: Set computer_use.permission_mode: bounded with a capability_manifest naming the apps, browser profile kinds, origins and typed tools the session may use; anything outside the manifest fails closed inside cua-driver.

controls.note: Native on the per-tool rule: tools are allowed or removed per platform and per session, and argument or path limits apply to terminal commands, file writes, URL tools and computer_use, all enforced by the harness outside the model. Limits: MCP tools are on or off by name, not by argument; reads have no root (only secret files are read-denied); every tool runs with the user's own authority; delegate_task children inherit the parent's toolsets. The lists sit in ~/.hermes/config.yaml, which the agent's write_file can change on a local backend — pin them in /etc/hermes managed scope, as under action policy. --yolo lifts the approval layer but not a removed tool.

original.mechanism: hermes tools per-platform enable/disable persisted to config.yaml, toolsets: presets per platform and --toolsets per session, mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include/exclude, subagents inherit only the parent's toolsets

steps.title: Trim the tool surface per platform
body: Run hermes tools to toggle individual tools on or off for cli, telegram, discord and the other platforms; disabled tools are filtered out even when their toolset is enabled, and the result persists to config.yaml.

steps.title: Pin toolsets in config or per session
body: Set toolsets: per platform in ~/.hermes/config.yaml, or start a narrow session with hermes chat --toolsets "web,terminal"; opt-in sets such as a2a and x_search stay off until you enable them.

steps.title: Whitelist the tools each MCP server may contribute
body: Set mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include (or exclude) with names or globs, or disabled: true on a server; the catalog installer writes the same filter from its tool-selection checklist.

steps.title: Keep subagents at or below the parent's rights
body: delegate_task has no toolsets parameter — children inherit the parent's enabled toolsets and leaf subagents cannot delegate; raise delegation.max_spawn_depth above the default 1 only deliberately.

original.note: Toolsets hide tools per platform and session; approvals gate; argument limits come from approvals.deny globs and the write-safe root. --yolo pre-approves everything except the hardline blocklist.

controls.mechanism: Stdio MCP servers get a filtered environment plus only their own mcp_servers.<name>.env block, and OAuth MCP tokens are cached per server under ~/.hermes/mcp-tokens/; terminal, execute_code and cron scripts drop Hermes-managed credentials unless declared in terminal.env_passthrough; the iron-proxy egress proxy gives Docker sandboxes proxy tokens and swaps in model-provider keys on the host

steps.title: Scope MCP credentials to the one server that needs them
body: Put each server's token in its own mcp_servers.<name>.env block; stdio servers otherwise receive only PATH, HOME, USER, LANG, LC_ALL, TERM, SHELL, TMPDIR and XDG_* variables, and MCP error text is redacted for PATs, sk- keys and bearer tokens before the model sees it.

steps.title: Leave the child-process env filters at their defaults
body: Only variables a loaded skill declares in required_environment_variables or that you list under terminal.env_passthrough reach terminal, execute_code and cron scripts; provider keys and gateway tokens cannot be declared.

steps.title: Keep model keys out of the Docker sandbox
body: Run hermes egress install, hermes egress setup and hermes egress start, keeping proxy.enabled and proxy.enforce_on_docker true; the sandbox gets opaque proxy tokens under the usual env names and iron-proxy substitutes the real key on the host only for requests to allowlisted upstreams.

steps.title: Forward nothing else into the sandbox
body: Keep terminal.docker_forward_env: [] and set auth.adopt_external_logins: false so Hermes neither injects task tokens into the container nor borrows the Codex CLI and Claude Code logins on the host.

controls.note: Partial on the D3-CTS rule: credentials are separated per MCP server and per child process, and model provider keys reach a Docker sandbox only as proxy tokens swapped on the host, but nothing narrows a credential to the task — each MCP server, forwarded token (docker_forward_env, env_passthrough) and adopted CLI login carries the owner's standing grant, and there is no token exchange or on-behalf-of flow. The proxy covers header-swappable provider keys on the Docker backend only; SigV4 (AWS) and service-account file (GCP) credentials stay real, and Modal, Daytona, SSH and Singularity get no proxy.

original.mechanism: execute_code and terminal strip credential-shaped env vars from child processes, MCP subprocesses get a filtered environment plus only their own env: block, Docker forwards nothing unless listed, and the iron-proxy egress proxy replaces real keys with opaque proxy tokens inside sandboxes

steps.title: Leave the sandbox env filters at their defaults
body: Only variables a loaded skill declares in required_environment_variables or that you list under terminal.env_passthrough reach execute_code, terminal and remote backends; the docs say never to add provider keys or gateway tokens to env_passthrough.

steps.title: Scope MCP credentials to the one server that needs them
body: Stdio MCP servers receive only PATH, HOME, USER, LANG, LC_ALL, TERM, SHELL, TMPDIR and XDG_* plus whatever you put in mcp_servers.<name>.env; error messages are redacted for PATs, sk- keys and bearer tokens before the model sees them.

steps.title: Keep real keys out of the Docker sandbox with the egress proxy
body: Run hermes egress setup then hermes egress start; the sandbox is given HTTPS_PROXY plus proxy tokens in the usual env names and iron-proxy swaps them for the real credential on the host, so a printenv inside the sandbox yields nothing usable elsewhere.

steps.title: Forward nothing into containers by default
body: Keep terminal.docker_forward_env: [] — anything you add is deliberately injected into the container for task credentials and can be read and exfiltrated by code running there.

original.note: Covers credential-shaped environment variables and provider keys for child processes, MCP subprocesses and Docker; a local (unsandboxed) terminal backend and the gateway process itself hold the real values. Single-user product, so on-behalf-of exchange does not arise.

controls.mechanism: secrets.bitwarden, secrets.onepassword and the command helper pull keys from a vault into the Hermes process at startup so only the bootstrap token stays in ~/.hermes/.env; proxy.credential_source: bitwarden feeds iron-proxy, which injects model-provider keys on the host for Docker sandboxes; write_file refuses .env and credential stores

steps.title: Pull keys from Bitwarden Secrets Manager
body: Run hermes secrets bitwarden setup (installs the pinned bws binary, stores the access token, picks a project) and set secrets.bitwarden.enabled: true with project_id in config.yaml; rotate the bootstrap token with hermes secrets bitwarden token.

steps.title: Or reference 1Password items or any CLI vault
body: Set secrets.onepassword.enabled: true and map env var names to op:// references under secrets.onepassword.env, or point the command source at keepassxc-cli, secret-tool or pass printing KEY=VALUE lines.

steps.title: Inject model keys outside the sandbox
body: Run hermes egress setup --from-bitwarden so iron-proxy refetches provider keys from Bitwarden on every start (proxy.credential_source: bitwarden, allow_env_fallback: false) and the Docker sandbox holds only proxy tokens.

steps.title: Lock the file that remains and rotate after a leak
body: Run chmod 600 ~/.hermes/.env, and after a suspected leak mint fresh proxy tokens with hermes egress setup --rotate-tokens, restart running sandboxes and rotate the provider keys in the vault.

controls.note: Partial on the D3-CH rule: vault references and host-side injection both exist, but the pulled values live in the environment of the Hermes process that runs the agent loop for its lifetime (child processes get a scrubbed copy), injection outside the boundary covers header-swappable model-provider keys on the Docker backend only, MCP server credentials sit in config.yaml env blocks or .env, the Bitwarden machine-account token in .env can be issued with no expiry, and auth.adopt_external_logins (default true) reads and refreshes the Codex CLI and Claude Code credential files. steps.title: Bound the self-waking loop
