tools.name: OpenAI Agents SDK

variants.name: openai-agents (Python)
@openai/agents (TypeScript: agents-core, agents-openai, agents-extensions)

summary: An open-source library (Python and TypeScript, MIT) that runs the agent loop inside the customer's own process: agents with instructions, typed function tools, handoffs and agents-as-tools, input, output and tool guardrails, tool approvals that pause a run as serialisable RunState, sessions for conversation history, MCP servers (local or hosted), and sandbox agents that run shell and file tools in Unix-local, Docker or hosted-provider sandboxes. Inference goes to the OpenAI Responses API by default (or Chat Completions and other providers through adapters) with the key or client the application supplies.

Every control is a parameter or a function the deployer writes: max_turns (default 10), needs_approval and require_approval, guardrail functions, is_enabled and MCP tool filters, trace processors. Tracing is on by default and ships each run to OpenAI's Traces dashboard with model inputs, outputs and tool arguments included unless trace_include_sensitive_data is turned off or the processors are replaced; tracing is unavailable to Zero Data Retention organisations. Nothing is hosted by the SDK itself: storage, identity, egress and isolation are the application's.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Free, MIT-licensed packages (pip install openai-agents, npm install @openai/agents); model calls, hosted tools and containers bill to the OpenAI API organisation at API rates.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: OpenAI Responses API by default with OPENAI_API_KEY (or set_default_openai_key / set_default_openai_client, OPENAI_BASE_URL); set_default_openai_api switches to Chat Completions; other providers through a ModelProvider, a Model instance per agent, or the Any-LLM / LiteLLM adapters.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Instructions, history and tool results to the model provider; traces to OpenAI's backend by default (generation inputs and outputs and function-call inputs and outputs unless trace_include_sensitive_data is False); session history wherever the chosen session store lives (OpenAIConversationsSession keeps it in OpenAI's Conversations API); hosted tools and hosted containers run at OpenAI.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: API data is not used for training by default; /v1/responses keeps abuse-monitoring logs up to 30 days and is ZDR-eligible; /v1/conversations (OpenAIConversationsSession) keeps items until deleted and is not ZDR-eligible; tracing is unavailable to ZDR organisations and trace retention is not documented on the tracing pages.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: openai.github.io/openai-agents-python and openai.github.io/openai-agents-js, with platform guides at developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents

facts.label: Security policy
facts.value: Reports go through OpenAI's Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure Policy; SECURITY.md states that tool implementations run with the host application's privileges and that the application must authorise them and isolate untrusted execution.

items.title: Keep traces in your own store
body: Tracing starts on and exports to OpenAI. Install your collector's processor with set_trace_processors (which replaces the OpenAI exporter) before the first run, and set trace_include_sensitive_data to False unless that store is approved for prompts and tool arguments.

items.title: Choose a sandbox client that isolates
body: UnixLocalSandboxClient adds no OS-level confinement on Linux and no network isolation on macOS; use Docker with network_mode "none", a hosted sandbox client, or external isolation for commands influenced by untrusted input.

riskNotes.note: Input guardrails run only on the first agent and by default in parallel with it, so the model can already have called tools when a tripwire fires; results of hosted tools (web search, file search, hosted MCP) reach the model inside the Responses call with no SDK hook.
Approval is opt-in per tool: function tools run unapproved unless needs_approval is set, and local ShellTool and ApplyPatchTool default to needs_approval=False on a host the SDK does not sandbox.
Tracing defaults to on, to OpenAI, with model and tool payloads included; serialised RunState carries the application context and approval state, so secrets placed in context travel with it.
max_turns defaults to 10 model calls per run and max_turns=None removes it; usage is counted on the run context but no token or cost ceiling stops a run.
Each run calls list_tools() on every MCP server, so a server can add or redefine tools between runs unless a static tool_filter narrows the list; cache_tools_list is a latency cache, not a pin.

controls.mechanism: The run context (Runner.run(..., context=...)) carrying the caller's grant to every tool, FunctionTool.is_enabled, Handoff.is_enabled, MCP tool_filter, needs_approval callables and guardrails; who may start, resume or cancel a run is the application's endpoint

steps.title: Bind the grant at ingress
body: Pass the principal the run acts for and its grant (a service principal's scope or the on-behalf-of token from the message) as the context object to Runner.run(..., context=...); tools, hooks and guardrails read it from RunContextWrapper.context.

steps.title: Gate capabilities on the grant
body: Return False from FunctionTool.is_enabled, Handoff.is_enabled or a callable MCP tool_filter when the context's grant does not cover the capability; the runner re-evaluates is_enabled before invoking a local function tool.

steps.title: Rebuild the context on resume
body: Resume a parked run with the authenticated caller's context, not the serialised one — in TypeScript RunState.fromStringWithContext(agent, state, context, { contextStrategy: 'replace' }).

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule for D3-APA (a run context carrying the caller's grant is an attach point). The SDK carries the grant to every callback but decides nothing with it: it has no listener, is_enabled "controls visibility and dispatch; it does not replace authorization that depends on the tool arguments or the resource", and the grant is whatever the application places in context. Who may start, resume or cancel a run — including whether the event that resumes a parked proposal carries an authorised approver — is the application's endpoint behind its IdP or API gateway. Serialised RunState includes the context and approval state (TypeScript's default contextStrategy 'merge' merges the serialised approvals), so where it is stored is part of the trust boundary.

controls.mechanism: Agent.tools, handoffs and mcp_servers declared per agent in application code; a call to an unlisted function tool raises ModelBehaviorError by default (tool_not_found_behavior); MCP tool lists fetched from each server on every run and narrowed by create_static_tool_filter

steps.title: Declare each agent's catalogue in reviewed code
body: Give every Agent an explicit tools and handoffs list and keep RunConfig.tool_not_found_behavior at its default, so a model-named tool that is not on the current agent raises ModelBehaviorError.

steps.title: Fix each MCP server's tool list
body: Set tool_filter=create_static_tool_filter(allowed_tool_names=[...]) (TypeScript createMCPToolStaticFilter) on every MCP server so tools a server adds later are not exposed.

steps.title: Label runs for reconciliation
body: Set RunConfig workflow_name, group_id and trace_metadata (owner, release) on each run so traces can be reconciled against the organisation's registry.

controls.note: Partial by this drawing's rule (tools declared per agent in code; admission is code review). There is no registry with owner, version or approval state and nothing consults one before a tool is offered; the catalogue is whatever the process constructs. MCP tool definitions arrive from the server on each run, so a server adds tools unless a static filter narrows them, and HostedMCPTool servers list their tools inside the Responses API. set_default_openai_harness only adds an agent_harness_id to trace metadata — a label, not an admission check. Change gating is the organisation's pipeline.

controls.mechanism: None in the SDK; an evaluation platform in CI runs the agent against a protected test set before a model, instruction or tool change ships

evidence.title: Testing — deterministic, provider-neutral utilities; model behaviour needs real providers (2026-09-25)
Evaluate agent workflows — trace grading and eval runs on the OpenAI Platform (2026-09-25)
Evals platform deprecation — read-only 2026-10-31, shutdown 2026-11-30 (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External (evaluation or red-team platform in CI), as for the Claude Agent SDK and Codex SDK: the SDK's testing utilities (ScriptedModel, provider-neutral fakes) make no model requests and test the orchestration the application owns — the page says to use real providers for behaviour owned by the model — so they cannot validate a model or prompt change. OpenAI's trace grading and Evals run on the platform and gate nothing; the Evals platform becomes read-only on 2026-10-31 and shuts down on 2026-11-30. Integration point: run the agent headless in CI against the evaluation platform's suite with a pinned model and output_type, and gate the release on its result.

controls.mechanism: @function_tool / tool() schemas generated from Pydantic or Zod types with strict_mode True by default, arguments validated (Field constraints included) before the function runs; per-agent tools lists and is_enabled; create_static_tool_filter on MCP servers

steps.title: Type and constrain every action
body: Declare each action with @function_tool (TypeScript tool({ parameters: z.object(...) })) using constrained types such as Field(ge=, le=, pattern=) and leave strict_mode True; arguments that fail validation never reach the function.

steps.title: Give each agent only its own actions
body: Set Agent.tools per agent and use is_enabled for request-scoped exposure; a specialist reached by handoff runs with its own tools, not the triage agent's.

steps.title: Allowlist tools from MCP servers
body: Set tool_filter=create_static_tool_filter(allowed_tool_names=[...]) on each MCP server; the allow-list is applied first and blocked_tool_names removes from what remains.

steps.title: Validate in hand-built tools
body: In a hand-built FunctionTool, validate the raw JSON string on_invoke_tool receives (for example model_validate_json) before acting on it.

controls.note: Native on this drawing's rule for AML.M0028 (typed schemas strictly validated by the SDK before execution, plus per-agent tool lists): the decorator path builds a strict JSON schema and re-validates the parsed arguments with Pydantic, so a malformed or out-of-range call is refused outside the model. Outside that boundary: hand-built FunctionTool receives raw JSON; MCP tool schemas are converted to strict best-effort and validated by the server; hosted tools and local shell, apply-patch and computer tools take free-form arguments; is_enabled governs visibility, not authorisation. Every tool runs with the process's authority unless the tool reads the caller's grant from context, and a declared blast radius or compensating transaction is the tool author's, not an SDK concept. The multi-agent drawing's SDK rows are partial on that drawing's per-hop rule, which this drawing does not apply.

controls.mechanism: needs_approval (True or an async callable over context, parsed arguments and call ID) on function tools, Agent.as_tool, ShellTool and ApplyPatchTool; require_approval on local and hosted MCP servers; the run pauses with RunResult.interruptions (ToolApprovalItem with agent.name, tool_name, arguments) and resumes after state.approve or state.reject for that call ID

steps.title: Key approval to consequence
body: Set needs_approval on each consequential tool to an async callable that returns True above the irreversibility or value threshold (TypeScript needsApproval), or True to always ask.

steps.title: Park the run and resume on a decision
body: Store result.to_state() with state.to_json() (TypeScript result.state.toString()), show the approver each interruption's agent, tool_name and arguments, and resume with Runner.run(agent, state) only after state.approve or state.reject.

steps.title: Gate MCP and shell actions too
body: Set require_approval on MCPServerStdio, MCPServerSse and MCPServerStreamableHttp, tool_config require_approval "always" on HostedMCPTool, and needs_approval=True on local ShellTool and ApplyPatchTool (default False).

steps.title: Keep decisions per call
body: Do not pass always_approve=True for consequential tools; it approves every later call to that tool for the rest of the run and survives serialisation.

controls.note: Native on the same rule as the Claude Agent SDK's canUseTool: a built-in primitive holds the exact call (per call ID, with its arguments) until the application records a decision, callable rules fail closed on malformed arguments, and nested, handed-off and agent-as-tool approvals surface on the outer run. The deployer supplies the approver, the UI, authentication, expiry and the rule that the requester never approves — the SDK records no approver identity. Boundaries: approval is opt-in per tool; hosted tools, hosted-container shell (which must not set needs_approval) and handoffs have none; on_approval and on_approval_request callbacks decide in code and are not human approval; always_approve is sticky for the run; the serialised RunState carries the approval state, so its storage must be tamper-protected.

controls.mechanism: Tool input guardrails (@tool_input_guardrail with ToolContext tool_name, tool_call_id, tool_arguments) returning reject_content or raising a tripwire, per function tool or server-wide on local MCP servers; needs_approval callables as the escalate path; no declarative policy language

steps.title: Decide every function-tool call in a guardrail
body: Attach tool_input_guardrails to each function tool (TypeScript inputGuardrails on tool()) that checks the context's principal, the tool and its arguments and returns ToolGuardrailFunctionOutput.reject_content(...) or raises a tripwire.

steps.title: Apply it to MCP tools
body: Pass tool_input_guardrails on MCPServerStdio, MCPServerSse or MCPServerStreamableHttp so the SDK attaches it to every tool the server exposes after filtering.

steps.title: Decide before the approval prompt
body: Set RunConfig.tool_execution=ToolExecutionConfig(pre_approval_tool_input_guardrails=True) so the policy runs before an approval interruption and again after approval.

controls.note: Partial by this drawing's rule (tool guardrail functions the deployer writes). The guardrail runs outside the model, per call, before the function executes, and deny, allow and escalate (via needs_approval) are all expressible — but the rules are the deployer's code and the decision is recorded only as a guardrail span. Not covered: handoffs, Agent.as_tool, hosted tools (WebSearchTool, FileSearchTool, HostedMCPTool, CodeInterpreterTool, ImageGenerationTool) and built-in execution tools (ComputerTool, ShellTool, ApplyPatchTool, LocalShellTool), which bypass the guardrail pipeline. A hosted MCP server can be pointed at an MCP gateway that decides per call.

controls.mechanism: No agent identity in the SDK; the process authenticates to OpenAI with OPENAI_API_KEY, set_default_openai_key or a client from set_default_openai_client, or per agent with a Model instance on its own AsyncOpenAI client; a project service account through workload identity federation is the revocable workload identity

steps.title: Federate a workload identity per agent workload
body: In Organization Settings > Security > Workload Identity Provider map each agent workload's OIDC, SPIFFE or X.509 identity to its own project service account with only the permissions it needs.

steps.title: Give an agent its own model client
body: Pass the agent a Model instance on its own client (the models guide shows OpenAIChatCompletionsModel(model=..., openai_client=AsyncOpenAI())) instead of the process default.

steps.title: Give an agent its own tool credential
body: Construct that agent's MCP servers with headers carrying a token minted for the agent, and list them only in its mcp_servers.

controls.note: Partial by this drawing's rule (the SDK neither mints nor authenticates agent identities). Agent.name labels spans and approvals but is not a principal; handed-off and nested agents run in the same process and environment, and nested Agent.as_tool runs share the app context by default. Per-agent model clients and MCP credentials are configurable, but minting, rotating and revoking them is the application's; the federated identity is per workload and revocable in the platform (disable the service account or its mapping).

controls.mechanism: The requester's token carried in the run context to function tools, per MCP server in headers, per call in _meta through tool_meta_resolver, and per HostedMCPTool connector in authorization; no OAuth flow, on-behalf-of exchange or built-in identity passthrough

steps.title: Carry the requester's token to each data tool
body: Put the account-scoped access token from your own OAuth or on-behalf-of flow in the run context and use it inside each function tool's data call.

steps.title: Scope each MCP call to the account
body: Construct the MCP server per request with the requester's token in headers, and set tool_meta_resolver to put the account or tenant ID into each call's _meta.

steps.title: Pass the user's grant to hosted connectors
body: For a HostedMCPTool connector, set tool_config authorization to the requesting user's access token for that run.

controls.note: Partial on the same rule as the Claude Agent SDK's per-query MCP headers (a per-call context attach point): retrieval runs with the requester's entitlements only when the application obtains and passes that token, and the docs say MCP servers must authorise their own protected operations. The SDK runs no OAuth flow or token exchange; FileSearchTool reads OpenAI vector stores with the project key, sandbox mounts read with the mount's credentials, and function tools use whatever the application gives them. Oversharing analysis of the sources is outside the SDK.

controls.mechanism: @input_guardrail on the starting agent (run_in_parallel=False to block before the model), tool_output_guardrails on function tools and local MCP servers, and RunConfig.call_model_input_filter, as attach points for the deployer's classifier; none ships

steps.title: Classify the payload before the loop
body: Attach an input guardrail that runs your injection classifier to the starting agent with run_in_parallel=False (TypeScript runInParallel: false), so a tripwire stops the run before any model call or tool.

steps.title: Screen returned content before it re-enters context
body: Attach tool_output_guardrails to each data-returning function tool, and server-wide on local MCP servers, returning reject_content to replace a flagged result before the model sees it.

steps.title: Filter the assembled input
body: Set RunConfig.call_model_input_filter to inspect and strip the prepared input, session history included, immediately before each model call.

controls.note: Partial by this drawing's rule: the guardrails are attach points and no injection classifier ships. Returned content can be screened before it re-enters context for function tools and local MCP tools only; hosted tools' results (web search, file search, hosted MCP, code interpreter) are read by the model inside the Responses call, and shell, apply-patch and computer outputs bypass the pipeline. Input guardrails run only for the first agent and by default in parallel, so the model may already have spent tokens and run tools when one trips; handoff inputs are not screened.

controls.mechanism: Session stores keyed by a session_id the application chooses (SQLiteSession, RedisSession, SQLAlchemySession, MongoDBSession, DaprSession, OpenAIConversationsSession) with clear_session(); EncryptedSession with per-session derived keys and ttl; sandbox Memory() separated by MemoryLayoutConfig

steps.title: Key each session to one case
body: Construct the session with the case ID (for example SQLAlchemySession(case_id, engine=...)), never reuse it for another case, and call clear_session() when the case closes.

steps.title: Encrypt and expire case history
body: Wrap the store in EncryptedSession(session_id, underlying_session, encryption_key, ttl=...) with the master key from your secret manager; items past ttl are skipped on read.

steps.title: Separate sandbox memory by case or tenant
body: Give Memory() a MemoryLayoutConfig per case or tenant (memories_dir, sessions_dir), and use Memory(generate=None) for agents that must not write memory.

controls.note: Partial by this drawing's rule (session objects the deployer scopes): the boundary is the session_id and layout the application picks — a run reads whatever session it is handed, and TypeScript tenant routing is a RunContextAwareSession the deployer writes. Nothing validates what a turn writes: tool results persist in history, and sandbox memory consolidates lessons across every conversation sharing a layout, with live updates to MEMORY.md on by default. ttl skips expired items rather than deleting them; deletion is clear_session() or the store's own TTL (Dapr).

controls.mechanism: OPENAI_API_KEY by default, or set_default_openai_key / set_default_openai_client; a short-lived access token from workload identity federation passed to the client; set_tracing_export_api_key for a separate tracing key; UnixLocalSandboxClient inherit_host_environment=False

steps.title: Replace the standing key with federation
body: Map the workload to a project service account under Organization Settings > Security > Workload Identity Provider and exchange its identity token for a short-lived access token, renewing before expires_at.

steps.title: Hand the brokered credential to the SDK
body: Build an AsyncOpenAI client with that token and install it with set_default_openai_client(client, use_for_tracing=False), then set_tracing_export_api_key for the tracing credential.

steps.title: Keep host secrets out of sandbox commands
body: Create UnixLocalSandboxClient(inherit_host_environment=False) with a host_environment_allowlist, so commands do not inherit the process's keys.

controls.note: Partial by this drawing's rule: the SDK takes whatever key or client the application gives it — by default a standing OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment — and brokers nothing per workload or per step. Federation gives an expiring token with no refresh token, so renewal is the application's code, and whether the default tracing exporter accepts a federated token is not documented (it needs an API key of its own when the model client is not used for tracing). The docs warn that RunContextWrapper.context travels with serialised RunState; TypeScript omits the tracing key from serialised state by default.

controls.mechanism: max_turns (default 10; None disables) raising MaxTurnsExceeded; function-tool timeout and max_function_tool_concurrency; ModelSettings.timeout per model call; usage counted on RunContextWrapper.usage with no budget that stops the run

steps.title: Cap turns on every run
body: Pass max_turns to Runner.run (TypeScript maxTurns) and never None; the run ends with MaxTurnsExceeded or the error_handlers "max_turns" output.

steps.title: Bound tool fan-out and time
body: Set RunConfig.tool_execution=ToolExecutionConfig(max_function_tool_concurrency=N) and @function_tool(timeout=...) on slow tools.

steps.title: Enforce a token budget in a hook
body: In RunHooks.on_llm_end read context.usage and stop the run (raise, or cancel a streamed run) when it passes the run's allowance.

controls.note: Partial by this drawing's rule (max_turns only; no token or cost budget ships). The turn limit counts model calls per run and is on by default; usage (requests, tokens) is tracked but only a hook the deployer writes can act on it, hosted tool and container charges are not in it, and no wall-clock deadline covers the whole run (ModelSettings.timeout bounds one model call; TypeScript can pass AbortSignal.timeout as signal). Quotas and cost ceilings "on the crossing" belong to the AI gateway or the project's budget.

controls.mechanism: Hosted-container ShellTool environment network_policy (disabled or allowlist with allowed_domains, within the org allow list); DockerSandboxClientOptions network_mode "none"; no network control for UnixLocalSandboxClient, function tools or local MCP servers

steps.title: Allowlist the hosted shell
body: Configure ShellTool(environment={"type": "container_auto", "network_policy": {"type": "allowlist", "allowed_domains": [...]}}) with only the package mirror and the hosts the task needs; hosted containers have no outbound access by default.

steps.title: Cut networking in Docker sandboxes
body: Set DockerSandboxClientOptions(network_mode="none") (TypeScript networkMode: 'none'), the only explicit mode supported.

steps.title: Bound the host at the network
body: Run the application, its function tools, local MCP servers and any Unix-local sandbox in a subnet or namespace whose egress proxy allows only the AI gateway and the package mirror.

controls.note: Partial on the same finding as the Claude Agent SDK: a domain allowlist exists only for the OpenAI-hosted container shell, enforced by OpenAI within the org allow list set in the dashboard. Docker sandboxes are on or off, Unix-local adds no network isolation, and the hosted sandbox provider clients document no allowlist. In-process function tools (the local tools this pin sits on), local MCP servers and local ShellTool leave through the host network, which is the deployer's to restrict.

controls.mechanism: Credentials scoped per MCP server (headers), per HostedMCPTool (authorization), per agent model client and per hosted-shell domain (network_policy.domain_secrets); per-user tokens in the run context for function tools; no on-behalf-of exchange or passthrough guard

steps.title: Scope each credential to one server
body: Put each tool credential in that MCP server's headers (an Authorization header, never the URL) rather than the process environment.

steps.title: Bind sandbox secrets to their domain
body: In a hosted-shell allowlist use network_policy.domain_secrets so a secret is injected only for its domain.

steps.title: Keep the host environment out of commands
body: Set inherit_host_environment=False with an explicit host_environment_allowlist on UnixLocalSandboxClient.

controls.note: Partial by this drawing's rule (per-tool credential context). The intersection of requester grant, agent identity, policy and record is the application's: the SDK does not compute it, an MCP server receives whatever token the application put in its headers (no audience check or passthrough guard), function tools run with the process's credentials, and the app context is shared by every agent in a run, nested Agent.as_tool runs included.

controls.mechanism: Built-in tracing, on by default: a trace per run with agent, generation (model input and output), function (tool arguments and results), guardrail and handoff spans, correlated by trace_id and group_id; add_trace_processor / set_trace_processors route spans to the customer's store; trace_include_sensitive_data controls payload capture

steps.title: Send traces to your own store
body: Call set_trace_processors([...]) (TypeScript setTraceProcessors) with your collector's processor — a listed integration or your own exporter — before the first run; add_trace_processor keeps the OpenAI exporter as well.

steps.title: Decide what payload is captured
body: Set trace_include_sensitive_data (OPENAI_AGENTS_TRACE_INCLUDE_SENSITIVE_DATA), True by default, to False where the store is not approved for prompts and tool arguments, or redact inside your own exporter.

steps.title: Correlate runs to the case and principal
body: Set RunConfig group_id to the case ID and trace_metadata to the principal and agent release on each run.

steps.title: Flush before workers exit
body: Call flush_traces() after each job's trace closes so batched spans are exported before a worker is recycled.

controls.note: Native on the rule applied to the Claude Agent SDK: every model call, function-tool call with arguments and results, guardrail and handoff is a span, the whole run is one trace, and a processor sends it to the customer's store. Defaults: on in server runtimes (TypeScript turns it off in browsers and under NODE_ENV=test), exported to OpenAI's Traces dashboard with payloads included, and unavailable to ZDR organisations. No first-party OTLP exporter is documented — export elsewhere uses a third-party processor or the deployer's own. Limits: hosted-tool work appears only inside generation output, session and memory reads and writes are not spans, identity is whatever metadata the application adds, and a processor is an in-process observer, so append-only retention is the collector's.

controls.mechanism: RunResultStreaming.cancel() (immediately or mode "after_turn"); TypeScript signal: AbortSignal on run(); revoking the API key or disabling the workload identity mapping; clear_session() and sandbox session teardown by the application

steps.title: Cancel the running run
body: Call result.cancel() on a streamed run (TypeScript: abort the AbortSignal passed as signal) and keep consuming stream_events() until it finishes.

steps.title: Revoke what it authenticates with
body: Disable the service account's workload identity mapping or revoke the project key the process uses so later model calls fail.

steps.title: Discard what it stored
body: Discard any parked RunState, call clear_session() on its session, and close its sandbox session.

controls.note: Partial by this drawing's rule (in-process cancellation only): the stop is a call by the process that holds the result handle; no runtime or remote cancel exists, and the Python docs document cancel() for streamed runs only. Whether an in-flight function tool, local shell command, MCP call or hosted container stops is not documented. A parked RunState can be resumed by whoever holds it, so quarantine means discarding it. Revoking the key or mapping refuses later model requests only (delay not documented); quarantine from peers and secure deletion are the deployer's steps.

evidence.title: Tools — FileSearchTool retrieves from OpenAI Vector Stores as a hosted tool (2026-09-25)
Agents SDK documentation index, reviewed for applicability (2026-09-25)

controls.note: Not applicable: the SDK has no retrieval corpus or index of its own. FileSearchTool queries OpenAI Vector Stores inside the Responses API, and anything else is a store the application attaches through a function tool or MCP server; ingest trust, per-tenant index isolation and grounding checks belong to that store or the OpenAI API's vector stores. Sandbox memory is covered on AML.M0031.

controls.mechanism: MCP servers declared in code per agent; create_static_tool_filter allowlist or a callable tool_filter that sees each tool definition; require_approval; list_tools() on every run unless cache_tools_list (a latency cache cleared by invalidate_tools_cache()); no hashing or pinning of definitions

steps.title: Admit only named tools
body: Set tool_filter=create_static_tool_filter(allowed_tool_names=[...]) on every MCP server.

steps.title: Refuse redefined tools in a callable filter
body: Pass a callable tool_filter that hashes the name, description and input schema of the tool object it receives and returns False when they differ from the approved value; leave cache_tools_list off.

steps.title: Require approval on write tools
body: Set require_approval with a per-tool map on local servers and "always" on HostedMCPTool for tools that change records.

controls.note: Partial by core rule 1: declared servers and a tool allowlist admit tools by name but verify nothing a server serves, and the docs describe no hashing, pinning or re-approval when a definition changes. A callable tool_filter is the attach point where the deployer can pin definition hashes; it runs for local servers only — HostedMCPTool definitions are listed inside the Responses API. Stdio server versions are whatever command the application starts.

controls.mechanism: None in the SDK; admission scanning at the package mirror or artifact repository the sandbox image and the hosted-shell allowlist point at

evidence.title: Sandbox clients — image choice, Unix-local host execution, hosted providers (2026-09-25)
Tools — hosted shell skills and network_policy allowlist (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External (package firewall or artifact-repository scanning at the mirror): the SDK scans nothing it loads or its agents install — skills load from local directories or skill references, stdio MCP servers start from the command the application gives, and packages a sandbox shell installs come from whatever registry the network allows. Integration points: point the sandbox image's package managers at the scanning mirror and allow only its host in the hosted-shell allowlist and the egress proxy; pin the SDK in the lockfile. No model weights load in the SDK.

ChatGPT web (chatgpt.com)
ChatGPT Work (Work Local and Work Cloud)
Built-in browser (browser_use) and Chrome extension

summary: The current desktop app bundles Chat, Work and Codex, and is governed by the same managed-configuration system as Codex — requirements.toml cloud policies and the com.openai.codex MDM domain — plus workspace admin controls for plugins, apps, memory and identity from the ChatGPT admin panel.

Inference is at OpenAI for every mode. Chat and Work Cloud run entirely on OpenAI infrastructure (Work Cloud in VM-backed sandboxes with a hosted browser whose cookies stay separate from the device); Work Local runs on the desktop app with the Codex sandbox, computer use and the built-in browser, and the vendor states that relevant file excerpts, prompts, screenshots and browser content may be sent to OpenAI to complete a task.

Enterprise administration is role-based (Owner, Admin, Member, Analytics Viewer plus custom roles, with an explicit Off in any role denying), provisioned by SCIM, with plugins and apps off by default on Enterprise and Edu (new workspaces start with a vendor-selected set of apps enabled), per-connection action controls, a GPT actions domain allowlist, access-token lifetime limits, service accounts, and a Compliance API whose records live 30 days at source.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Business, Enterprise and Edu carry the admin controls; apps and plugins default on for Business and off for Enterprise and Edu, except that new Enterprise and Edu workspaces start with a vendor-selected set of apps enabled.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Work Cloud runs the Codex harness in an isolated OpenAI environment; the web cannot access local files, apps or tabs.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Local execution does not mean device-only inference; file excerpts, prompts, screenshots, browser content and tool results may be sent to OpenAI.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: Conversations follow workspace retention settings with deletion scheduled within 30 days; Compliance Logs Platform keeps 30 days; connected-app data follows the source system.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/chatgpt-work-overview (links every admin page)

items.title: Managed deployment and update control
body: Windows ships only as a Store-signed MSIX (no MSI or standalone EXE), deployable via Intune, MECM or winget with offline packages available; macOS deploys from the enterprise DMG, with device management arriving through the com.openai.codex MDM payload rather than a dedicated packaging guide. The built-in updater is disabled with an enforced requirements.toml feature pin, targeted by group, user or platform from the managed-configs console.

items.title: Workspace controls over connectors, apps and memory
body: On Enterprise and Edu workspaces, new plugins and apps are disabled by default (new workspaces start with a vendor-selected set of apps enabled) and enabled per role, with per-app configuration for real-time access, actions, approvals and domain restrictions — one control set that applies across web, mobile, desktop and Codex. Memory and record mode are workspace-level toggles (record off by default), and the Compliance Logs Platform exports immutable audit, authentication and usage events with 30-day source retention, so longer retention requires continuous export.

links.title: Admin controls, security, and compliance for plugins and apps
OpenAI Compliance Platform for Enterprise and Edu customers

riskNotes.note: Shared connections use the connected account's permissions, which the vendor warns may be broader than the individual user's; Work Local ships file excerpts and screenshots.

The hosted and built-in browsers and connected apps feed arbitrary content to the model; OpenAI's screening (MCP content monitoring, link-generation controls, a sign-in review model) is vendor-internal and not admin-tunable, and a Lockdown Mode role cuts exfiltration paths without screening content.
Agent-owned and shared connected accounts act for whoever triggers the task; action control (read-only or a custom set) is the bound.

Plugins can carry MCP servers, hooks and browser extensions from a GitHub marketplace that syncs daily unless pinned to a commit; custom MCP apps stay on the admin-approved tool snapshot until an admin refreshes and republishes them.

controls.mechanism: Admin Console > Global settings > Access > Single Sign-On with the ChatGPT sign-in policy set to Required, verified domains under Access > Domains; MFA itself is enforced by the organisation's IdP

steps.title: Require SSO for the workspace
body: In Admin Console (admin.openai.com) open Global settings > Access > Single Sign-On and, after testing the connection, set the ChatGPT product policy (or the workspace override) to Required; Required applies to members whose email is on a verified domain the policy covers.

steps.title: Verify every sign-in domain
body: Under Global settings > Access > Domains add each exact domain and subdomain, publish the DNS TXT record, select Check Domain, then use Manage eligibility to scope it to the intended workspaces.

steps.title: Enforce MFA in the identity provider
body: ChatGPT doesn't provide workspace-wide MFA enforcement, so require MFA and conditional access on the IdP application behind the SSO connection.

steps.title: Bound the token paths that skip the IdP
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles set Access token expiration limit and grant token creation only to named owners; revoke tokens at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor on this drawing: the product can enforce SSO-only sign-in for verified-domain members (policy Required), so the IdP's MFA governs each interactive login, but MFA lives in the IdP — the MFA article says MFA "cannot currently be enforced at the ChatGPT workspace" level, and the Work admin FAQ says the same. Paths that skip the IdP prompt: invited members from other domains may still use another permitted sign-in method (turning off Allow External Domain Invites stops only new invitations); personal accounts, which the allowed-workspace header rather than SSO keeps off managed networks (see D3-OTF); Codex and Workspace Agent access tokens and service-account tokens (the expiration limit applies to new tokens only); workspace Admin keys, whose expiry can be Never; and existing sessions — switching the policy to Required can sign affected users out, but session lifetime is not documented and a user's Log out of all devices takes up to 30 minutes. Domain claiming (a separate request to OpenAI) also blocks corporate app connections from personal or other workspaces.

original.mechanism: SCIM provisioning, workspace roles and custom roles (Permissions & roles), access-token expiration limit
original.note: SAML/OIDC setup lives in the Help Center, which returned 403 today; the roles model is verified.

steps.title: Provision from the IdP
body: SCIM provisions membership and groups (manually managed or IdP managed); group membership alone grants no feature permission.

steps.title: Assign roles with deny-wins semantics
body: Owner, Admin, Member, Analytics Viewer and custom roles carry Default / On / Off per feature; an explicit Off in any role blocks access.

steps.title: Bound token lifetime
body: Owners set "Access token expiration limit" in Permissions & roles.

controls.mechanism: Workspace settings > Permissions & roles custom roles (Default / On / Off, explicit Off wins) over Work, plugins and apps, developer mode, agents and GPTs; target-tenant admin consent for connector apps (Admin > Plugins > Configure Microsoft permissions to Entra organisation-wide consent, Google Workspace scope authorisation)

steps.title: Model feature access as custom roles
body: Workspace owners create roles under Permissions & roles > Custom roles, assign them to SCIM groups and use Off to deny Work, plugins, developer mode, agent building or publishing and GPT sharing; an explicit Off in any role wins.

steps.title: Grant Microsoft permissions through Entra admin consent
body: In Admin > Plugins select Configure Microsoft permissions, keep only the permissions you intend to grant, then have an Entra administrator grant organisation-wide consent to the verified ChatGPT / OpenAI, L.L.C. application; actions stay off until enabled in ChatGPT.

steps.title: Authorise Google scopes in Google Workspace
body: Have the Google Workspace administrator authorise the Drive, Docs, Sheets and Slides scopes (and domain-wide delegation for administrator-managed sync), or turn off the actions whose scopes you will not grant.

controls.note: Native by the rule applied to every vendor: the console administers role- and group-based authorisation over connectors, agents and features (deny-wins custom roles on SCIM-synced groups), and OpenAI documents the target-tenant consent path for its connector apps — Entra organisation-wide consent to the verified ChatGPT / OpenAI, L.L.C. application for Outlook, Teams and SharePoint, Google Workspace scope authorisation and domain-wide delegation, and Slack admin approval for the ChatGPT Agents app. The target-tenant consent itself is the other tenant's control (Entra, Google Workspace, Slack, GitHub organisation approval); OpenAI does not publish the Entra app ID, so confirm the app identity on the consent screen. Custom roles are Enterprise, Edu and Healthcare only and take about five minutes to apply. Policy administration is not the runtime decision, which OpenAI makes per request.

steps.title: Test with a least-privileged account
body: A member can use an MCP server only when the plugin is available to their role and they have access to the connected service; verify with an account holding only intended permissions.

controls.mechanism: ChatGPT-Allowed-Workspace-Id header injected on https://chatgpt.com/* by the organisation's SASE or TLS-inspecting proxy and enforced by OpenAI; workspace IP allowlisting (inbound) and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces for the desktop app's local runtime

steps.title: Inject the allowed-workspace header
body: Have the SASE or proxy add ChatGPT-Allowed-Workspace-Id with the workspace UUID(s), comma-separated without spaces, to requests for https://chatgpt.com/*; OpenAI filters out every other workspace, personal ones included, and returns 403 when none remain.

steps.title: Block logged-out use and cover the apps
body: Block URLs starting https://chatgpt.com/backend-anon/, and add the proxy's certificates to the desktop and mobile apps' pin list by MDM (the apps pin certificates), or block desktop.chatgpt.com, ios.chat.openai.com and android.chat.openai.com outright.

steps.title: Restrict where the workspace is reachable from
body: Workspace Settings > Identity & access > Access Restrictions, add IP ranges for Workspace and Compliance API, then toggle Activate IP Allowlist (changes take 5-15 minutes).

steps.title: Pin the desktop app's local runtime to the workspace
body: Set allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces = ["<uuid>"] in the system requirements.toml or macOS MDM; both keys are ignored in cloud-managed requirements.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: OpenAI honours a documented allowed-workspace header that the organisation's proxy injects and enforces the block server-side; the SSE only admits the destination, and a pinned session to the approved tenant is not readable. It holds only on traffic the proxy sees and can decrypt — the desktop and mobile apps pin certificates, so devices without the MDM pin exception are outside it. A customer proxy does not control OpenAI's own egress: Work Cloud code and shell (public internet toggle and managed allowlist), the cloud browser, deep research, agent mode and connector calls leave from OpenAI infrastructure; the vendor-side levers are the Work network setting and a Lockdown Mode role (live browsing, agent mode, deep research and file downloads off; Codex unaffected). IP allowlisting limits inbound access to the workspace and Compliance API, not outbound traffic. Work Local commands follow [experimental_network] (experimental); browser use, computer use and MCP are outside it.

original.mechanism: Tenancy pinning in product (allowed_chatgpt_workspaces for the desktop app, IP access restrictions referenced); inline inspection is a third-party SSE
original.note: Comparable to Claude chat: the vendor pins tenancy (allowed_chatgpt_workspaces) and offers workspace IP access restrictions, and the inline inspection is the customer's SSE; rated partial for the same reason.

steps.title: Pin the desktop app to the workspace
body: allowed_chatgpt_workspaces in requirements.toml restricts sign-in to listed workspace UUIDs.

original.mechanism: "Allow public internet access" for Work Cloud code/shell (managed allowlist when off); [experimental_network] for Work Local

steps.title: Turn off public internet for cloud code and shell
body: When disabled, commands reach only required hostnames from a managed allowlist; this controls destinations, not commands.

steps.title: Allowlist domains for local commands
body: [experimental_network] with managed_allowed_domains_only = true; browser tools and MCP are outside it.

original.note: Work Cloud code and shell follow the managed allowlist when public internet access is off; Work Local commands follow [experimental_network]. Browser, computer use and connector traffic are outside both and need a network-layer control.

controls.mechanism: SharePoint app Safety & Security Controls > Excluded sensitivity labels without encryption (label-based restriction); no in-product inspection of prompts, uploads or responses in Chat or Work

steps.title: Exclude labelled SharePoint files
body: In the SharePoint app's Safety & Security Controls enter each non-encrypting Microsoft Purview label GUID under Excluded sensitivity labels without encryption; files with encrypting labels are already excluded.

steps.title: Inspect prompts at the endpoint or browser
body: Apply endpoint, browser or SSE DLP inline to chatgpt.com; the desktop and mobile apps need the proxy certificate added to their pin list by MDM before SSL inspection works.

steps.title: Scan conversations after the fact
body: Have a workspace owner create an Admin key with Conversation messages and app-log access and feed the Compliance Logs Platform to a DLP partner such as Microsoft Purview, Netskope, Cyberhaven, Forcepoint or Palo Alto Networks.

controls.note: Partial only by the label-restriction clause of the rule applied to every vendor: the SharePoint sensitivity-label exclusion, enforced by OpenAI, keeps labelled files out of SharePoint app results (supported Office, PDF and MP4 files; TXT and CSV are treated as unlabelled; OneDrive is separate). Nothing in Chat or Work detects identifiers, secrets or classified content in what an employee types or uploads, in connector payloads or in responses, and nothing masks them; Prisma AIRS external guardrails scan Codex prompts only. The pin's objective — classification before material leaves the person — is met by endpoint or browser DLP inline; Compliance Logs Platform partners scan conversations after they reach OpenAI (detection after the fact, 30-day source window). Action controls, parameter constraints, deny_read and allow_appshots limit where data can go or what the agent can read but inspect nothing.

original.mechanism: Action control per connection and requirements.toml deny_read / allow_appshots
original.note: In-product controls limit what agents can reach and screenshot; nothing inspects prompt or upload content.

steps.title: Limit what connections may do
body: Action control allows read-only, all or a custom set of actions per connection.

steps.title: Stop screenshots and secret reads on the desktop
body: allow_appshots = false and [permissions.filesystem] deny_read in requirements.toml.

original.mechanism: Managed browser controls for the built-in browser (origins, uploads, downloads, developer access; browser_use flags)
original.note: Covers the agent's browser, not the employee's browser session on chatgpt.com. Rated partial for the managed agent browser only; the employee's own browser on chatgpt.com is secured by the organisation's browser tooling, which is external here as for every other chat SaaS.

steps.title: Restrict the built-in browser
body: Set [features] browser_use and browser_use_full_cdp_access = false, or use the managed browser controls to restrict origins, uploads, downloads and developer access.

controls.mechanism: Vendor-operated screening of returned content (online and offline monitoring of MCP content for prompt injection, policy screening of MCP prompts, known-malicious-domain blocking, link-generation controls, a cloud-browser sign-in review model); none of it is admin-configurable

steps.title: Verify the vendor's returned-content defenses
body: Assess the app and MCP safeguards the App security whitepaper describes (injection monitoring, malicious-domain blocking, link-generation controls) and record that no admin toggle, threshold or detection event exists for them.

steps.title: Limit untrusted MCP sources
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles > Connected Data grant Developer mode / Create custom MCP connectors only to vetted builders; only admins and owners can publish a custom app.

steps.title: Put high-risk groups in a Lockdown Mode role
body: Designate a custom role as a Lockdown Mode role and assign the groups that handle sensitive data, which turns off live browsing, agent mode and deep research; it limits exfiltration and does not screen content.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: OpenAI documents vendor-internal screening of returned content — online and offline monitoring for prompt injection originating from MCP servers, policy screening of MCP prompts, blocking of known malicious domains, link-generation controls against URL-based exfiltration and a review model on cloud-browser sign-in pages — but none of it can be switched on, tuned or set to block by the admin, and no detection event is a documented Compliance Logs Platform type. Lockdown Mode cuts outbound paths and, per the vendor, does not prevent prompt injections from appearing in the content ChatGPT processes; Auto approve and Allow low-risk actions classify actions, not input; the frozen tool snapshot of custom MCP apps guards definitions, not results; Prisma AIRS (Codex only) screens prompts, not tool results. Records read through the organisation's own MCP tier can be classified by its gateway (the drawing's second pin).

original.mechanism: Sign-in review model in the built-in browser, automated risk checks on Auto approve, safety review pauses

steps.title: Know what the vendor checks
body: A review model checks sign-in requests for phishing or deception; the feature is tested against prompt injection.

original.note: Vendor-operated review on browser sign-in and Auto approve actions; page and file content the assistant reads is not classified for injected instructions, and nothing is customer-tunable.

controls.mechanism: Vendor evidence from the OpenAI Trust Portal and the App security and Workspace agents security papers, consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

evidence.title: OpenAI Trust Portal (SafeBase) — SOC 2 Type 2, SOC 3, ISO/IEC 27001/27017/27018/27701 and 42001, CSA STAR, PCI DSS, FedRAMP 20x, pentest report, subprocessors and DPA (2026-09-25)
App security whitepaper (June 2026)
Workspace agents security overview

controls.note: External by the rule applied to every vendor: the assessment runs in the organisation's TPRM platform. The portal describes itself as covering ChatGPT Enterprise and Edu and lists SOC 2 Type 2 (the 2026 report covers 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026 and needs an authenticated account), SOC 3, ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, 27018, 27701 and 42001, CSA STAR, PCI DSS, TX-RAMP, FedRAMP 20x, a pentest report, data-flow diagram, CAIQ and HECVAT, the subprocessor list and the DPA; most reports require an access request. Re-assess on the vendor's release clock: new Enterprise workspaces start with a vendor-selected set of apps enabled, Work is on by default for the default role on eligible workspaces, and custom GPTs retire for Enterprise on 2026-12-11 in favour of plugins. Custom MCP servers and third-party apps sit outside OpenAI's trust boundary and need their own assessment.

body: SOC 2 / SOC 3 reports, pen-test reports, subprocessor list and DPA are on the trust portal.

controls.mechanism: Workspace settings > General > Plugin permissions (workspace default) and per-app Permissions in Admin > Plugins (Always ask, Allow read actions, Allow low-risk actions, Allow all actions); Workspace Agent write approvals set by each agent's builder; persistent-approval keys under [computer_use] and [browser_use] in requirements.toml

steps.title: Set the workspace default to ask before changes
body: In Workspace settings > General > Settings > Plugin permissions select Always ask or Allow read actions; the workspace-wide selector does not offer Allow all actions.

steps.title: Keep write-capable apps off Allow all actions
body: In Admin > Plugins open each included app's Permissions control and keep Workspace default or Always ask; never select Allow all actions for an app that can write.

steps.title: Stop saved approvals on the desktop
body: In requirements.toml set [computer_use] allow_persistent_approval = false, [browser_use] allow_global_persistent_approval = false with persistent_approval = false per origin, and browser_use.disable_auto_review = true.

steps.title: Restrict who publishes agents that write
body: In Permissions & roles grant Enable agent publishing and Enable agent publishing with agent-owned connections only to reviewed builders, because each agent's builder sets its write approvals.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: a person approves app actions on a card that shows the app and the proposed action, the admin decides when ChatGPT asks (workspace default plus a per-app override), and managed-workspace members are not offered Always allow as a persistent approval for app actions. Below native because the requirement is set per app, not per action; Allow low-risk actions lets ChatGPT's own risk evaluation auto-approve what it deems low risk (an automated reviewer), and the approval card can offer members Allow low-risk actions for future calls on the same connected account — whether a workspace Always ask policy suppresses that choice is not stated; Workspace Agents' write approvals (Always ask by default, or Never ask or Custom) are set by the builder, not the admin, and scheduled or event-triggered runs execute without the requester present; Computer Use, Apple Messages (Always allow sending to this chat) and the local browser save user approvals unless the device carries the requirements.toml keys; cloud-browser website access has an Auto approve risk check, though admins can remove Always allow workspace-wide. Some risky actions are denied rather than prompted. Binding an approval to the exact arguments, and voiding it if they change, is not documented.

original.mechanism: App permissions (when ChatGPT asks before using a connection), website approval levels, per-app computer-use approval

steps.title: Require confirmation on connections
body: App permissions decide when ChatGPT asks before using a connection; start with read actions.

steps.title: Limit website approval levels
body: Always ask, Auto approve, Always allow; administrators can limit which levels users may select.

steps.title: Keep computer use per-app
body: ChatGPT asks before using each application; "Always allow" is per app and listed under Always-allowed apps.

controls.mechanism: App Disable in Admin > Plugins (ends every grant to an app), APP_AUTH_LOG link and unlink events in the Compliance Logs Platform, the admin agent list, and Codex service accounts; per-grant disconnect is the user's action

steps.title: Build the grant inventory from the log
body: Pull APP_AUTH_LOG (link or unlink, link_id, actor) from the Compliance Logs Platform with an Admin key holding the Apps Auth log scope and keep the grant inventory in the identity-governance tool.

steps.title: End every grant to an app
body: In Admin > Plugins select Disable on the app or remove its role access; the vendor lists an administrator toggling an app off as a trigger for token revocation and deletion.

steps.title: Give automation its own identity
body: Create a Codex service account per workflow with a finite token ttl under one year; disabling or deleting the account revokes all of its tokens.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: connector grants are per-user OAuth links, or an agent-owned shared connection in a Workspace Agent, held by OpenAI; the admin can end all grants to an app by disabling it and sees link and unlink events, but neither the console nor the Admin API lists each user's live grants with a per-grant revoke — disconnecting an individual account is the user's action — and no admin-set grant expiry exists (per the App security whitepaper, refresh credentials last until user deletion, an app toggled off or lost upstream permission). The user-lifecycle guide tells admins to review connected apps separately after removing someone, so deprovisioning alone is not the documented revocation. Agent-owned connections act with the connected account's permissions for everyone who runs the agent; the admin console lists agents with their connected apps. Codex service accounts are the only first-class non-human principals; Chat and Work actions carry the member's identity.

original.mechanism: Service accounts and workload identity federation

steps.title: Create service accounts for automation
body: Owners and admins create them; roles User / Configure / Manager; SCIM userType "ServiceAccount".

steps.title: Federate short-lived tokens
body: OIDC or SPIFFE tokens exchange for workspace tokens capped at one hour; disabling a rule revokes issued tokens.

original.note: Service accounts and federated workload identities are principals for automation against the workspace APIs; chat and agent actions on a member's behalf carry the member's identity, not a distinct agent principal.

controls.mechanism: Administrator-managed sync source selection (SharePoint sites or folders, Google Drive shared drives or folders), the Admin > Plugins app list and public-catalog CSV export; classification and oversharing analysis by DSPM partners reading the Compliance Platform

steps.title: Choose exactly what is indexed
body: When setting up Indexed search for an app in Admin > Plugins, select the specific sites, folders or shared drives to include rather than all supported content.

steps.title: Export the app catalogue for review
body: In Admin > Plugins select Public, then Export CSV (public-plugins-security-review.csv) to list each plugin with its MCP servers and skills.

steps.title: Classify what sits behind the connectors
body: Feed the Compliance Platform to a DSPM partner such as Varonis, Concentric AI, Microsoft Purview or Teleskope and run oversharing analysis in the source system before enabling sync.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the product lists the connected sources — which apps are enabled and which sites, folders or drives the administrator-managed index covers — but does not inventory or classify the content behind them or report oversharing; the assistant surfaces whatever the source permissions already allow. Live, non-synced connections retrieve on demand from anything the user's account can reach, so the index scope does not bound them. Retention settings and the Compliance API's 30-day window are lifecycle controls, not inventory. DSPM products (Compliance Platform partners) or the source system's own data-security tooling classify content and find the oversharing.

original.mechanism: Workspace retention settings, Compliance API 30-day window, HIPAA configuration

steps.title: Set retention and export
body: Conversations follow workspace settings with deletion within 30 days; export compliance records before the 30-day source window lapses.

steps.title: Apply the regulated-workspace profile where PHI is possible
body: Keep [mcp_servers] empty by default, restrict sign-in with allowed_login_methods, and do not use Codex cloud with PHI.

original.note: Retention and the Compliance API window are lifecycle controls; discovery, classification and exposure assessment of workspace content are the customer's DSPM product reading the Compliance API.

controls.mechanism: OpenAI-held connector OAuth tokens (encrypted, never in model context), workspace Admin keys (scoped, expiry 30-365 days or Never, revocable) and the Access token expiration limit for Codex and Workspace Agent tokens; no tunnel in this product

steps.title: Scope and expire Admin keys
body: In Admin Console open the workspace's Credentials > Admin keys, choose Custom permissions and a 30, 60, 90-day or custom expiration up to 365 days instead of the Never default, and revoke keys no longer used.

steps.title: Cap access-token lifetime
body: In Permissions & roles set Access token expiration limit; revoke tokens at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens.

steps.title: Revoke connector credentials in bulk
body: Disable the app in Admin > Plugins to trigger revocation and deletion of its stored tokens; the admin cannot rotate or expire them individually.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: connector refresh credentials are held by OpenAI, encrypted at rest (AES-256 under Azure Key Vault keys, EKM-capable), minted into short-lived access tokens per call and never placed in prompts, per the App security whitepaper; the admin can revoke them only in bulk by disabling an app and cannot bound their lifetime or rotation. Admin keys are scoped and revocable, but an owner can still create one with no expiry and existing expirations cannot be changed; the access-token expiration limit bounds new Codex and Workspace Agent tokens only. This product has no tunnel of its own: the drawing's tunnel credential belongs to Secure MCP Tunnel (toolOpenaiMcpTunnel) and is rated there. mTLS to custom MCP servers uses an OpenAI-managed client certificate.

original.mechanism: Access-token expiration limit, service-account token lifetime (maximum one year), federation

steps.title: Bound and rotate tokens
body: Tokens require an expiry at creation; owners set the workspace-wide limit; treat tokens as automation secrets.

original.note: Token lifetime limits bound how long a stored credential works; nothing issues per-request credentials. Connector tokens are held by OpenAI and never shown to the model.

controls.mechanism: Permissions & roles > Custom roles > Plugins & connected data (apps per role), Admin > Plugins app Actions (read, write and individual actions; New actions set to Disable new actions), admin-only publishing of custom MCP apps with a frozen tool snapshot, GPT actions domain allowlist

steps.title: Allow apps per role
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles > Custom roles open the role, turn on Allow members to use plugins under Plugins & connected data and use Select to choose its apps.

steps.title: Scope each app's actions
body: In Admin > Plugins open the app's Actions, enable only the Read or Write actions needed and set New actions to Disable new actions so later actions wait for admin review.

steps.title: Gate custom MCP servers
body: Grant Developer mode / Create custom MCP connectors only to vetted builders; only admins and owners publish, choosing actions with Configure Actions and groups with Configure Access, and tool changes need Refresh and republish.

steps.title: Constrain GPT actions until GPTs retire
body: In Workspace settings > GPTs > Actions allow only approved domains; with no domains listed, custom GPT actions cannot execute.

controls.note: Native by the rule applied to every vendor: the admin allowlists apps (off by default apart from the vendor-selected set in new workspaces), assigns them per role and scopes each app's read, write and individual actions, enforced server-side by OpenAI across Chat, Work, deep research and plugins; custom MCP servers need an admin to publish them. Action scoping is per app for the whole workspace, not per role; Workspace Agent builders can narrow further with per-agent actions and Connector Action Constraints but cannot exceed what the admin enabled. Argument-level limits are SharePoint site-collection lists and the parameter constraints the App security whitepaper describes; otherwise the connector's own OAuth scope bounds the call. MCP servers configured locally in the desktop app follow requirements.toml, not these workspace controls. Custom GPTs retire for Enterprise on 2026-12-11.

original.mechanism: Admin > Plugins availability per role, action control per connection, GPT actions domain allowlist

steps.title: Enable plugins per role
body: Plugins are off by default on Enterprise and Edu; limit availability to a role or pilot group in Admin > Plugins.

steps.title: Restrict GPT actions to approved domains
body: If no domains are allowed, custom GPT actions cannot execute (Administration > Workspace access, policy, and models > GPTs and Sharing).

original.note: Plugin availability hides tools per role; action control per connection gates; the GPT actions domain allowlist limits destinations. No argument-level scoping inside a connector beyond its own authorisation.

controls.mechanism: Retrieval with each user's provider permissions (live OAuth apps; administrator-managed index with replicated ACLs), SharePoint app Safety & Security Controls site-collection allowlist or deny list, administrator-managed sync source selection

steps.title: Restrict SharePoint to approved site collections
body: In the SharePoint app's Safety & Security Controls choose Access mode Allowed sites and add the site-collection GUIDs (UI, CSV or the Admin API with an Apps-write Admin key); the rule covers search, browsing, retrieval and actions.

steps.title: Scope the administrator-managed index
body: When setting up Indexed search select the SharePoint sites or folders or Google Drive shared drives or folders to include; each member retrieves only what their provider permissions allow.

steps.title: Keep shared agents on the caller's identity
body: Grant Enable agent publishing with agent-owned connections only to reviewed builders so published agents authenticate each end user rather than a shared account.

controls.note: Native by the rule applied to every vendor: retrieval runs with the requesting user's provider permissions — live apps call the source with the user's OAuth grant, and the administrator-managed index replicates source ACLs and filters results per member — and the admin restricts what may be returned (SharePoint site-collection allow or deny lists, enforced by OpenAI before results reach the model; sync source selection). Boundaries: the site controls need enabling for the workspace and cover whole site collections, not subsites, folders or OneDrive; index scope does not restrict a separately enabled live connection; permission changes reach the index only on refresh; administrator-managed SharePoint sync reads ACLs with a broad Microsoft grant (Sites.FullControl.All); for other apps the connector's OAuth scope is the only corpus bound; agent-owned or shared connections retrieve with the connected account's permissions, which the vendor warns can exceed the requester's. Oversharing analysis of indexed repositories is not provided (see D3-DI).

original.mechanism: Connected-service permissions govern retrieval; source-system permission mapping
original.note: Shared connections use the connected account's permissions, potentially broader than the user's.

steps.title: Test with a least-privileged account
body: A member can use an MCP server only when the plugin is available to their role and they have access to the connected service; verify with an account holding only intended permissions.

controls.mechanism: Admin > Plugins catalogue (apps off by default; admin-published custom MCP apps pinned to a tool snapshot) and the Stateful Compliance API List Workspace Plugins, List Workspace Agents and List GPTs

steps.title: Pull the inventory by API
body: With an Admin key call List Workspace Plugins (creator, marketplace, version, installation policy, status), List Workspace Agents (owner, status; draft-only agents excluded) and List GPTs.

steps.title: Keep the connector catalogue in allowlist mode
body: Leave new apps disabled, enable each one deliberately in Admin > Plugins, and publish custom MCP apps only after review; an approved app keeps its tool snapshot until an admin refreshes it.

steps.title: Limit third-party GPTs and agent publishing
body: In Permissions & roles allow only owner-approved third-party GPTs and grant Enable agent publishing only to reviewed builders.

steps.title: Record owner and approval yourself
body: For each connected service record the business owner, approved actions, authentication method and removal contact, as the Plugin controls guide instructs.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: enforcement exists — apps are off by default on Enterprise and Edu (new workspaces start with a vendor-selected set enabled), only admins publish custom MCP apps and a published app stays on its approved tool snapshot, and third-party GPTs can be limited to owner-approved ones — and the Admin API lists workspace plugins, agents and GPTs with creator or owner. Missing is an owner-and-approval record on the same entry: public-directory apps carry the developer's name, not an organisational owner (the vendor tells admins to keep that record themselves), and Workspace Agents and custom GPTs carry an owner and a publication status but no admin approval — a member holding the building and publishing permissions ships one without review. Draft-only agents are absent from the API list, and nothing reconciles connectors found outside the workspace. Custom GPTs retire for Enterprise on 2026-12-11.

original.mechanism: Admin > Plugins (marketplace import and sync) and the GPT management dashboard

steps.title: Manage the plugin catalogue
body: Import a GitHub marketplace, sync daily, mark plugins Available or Installed per role, and flag "No longer in source".

steps.title: Inventory GPTs
body: The dashboard shows builder, custom actions, who can access, activity and ownership for every workspace GPT.

controls.mechanism: Nothing in the product lists personal accounts on verified domains; SSE or CASB discovery of chatgpt.com use, with the allowed-workspace header, domain claiming and automatic account creation as prevention and enrolment

controls.note: External by the rule applied to every vendor: no page documents a report of personal or unmanaged ChatGPT accounts on the organisation's verified domains. Automatic account creation invites verified-domain users into the workspace when they sign in (enrolment, not discovery); domain claiming, by request to OpenAI, blocks corporate app connections from personal or other workspaces; the ChatGPT-Allowed-Workspace-Id header refuses other workspaces and anonymous use on managed networks — prevention, credited here only. Finding personal accounts, other AI chat tenants and unsanctioned connectors is the SSE or CASB's job (chatgpt.com, backend-anon and the app hostnames in proxy logs), with endpoint inventory for the desktop app.

original.mechanism: None in product beyond workspace pinning of the desktop app

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for the integration point (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: Compliance Logs Platform (immutable JSONL: conversation messages, APP_LOG request and response, APP_AUTH_LOG, audit, auth, Workspace Agent and Codex events) pulled with a workspace Admin key; 30-day source retention

steps.title: Create an Admin key for log export
body: In Admin Console open the workspace's Credentials > Admin keys; a workspace owner grants Conversation messages plus the audit, authentication and app log categories.

steps.title: Collect continuously
body: Run download_compliance_files.sh or .ps1 (or the List Files and Download File endpoints) per event type into the SIEM before the 30-day source window lapses.

steps.title: Pin the collector's addresses
body: IP allowlisting is always enforced for Compliance API keys; add the collector's egress IPs under Identity & access > Access Restrictions.

controls.note: Native by the rule applied to every vendor: the Compliance Logs Platform exports conversation messages and connector and tool events — APP_LOG records the request payload and normalised response of each app call, APP_AUTH_LOG each link and unlink, and Workspace Agent logs carry run, connector-call, trigger and memory events — as immutable JSONL files with a p99 target under 30 minutes, ready to fuse with the organisation's gateway record. Boundaries: 30 days at source with no backfill; the vendor says the export does not establish a complete trail for every hosted shell command, browser interaction, file operation or approval; Work Local, Computer Use and Chrome-extension actions are not fully recorded (local OpenTelemetry is a separate opt-in path); app-log coverage varies by app. Capture only: tamper resistance and retention beyond 30 days are the receiving store's.

original.mechanism: Compliance API (30-day source retention) and workspace analytics
original.note: Not every local file operation, screenshot or Chrome-extension action appears in the Compliance API.

steps.title: Export continuously
body: Use COMPLIANCE_API_KEY against the Admin API; the source window does not replace your retention policy.

controls.mechanism: Permissions & roles Off for Work Cloud, Work Local and Enable agents; app Disable in Admin > Plugins; Unpublish or Delete Workspace Agent and Delete User Automation on the Admin API; access-token and service-account revocation

steps.title: Turn the agent surfaces off
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles set Work Cloud, Work Local and Enable agents to Off for the affected roles; an explicit Off in any role denies.

steps.title: Revoke connector access in bulk
body: In Admin > Plugins select Disable on each affected app; turning an app off triggers revocation of its stored tokens.

steps.title: Stop agents and scheduled tasks
body: Call Unpublish Workspace Agent or Delete Workspace Agent and Delete User Automation on the Admin API, or use the agent area of the admin console.

steps.title: Revoke automation credentials
body: Revoke tokens at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens and disable service accounts, which revokes all of their tokens.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the admin can switch the agent surfaces off org-wide, revoke connector grants in bulk by disabling apps, unpublish or delete agents and delete scheduled tasks, but no page says a Work task, agent run or deep research already in progress stops. Documented timings are custom-role changes in about five minutes, IdP sync every 30 to 40 minutes (it cannot be forced), IP allowlist 5 to 15 minutes, and a Work network change after the current command finishes; the delay for stopping running work is not documented. Removing local Codex permission suspends tokens without revoking them, and per-user grant revocation is the user's action. Measure the stop before relying on it.

original.mechanism: Role Off for Work Local / Work Cloud / plugins, token revocation, service-account disable

steps.title: Turn surfaces off by role
body: Work Cloud and Work Local are distinct toggles in Permissions & roles; plugins can be made unavailable in Admin > Plugins.

steps.title: Revoke credentials
body: Owners and admins revoke any token; disabling a service account revokes all of its tokens.

original.note: Role and token changes apply at the next request; an in-flight request completes. The docs state no propagation delay, so measure it before relying on it.

Codex IDE extension (openai.chatgpt)
Codex app (ChatGPT desktop, macOS / Windows / Linux)
Codex Remote (phone controls the local app)
