summary: One agent across the CLI, the IDE extension and the ChatGPT desktop app, configured through TOML with a documented precedence chain and a genuine enterprise enforcement layer: an admin-authored requirements.toml that constrains approval policies, sandbox profiles, network, MCP servers and feature flags, and that users cannot override.

Inference runs at OpenAI; the local runtime executes commands inside an OS sandbox (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap plus seccomp on Linux, a native Windows sandbox) and sends prompts, file excerpts, command output and — when browser or computer use is on — screenshots and page content to OpenAI services. Work Local is explicit that "local execution does not mean offline or device-only model inference". Structured OTel export is opt-in; a separate anonymous usage and health ping to OpenAI is on by default.

Policy arrives by four channels with a fixed precedence (macOS MDM com.openai.codex, the cloud-managed requirements bundle assigned at chatgpt.com, /etc/codex/requirements.toml or %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml, then managed_config.toml defaults). A cloud bundle that cannot be fetched and has no cache stops the client rather than starting unmanaged. Codex Remote, the GitHub Action and Codex Security are shells of the same runtime; Codex cloud and the SDK are separate entities below.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Codex is in Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu; API-key sign-in pays per token and loses cloud features (GitHub reviews, Slack). Business, Enterprise and Edu add admin controls, Compliance API audit and spend limits.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Model calls go to OpenAI; chatgpt_base_url and model_providers.<id>.base_url can redirect to a proxy, and "Codex respects workspace residency settings when you sign in with ChatGPT".

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Prompts, relevant file excerpts, screenshots, browser content and tool results may be sent to OpenAI to complete a task; not every local file operation, screenshot or browser action appears in the Compliance API.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: learn.chatgpt.com/docs (Codex, configuration, enterprise, security sections)

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Workspace audit records are retained up to 30 days for the Compliance API; the BAA does not cover Codex cloud. API-key usage falls under the API data policy (no training by default, 30-day abuse-monitoring logs, ZDR by approval).

items.title: Admin-enforced requirements.toml
body: Requirements arrive by system file (/etc/codex/requirements.toml on Unix, %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml on Windows), as a cloud-managed policy bundle assigned from chatgpt.com and delivered at sign-in, or via macOS MDM under com.openai.codex (base64-encoded TOML; the highest-precedence channel). If the cloud policy fetch fails with no valid cache, the client refuses to start unmanaged rather than failing open.

Enforceable keys cover the surfaces that matter: allowed_approval_policies and allowed_permission_profiles with default_permissions (e.g. pin ":workspace" and allow only read-only and workspace profiles), filesystem deny_read patterns for secrets paths, prefix command rules, managed hooks with allow_managed_hooks_only, experimental network domain allow/deny lists, and feature pins that disable computer use and browser surfaces org-wide.

items.title: Sandbox, approvals and network posture
body: Sandboxing is OS-enforced (Seatbelt on macOS, bwrap plus seccomp on Linux, a native Windows sandbox) with permission profiles from read-only through workspace-write to an explicit danger-full-access escape hatch. The agent runs with network access off by default; enabling it can route through a domain-filtering proxy, and .git, .codex and .agents stay read-only inside writable roots. Codex cloud blocks internet access during the agent phase by default, with per-environment allowlists and method restrictions.

items.title: Workspace gating and compliance export
body: Workspace admins gate Codex Local (desktop app, CLI and IDE extension together) and Codex cloud separately, assign access by role with SCIM-synced groups, and set starting model defaults — enforced requirements still win. Codex usage, including the local clients, exports through the Compliance API and the immutable Compliance Logs Platform alongside workspace audit and authentication logs.

links.title: Using Codex with your ChatGPT plan

riskNotes.note: The vendor's own guidance says prompt injection can make the agent fetch and follow untrusted instructions when network access or web search is on; the 2026 web.run research chained exactly that into out-of-sandbox execution on Windows.
--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox (--yolo) removes both boundaries; the admin answer is allowed_approval_policies and allowed_sandbox_modes in requirements.toml, which users cannot loosen.
Plugins bundle MCP servers, skills and hooks from Git marketplaces; without marketplaces.restrict_to_allowed_sources and an [mcp_servers] identity allowlist any developer can add a tool source.
Three 2026 sandbox findings (git show allowlist, Docker socket, ProgramData config trust) were escapes through components the sandbox trusted, not model failures.
File excerpts, screenshots and browser content leave the device on every task; deny_read globs and shell_environment_policy are the only in-product data minimisation.

controls.mechanism: allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces in the system requirements.toml or macOS MDM (cloud-managed values are ignored); MFA itself is enforced by the organisation's SSO IdP

steps.title: Pin every client to the org workspace
body: In /etc/codex/requirements.toml, %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml or MDM com.openai.codex requirements_toml_base64, set allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces = ["<workspace-uuid>"]; Codex ignores both keys in cloud-managed requirements and refuses to start when no permitted login remains.

steps.title: Enforce MFA in the identity provider
body: ChatGPT has no workspace-wide MFA enforcement, so require SSO with MFA at the IdP and manage SSO in the Global Admin Console.

steps.title: Bound the token paths that skip the IdP
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles grant "Allow users to create personal access tokens" only to named owners and set "Access token expiration limit"; revoke tokens at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens.

steps.title: Leave device-code login off unless needed
body: codex login --device-auth works only after a workspace admin enables device code login in ChatGPT workspace permissions.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: Codex pins the local client to the org's ChatGPT workspace, so the IdP's MFA policy governs each interactive browser sign-in, but MFA is configured in the IdP, not the product — the admin FAQ states ChatGPT doesn't provide workspace-wide MFA enforcement (Codex cloud requires MFA only for email-and-password accounts). Paths that skip the IdP prompt: Platform API keys (blocked by allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"]; "api" also admits Amazon Bedrock), Codex access tokens and service-account tokens (bounded by the expiration limit for new tokens only; the page warns an earlier dialog can offer No expiration), cached ChatGPT credentials that refresh automatically (lifetime not documented), device-code login (admin-enabled) and workload identity. Personal accounts are refused by allowed_chatgpt_workspaces, which also applies to access tokens. The pin holds only on machines that carry the system file or MDM payload; whether SSO-only sign-in can be enforced is on Help Center pages that returned 403.

original.mechanism: requirements.toml forced_login_method / forced_chatgpt_workspace_id (config) and allowed_login_methods / allowed_chatgpt_workspaces (managed), plus workspace roles and SCIM groups

steps.title: Pin the sign-in method and workspace
body: Set forced_login_method = "chatgpt" and forced_chatgpt_workspace_id = "<uuid>" so the client cannot run on a personal account or an API key.

steps.title: Enforce it from the managed bundle
body: In requirements.toml use allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces as the UUID allowlist; deliver by MDM, cloud policy or the system path.

steps.title: Gate Codex Local by role
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles, set the Codex Local / Work Local permission per role; an explicit Off in any role denies even when another grants.

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [rules] prefix_rules (decision "prompt" or "forbidden") and a managed [hooks] PreToolUse hook with allow_managed_hooks_only = true and [features].hooks = true

steps.title: Enforce restrictive command rules
body: In requirements.toml add [rules] prefix_rules with decision "forbidden" or "prompt" (requirements rules can't allow); they merge with .rules files and the most restrictive decision wins.

steps.title: Deploy a managed PreToolUse hook
body: Define [[hooks.PreToolUse]] in requirements.toml with hooks.managed_dir, set allow_managed_hooks_only = true and [features].hooks = true, and ship the script by MDM (Codex doesn't distribute it).

steps.title: Deny from the hook
body: Return permissionDecision "deny" (or exit code 2); matchers cover Bash, apply_patch, MCP tool names and other local function tools, not hosted tools such as WebSearch.

steps.title: Test the rule set
body: Run codex execpolicy check --rules <file> -- <command> to see the strictest decision and the matching rules before deploying.

controls.note: Partial: the declarative [rules] layer covers shell command prefixes only (the Rules page frames it as controlling commands run outside the sandbox), and the only per-call gate over files and MCP tools is the organisation's own hook script. The vendor says hosted tools skip the hook path, "some specialized tool paths can opt out" and hooks are "a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary"; a PreToolUse "ask" is not supported and fails open (the call continues), so escalate-to-human exists only through prompt rules for shell prefixes. Enforced on the device by the Codex runtime from requirements.toml, which users can't override; decisions reach the org's collector as codex.tool_decision only when OTel export is configured. The Guardian auto-review is a classifier, not a rule. What an allowed MCP server does downstream is outside.

original.mechanism: requirements.toml [rules] (forbidden / prompt) and managed [hooks] with allow_managed_hooks_only

steps.title: Write managed command rules
body: Add [rules] entries in requirements.toml with decision "forbidden" or "prompt" for command prefixes; users cannot weaken them.

steps.title: Add a PreToolUse or PermissionRequest hook
body: A managed hook returning permissionDecision "deny" (or exit code 2) blocks the call; set allow_managed_hooks_only = true so user, project and plugin hooks are ignored.

original.note: [rules] forbidden entries are deterministic; managed hooks are an integration point. The Guardian reviewer is a classifier, not a rule. MCP tool calls pass the rules; a server's own actions are outside them.

controls.mechanism: Vendor evidence from the OpenAI trust portal consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

evidence.title: OpenAI Trust Portal (SafeBase) — SOC 2, ISO, pen-test and subprocessor artifacts (2026-09-25)
OpenAI Trust Portal — Security Whitepaper, linked from the Codex docs as the Codex security white paper

controls.note: External: the assessment runs in the organisation's TPRM platform. The trust portal lists a SOC 2 Type 2 report (described as covering the ChatGPT and API products), ISO 27001, 27017, 27018 and 27701 and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certifications, a Pentest Report, CSA STAR Level 1, the subprocessor list and a Security Whitepaper; most reports require an access request. Codex is not named as its own SOC 2 scope, so the assessment inherits the ChatGPT scope. API-key sign-in moves Codex under the API organisation's data terms instead of the workspace's.

original.mechanism: Vendor evidence from trust.openai.com consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform
original.note: OpenAI publishes SOC 2 Type 2 (scope includes API Platform, ChatGPT Enterprise, Edu and Team), ISO 27001/27017/27018/27701/42001, pen-test reports and the subprocessor list on the trust portal; Codex is not named separately, so the assessment inherits the ChatGPT Enterprise scope.

steps.title: Pull vendor evidence
body: Request the SOC 2 report, pen-test summary and subprocessor list from the trust portal and load them into the TPRM record.

controls.mechanism: Prisma AIRS under Codex Data controls > External guardrails (prompt scanning, Block mode) and managed UserPromptSubmit / PreToolUse hooks; deny_read and shell_environment_policy are minimisation only

steps.title: Connect Prisma AIRS as the prompt inspector
body: In Codex Data controls (chatgpt.com/codex/cloud/settings/data) > External guardrails > Prisma AIRS, save the key, security profile and endpoint, choose Enforcement mode Block and On AIRS failure Block prompts, then turn on Enable Prisma AIRS.

steps.title: Close the uncovered sign-in path
body: Set allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces in the system requirements.toml or MDM, because sessions signed in with a Platform API key are not scanned.

steps.title: Inspect prompts and tool arguments in managed hooks
body: A managed UserPromptSubmit hook can block a prompt and a PreToolUse hook can deny a Bash, apply_patch or MCP call after the org's own detector reads it.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: Codex hands content to an inspector the organisation runs rather than detecting it itself. Prisma AIRS scans newly submitted prompt text across the desktop app, CLI, IDE extension and cloud when users sign in to the configured workspace; it does not scan assistant responses, tool calls, tool results, files or images, access must be enabled by the OpenAI account team, and the default On AIRS failure is Allow prompts. Hooks are an attach point that sees prompts and local tool arguments, not hosted tools. Codex itself only redacts secrets from generated memory fields. [permissions.filesystem] deny_read and shell_environment_policy keep named paths and variables away from the agent (data minimisation, credited here) but inspect nothing; endpoint DLP or an AI gateway covers the rest.

original.mechanism: permissions.filesystem.deny_read globs and shell_environment_policy in requirements.toml
original.note: These stop the agent reading named paths and environment variables; nothing in the product inspects prompt or upload content. Endpoint DLP is external.

steps.title: Deny reads of secret paths
body: Set [permissions.filesystem] deny_read globs (SSH keys, cloud credentials, .env); full-access profiles are rejected while deny-read rules exist.

steps.title: Strip secrets from the shell environment
body: Set shell_environment_policy.inherit = "core" and exclude patterns so tokens in the developer's environment never reach subprocesses.

controls.mechanism: Managed PostToolUse hook (attach point), Prisma AIRS prompt scanning, and allowed_web_search_modes in requirements.toml

steps.title: Screen tool output in a managed PostToolUse hook
body: A PostToolUse hook returning decision "block" (or continue false) replaces the tool result with the hook's feedback before the model continues; it covers Bash, apply_patch, MCP and local function tools.

steps.title: Scan submitted prompts with Prisma AIRS
body: Under Codex Data controls > External guardrails, a Prisma AIRS security profile with prompt injection detection in Block mode stops flagged prompts before they reach the model.

steps.title: Keep web search on the cached index
body: Set allowed_web_search_modes = ["cached"] (or [] to allow only disabled) so live web search is unavailable even in full-access sessions.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the product-side path is a post-tool hook that can replace a tool result before the model reasons over it — an attach point whose classifier the organisation supplies — plus Prisma AIRS, which screens user prompts only, not tool results, files or fetched pages. Hosted web search skips the hook path. The Guardian auto-review judges proposed actions (credited under action policy) and GPT-6 safety monitoring pauses a task after the fact; neither screens input before it enters context. Cached web search reduces exposure to live content without classifying it. An AI or MCP gateway classifier on the brokered path covers the rest.

original.mechanism: Guardian automatic review (allowed_approvals_reviewers, guardian_policy_config) and the browser sign-in review model
original.note: The vendor ships a reviewing model for out-of-sandbox requests and for browser sign-in pages, and warns that refusal is probabilistic; no admin-tunable classifier on inputs.

steps.title: Decide whether automatic review may replace the human
body: allowed_approvals_reviewers controls whether ["auto_review"] is permitted; guardian_policy_config overrides the review policy text.

steps.title: Keep web access off where it is not needed
body: Network access defaults off in workspace-write; the docs say prompt injection can make the agent fetch and follow untrusted instructions once it is on.

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [allowed_permission_profiles] with managed default_permissions and profile filesystem rules, [permissions.filesystem] deny_read, [rules] prefix_rules, [mcp_servers] identity allowlist, apps.<id> requirements and [features] / [browser_use] / [computer_use] pins

steps.title: Fix the permission profile set
body: Set default_permissions = ":workspace" (or a managed custom profile) and [allowed_permission_profiles] without ":danger-full-access"; omitted profiles are denied (Codex 0.138.0 or later).

steps.title: Scope paths inside the managed profile
body: In [permissions.<name>.filesystem] mark globs such as "**/*.env" = "deny", and add [permissions.filesystem] deny_read for paths no profile may read.

steps.title: Scope commands, MCP servers and app tools
body: Use [rules] prefix_rules (prompt or forbidden), the [mcp_servers.<id>] identity allowlist, and apps.<id>.enabled = false or apps.<id>.tools.<tool>.approval_mode in requirements.toml.

steps.title: Pin high-agency surfaces off
body: Set [features] computer_use, browser_use, browser_use_external, browser_use_full_cdp_access and in_app_browser = false, or restrict sites with [browser_use.origins] policies.

controls.note: Native: shell commands (by prefix), filesystem paths, MCP servers, app tools and the browser and computer-use surfaces are all scoped in requirements.toml, which users can't loosen, and Full access is removable. Enforced by the Codex runtime on the device; principal scoping comes from assigning cloud-managed requirements to groups. Limits: per-tool deny within an allowlisted MCP server is not a requirements key (enabled_tools / disabled_tools live in user config.toml), so use a managed PreToolUse matcher such as mcp__server__tool; [rules] can only restrict; on native Windows managed deny_read covers direct file tools but not shell subprocess reads; [[remote_sandbox_config]] can widen sandbox modes by hostname, which is not authenticated device proof; clients older than 0.138.0 ignore profile allowlists.

original.mechanism: allowed_permission_profiles, default_permissions, allowed_sandbox_modes, [mcp_servers] enabled_tools / disabled_tools and [features] pins in requirements.toml

steps.title: Fix the permission profile set
body: Set allowed_permission_profiles (the complete allowlist; omitted profiles are denied) and default_permissions = ":workspace"; add allowed_sandbox_modes.

steps.title: Scope MCP tools per server
body: In each [mcp_servers.<name>] set enabled_tools or disabled_tools and a default_tools_approval_mode.

steps.title: Pin high-agency features off
body: Set [features] computer_use = false, browser_use = false and browser_use_full_cdp_access = false where the fleet does not need them.

original.note: enabled_tools/disabled_tools hide MCP tools, permission profiles and sandbox modes limit filesystem and network reach, feature pins remove surfaces; approval policy pre-approves. All enforced by requirements.toml, which users cannot loosen.

controls.mechanism: OS sandbox around spawned commands (Seatbelt / bubblewrap plus seccomp / native Windows sandbox), required by [allowed_permission_profiles] without ":danger-full-access" or allowed_sandbox_modes, with windows.allowed_sandbox_implementations = ["elevated"]

steps.title: Remove the escape hatch
body: Omit ":danger-full-access" from [allowed_permission_profiles], or set allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"], so --sandbox danger-full-access and --yolo are refused.

steps.title: Decide what may escalate out of the sandbox
body: Under on-request, add [rules] prefix_rules with decision forbidden for command prefixes that must never run outside the sandbox, or pin allowed_approval_policies = ["never"] to refuse every escalation.

steps.title: Require the stronger Windows sandbox
body: Set [windows] allowed_sandbox_implementations = ["elevated"] so native Windows runs commands as dedicated lower-privilege sandbox users rather than the weaker unelevated fallback.

steps.title: Install bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2
body: Package bwrap on every Linux host; without it Codex falls back to a bundled helper that needs unprivileged user namespaces, and surfaces a startup warning when neither works.

controls.note: Partial on the rule applied to every vendor (Cursor, Claude Code): the sandbox can be required but is not fail-closed, because under on-request approval a command that needs to go beyond the boundary is run outside it once the user approves the escalation. The only admin-pinnable way to refuse escalations is allowed_approval_policies = ["never"], which also removes human approval; the granular policy's sandbox_approval = false rejects them while keeping other prompts, but requirements.toml is not documented to pin it. Inside the boundary: the OS sandbox wraps every command the agent spawns and their children, and requirements.toml stops users choosing full access; in workspace-write, .git, .agents and .codex under writable roots stay read-only and network is off by default. Platforms: Seatbelt on macOS, bwrap plus seccomp on Linux and WSL2 (fail-closed behaviour without bwrap or user namespaces is not documented), elevated or unelevated sandbox on native Windows; inside Docker the sandbox may not start and the vendor tells users to make the container the boundary. Outside the boundary: the Codex process itself, MCP servers, hooks, web search and browser or Computer Use, which have their own controls; [[remote_sandbox_config]] can widen modes on matching hosts. Three 2026 escapes (git show allowlist, Docker socket, ProgramData config trust) are in advisories.

original.mechanism: OS sandbox (Seatbelt / bubblewrap+seccomp / Windows sandbox) selected by sandbox_mode and pinned by allowed_sandbox_modes
original.note: Three 2026 escapes (git show allowlist, Docker socket, ProgramData config trust) sit in advisories; the Docker-socket one is by design unless a socket is explicitly allowed. Inside the boundary: commands the agent runs. Outside: browser tools, web search and MCP servers, which are bounded by their own controls. Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap plus seccomp on Linux, a native Windows sandbox.

steps.title: Understand the boundary
body: workspace-write keeps writes inside the workspace and network off; .git, .agents and .codex under writable roots stay read-only.

steps.title: Remove the escape hatch
body: Pin allowed_sandbox_modes to ["read-only", "workspace-write"] so danger-full-access and --yolo are unavailable.

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [permissions.filesystem] deny_read for credential paths (OS-enforced for sandboxed commands), shell_environment_policy as a managed default, and mcp_servers.<id>.env_vars allowlists

steps.title: Deny the credential paths
body: Set [permissions.filesystem] deny_read for ~/.ssh, cloud CLI and git-credential files and "/**/*.env"; while deny rules exist the runtime rejects full access and keeps commands sandboxed.

steps.title: Strip secrets from spawned commands
body: Set [shell_environment_policy] inherit = "core", ignore_default_excludes = false and filters such as "AWS_*" = "exclude", shipped to every client as a managed default.

steps.title: Pass MCP servers only the variables they need
body: List each stdio server's variables in mcp_servers.<id>.env_vars instead of letting it inherit the developer's environment.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: read-denies are admin-locked and OS-enforced for sandboxed commands on macOS and Linux, but on native Windows managed deny_read applies to direct file tools only, not shell subprocess reads. Environment stripping is a managed default users can change during a run, and by default (ignore_default_excludes = true) variables named KEY, SECRET or TOKEN pass through; ship the policy in managed_config.toml or MDM config_toml_base64. Nothing holds credentials outside the agent and injects them per destination: commands still inherit whatever the developer's account reaches that no rule names — the git credential helper, cloud CLI config, the ssh-agent socket (Unix sockets are allowlist-only when the managed network proxy is active; otherwise not documented) — and Computer Use or the Chrome extension act in signed-in browser sessions. A dev container or secretless credential broker is the external fix.

original.mechanism: cli_auth_credentials_store, scoped access tokens and service accounts
original.note: Locally the agent acts as the signed-in developer with that developer's file and git rights; there is no on-behalf-of exchange. Automation can run as a service account so runs attribute to a non-human identity.

steps.title: Keep credentials out of auth.json
body: Set cli_auth_credentials_store = "keyring" (or "ephemeral" for CI) in requirements.toml.

steps.title: Run automation as a service account
body: Create a service account, assign it plugins and a role, and issue CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN from its Access tokens section (CLI 0.142.0+).

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [features].memories pin, the Computer History role permission, allow_managed_hooks_only, and read-only .codex / .agents inside the sandbox; AGENTS.md sources are not admin-lockable

steps.title: Pin local memories off or on deliberately
body: Set [features] memories = false in requirements.toml to keep agent-written memories out of managed clients; local memories are off by default.

steps.title: Gate Computer History by role
body: In Workspace Settings > Permissions & roles turn on Enable Computer History only for approved roles; it is off by default for Business and Enterprise and each member must still opt in.

steps.title: Load only managed hooks
body: Set allow_managed_hooks_only = true so user, project, session and plugin hooks are skipped.

steps.title: Keep instruction files under review
body: Codex merges ~/.codex/AGENTS.md (or AGENTS.override.md) with repo AGENTS.md files up to project_doc_max_bytes (32 KiB); review them as code.

controls.note: Partial: an administrator can switch agent-written memory off, gate Computer History, restrict hooks to managed ones, and the sandbox keeps .codex and .agents read-only to the agent's own commands; untrusted projects skip project .codex config, hooks and rules. Instruction sources cannot be locked — there is no admin-owned AGENTS.md and a user's AGENTS.override.md wins at its level — and memory contents are not validated or gated: Codex only redacts secrets from generated memory fields. memories.disable_on_external_context (keeps chats that used MCP or web search out of memory generation) and history.persistence are user config.toml keys, not requirements. Stores live under CODEX_HOME on the device.

original.mechanism: history.persistence and the Computer History role permission
original.note: Codex keeps session transcripts under CODEX_HOME and, on the desktop app, a searchable Computer History; there is no admin validation or quarantine of that store.

steps.title: Disable local transcript persistence
body: Set [history] persistence = "none" (and max_bytes) in the managed config.

steps.title: Gate Computer History by role
body: Workspace settings > Permissions & roles carries the Computer History permission.

original.mechanism: AGENTS.md hierarchy with project_doc_max_bytes and project trust
original.note: Instructions load from ~/.codex/AGENTS.md then repo-root-to-cwd AGENTS.md files; project config loads only for trusted projects. There is no admin-owned instruction file.

steps.title: Own the instruction files
body: Keep AGENTS.md under code review; AGENTS.override.md wins at each level and project_doc_max_bytes (32 KiB default) truncates the merged set.

controls.mechanism: cli_auth_credentials_store = "keyring" and allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] in the system requirements.toml or MDM, the workspace Access token expiration limit, and workload identity federation

steps.title: Require the OS credential store and forbid API keys
body: In the system requirements.toml or MDM set cli_auth_credentials_store = "keyring" and allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"]; cloud-managed requirements ignore both keys.

steps.title: Cap access-token lifetime
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles set "Access token expiration limit"; owners and admins revoke any token at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens.

steps.title: Use federation instead of stored tokens for automation
body: Set OPENAI_FEDERATION_RULE_ID and OPENAI_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE (an OIDC token or SPIFFE JWT-SVID) so the workload authenticates without a stored Codex credential.

controls.note: Native for the product's own credential: it can be forced into the OS credential store (keyring fails rather than falling back to the plaintext ~/.codex/auth.json), ChatGPT sign-in tokens refresh automatically, workload identity and model_providers.<id>.auth.command give keyless or rotating options, and an admin can forbid API keys and bound new access tokens. Enforced on the device by the Codex runtime, only where the system file or MDM payload is present. Limits: the expiration limit applies to new tokens and the page warns an earlier Codex-only dialog can offer No expiration; MCP server credentials (bearer_token_env_var, mcp_oauth_credentials_store) are user config, not requirements; the workload identity page cited on 2026-09-10 now returns 404, so its token lifetime is not re-verified.

original.mechanism: OS keyring credential store, workspace access-token expiration limit, workload identity federation

steps.title: Cap token lifetime
body: Owners set "Access token expiration limit" in Permissions & roles; tokens are created at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens with a required expiry.

steps.title: Replace stored tokens with federation
body: Exchange an OIDC or SPIFFE token via OPENAI_FEDERATION_RULE_ID / OPENAI_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE; the resulting token never lasts longer than one hour.

original.note: The keyring stores the sign-in credential; federation is the ephemeral path for automation. Shell commands read the developer's environment unless shell_environment_policy strips it, and the model sees a secret only if a command prints it.

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [mcp_servers.<id>] identity allowlist (command executable and args, or url) and [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources with Git source and ref rules

steps.title: Allowlist MCP servers by name and identity
body: Add [mcp_servers.<id>] identity = { command = ... } for stdio or { url = ... } for streamable HTTP; a server whose name or identity doesn't match is disabled and an empty table disables all.

steps.title: Pin stdio invocations
body: Use the structured identity.command form with executable and args entries (match "exact", "prefix" or "regex") so the approved argument list, including a versioned package, must match.

steps.title: Restrict plugin sources
body: Set [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources = true with allowed_sources Git url and exact ref rules; unmatched marketplace adds, installs and refreshes are rejected.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: an allowlist admits servers but verifies nothing they serve. Exact argument matching can pin a package version for stdio servers only, and the match ignores cwd, env and env_vars; URL-matched remote servers stay unpinned. Nothing scans tool descriptions, hashes tool definitions or re-gates a server whose definitions change (hash-based trust review covers hooks, not MCP tools). Plugin-bundled servers use plugins.<plugin>.mcp_servers.<server>.identity. Enforced by the Codex runtime on the device from requirements.toml; an MCP gateway or registry supplies definition scanning and pinning.

original.mechanism: requirements.toml [mcp_servers] identity allowlist and [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources

steps.title: Allowlist MCP servers by identity
body: A server is enabled only when both its name and identity match an approved [mcp_servers] entry; an empty table disables all MCP servers.

steps.title: Restrict plugin sources
body: Set [marketplaces] with restrict_to_allowed_sources = true and pin features.plugins; unmatched marketplace operations are rejected.

original.note: Admission by identity: the [mcp_servers] allowlist and marketplace source restriction. Admission is not integrity — nothing pins the tool descriptions a server returns or detects a changed implementation.

controls.mechanism: allowed_approval_policies = ["on-request"], allowed_approvals_reviewers = ["user"], profiles without full access, [rules] prefix_rules decision "prompt", and browser / computer-use persistent-approval pins

steps.title: Remove the no-prompt modes
body: Set allowed_approval_policies = ["on-request"] and omit ":danger-full-access" from [allowed_permission_profiles] so "never", Full access and --yolo are refused.

steps.title: Make the reviewer a person
body: Set allowed_approvals_reviewers = ["user"]; "auto_review" routes approvals to a reviewer agent.

steps.title: Force a prompt for named commands
body: Add [rules] prefix_rules with decision = "prompt" (for example git push and commit); a managed prompt beats a user's allow rule for the same prefix.

steps.title: Stop saved approvals in the browser and Computer Use
body: Set browser_use.allow_global_persistent_approval = false and computer_use.allow_persistent_approval = false.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: a present person sees the exact command for each escalation, and an admin can remove never, Full access and the AI reviewer, but approval fires only for actions that leave the sandbox — commands inside it run unprompted unless a managed prompt rule names them. Users can still persist prefix allow rules to ~/.codex/rules/default.rules and accept Smart-approval suggestions; no requirement disables that, so a managed rule wins only for the prefixes the admin names. Scheduled tasks run with approval_policy "never" wherever requirements allow it. Enforced on the device by the Codex runtime.

original.mechanism: allowed_approval_policies and allowed_approvals_reviewers in requirements.toml, and the permission modes

steps.title: Require approval outside the sandbox
body: Set allowed_approval_policies = ["on-request"] so "never" is unavailable. Do not list "untrusted" — approval_policy = "untrusted" is retired and must be removed from managed defaults and user, project and profile configuration; project trust is now trust_level in project configuration.

steps.title: Make the reviewer a person
body: An "on-request" policy alone lets the reviewer be the automatic (AI) reviewer. Set allowed_approvals_reviewers = ["user"] where a human must decide; ["auto_review"] requires automatic review instead, and listing both leaves the choice to the user.

steps.title: Keep Full access out of the mode picker
body: Ask for approval, Approve for me (auto-review) and Full access are the user modes; admins decide which profiles the workspace allows.

original.note: Approval is requested only for actions that leave the sandbox; commands inside the permitted sandbox boundary run without a new prompt.

controls.mechanism: Admin > Plugins marketplace import with a per-role Installation policy, enforced on clients by the requirements.toml [marketplaces] and [mcp_servers] allowlists

steps.title: Keep the workspace plugin catalogue
body: Admin > Plugins > Add > Import marketplace from GitHub, optionally pinned to a branch, tag or commit; set Installation policy to Available or Installed per role.

steps.title: Refuse what the catalogue doesn't list
body: Set [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources = true and an [mcp_servers] identity allowlist in requirements.toml so unlisted sources and servers are rejected or disabled.

controls.note: Partial: the workspace catalogue records approved plugins with a role policy and a pinned source, and requirements refuse unlisted marketplace sources and MCP servers, but the client-side lists carry no owner, version or approval record and are not reconciled with the catalogue. Plugins are not available in the IDE extension. Nothing inventories agents or MCP servers a developer runs on a machine without the requirements file.

original.mechanism: Admin > Plugins marketplace import and the [mcp_servers] approved identities
original.note: Approved plugins and MCP servers are recorded centrally; nothing inventories the local agents or MCP servers a developer runs outside that list.

steps.title: Manage the plugin catalogue
body: Admin > Plugins imports a GitHub marketplace, syncs daily and sets Available or Installed per role.

controls.mechanism: None in product; EDR / MDM software inventory and SSE / CASB find unmanaged installs and personal-account use

evidence.title: Managed configuration — allowed_chatgpt_workspaces refuses other workspaces (prevention, 2026-09-25)
ChatGPT Work admin FAQ — identity features listed, no discovery of unmanaged use (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External: find unmanaged installs (the codex binary, npm @openai/codex, the openai.chatgpt IDE extension, the ChatGPT desktop app and MSIX) with EDR or MDM software inventory, and personal-account or unmanaged workspace use of chatgpt.com with SSE / CASB. The vendor lists domain verification among identity features, but no page fetched documents discovery of personal accounts on the org's domain (the Help Center pages returned 403). allowed_chatgpt_workspaces in the system requirements.toml is prevention on managed machines, credited here only.

original.mechanism: None in product; forced workspace login turns personal-account use into a detectable violation
original.note: Discover unmanaged installs (npm @openai/codex, the openai.chatgpt extension, the MSIX) with EDR or software inventory; allowed_chatgpt_workspaces then blocks personal accounts.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for the integration point (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: [otel] exporter / trace_exporter delivered as a managed default (managed_config.toml or MDM config_toml_base64) and the workspace Compliance API

steps.title: Point every client at the org collector
body: Ship [otel] exporter = "otlp-http" pointed at your collector, environment = "prod" and log_user_prompt = false in /etc/codex/managed_config.toml or MDM config_toml_base64.

steps.title: Know what the events carry
body: Events include codex.conversation_starts, codex.user_prompt (redacted by default), codex.tool_decision (approved or denied, config or user) and codex.tool_result, tagged with the conversation id.

steps.title: Collect workspace records continuously
body: Pull the append-only compliance log stream with COMPLIANCE_API_KEY into the SIEM; the Admin API reference defines which Codex events it covers.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: OTel carries per-session model, prompt and tool-decision events with correlation and prompt redaction, but [otel] is not a requirements.toml key — it arrives as a managed default that users can change during a run — and export is off by default and flushes on shutdown. The Compliance API is the workspace audit channel, and the Work Local page warns that not every local file operation, screenshot, browser action or approval appears there; its event list is in the Admin API reference, which returned 403. Capture only: tamper resistance is the receiving store's job.

original.mechanism: [otel] OTLP export from the client and the workspace Compliance API
original.note: The Compliance API keeps records 30 days; Work Local warns that not every local file operation, screenshot or browser action appears there. OTel is opt-in per client.

steps.title: Export client events
body: Set [otel] exporter = "otlp-http" or "otlp-grpc" with your endpoint; log_user_prompt defaults to false (redacted).

steps.title: Pull workspace records
body: Use the Compliance API with COMPLIANCE_API_KEY; the Admin API reference is the source of truth for event coverage and retention.

controls.mechanism: Codex Local role permission, access-token and service-account revocation, and allow_remote_control = false in requirements.toml

steps.title: Turn local Codex off for the affected roles
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles set "Allow members to use Codex locally" (or "Allow members to use Codex and Work Locally") to Off; an explicit Off in any role wins.

steps.title: Revoke automation credentials
body: Revoke tokens at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens; removing local permission only suspends them, while disabling or deleting a service account revokes all of its tokens.

steps.title: Cut phone steering
body: Set allow_remote_control = false in requirements.toml to disable device remote control.

controls.note: Partial: every lever blocks new access rather than stopping a session in progress. Custom-role changes take about five minutes to appear and revoked tokens can no longer start new authenticated runs; whether a running local session stops is not documented, so the delay for active work is not documented and the operator or EDR kills the process. Requirement changes load at the next client start (a background refresh doesn't replace the loaded policy, MDM is read at launch), and the admin FAQ says managed configuration isn't an access-revocation mechanism. The vendor's asynchronous safety monitoring can pause a task but is not an admin action.

original.mechanism: Role permission off, token revocation, service-account disable, federation rule disable

steps.title: Turn the surface off
body: Set "Allow members to use Codex locally" (or the combined Codex and Work Locally toggle) to Off for the affected roles.

steps.title: Revoke automation credentials
body: Owners and admins revoke any workspace access token; disabling a service account revokes all of its tokens.

original.note: The role toggle and token revocation block future access; a running local process and the commands inside its sandbox are not stopped remotely — the operator stops the process. A cloud-managed requirements bundle is re-fetched on its own schedule, so treat that interval as the cessation delay.

controls.mechanism: EDR on the endpoint; Codex exposes process identity (sandbox-exec, bwrap, dedicated Windows sandbox users) and OTel tool events for correlation

evidence.title: Agent approvals & security — sandbox-exec on macOS, bwrap on Linux, OTel event catalogue (2026-09-25)
Windows sandbox — elevated mode runs commands as dedicated lower-privilege sandbox users (2026-09-25)
Configuration Reference — log_dir enforceable in requirements.toml (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External: Codex does not analyse process behaviour; the organisation's EDR does. Integration points: agent commands run as children of the Codex process under sandbox-exec on macOS and bwrap on Linux, the elevated native Windows sandbox runs them as dedicated lower-privilege sandbox users, OTel codex.tool_decision and codex.tool_result events can be joined to EDR telemetry, log_dir can be enforced in requirements.toml, and a managed PreToolUse hook can log each command. Detections worth writing from the advisories: batch or executable files created in project roots (the web.run node.bat chain), Docker-socket use from the agent, and non-admin writes under %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex (pre-create and ACL it; Cymulate, 2026-08, no Codex CVE).

original.mechanism: EDR rules around the runtime; no vendor hook for endpoint security products
original.note: Watch for batch or executable files created in project roots (web.run node.bat chain), Docker-socket use from the agent, and non-admin writes under %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex; pre-create and ACL that directory (Cymulate ProgramData config-trust report, 2026-08; no Codex CVE assigned).

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for the integration point (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [experimental_network] (enabled, managed_allowed_domains_only, domains) over sandboxed commands, with command network off by default

steps.title: Enforce a managed domain allowlist
body: Set [experimental_network] enabled = true and managed_allowed_domains_only = true with [experimental_network.domains] "allow" and "deny" entries; deny wins.

steps.title: Keep command network off where it isn't needed
body: sandbox_workspace_write.network_access defaults to false; the managed proxy never grants network a sandbox keeps off.

steps.title: Close the paths the proxy doesn't see
body: Use allowed_web_search_modes, features.apps = false, the [mcp_servers] allowlist and [browser_use] origin policies for web search, connectors, MCP servers and the browser.

controls.note: Partial: the admin-owned allowlist is enforced on commands inside the sandbox, but the vendor marks [experimental_network] experimental, says not to enable it broadly without validation, and calls Windows support limited; DNS-rebinding protection is best effort. It does not filter web search, apps and connectors, MCP server connections, native-app traffic from Computer Use, or Codex's own model and service requests; browser tools check managed denies separately. An endpoint firewall or SSE policy covers the rest.

original.mechanism: [experimental_network] managed_allowed_domains_only and sandbox_workspace_write.network_access
original.note: Domain rules apply to command proxying inside the sandbox, not to browser tools, web search or MCP servers; those need a network-layer control.

steps.title: Allowlist domains for sandboxed commands
body: In requirements.toml set [experimental_network] allowed and denied domains with managed_allowed_domains_only = true.

steps.title: Keep network off by default
body: sandbox_workspace_write.network_access = false is the default; features.network_proxy adds allow/deny domain maps when it is on.

controls.mechanism: Package mirror or artifact repository with malware scanning; Codex's integration point is the [experimental_network.domains] allowlist that forces sandboxed installs through the mirror

evidence.title: Managed configuration — [experimental_network] domains and [marketplaces] allowed_sources (2026-09-25)
Plugin management — marketplace import pinned to a branch, tag or commit, no scanning (2026-09-25)
Configuration Reference — features.skill_mcp_dependency_install on by default (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External: Codex scans nothing it downloads or installs — plugins, skills, MCP dependencies installed for skills (features.skill_mcp_dependency_install, on by default) or packages its commands fetch. Admission scanning belongs at the organisation's package mirror; the integration point is an [experimental_network.domains] allowlist that admits only the mirror for sandboxed commands, with registry variables set through shell_environment_policy as a managed default. [marketplaces] allowed_sources pins plugin Git sources and refs, which is admission, not file analysis. No model weights load in Codex; inference is remote unless a user points model_provider at a local server, which loads them itself.

original.mechanism: Not applicable
original.note: No model artifacts are loaded by the product; inference is remote. model_provider can point at a local server (ollama, lmstudio) — that server, not Codex, loads the weights, and scanning them is the obligation of whoever runs it.

original.mechanism: Not offered
original.note: No signed manifest of runtime, plugins or MCP servers; the closest is codex-version pinning in the GitHub Action and marketplace sync from a Git source.

summary: Codex cloud runs coding tasks in OpenAI-hosted containers built from the universal image plus a per-environment setup script, checked out from a GitHub or GitLab repository and started from the web, the IDE extension, Slack, Linear, a pull request comment or a schedule. The same hosted harness is what ChatGPT Work calls Work Cloud, which the vendor describes as VM-backed sandboxes on OpenAI infrastructure.

Inference and execution are both at OpenAI: the repository, environment variables and the prompt leave the organisation, and the agent's output returns as a diff or pull request for a human to merge. Internet access during the agent phase is off by default and is set per environment (Off, or On restricted by a domain allowlist and GET/HEAD/OPTIONS-only methods); secrets are encrypted, exposed only to setup scripts and removed before the agent phase.

Admin gating is by workspace setting (Codex cloud chats, GitHub connector), by environment (internet, repositories, secrets) and by connector setting (the Slack posting toggle, Codex for Linear). Compliance API records are retained 30 days; the BAA does not cover Codex cloud.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Cloud features require Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise or Edu; not available on Free, Go or API-key sign-in.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Tasks run in OpenAI-hosted containers behind an HTTP/HTTPS proxy; caches are shared across users with access to the environment on Business and Enterprise.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: The repository checkout, environment variables, uploaded context, Slack thread history or Linear issue content are sent to create the cloud chat.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: learn.chatgpt.com/docs/cloud

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Conversations follow workspace retention with deletion scheduled within 30 days; execution snapshots and Library files follow separate lifecycles; Compliance Logs Platform keeps records 30 days.

riskNotes.note: The internet-access page shows hidden instructions in fetched web content driving secret exfiltration; the default Off and GET-only controls are the mitigation.
Cached containers are shared across every user with access to the environment for up to 12 hours, so anything a setup script writes is visible to the next user's task.
Output is a diff or PR, but automatic reviews and Slack posting act without a prompt; scope the GitHub app and the "post answers" toggle.
Environments and setup scripts are editable by anyone with access; they run with internet on.

controls.mechanism: Codex cloud chats workspace setting, Codex for Linear and the Slack posting toggle in admin settings, the "Allow event-triggered scheduled tasks" permission, and per-repository code review settings

steps.title: Turn on Codex cloud chats deliberately
body: In ChatGPT workspace settings (chatgpt.com/admin/settings) turn on Codex cloud chats only once hosted sessions are approved, and enable Codex for Linear in connector settings only where wanted.

steps.title: Keep Slack answers inside the chat
body: Clear "Allow Codex Slack app to post answers on task completion" in ChatGPT workspace settings so Slack receives only a link to the chat.

steps.title: Gate event triggers
body: Grant the "Allow event-triggered scheduled tasks" permission only to roles that should start runs from Gmail, Slack or GitHub events.

steps.title: Decide which repositories review automatically
body: In Codex settings > Code review turn on Code review and Automatic reviews per repository; changing them needs GitHub push or admin permission on the repository.

controls.note: Partial: hosted sessions are switched on in the vendor's admin settings and per integration (the rollout guide says to grant Codex cloud access to the intended audience through workspace controls; per-role granularity is on Help Center pages that returned 403), but who may start or steer a session is not documented as configurable — the docs do not restrict an @codex mention in a GitHub pull request or GitLab merge request, a Linear assignment or a Slack mention to people with write access, and no setting excludes Apps, bots or non-collaborators (GitLab's Review my, team or all MRs policy scopes automatic reviews, not invocation). Widening switches are partly admin-owned: personal access tokens are a workspace permission and device remote control is a local requirement (allow_remote_control); Codex cloud requires MFA only for email-and-password accounts.

original.mechanism: Workspace roles (Work Cloud / Codex cloud permission) and SCIM groups

steps.title: Gate cloud execution by role
body: Workspace settings > Permissions & roles carries Work Cloud and Work Local as distinct toggles; enable Work Cloud selectively.

steps.title: Provision membership from the IdP
body: SCIM provisions membership and group assignment; groups need explicit role grants and an Off in any role denies.

The Work cloud security page warns not to assume every shell command, browser interaction, app invocation, file operation or approval appears in a compliance export, and Compliance Logs Platform records are available for 30 days. body: Codex caches container state for up to 12 hours and invalidates it when the setup script, maintenance script, variables or secrets change; select Reset cache on the environment page to clear it.

body: Codex cloud requires ChatGPT sign-in, and ChatGPT-signed-in Codex usage follows the workspace's ChatGPT Enterprise retention and residency settings.

The container cache — setup-script output and anything written before the agent phase — persists for up to 12 hours and is shared by every user with access to the environment, with no admin setting beyond Reset cache and automatic invalidation; the Work Cloud page, which shares this harness, says execution snapshots follow a separate lifecycle the customer does not set. No agent-written memory is documented for Codex cloud sessions. AGENTS.md is read from the repository and is governed by repository review, not by the product; nothing validates what persists.

original.mechanism: Container cache lifetime and workspace retention
original.note: Caches are shared across all users with access to the environment; treat setup-script writes as shared state.

steps.title: Know the cache scope
body: Containers cache up to 12 hours and, on Business and Enterprise, are shared across users of the environment.

body: Set the workspace overage limit to zero where supported; No limit isn't a zero-spend cap, and usage alerts only notify.

body: Enterprise and Edu manage usage limits and overage; Business manages credits; user-level guardrails and notifications are plan-dependent.

body: In ChatGPT workspace settings turn Codex cloud chats off and disable Codex for Linear in connector settings.

body: In Codex Cloud > Settings > Connectors revoke the service-account token; Codex can't respond to GitLab activity until a valid token is configured.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: every documented lever stops new sessions; no page documents an administrator cancelling a cloud session that is already running, so the delay for active work is not documented. steps.title: Treat the environment as shared state
body: Codex creates a container and checks out the repository for each chat, but resumes cached container state for up to 12 hours, shared across all users with access to the environment.

steps.title: Read the isolation statement the vendor makes
body: Work Cloud, which uses the Codex task-execution harness, runs in VM-backed sandboxes on shared infrastructure and does not give every task a new container.

Inside the boundary: setup script and agent commands. Outside: the model, connectors and repository operations at OpenAI.

original.mechanism: Container per task from the universal image, behind an HTTP/HTTPS network proxy; the Work Cloud security page describes VM-backed sandboxes and states that tasks do not receive a new container per execution

steps.title: Treat the environment as shared state
body: Codex creates a container, checks out the branch or commit and runs your setup script for each prompt; caches and the workspace are shared across users of the environment, so setup-script writes and cache invalidation are your controls.

steps.title: Read the isolation statement the vendor makes
body: Work Cloud runs tasks in VM-backed sandboxes on shared hosted infrastructure the customer does not manage; the page states tasks do not receive a new container per execution.

original.note: The two vendor pages differ on per-task freshness (a fresh container per prompt on the environment page, no new container per execution on the security page); both are recorded and the safer reading — shared state within an environment — is the one to plan for. Inside the boundary: setup script and the agent's commands. Outside: the model and connector actions, which run at OpenAI.

Bypasses: repository clone and push, connector and integration traffic, and inference run outside the environment's policy. original.mechanism: Internet access per environment: Off by default during the agent phase, On, or On with controls (domain allowlist presets None, Common dependencies, All; methods limited to GET, HEAD and OPTIONS); setup scripts keep internet; the environment runs behind a proxy; Work Cloud "Allow public internet access" with a managed destination allowlist

steps.title: Leave the agent phase offline or restricted
body: Keep internet Off for the agent phase, or use On with controls with the None preset plus named domains and GET-only methods; the page shows how an injected instruction exfiltrates commit history when the agent can reach the web.

body: Allow public internet access for Work Cloud code and shell is a workspace setting; when off, a managed destination allowlist for required endpoints remains and the change applies after current runs complete.

controls.mechanism: Environment secrets (setup scripts only, removed before the agent phase) versus environment variables (whole chat); the repository credential's custody is not documented

body: Secrets are only available to setup scripts and are removed before the agent phase; environment variables stay set for the whole chat.

Environment variables persist into the agent phase, readable by the agent's commands and by everyone who shares the environment, and anything a setup script writes to disk with a secret survives into the agent phase and the shared cache. No git proxy substituting a scoped credential and no redaction of runtime secrets are documented, and the docs don't say how the credential used to clone and push is held, so plan as if it is in the sandbox. The vendor's HTTP/HTTPS proxy is for security and abuse prevention, not credential substitution.

original.mechanism: Environment secrets available only to setup scripts and removed before the agent phase starts, stored with an additional layer of encryption; environment variables persist for the whole task; connector tokens held at OpenAI

steps.title: Put credentials in secrets, not variables
body: Store anything sensitive as an environment secret so it exists only while the setup script runs and is gone before the agent acts; environment variables remain readable for the full task.

original.note: The designated secret path keeps values out of the agent's execution by design, which is the isolation this control asks for; anything placed in an environment variable is inside the boundary. No on-behalf-of exchange — a task acts as the workspace's connections.

original.mechanism: Environment secrets (encrypted, setup-script only) versus environment variables

steps.title: Put credentials in Secrets, not variables
body: Secrets get an additional layer of encryption, are only available to setup scripts and are removed before the agent phase; environment variables persist.

original.note: Environment secrets are readable by the setup script only and are not present when the agent runs; environment variables are readable by the agent's commands and so by the model. Stored secrets, not ephemeral issuance.

controls.mechanism: Encrypted environment secrets, the never-shown-again GitLab connector token with admin revoke and regenerate, and Secure MCP Tunnel's runtime API key scoped by Platform Tunnels permissions with optional control-plane mTLS

steps.title: Store setup credentials as Secrets
body: Environment secrets get an additional layer of encryption, are decrypted only for task execution and are removed before the agent phase.

steps.title: Rotate the GitLab connector token
body: In Codex Cloud > Settings > Connectors revoke the service-account token and generate a new one; a saved token is encrypted and never shown again.

steps.title: Scope the tunnel credential
body: Grant Tunnels Read + Use only to the identity running tunnel-client, keep its runtime API key in a secret store, and add control-plane mTLS where required.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: environment secrets are encrypted and setup-only, but whether a saved secret can be read back is not documented, and environment variables are plain values visible to the agent and to everyone sharing the environment. The GitLab connector token is encrypted, never shown again and admin-rotatable, but it is an api-scoped personal access token whose lifetime the org sets in GitLab; how the GitHub credential is held and how long it lives is not documented. A vendor tunnel exists: Secure MCP Tunnel serves ChatGPT, Codex and the Responses API, tunnel-client authenticates to OpenAI with a runtime Platform API key and optional control-plane mTLS, access is scoped by Platform RBAC (Tunnels Read, Use, Manage) and tunnel changes appear in Platform audit logs, but the tunnel page documents no rotation or revocation procedure for that key, and it does not say whether Codex cloud sessions can call a tunnel-backed server.

tools.name: Codex SDK

variants.name: @openai/codex-sdk (TypeScript)
openai-codex (Python)

summary: The SDK embeds the Codex agent in customer-hosted automation. The TypeScript library spawns the codex CLI (codex exec) and reads JSONL events over stdin/stdout; the Python library drives a local codex app-server over JSON-RPC and pins its own CLI runtime. Both expose a thread/turn API with sandbox presets (read-only, workspace-write, full access) settable per thread or per turn, and model selection. Inference is at OpenAI; execution is wherever the host runs.

Because both drive the Codex CLI runtime, the host's config.toml and any requirements.toml apply, and per-client config overrides are passed as --config flags; an omitted sandbox falls back to the runtime's configured default (read-only for codex exec). Python threads start with ApprovalMode.auto_review, so a reviewer agent answers escalations unless deny_all is passed. Unattended runs authenticate with CODEX_API_KEY (TypeScript), a service-account CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN or workload identity federation, which is the credential story that distinguishes this entity from the interactive shells.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: API-key usage bills at API rates; ChatGPT sign-in and service-account tokens use the workspace plan.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: The SDK controls a local runtime that calls OpenAI; model_provider / base_url overrides in config.toml apply.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Prompts, file contents the agent reads and command output go to OpenAI as with the CLI.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex-sdk

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: API-key traffic falls under the API data policy — not used for training by default, 30-day abuse-monitoring logs, ZDR by approval.

riskNotes.note: agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session is the only vendor bound on subagent fan-out; task duration and spend are yours to cap.
full_access is one argument away in the SDK; pin allowed_sandbox_modes on the host so the preset is rejected.
Runs act as whichever token the host holds; use a service account so actions attribute to the automation, not an engineer.
MCP servers and plugins configured on the host are inherited by SDK threads; allowlist them in requirements.toml.

controls.mechanism: Per-thread rollout files under CODEX_HOME (a per-tenant CODEX_HOME through the client's env), Python ephemeral threads, app-server thread/delete, and ExternalMessage for content from other agents; nothing validates stored state

steps.title: Give each tenant its own state root
body: Set CODEX_HOME in the client's env (TypeScript new Codex({ env }), Python CodexConfig(env=...)) to an existing per-tenant directory so sessions, logs, config and auth never share a root.

steps.title: Mark other agents' output as untrusted
body: Pass content from another agent, tool or application as ExternalMessage(tool_name=..., content=...) so it reaches the model with tool-level authority, below user and developer instructions.

steps.title: Keep short-lived runs off disk and delete the rest
body: Start Python threads with ephemeral=True, and remove stored threads with the app-server's thread/delete, which deletes the rollout files of the thread and its spawned descendants.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule (per-thread scoping, contents unvalidated). Threads are separate rollout files keyed by thread id, a per-tenant CODEX_HOME separates tenants, and delete exists at the app-server (the Python SDK exposes archive only, the TypeScript SDK neither). Nothing validates what a step writes: thread history, AGENTS.md files and memories are read back unscreened, and resumeThread / thread_resume opens any thread id the process can reach, so ownership checks are the host application's. ExternalMessage lowers the authority of another agent's text but does not screen it, and its tool name is not proof of identity. features.memories is off by default. Enforced by the Codex runtime on the host.

original.mechanism: Thread persistence (resumeThread) and history.persistence on the host

steps.title: Disable persisted transcripts on the host
body: Set [history] persistence = "none" if threads must not survive the process.

original.note: Retention only: thread persistence and history settings decide what is kept on the host. Nothing validates or restores it.

controls.mechanism: None in the SDK; an evaluation platform or CI suite runs SDK turns and gates the release, reading outputSchema structured output and the turn's items and usage

evidence.title: Codex SDK — thread/turn API, no evaluation harness or release gate (2026-09-25)
TypeScript SDK README — outputSchema structured output and streamed turn events (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External: the SDK ships no evaluation harness and nothing that can hold a model, prompt or agent change until tests pass. The integration point is the turn result — outputSchema makes the final response conform to a JSON schema, and the result carries the items, status and token usage — which an evaluation platform or the deployer's CI scores before promotion. Model and agent behaviour change with the pinned runtime (Python) or the installed CLI (TypeScript), so pin both and re-run the suite on every upgrade.

original.mechanism: Not offered
original.note: No vendor evaluation harness for SDK agents; structured output and streaming events let you build one.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed; no setting for this control (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: [otel] exporter and otel.trace_exporter to the deployer's collector (host config.toml or the client's config overrides), plus the SDK event stream (runStreamed items, Python turn.stream notifications) and the rollout files under CODEX_HOME/sessions

steps.title: Export the runtime's telemetry to your collector
body: Set [otel] exporter (logs) and otel.trace_exporter (traces) to otlp-http or otlp-grpc with your endpoint, environment = "prod" and log_user_prompt = false, in the host config.toml or the client's config overrides.

steps.title: Ship the full step record from the stream
body: Consume runStreamed() (TypeScript) or turn.stream() (Python) and forward item events, which carry the command and its output, file changes, and the MCP server, tool, arguments and result, to your store.

steps.title: Attribute runs to the automation
body: Run each workflow as its own service account so runs attribute to it; token creation and account changes appear in workspace audit records.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: the runtime's OTel export carries conversation starts, model requests, tool decisions (approved or denied, by config or user) and tool results (duration, success, output snippet) tagged with the conversation id, to a collector the deployer controls; export is off by default and flushes on shutdown. Tool arguments and subagent handoff correlation are not in the documented event catalogue, and the TypeScript event stream has no subagent items. Full arguments and results exist in the SDK event stream and the local rollout JSONL, which the host application must ship off the host itself. Emission is not detection or tamper resistance — the collector and SIEM supply those.

original.mechanism: Streaming turn events and [otel] export

steps.title: Export OTel logs

tools.name: Secure MCP Tunnel (tunnel-client)

variants.name: tunnel-client (binary and ghcr.io/openai/tunnel-client container)

summary: Secure MCP Tunnel lets a private or localhost MCP server serve ChatGPT developer-mode apps, the Responses API and Codex without inbound exposure: a customer-run tunnel-client polls api.openai.com (or mtls.api.openai.com) over outbound HTTPS, forwards each request to the local stdio or HTTP MCP server, and returns the response through the same tunnel.

The tunnel itself carries no inference; it is the connectivity leg between OpenAI's hosted chat and the organisation's tool server, which is why it sits on the enterprise-chat architecture. Tunnels are created, edited and deleted in Platform tunnel settings and associated with one or more Platform organisations or ChatGPT workspaces; tunnel-client authenticates with a Restricted runtime API key (CONTROL_PLANE_API_KEY, Tunnels Read + Use) created and revoked on the Platform API keys page, optionally adds control-plane mTLS, can present its own mTLS certificate to the MCP server, and supports outbound proxies and custom CA bundles.

Audit is split: tunnel.created / updated / deleted appear in Platform audit logs, but control-plane tunnel traffic is not emitted as Compliance Platform app events; app-level invocation and auth-lifecycle logging still applies when ChatGPT reaches the app through the tunnel.

steps.title: Mint a least-privilege runtime key

body: Activate a trust anchor at Organization settings > Security > Mutual TLS for the key's organisation or project and give tunnel-client control_plane.client_cert and client_key; a request with the key but no accepted certificate fails with certificate_required.

controls.note: Native by the drawing rule for a tunnel credential: it is scoped (a Restricted key with Tunnels Read + Use), held as a reference to the host's secret store rather than in the profile, rotatable under an enforced maximum lifetime, bindable to a client certificate so the key alone is not enough, and revocable centrally without redeploying — delete the key on the API keys page or through the Admin API, remove the principal's Tunnels Use, or delete the tunnel. Boundaries: the key is a bearer token sent to OpenAI on every poll and readable by whoever can read the host's environment or secret file; tunnel-client does not encrypt it (custody is the Kubernetes Secret, systemd credential or secrets manager the operator uses) and still accepts a literal value for compatibility; the reference is resolved at startup, so rotation needs a restart, and stdio bindings allow one instance per tunnel ID (a brief gap); the maximum lifetime binds only keys created after it is set; the propagation delay of a revocation is not documented. Other credentials on the path: a connector-forwarded Authorization bearer crosses OpenAI (strict-local-auth is unsupported), while MCP_EXTRA_HEADERS and MCP-side mTLS keep a backend credential on the final hop.
