tools.name: OpenClaw
summary: A self-hosted personal agent whose gateway is the control plane — channels, tool policy and auth under an explicit single-trusted-operator model. Official hardening is real and specific: loopback-plus-token gateway auth, DM pairing, high-risk tools disabled or sandboxed, and a container sandbox whose defaults are no network, a read-only root and all capabilities dropped. Sandboxing itself is off by default (agents.defaults.sandbox); latest release 2026.9.6 (2026-09-23).

The operator model is the single trusted user: the person who runs the gateway is the administrator, everything below is a config key in openclaw.json, a CLI command or a Control UI setting that user sets, and the trust-model page says plainly that one gateway is one trust boundary and not hostile multi-tenant isolation.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Open source, self-hosted; no vendor plan tiers. ClawHub is the public marketplace for skills and plugins.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: The user picks the model provider under models.providers (hosted APIs, subscription OAuth, or local servers); every reply and tool call runs on that provider, and web search, embeddings and media features can call further paid APIs with their own keys.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Prompts, tool results and attachments go to the configured model and tool providers; runtime traffic can be forced through an operator proxy (proxy.proxyUrl). Feature telemetry is off by default (telemetry.enabled false) and rides the daily update check when enabled.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: Everything is local under ~/.openclaw: config, credentials, SQLite state and session transcripts (JSONL). The metadata-only audit ledger keeps 30 days and at most 100,000 rows. No vendor training; provider terms apply to what is sent for inference.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: https://docs.openclaw.ai/llms.txt

items.title: Gateway lockdown and the version floor
body: gateway.bind defaults to loopback (container images default to an exposed bind); the network-exposure page says plainly never to expose it unauthenticated on 0.0.0.0, and gateway.auth.mode token is the recommended mode. DM hardening is dmPolicy pairing (codes expire after one hour for unknown senders), allowFrom contact allowlists and requireMention in groups; `openclaw security audit` checks a deployment and `--fix` applies safe fixes (open group policies to allowlist, file permissions). Enforce a version floor of 2026.1.29: earlier Control UI builds auto-connected to an attacker-supplied gatewayUrl and sent the operator token (CVE-2026-25253, CVSS 8.8), and internet scans found thousands of exposed instances.

links.title: GitHub Advisory GHSA-g8p2-7wf7-98mq — CVE-2026-25253 (readable primary advisory)
NVD — CVE-2026-25253 (record; client-rendered, thin to automated fetch)

items.title: Sandbox defaults and proxy-injected credentials
body: With the Docker sandbox backend enabled, tool execution runs in a container whose defaults are network none, readOnlyRoot true, capDrop ALL, an init process and no-new-privileges, with the workspace mounted read-only at /agent (workspaceAccess ro) or read-write by policy; per-agent sandbox and tool-policy overrides layer on top, and the docs warn never to mount the host Docker socket into a sandbox container. Docker's own Sandboxes product wraps the same agent with a configurable egress proxy that denies arbitrary hosts and injects provider API keys at the proxy, so the agent process never holds them.

links.title: Docker: Run OpenClaw securely in Docker Sandboxes

riskNotes.note: The docs treat every fetched page, email, attachment and hook payload as hostile even when only the operator can message the bot; the shipped defences are boundary markers and token stripping, not a classifier, so the recommended shape is a tool-less reader agent plus tool policy, exec approvals and sandboxing.

The trusted-operator default is host exec with security full and ask off; nothing prompts until the user sets tools.exec.mode to allowlist or ask, and tools.elevated lets exec leave the sandbox for allowlisted senders.

controls.mechanism: External content (web, mail, hook payloads, attachments) is wrapped in <<<EXTERNAL_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT>>> boundary markers with chat-template special tokens stripped; nothing classifies it. The attach point is a plugin before_agent_run gate hook, which sees the final prompt and session messages before model submission and can block the run (it fails closed on error or timeout); tool_result_persist and before_message_write can rewrite a tool result before it is persisted.

steps.title: Keep the unsafe-content bypass flags off
body: Leave hooks.mappings[].allowUnsafeExternalContent, hooks.gmail.allowUnsafeExternalContent and the cron payload field allowUnsafeExternalContent unset so external content keeps its boundary markers.

steps.title: Attach your own screening to the run gate
body: Register a plugin before_agent_run handler that runs your injection classifier over the assembled prompt and session messages and blocks the run on a hit; the runner also blocks the run when the handler throws or exceeds its 15-second default timeout.

steps.title: Summarise untrusted content in a reader agent
body: Route web, mail and hook content to a read-only or tool-disabled agent under agents.entries.<id> and pass only its summary to the main agent, constraining the handoff with tools.agentToAgent.allow.

steps.title: Let the audit catch weak-model exposure
body: `openclaw security audit` warns when a model of 300B parameters or fewer runs unsandboxed with web or browser tools enabled; fix that finding before exposing the agent to untrusted inboxes.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the product ships a hook that can block, not a classifier. Boundary markers and token stripping lower the odds that an injected instruction is obeyed but detect nothing, so inbound channel messages (the owner's included) and tool results reach the model unscreened unless a plugin gates the run. The memory taint on network-sourced tool results governs promotion into long-term memory, not what the model reads in the current turn. Enforcing actor: the Gateway process on the host, for every channel and agent once the plugin is loaded.

original.mechanism: External content is wrapped in <<<EXTERNAL_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT>>> boundary markers with chat-template special tokens stripped, and an outbound sanitizer strips leaked tool-call scaffolding from replies; there is no injection classifier. Hardening is the reader-agent pattern, tool policy and the audit's small-model warning.

steps.title: Keep the unsafe-content bypass flags off
body: Leave hooks.mappings[].allowUnsafeExternalContent, hooks.gmail.allowUnsafeExternalContent and the cron payload field allowUnsafeExternalContent unset; if one is needed for debugging, isolate that agent with a sandbox, minimal tools and its own session namespace.

steps.title: Summarise untrusted content in a reader agent
body: Route web, mail and hook content to a read-only or tool-disabled agent under agents.entries.<id> (sandbox mode all, tools.deny for exec/browser/write) and pass only its summary to the main agent; constrain the handoff with tools.agentToAgent.allow.

steps.title: Deny the high-risk tools unless needed
body: Keep web_search, web_fetch and browser out of tool-enabled agents via tools.deny, and set tools.exec.strictInlineEval true whenever interpreters (python, node, ruby, osascript) are allowlisted so -c/-e forms still need approval.

steps.title: Let the audit catch weak-model exposure
body: `openclaw security audit` warns when a model of 300B parameters or fewer runs unsandboxed with web or browser tools enabled; fix that finding before exposing the agent to untrusted inboxes.

original.note: Boundary markers and token stripping reduce the chance an injected instruction is obeyed; they detect nothing. Detection would be a scanner the operator adds in front of tool results.

controls.mechanism: plugins.entries.amazon-bedrock.config.guardrail applies an Amazon Bedrock Guardrail (content filters, topic denial, word filters) to every Bedrock model invocation; for any other provider the only points are plugin hooks — before_agent_run can block a run before model submission, and message_sending / reply_payload_sending can rewrite or cancel a reply before delivery.

steps.title: Apply a Bedrock Guardrail when the provider is Bedrock
body: Set plugins.entries.amazon-bedrock.config.guardrail with guardrailIdentifier and guardrailVersion (streamProcessingMode "sync" or "async" for streamed output) and grant the Gateway's IAM principal bedrock:ApplyGuardrail.

steps.title: Gate requests with your own classifier
body: A plugin before_agent_run handler can run your harm or denied-topic classifier on the final prompt and block the run; it fails closed on error or timeout.

steps.title: Hold replies with your own classifier
body: A plugin message_sending handler can rewrite the outbound content or return { cancel: true }; a handler that throws or times out is logged and skipped, so this gate fails open.

controls.note: Partial by the attach-point rule: a config switch classifies model traffic only on the Amazon Bedrock provider, where AWS runs the classifier; every other provider gets nothing unless the user attaches a plugin. No harm-category, denied-topic or blocked-term filter ships in OpenClaw itself, and the only built-in output processing is the sanitizer that strips leaked tool-call scaffolding. The decision models API (onnx, TypeSafe) has no automatic consumer wired to it.

original.note: No harm-category, denied-topic or blocked-term filter on model inputs or outputs is documented; the only output processing is the scaffolding sanitizer. Apply guardrails at the provider (the Amazon Bedrock plugin advertises guardrail support but documents no key) and keep /reasoning, /verbose and /trace off in shared rooms.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed; no setting for this control (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: Attach points on both legs: plugin message_sending / reply_payload_sending hooks can rewrite or cancel an outbound reply, and before_tool_call can rewrite a tool call's params or block it; a Bedrock Guardrail's sensitive-information filters apply on the Bedrock provider only. Built in: pattern and exact-value redaction of logs and operator surfaces (logging.redactPatterns) and tools.fs.workspaceOnly path fences.

steps.title: Redact replies and tool calls in a plugin
body: Register message_sending (rewrite content or cancel delivery) and before_tool_call (rewrite params or block) handlers that call your DLP detector; message_sending fails open when a handler errors, before_tool_call fails closed.

steps.title: Use the Bedrock Guardrail's sensitive-information filters
body: A guardrail referenced from plugins.entries.amazon-bedrock.config.guardrail applies its sensitive-information filters to Bedrock invocations; other providers are not covered.

steps.title: Extend log redaction
body: Set logging.redactPatterns (regex strings) for tokens, hostnames and internal URLs; the setting replaces the default string list, so include the defaults you still want.

steps.title: Keep file tools inside the workspace
body: Set tools.fs.workspaceOnly true and leave tools.exec.applyPatch.workspaceOnly at its default true; avoid broad workspace roots such as the home directory.

controls.note: Partial by the rule: detection on the reply and tool-call legs is the user's own detector at a hook, or AWS's filter on the Bedrock path only. The built-in redaction matches known secret patterns in logs, Control UI tool events, diagnostics exports and approval displays; it does not inspect prompts sent to the provider or replies sent to a channel. workspaceOnly is data minimisation, not detection.

original.mechanism: Always-on secret redaction across console, file logs, OTLP records and transcripts with logging.redactPatterns for custom patterns, tools.fs.workspaceOnly and tools.exec.applyPatch.workspaceOnly to keep file tools inside the workspace, write-only store secrets, and channel contextVisibility. No policy inspection of prompt or response content for sensitive data.

steps.title: Add your own redaction patterns
body: Set logging.redactPatterns (regex strings) for tokens, hostnames and internal URLs; note that setting it replaces the built-in defaults, so include the ones you still want.

steps.title: Keep file tools inside the workspace
body: Set tools.fs.workspaceOnly true and leave tools.exec.applyPatch.workspaceOnly at its default true; avoid broad workspace roots such as the home directory.

steps.title: Limit what rooms feed the prompt
body: Use contextVisibility on group channels so the agent reads only what it needs, and keep /reasoning, /verbose and /trace disabled outside trusted DMs.

original.note: Redaction is pattern-based and applied to logs, transcripts and telemetry after the fact; prompts sent to the model provider and tool results are not inspected. Treat it as log hygiene, not prompt DLP.

controls.mechanism: Per-channel dmPolicy (pairing by default, allowlist, open, disabled) with allowFrom and groupAllowFrom, reusable accessGroups referenced as accessGroup:<name> from any channel's lists, commands.allowFrom and commands.ownerAllowFrom for commands and directives, and explicit approval of paired devices and nodes.

steps.title: Define approved senders once
body: Put approved senders in accessGroups.<name> (type "message.senders", members keyed "*" for every channel or by channel) and set each channel's allowFrom to ["accessGroup:<name>"] with dmPolicy "allowlist".

steps.title: Keep unknown senders out
body: Leave dmPolicy "pairing" or use "allowlist"; approve a request with `openclaw pairing approve <channel> <code>` (codes expire after one hour and pending requests cap at three per channel account).

steps.title: Restrict who may issue commands
body: Set commands.allowFrom per provider (when set it is the only authorization source for commands and directives such as /exec) and commands.ownerAllowFrom for owner-only commands.

steps.title: Approve devices explicitly
body: Review pending and paired devices with `openclaw devices list`, approve a request with `openclaw devices approve <requestId>` and remove strays with `openclaw devices remove <deviceId>`.

controls.note: Partial by the architecture rule: admission is set channel by channel and an approved sender never expires or gets re-checked — the pairing page says approvals persist until removed. accessGroups let every bridge use one list, but each channel has to reference it and group policies stay separate. No directory binding: members are platform IDs, except Discord's channelAudience type, which resolves membership through Discord at authorization time. The 2026-09-11 advisory batch fixed per-channel admission bypasses in 2026.8.1 (GHSA-58qx-6m8p-wh2j Slack group DMs, GHSA-8938-r7c6-54vq Microsoft Teams access groups).

original.mechanism: gateway.auth.mode (token | password | trusted-proxy; required by default, fail-closed), dmPolicy pairing plus allowFrom allowlists per channel, device and node pairing approvals, and gateway.roles / gateway.auth.identityScopes for operator.read | write | admin scopes on team gateways

steps.title: Require gateway authentication
body: Set gateway.auth.mode "token" and a real gateway.auth.token (24+ characters; `openclaw doctor --generate-gateway-token` mints one); startup rejects blank or placeholder secrets and the audit flags short ones.

steps.title: Gate who can message the agent
body: Keep dmPolicy "pairing" (the default) and approve senders with `openclaw pairing approve <channel> <code>`, or switch to "allowlist" with an explicit allowFrom list; "open" requires allowFrom to contain "*".

steps.title: Approve devices and nodes explicitly
body: Review `openclaw devices list`, remove strays with `openclaw devices remove <deviceId>`, and set gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveLocal false to require a decision for every device; leave autoApproveCidrs unset.

steps.title: Scope operator connections
body: On a shared gateway define gateway.roles with per-role scopes (operator.read, operator.write, operator.approvals, operator.admin) and map identities with gateway.auth.identityScopes; a required gateway.roles.default caps everyone else.

controls.mechanism: tools.exec.mode (deny | allowlist | ask | auto | full) under a host approvals floor (the stricter of config and host approvals wins), with approval-backed runs bound to resolved executables, argv, cwd and one file operand; tools.allow / tools.deny, tools.toolsBySender and per-agent tools; tools.fs.workspaceOnly; plugin before_tool_call hooks (block or require approval, fail closed). Stored automation jobs carry an explicit tool list. The default is full host exec with no prompts.

steps.title: Choose an exec mode that enforces policy
body: `openclaw config set tools.exec.mode allowlist` (misses are denied) or `ask` (misses go to a human); `deny` blocks host exec, and `auto` adds a model reviewer, which is not a deterministic rule.

steps.title: Stop the agent rewriting its own policy
body: Put group:automation (or at least the openclaw tool) in tools.deny, or run the messaging, coding or minimal profile, which omits openclaw; under Full Access, including the default, a config change the agent delegates through openclaw is applied without an approval prompt.

steps.title: Bind unattended jobs to a tool list
body: Create agent-turn automations with `--tools` naming only what the job needs (`--tools ""` disables every tool); jobs an agent creates are capped to that turn's tools and it cannot widen the stored list.

steps.title: Add a deterministic plugin gate
body: A plugin before_tool_call handler returning block true, or a requireApproval decision, is terminal for that tool call; the runner blocks the call when the handler throws or times out.

controls.note: Native by the same rule as Claude Code: deterministic config rules over tool name and, for exec, the arguments and resolved binary, evaluated by the Gateway before the call runs and outside the model. Unattended turns: automation jobs store an explicit tool policy that agent-created jobs cannot widen, but heartbeat turns run with the agent's ordinary tools — there is no restricted class for them. Outside the decision point: a remote MCP server's own actions; the auto-mode and workspace-mode LLM reviewer, a second gate that is not deterministic; and the Policy plugin's policy.jsonc, a conformance check rather than a runtime decision. Exec allowlist parsing bypasses were fixed in 2026.8.1 (GHSA-ghpx-6xwq-2w4w, GHSA-9f86-pvv5-rxfw), which sets the version floor.

original.mechanism: tools.exec.mode (deny | allowlist | ask | auto | full) evaluated on the execution host against the per-agent allowlist, with approval-backed runs bound to resolved executables and one file operand and denied on drift; plugin before_tool_call hooks can block or require approval for any tool call. The trusted-operator default resolves to full/off.

steps.title: Choose an exec mode that enforces policy
body: `openclaw config set tools.exec.mode allowlist` (silent deny on miss) or `ask` (human prompt on miss); the default for gateway and node hosts is security full with ask off, and `deny` blocks host exec entirely.

steps.title: Verify the effective policy
body: Run `openclaw approvals get` and `openclaw exec-policy show`; effective policy is the stricter of tools.exec.* and the host approvals file, and askFallback defaults to deny when no UI can answer a prompt.

steps.title: Rely on approval binding
body: Approved commands bind cwd, exact argv, resolved executable identity (content hash for writable binaries) and one concrete script or file operand; a change after approval denies the run instead of executing drifted content.

steps.title: Add a deterministic plugin gate
body: A plugin before_tool_call handler returning block true (or requiring an allow-once | allow-always | deny decision) is terminal for that tool call and is recorded as an enforced decision in the audit ledger.

original.note: exec mode and allowlists are deterministic and bound to resolved executables; before_tool_call plugin hooks are an integration point. MCP tool calls pass tool policy; a server's own actions are outside it.

controls.mechanism: gateway.bind "loopback" by default; gateway.auth required by default (token | password | trusted-proxy; non-loopback binds require auth and "none" is an explicit opt-in); gateway.controlUi.allowedOrigins (defaulting to gateway.publicOrigin) for browser origins; device clients sign the server's connect.challenge nonce; gateway.tls with gateway.remote.tlsFingerprint pinning for remote clients.

steps.title: Keep the Gateway on loopback with token auth
body: Leave gateway.bind "loopback" and set gateway.auth.mode "token" with a long gateway.auth.token (onboarding generates one); reach it remotely through Tailscale Serve or an SSH tunnel rather than a LAN bind.

steps.title: Pin browser origins
body: Set gateway.controlUi.allowedOrigins (or gateway.publicOrigin) to the exact Control UI origin and leave gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback unset.

steps.title: Pin remote connections
body: Use wss:// with gateway.remote.tlsFingerprint set to the expected SHA-256 certificate fingerprint; plaintext ws:// is accepted only for loopback, private IP literals, .local and *.ts.net, and OPENCLAW_ALLOW_INSECURE_PRIVATE_WS is break-glass.

steps.title: Approve every device
body: Set gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveLocal false (default true) so pairing, role and scope upgrades from local connections need an explicit decision.

controls.note: Native: loopback binding, fail-closed authentication and a browser-origin allowlist are all settings the user controls, and device handshakes sign a server nonce with a timestamp, which protects the handshake against replay. Outside it: gateway.auth.mode "none" on loopback; Tailscale Serve identity-header auth (gateway.auth.allowTailscale defaults to true under Serve) trusts the tailnet; same-origin LAN and tailnet UI loads are accepted without an explicit origin; stdio MCP servers have no transport authentication and HTTP MCP servers rely on their own TLS or OAuth; a bearer token alone carries no replay protection. Upgrade-like requests could keep unauthenticated sockets before 2026.8.1 (GHSA-4r25-35qc-fr6j).

original.mechanism: Authenticated Gateway WebSocket (token/password/device identity, fail-closed), gateway.tls for HTTPS/WSS termination, gateway.remote.tlsFingerprint pinning for remote clients, SSH-verified node pairing, and TLS / mTLS / OAuth settings per MCP server

steps.title: Terminate TLS at the gateway or pin the proxy
body: Set gateway.tls.enabled true with certPath, keyPath and optional caPath (autoGenerate produces a self-signed pair for local use only), or terminate TLS at a reverse proxy listed in gateway.trustedProxies.

steps.title: Pin remote gateway connections
body: Use wss:// with gateway.remote.tlsFingerprint set to the expected SHA-256 certificate fingerprint; plaintext ws:// is accepted only for loopback, private IP literals, .local and *.ts.net, and OPENCLAW_ALLOW_INSECURE_PRIVATE_WS is break-glass.

steps.title: Authenticate MCP servers
body: Configure HTTP MCP servers with TLS verification and mTLS certificate/key paths through `openclaw mcp add` / `openclaw mcp configure`, prefer auth "oauth" with `openclaw mcp login <name>`, and keep literal bearer tokens out of config.

steps.title: Keep node pairing key-verified
body: gateway.nodes.pairing.sshVerify (default on) approves a node only on an exact device-key match read back over SSH with strict host keys; leave gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveCidrs unset.

original.note: By channel: gateway WebSocket (authenticated, TLS when gateway.tls is set, fingerprint pinning for remote clients); node pairing (SSH-verified); HTTPS MCP servers (TLS, optional mTLS, OAuth); stdio MCP servers (a local process boundary, no transport authentication — do not expect mTLS there). Bearer tokens over TLS give no replay protection, and message schema validation is each server's job.

controls.mechanism: Provenance on every memory entry, in SQLite columns the model cannot write (owner | agent | untrusted | system); curated MEMORY.md and USER.md are injected only when their provenance is eligible; the dreaming consolidation pass is the primary durable writer and excludes untrusted, system, cron, heartbeat and sub-agent candidates, validates each rewrite, keeps its pre-image and logs a summary to DREAMS.md; memoryPolicy.excludeSessions and `openclaw memory forget` scope and purge by lineage.

steps.title: Exclude untrusted sources from memory ingestion
body: Set plugins.entries.memory-core.config.memoryPolicy.excludeSessions with hookExternalContentSources (for example ["email", "gmail"]), channels or chatTypes so those sessions never enter dreaming ingestion or backfill.

steps.title: Decide which writers run
body: plugins.entries.memory-core.config.dreaming.enabled false stops consolidation, and agents.defaults.compaction.memoryFlush.enabled false stops the silent save turn before compaction.

steps.title: Purge what a session wrote
body: `openclaw memory forget --agent <id> --session <id-or-key> --dry-run --json` previews lineage-based removal; rerun without --dry-run to delete, or purge by --participant or --hook-source.

steps.title: Give each agent its own workspace and sandbox scope
body: Set agents.entries.<id>.workspace per agent and keep agents.defaults.sandbox.scope "agent" (or "session"); "shared" removes cross-session isolation.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: disabling and scoping are native and the consolidation path is gated, validated and reviewable, but not every write is. The agent writes USER.md, MEMORY.md and daily notes directly with its file tools when asked; the admission policy does not restrict workspace writes; turn taint covers only tools that declare network-sourced output. Nothing scans memory content, and recovery is forget and re-ingest plus stored pre-images, not a versioned store. Dreaming could widen restricted sender authority before 2026.8.1 (GHSA-62qm-6fjj-6g23).

original.mechanism: Per-agent workspaces and sandbox scope isolate memory files; a memory admission policy keeps chosen sources out of dreaming ingestion; dreaming taint-gates untrusted candidates; `openclaw memory forget` purges by session, participant or hook source using recorded lineage. Memory is plain Markdown the agent writes; there is no write validation, quarantine or rollback beyond forget.

steps.title: Give each agent its own workspace and sandbox scope
body: Set agents.entries.<id>.workspace per agent and keep agents.defaults.sandbox.scope "agent" (or "session" for per-session isolation); "shared" removes cross-session isolation.

steps.title: Exclude untrusted sources from long-term memory
body: Set plugins.entries.memory-core.config.memoryPolicy.excludeSessions with hookExternalContentSources (for example ["email", "gmail"]), channels or chatTypes so those sessions never enter dreaming ingestion or backfill.

steps.title: Purge what a session wrote
body: `openclaw memory forget --agent <id> --session <id-or-key> --dry-run --json` previews lineage-based removal; rerun without --dry-run to delete, or purge by --participant or --hook-source.

steps.title: Control background promotion
body: Dreaming promotes only scored, provenance-gated candidates into MEMORY.md and writes a reviewable DREAMS.md diary; disable it with plugins.entries.memory-core.config.dreaming.enabled false.

original.note: Admission policy and taint-gating are integrity contributions at ingestion; per-agent workspaces are the boundary. What can still write: the agent's own turns. Recovery is forget and re-ingest, not a versioned store.

controls.mechanism: agents.defaults.sandbox (mode off | non-main | all; backend docker | podman | ssh | openshell | crabbox; scope agent | session | shared; workspaceAccess none | ro | rw) with Docker defaults of network none, readOnlyRoot, capDrop ALL, user 1000:1000, pids/memory/cpu limits and the openclaw-sandbox AppArmor profile; per-call host overrides are rejected while a sandbox is active; off by default.

steps.title: Sandbox every session
body: Set agents.defaults.sandbox.mode "all"; "non-main" leaves each agent's main session, the owner's DM, on the host.

steps.title: Keep the container defaults
body: The documented defaults are docker.network "none", readOnlyRoot true, capDrop ["ALL"], user 1000:1000, pidsLimit 256, memory 1g, cpus 1 and apparmorProfile openclaw-sandbox; add a seccompProfile, and note that "host" networking is blocked.

steps.title: Close the escape hatches
body: Set tools.elevated.enabled false (both the global and any per-agent gate must be true for elevated to work), which stops exec calls with elevated true from leaving the sandbox and also locks out ! shell commands.

steps.title: Keep the agent out of its own config
body: Put group:automation (or the openclaw tool) in tools.deny so a Full Access run cannot apply a sandbox or tool change it delegates without your approval; group denies override an explicit openclaw allow.

controls.note: Native on the architecture rule: with mode "all", tools.elevated.enabled false and the openclaw delegation tool denied, the container is a boundary the agent cannot leave or reconfigure from inside; while a sandbox is active, per-call host=gateway and host=node requests are rejected. The defaults are the opposite (sandbox off, openclaw available under Full Access), so the rating holds only once those keys are set. An authorized sender's /exec host=gateway directive still moves a session's exec to the host, so limit commands.allowFrom to yourself; only a team-gateway role with sandbox "required" is immune to it. Outside the boundary: the Gateway process and what runs in it (channel adapters, plugins, the MCP servers its client launches). Browser node targets could bypass sandbox host control before 2026.7.1 (GHSA-9x88-f7rh-4c83).

original.mechanism: agents.defaults.sandbox (mode off | non-main | all; backend docker | podman | openshell | ssh; scope session | agent | shared; workspaceAccess none | ro | rw) with container defaults of network none, readOnlyRoot, capDrop ALL, non-root user, pids/memory/cpu limits and optional seccomp/AppArmor profiles; off by default

steps.title: Turn the tool sandbox on
body: Set agents.defaults.sandbox.mode "all" (or "non-main" to sandbox everything but the main session) and pick a backend; the audit warns when Docker settings exist while mode is still off.

steps.title: Keep the container defaults
body: The documented defaults are docker.network "none", readOnlyRoot true, capDrop ["ALL"], user 1000:1000, tmpfs for /tmp, and pidsLimit/memory/cpus caps; add seccompProfile or apparmorProfile paths and never use network "host".

steps.title: Limit what the sandbox can see
body: workspaceAccess "none" (default) hides the agent workspace, "ro" mounts it read-only at /agent; extra docker.binds are validated against a denylist covering /etc, /proc, the Docker socket paths and ~/.ssh, ~/.aws and similar.

steps.title: Close the escape hatch
body: Set tools.elevated.enabled false (and per agent agents.entries.<id>.tools.elevated) so exec cannot leave the sandbox onto the gateway or node host.

original.note: Mode is off by default and non-main sandboxes only non-main agents; set all to cover every agent. Inside the boundary: exec and file tools of sandboxed agents. Outside: the gateway process, channel adapters and any MCP server launched on the host.

controls.mechanism: tools.profile (minimal | coding | messaging | full) plus tools.allow / tools.deny (deny wins, wildcards, groups such as group:runtime, group:fs and group:automation), layered per provider (tools.byProvider), per sender (tools.toolsBySender), per agent (agents.entries.*.tools), for sandboxed sessions (tools.sandbox.tools) and per sub-agent (tools.subagents.tools), with path scoping from tools.fs.workspaceOnly and argument scoping from the exec allowlist

steps.title: Start from a profile and deny the rest
body: Set tools.profile ("messaging" or "minimal" for a chat-facing agent; an unset profile leaves core tools unfiltered) and list tools.deny entries such as group:runtime, group:fs and browser; deny always wins, and write and apply_patch are separate tool ids.

steps.title: Fence file tools to the workspace
body: Set tools.fs.workspaceOnly true to restrict read, write, edit and apply_patch paths to the workspace; tools.exec.applyPatch.workspaceOnly is already true by default.

steps.title: Scope per agent and per sender
body: Override with agents.entries.<id>.tools.{profile,allow,deny} and restrict specific requesters with tools.toolsBySender keys such as "id:<senderId>" or "*" (defence in depth on top of channel allowlists).

steps.title: Bound sub-agents and cross-agent reach
body: Narrow tools.subagents.tools.deny/allow and agents.defaults.subagents.allowAgents; set tools.sessions.visibility "agent" and tools.agentToAgent.enabled false as in the hardened baseline.

controls.note: Native by the same rule as Claude Code: per-tool allow and deny with path scoping (workspaceOnly) and, for exec, argument scoping (an allowlist bound to the resolved binary), set in config and enforced by the Gateway outside the model. Limits: MCP tools are scoped by server and tool name (server__* globs), not arguments; message, browser and web tools are on or off per agent or sender, with host policies of their own (cross-context messaging, SSRF host lists); tools run with the owner's own authority; and the full profile, the onboarding default, pre-approves everything.

original.mechanism: tools.profile (minimal | coding | messaging | full) plus tools.allow / tools.deny (deny wins, wildcards, tool groups such as group:runtime and group:fs), layered per provider (tools.byProvider), per sender (tools.toolsBySender), per agent (agents.entries.*.tools) and per sub-agent (tools.subagents.tools)

steps.title: Start from a profile and deny the rest
body: Set tools.profile ("messaging" or "minimal" for a chat-facing agent) and list tools.deny entries such as group:runtime, group:fs, browser; deny always wins and applies even when the sandbox is off.

steps.title: Deny control-plane tools where untrusted content flows
body: For any agent or surface that reads untrusted content set tools.deny to include gateway, cron, sessions_spawn and sessions_send; non-owner senders already cannot use cron or gateway.

steps.title: Scope per agent and per sender
body: Override with agents.entries.<id>.tools.{profile,allow,deny} and restrict specific requesters with tools.toolsBySender keys such as "id:<senderId>" or "*" (defence in depth on top of channel allowlists).

steps.title: Bound sub-agents and cross-agent reach
body: Narrow tools.subagents.tools.deny/allow and agents.defaults.subagents.allowAgents; set tools.sessions.visibility "agent" and tools.agentToAgent.enabled false as in the hardened baseline.

original.note: Profiles and allow/deny lists hide tools per provider, sender and agent; exec approvals gate; argument limits come from exec allowlists bound to resolved executables. full profile pre-approves everything.

controls.mechanism: The secret egress proxy (secrets.egressProxy.enabled, off by default) gives Gateway-hosted exec an authenticated sentinel that a loopback proxy swaps for the real value only on the exact HTTPS hosts bound with --allow-host, refusing every other destination; SecretRef provider keys travel the model-call chain as sentinels until egress; HTTP MCP servers hold their own OAuth grants; tools.github gives agent exec a separate, auto-refreshed GitHub identity instead of the owner's gh login.

steps.title: Bind each secret to its destination
body: `openclaw secrets store set OPENAI_API_KEY --allow-host api.openai.com`, then `openclaw config set secrets.egressProxy.enabled true --strict-json` and restart; a sentinel sent to any other host is refused before the plaintext leaves.

steps.title: Keep provider keys in SecretRefs
body: Point models.providers.<id>.apiKey at { source: "store" | "file" | "env" | "exec", provider, id } so the model-call chain carries a sentinel and an unresolved one is never sent.

steps.title: Give agent GitHub work its own identity
body: Configure tools.github (Settings → Profile → GitHub connections, For the system) with a fine-grained PAT or the device flow so agent exec uses a dedicated credential, refreshed about every eight hours, rather than your own gh login.

steps.title: Give MCP servers their own grants
body: Configure HTTP servers with auth "oauth", authorise with `openclaw mcp login <name>` and revoke with `openclaw mcp logout <name>`.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: credentials are separated per destination and per server, and a destination-bound sentinel stays useless even if the proxy is bypassed, but nothing narrows a grant to the task — each call carries the owner's standing key, token or OAuth scope (the managed GitHub identity requests repo, workflow, read:org and gist). The proxy covers Gateway-hosted exec only; sandbox and node exec receive no store secrets through it, while agent-readable env entries and the inherited Gateway environment reach host commands in plaintext. There is no on-behalf-of exchange.

original.mechanism: SecretRefs keep provider credentials out of config and hand the model-call chain a process-local sentinel; the default-off secret egress proxy gives Gateway-hosted subprocesses sentinels that a loopback proxy swaps in only for host-bound destinations; workspace .env cannot inject provider keys; MCP servers hold their own OAuth grants. The agent still acts with the operator's own accounts — there is no on-behalf-of exchange.

steps.title: Replace plaintext credentials with SecretRefs
body: Point models.providers.<id>.apiKey and other supported fields at { source: "store" | "file" | "env" | "exec", provider, id }; the runtime mints an oc-sent-v2 sentinel and refuses to send an unresolved one.

steps.title: Bind subprocess secrets to destinations
body: `openclaw secrets store set OPENAI_API_KEY --allow-host api.openai.com`, then `openclaw config set secrets.egressProxy.enabled true --strict-json` and restart; exec commands receive sentinels the proxy substitutes only for the bound host.

steps.title: Keep workspace .env files powerless
body: Provider API-key variables, every OPENCLAW_* key and endpoint-routing variables are blocked from untrusted workspace .env files; put credentials in the gateway process environment, ~/.openclaw/.env or config instead.

steps.title: Give MCP servers their own grants
body: Configure HTTP servers with auth "oauth", authorise with `openclaw mcp login <name>` and revoke with `openclaw mcp logout <name>`; tokens live in state/openclaw.sqlite.

original.note: SecretRefs keep provider credentials out of the model-call chain by default; the secret egress proxy for subprocesses is off by default, and workspace .env files are readable by tools unless moved. Single-user gateway, so on-behalf-of exchange does not arise unless several people share it — then every tool call carries the gateway's credentials, not the requester's.

controls.mechanism: SecretRefs (source env | file | exec | store) resolve into an in-memory snapshot, with exec providers for external managers (a Vault resolver command, the 1Password plugin); write-only kind "secret" store entries; model-provider credentials held as sentinels until the final adapter boundary; `openclaw secrets audit --check` finds plaintext residue. The built-in store is unencrypted at rest (0600/0700 permissions).

steps.title: Pull credentials from an external manager
body: Declare secrets.providers with an exec provider (for example a Vault resolver command) and reference it from credential fields as { source "exec", provider, id } instead of the built-in store, which is not encrypted at rest.

steps.title: Store the rest as write-only
body: `openclaw secrets store set <NAME>` (kind secret) values are never returned by list/get or the Control UI and stay inert until a SecretRef or the egress proxy uses them; kind env values are agent-readable by design.

steps.title: Audit and scrub plaintext residue
body: Run `openclaw secrets audit --check`, then `secrets configure` and `secrets apply` until the audit is clean; residue in openclaw.json, the SQLite auth store, .env and generated models.json stays agent-readable until scrubbed.

steps.title: Lock down the state directory
body: Keep ~/.openclaw at 700 and openclaw.json plus credential files at 600; `openclaw security audit --fix` tightens them, and full-disk encryption plus a dedicated OS user are the documented host baseline.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: secrets can come from a manager and stay out of config, transcripts and the model's context, but the Gateway process that runs the agent loop holds the resolved values in memory — the vendor says sentinels are not process isolation — the built-in store is unencrypted, and agent-readable env entries, plain environment variables and unscrubbed residue stay readable to unsandboxed tools. Short-lived issuance covers the egress proxy's per-process grants and the tools.github OAuth token, not provider keys.

original.mechanism: SecretRef providers env | file | exec | store, exec recipes for 1Password, Bitwarden, HashiCorp Vault, pass and sops, a shared secret store with write-only "secret" entries, per-run proxy credentials that expire when the agent run closes, and `openclaw secrets audit --check` as the migration gate. The store itself is not encrypted at rest (0600/0700 permissions only).

steps.title: Configure SecretRef providers
body: Declare secrets.providers (for example a file provider with mode "singleValue") and reference entries from credential fields; the exec provider runs a trusted local command such as a 1Password, Bitwarden, Vault, pass or sops CLI.

steps.title: Use the shared store for write-only values
body: `openclaw secrets store set <NAME>` (kind secret) values are never returned by list/get or the Control UI and are inert until a SecretRef or the egress proxy uses them; kind env values stay agent-readable by design.

steps.title: Audit and scrub plaintext residue
body: Run `openclaw secrets audit --check`, then `secrets configure` and `secrets apply` until the audit is clean; residue in openclaw.json, the SQLite auth store, .env and generated models.json stays agent-readable until scrubbed.

steps.title: Lock down the state directory
body: Keep ~/.openclaw at 700 and openclaw.json plus credential files at 600; `openclaw security audit --fix` tightens them and full-disk encryption plus a dedicated OS user are the documented host baseline.

original.note: SecretRefs pull from a vault and hand the model-call chain a sentinel; per-run proxy credentials are the ephemeral path and expire with the run. Exec tools still read the gateway process environment unless the secret egress proxy is on.

controls.mechanism: Plugins: plugins.allow exclusive allowlist, `--pin` exact npm versions, ClawHub digest verification and recorded integrity, and audit findings for unpinned, integrity-less or drifted records. Skills: recorded install digests with local-edit detection on update and `openclaw skills verify`. Both: security.installPolicy (allow | warn | block). MCP servers: mcp.servers definitions with toolFilter; tool definitions are neither pinned nor re-approved when they change.

steps.title: Allowlist plugins explicitly
body: Set plugins.allow to the plugin ids you trust (plugins.deny wins over it); the Gateway logs "plugins.allow is empty; discovered non-bundled plugins may auto-load" and the audit flags plugins.extensions_no_allowlist.

steps.title: Pin and verify installs
body: `openclaw plugins install <package> --pin` records the exact npm version; ClawHub installs verify the digest header and artifact digest, and `openclaw security audit` warns on plugins.installs_unpinned_npm_specs, plugins.installs_missing_integrity and plugins.installs_version_drift.

steps.title: Run your own install policy
body: Configure security.installPolicy (enabled, targets ["skill", "plugin"], exec.command) to run a trusted local command that returns allow, warn or block before any skill or plugin install commits; --force never overrides block.

steps.title: Filter MCP tools
body: Restrict each server with mcp.servers.<name>.toolFilter.include or exclude, check it with `openclaw mcp doctor <name> --probe`, and put bundle-mcp in tools.deny when no MCP server is needed.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: an allowlist admits servers but pins nothing they serve. Plugins and ClawHub skills get content pinning (digest-verified artifacts, recorded integrity, drift warnings), but MCP servers do not: a tool-list change invalidates the cached catalog and the next discovery takes the server's new definitions without re-approval, nothing scans tool descriptions, and a stdio server is pinned only if its command names a versioned package. Official ClawHub packages and bundled plugins skip the release-trust check.

original.mechanism: plugins.allow exclusive allowlist plus plugins.deny, `--pin` exact versions with digest-verified ClawHub artifacts and a security-audit trust check before download, a security.installPolicy exec hook (allow | warn | block) for skill and plugin installs, and per-MCP-server toolFilter and probes. MCP tool definitions are not hash-pinned and there is no built-in static analysis of installed code.

steps.title: Allowlist plugins explicitly
body: Set plugins.allow to the plugin ids you trust (plugins.deny wins over it); the gateway logs "plugins.allow is empty; discovered non-bundled plugins may auto-load" and the audit flags loading without an allowlist.

steps.title: Pin and verify installs
body: `openclaw plugins install <package> --pin` records the exact npm version; ClawHub installs verify the artifact digest and print the release's security-audit outcome, and `openclaw security audit` warns on unpinned or integrity-less records.

steps.title: Run your own install policy
body: Configure security.installPolicy (enabled, targets ["skill", "plugin"], exec.command) to run a trusted local command that returns allow, warn or block before any skill or plugin install commits; --force never bypasses it.

steps.title: Filter and probe MCP servers
body: Restrict each server with mcp.servers.<name>.toolFilter.include, verify it with `openclaw mcp doctor <name> --probe`, and disable all configured servers with tools.deny ["bundle-mcp"] when none are needed.

original.note: Rated native on the personal-agent rule: the user can make plugins.allow exclusive and pin digest-verified versions in the product's own config. Admission is not integrity — tool definitions an MCP server returns are not pinned or re-verified between sessions.

controls.mechanism: tools.exec.mode ask (allowlist misses go to a human) or tools.exec.ask "always" (every command, and allow-always grants do not suppress the prompt), with askFallback deny when no approval surface answers; per-server MCP approval (`openclaw mcp configure <server> --approval prompt`); human approval of config changes an agent delegates through the openclaw tool in restricted permission modes; requireApproval from plugin before_tool_call hooks.

steps.title: Require a human on host commands
body: Set tools.exec.mode "ask" (allowlist matches run, misses prompt) or tools.exec.ask "always" for every command; leave askFallback at its default deny so an unanswered prompt blocks rather than allows.

steps.title: Keep the bypass modes off
body: Avoid tools.exec.mode "full" or "auto" and the "workspace" session mode (their reviewer is a model), keep "full" sessions to operator.admin, and leave tools.elevated off so /elevated full cannot skip prompts.

steps.title: Prompt on MCP tools
body: `openclaw mcp configure <server> --approval prompt` keeps asking for that server's tools regardless of stored grants; `auto` honours per-agent Allow Always grants.

steps.title: Answer prompts where you are
body: Approvals arrive as exec.approval.requested in the Control UI, the macOS app and chat channels; choose Allow Once, or Always Allow Here where the policy permits durable trust.

controls.note: Native: a person approves each named action with its bound command, cwd and executable, and every mode or grant that would skip the prompt is a config choice the user can remove. Unattended turns: with no approval surface reachable askFallback denies; automation runs deliver the approval card and wait, and answering Always allow there mints a standing grant unless ask is "always". Boundaries: approvals cover host exec, MCP tools, delegated config changes and plugin-declared approvals — the message, browser and file tools have no prompt of their own (deny them or gate them with before_tool_call); the auto and workspace reviewers are a model, not human approval. Reusable approvals could authorize changed arguments before 2026.8.1 (GHSA-74gc-hg2m-79p9).

original.mechanism: Exec approvals (tools.exec.mode ask, exec.ask always, askFallback deny) broadcast exec.approval.requested to the Control UI, macOS app and chat channels with Allow Once / Always Allow Here; MCP tool approval mode per server; typed acknowledgement for install-policy warnings; operator.approvals scope gates who may answer

steps.title: Require a human on new commands
body: Set tools.exec.mode "ask" (allowlist matches run, misses prompt) or exec.ask "always" for every command; leave askFallback at its default deny so an unanswered prompt blocks rather than allows.

steps.title: Answer prompts where you are
body: Approvals arrive as exec.approval.requested; choose Allow Once (Command-Return on macOS) or Always Allow Here, and the gateway forwards the stored plan, rejecting any caller edits to command, cwd or session after the request was created.

steps.title: Prompt on MCP tools
body: `openclaw mcp configure <server> --approval prompt` keeps asking for that server's tools regardless of stored grants; `auto` honours per-agent Allow Always grants.

steps.title: Acknowledge install warnings deliberately
body: A security.installPolicy warn result stops the install until the operator types the plugin or skill name (or passes --acknowledge-install-policy-warning after review); Gateway-backed installs with no confirmation flow stay blocked.

controls.mechanism: agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds (elapsed run budget, default 172800 s, aborting on expiry), tools.loopDetection (off by default; blocks a repeating tool batch, then ends the run), sub-agent maxConcurrent 8, maxChildrenPerAgent 5 and maxSpawnDepth (default 5), tools.exec.timeoutSeconds, and cadence for self-waking turns (heartbeat every and activeHours, automation pacing.min / pacing.max, cron.enabled). No turn or tool-call count and no token or spend ceiling.

steps.title: Cap each run's lifetime
body: Set agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds (default 172800, 48 hours; 0 is unlimited) to the longest run you accept; approval waits pause the budget.

steps.title: Break tool loops
body: Set tools.loopDetection.enabled true (off by default; the post-compaction guard stays on unless explicitly false) so repeated tool patterns warn, then block the batch and end the run.

steps.title: Cap delegation fan-out
body: agents.defaults.subagents.maxConcurrent (8), maxChildrenPerAgent (5) and maxSpawnDepth (default 5; 1 makes direct children leaves) bound sub-agent trees.

steps.title: Pace the self-waking loop
body: Set agents.defaults.heartbeat.every (default 30m; "0m" stops the cadence) and activeHours, and isolatedSession plus lightContext to shrink each heartbeat turn.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: the run-time budget, loop breaker, fan-out caps and schedule cadence are hard, config-level bounds, but there is no ceiling on turns or tool calls within a run and no token or spend budget — usage and cost are reported, not enforced, so a run under the 48-hour default can spend freely. Set hard budgets on the provider account. gateway.auth.rateLimit throttles failed logins, which is access protection, not resource control.

original.mechanism: gateway.auth.rateLimit for failed auth, fixed control-plane write and webhook throttles, tools.loopDetection with a post-compaction guard, sub-agent concurrency and depth caps, tools.exec.timeoutSeconds, and usage/quota visibility per provider. No hard token or spend cap is offered.

steps.title: Tune the brute-force limiter
body: gateway.auth.rateLimit { maxAttempts 10, windowMs 60000, lockoutMs 300000, exemptLoopback true } are the defaults; webhook and control-plane write limits are fixed.

steps.title: Break tool loops
body: Set tools.loopDetection.enabled true (off by default; the post-compaction guard stays on unless explicitly false) so repeated (tool, args, result) patterns warn, then block the batch and end the run.

steps.title: Cap delegation fan-out and command lifetime
body: agents.defaults.subagents.maxConcurrent (8), maxChildrenPerAgent (5) and maxSpawnDepth (1-5) bound sub-agent trees; tools.exec.timeoutSeconds terminates long commands even when backgrounded.

steps.title: Watch spend
body: `openclaw status --usage`, /usage cost and the Control UI Usage page show provider quota windows and local cost estimates; set hard budgets on the provider account since OpenClaw enforces none.

original.note: Rated native on the same rule as Hermes: exec.timeoutSeconds, loopDetection and the sub-agent concurrency and depth caps are hard bounds on runtime and iterations. No token or currency spend cap exists — usage is visible per provider, not enforced. gateway.auth.rateLimit throttles failed logins, which is access protection, not agent resource control.

controls.mechanism: The diagnostics-otel plugin with diagnostics.otel exports OTLP traces (openclaw.run, model-call and openclaw.tool.execution spans with tool name, call id and params, message processed and delivery spans), metrics and optional logs to the user's collector, with content capture opt-in (captureContent); locally, a metadata-only audit ledger (logging.audit, 30 days, 100,000 rows) queried with `openclaw audit`.

steps.title: Export traces off the host
body: `openclaw plugins install clawhub:@openclaw/diagnostics-otel`, add it to plugins.allow and enable it, then set diagnostics.enabled and diagnostics.otel.enabled true with your endpoint, traces true and sampleRate 1.0 so no run is dropped.

steps.title: Decide what content is captured
body: diagnostics.otel.captureContent (off by default) adds message, tool and tool-definition content to spans and OTLP log bodies; leave it off unless the collector is cleared to hold it.

steps.title: Turn on identity and message records
body: `openclaw config set logging.audit.executionIdentity true` (off by default) and logging.audit.messages "direct" or "all", then restart the Gateway; keep logging.audit.enabled true.

steps.title: Query who did what
body: `openclaw audit --kind tool_action --json` and `openclaw audit --run <id> --explain` for the execution identity and decision receipts (approvals, plugin hook blocks).

controls.note: Native: the export is a config switch, carries each run's model calls and tool executions with their parameters, and lands in a collector off the agent's filesystem. Capture is not tamper resistance; durability belongs to the collector. Gaps: the plugin must be installed and allowed; a sampleRate below 1 drops traces; usage spans omit session identifiers (sessions.usage supplies them); prompt and result content is absent unless captureContent is on; the local ledger and the JSONL logs under /tmp/openclaw are files an unsandboxed agent can modify.

original.mechanism: Metadata-only activity ledger (logging.audit.enabled on by default) with optional execution identity and message lifecycle records, HMAC-pseudonymised identifiers, 30-day retention and a 100,000-row cap, queried with `openclaw audit`; OTLP export via diagnostics.otel. Persistence is best-effort and the store is a local SQLite file, so it is not tamper-evident on its own.

steps.title: Turn on identity and message records
body: `openclaw config set logging.audit.executionIdentity true` (off by default) and logging.audit.messages "direct" or "all", then restart the gateway; keep logging.audit.enabled true.

steps.title: Query who did what
body: `openclaw audit --kind tool_action --json`, `--agent`, `--session`, `--after`, and `openclaw audit --run <id> --explain` for the immutable execution identity and decision receipts (approvals, plugin hook blocks).

steps.title: Export off the host
body: Set diagnostics.otel.enabled true with endpoint, traces/metrics/logs and captureContent false to ship spans and log records to a collector you retain beyond 30 days.

original.note: No baselining of goals or tool-use profiles is documented; tools.loopDetection catches repetition only. Export /export-trajectory bundles or OTLP traces (diagnostics.otel) to an external analyser if drift detection is required.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed; no setting for this control (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: `openclaw gateway stop` drains and then cancels the Gateway's remaining runs (a drain of at most 315 seconds), which also halts automations and heartbeats because they run inside the Gateway; a standalone "stop" message aborts the current run; cron.enabled false pauses every automation without deleting it; the incident runbook covers contain, rotate and audit; `openclaw devices remove` drops paired devices.

steps.title: Stop the agent
body: `openclaw gateway stop` drains work, then cancels the remaining runs and waits for their commands to settle; `openclaw gateway uninstall` removes the service so it does not return at next login.

steps.title: Keep schedules from resuming
body: Set cron.enabled false before any restart; missed recurring slots are caught up at startup unless cron.skipMissedJobs is true.

steps.title: Rotate
body: Rotate gateway.auth.token or gateway.auth.password, gateway.remote.* on every client, and provider, channel and model credentials; then re-run `openclaw security audit --deep`.

steps.title: Revoke devices and sessions
body: `openclaw devices remove <deviceId>` drops a paired device; `openclaw sessions delete <sessionKey> --yes` removes a session's state.

controls.note: Native on the architecture rule: one documented command halts running turns and scheduled jobs, and the vendor's incident runbook lists every credential to rotate. Delay: running work gets the drain window (the Gateway runbook sets a 315-second maximum) before the remaining runs are cancelled; a "stop" chat message aborts the current run. A launchd stop does not change persistent enablement, so the service returns at next login unless uninstalled. Provider keys and channel tokens stay valid until rotated.

original.mechanism: `openclaw gateway stop`, the documented contain / rotate / audit runbook (bind loopback, dmPolicy disabled, rotate gateway.auth and provider credentials), `openclaw devices remove`, `openclaw sessions delete`, and commands.restart false to disable remote restarts

steps.title: Stop the agent
body: `openclaw gateway stop` (add --force in a non-interactive shell) halts the managed service; `openclaw gateway uninstall` removes it.

steps.title: Contain
body: Set gateway.bind "loopback" (or disable Tailscale Funnel/Serve), switch risky channels to dmPolicy "disabled" or require mentions, and remove any "*" allow-all entries.

steps.title: Rotate
body: Rotate gateway.auth.token or gateway.auth.password, gateway.remote.* on every client, and provider, channel and model credentials; then re-run `openclaw security audit --deep`.

steps.title: Revoke devices and sessions
body: `openclaw devices remove <deviceId>` drops a paired device; `openclaw sessions delete <sessionKey> --yes` removes a session's state.

controls.mechanism: `openclaw gateway discover` scans mDNS and wide-area DNS-SD for other OpenClaw Gateway beacons (_openclaw-gw._tcp); `openclaw security audit` reports plugins installed without plugins.allow and unpinned, integrity-less or drifted install records; the Gateway logs discovered non-bundled plugins at startup.

steps.title: Find other Gateways on the network
body: `openclaw gateway discover --json` lists beacons on local. and any configured wide-area domain; only Gateways with Bonjour discovery on (the default) advertise.

steps.title: Audit for unregistered extensions
body: Run `openclaw security audit`; plugins.extensions_no_allowlist, plugins.installs_unpinned_npm_specs and plugins.installs_missing_integrity flag extensions this Gateway never explicitly admitted.

steps.title: Act on discovery diagnostics
body: Treat the startup warning "plugins.allow is empty; discovered non-bundled plugins may auto-load" as unregistered code; pin it in plugins.allow or reinstall from a trusted source.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the project ships two discovery aids — a beacon scan that finds other OpenClaw Gateways that advertise, and an audit that finds extensions this Gateway did not explicitly allow. Gateways with discovery turned off, other agent products, personal accounts and API keys are not found; EDR/MDM inventory (the openclaw binary, ~/.openclaw, the ai.openclaw.gateway LaunchAgent or openclaw-gateway.service unit) and network monitoring cover those.

Scope is this gateway's own extension roots — nothing discovers other agents or accounts on the device.

steps.title: Audit for unregistered extensions
body: Run `openclaw security audit`; findings prefixed plugins.* and skills.* cover loading without plugins.allow, unpinned npm records and missing integrity metadata.

original.note: A narrow but real discovery contribution: it finds plugins and installs this gateway did not explicitly allow. Its scope is one installation's extension root; other OpenClaw installs on the estate are found by endpoint inventory.

controls.mechanism: plugins.allow is an exclusive allowlist backed by a persisted plugin registry that records source and install metadata (`openclaw plugins registry`, `plugins inspect`); ClawHub skills keep origin and install digests; agents.entries and `openclaw agents list --bindings` declare agents; mcp.servers and `openclaw mcp status` list tool servers with no version or source record.

steps.title: Approve extensions through the allowlist
body: plugins.allow is exclusive; a plugin outside it stays unavailable even when tools.allow contains "*", and plugins.entries.<id>.enabled false disables one.

steps.title: Read the recorded inventory
body: `openclaw plugins registry --json` shows the persisted identity, enablement and source metadata, and `openclaw plugins inspect <id>` the install metadata and declared capabilities.

steps.title: Declare agents explicitly

steps.title: Inventory tool servers
body: `openclaw mcp status --verbose` lists every mcp.servers definition with transport, auth and filter state.

An organisation running several gateways records them in its own agent register.

steps.title: Declare agents explicitly
body: `openclaw agents list --bindings` (or `--json`) enumerates agents, workspaces and channel bindings; add or remove them with `openclaw agents add|delete` rather than ad-hoc config.

steps.title: Approve extensions through the allowlist

body: `openclaw mcp status --verbose` lists every mcp.servers definition with enablement, OAuth and filter state; Settings → MCP in the Control UI shows the same inventory.

original.note: Native on the personal-agent rule: the config is the authoritative declaration of this gateway's agents, plugins and servers. It is scoped to one installation and carries no owner or approval workflow — a single-user product does not need one, but an organisation running several gateways records them centrally.

controls.note: External (EDR): OpenClaw analyses no process behaviour. Integration points for the sensor: the Gateway service (LaunchAgent label ai.openclaw.gateway, or ai.openclaw.<profile>, on macOS; systemd user unit openclaw-gateway.service on Linux) and the exec processes it spawns; the daily JSONL logs under /tmp/openclaw/; OpenTelemetry openclaw.tool.execution spans carrying each tool call's parameters for SIEM correlation; and a plugin before_tool_call hook, which fails closed, where a sensor's verdict can block a tool call. Run the Gateway as a dedicated OS user so its processes are attributable.

original.note: Nothing device-resident ships with the product; run the host's own EDR and a dedicated OS user. The documented integration point for a security agent is a plugin before_tool_call hook (block or require approval on every tool call) plus `openclaw security audit --deep` for live probes.

controls.mechanism: The Docker sandbox takes agents.defaults.sandbox.docker.network "none" (default), "bridge" or a custom network — on or off, with no destination list; the OpenShell backend applies an OpenShell policy file (plugins.entries.openshell.config.policy) that permits named destinations; secrets.egressProxy.allowedHosts restricts Gateway-hosted exec traffic for clients that honour the proxy; tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy host lists bound web_fetch; proxy.proxyUrl routes runtime traffic through the user's forward proxy.

steps.title: Keep the sandbox offline
body: Leave agents.defaults.sandbox.docker.network at its default "none"; "host" is blocked and container namespace joins need the dangerouslyAllowContainerNamespaceJoin break-glass key.

steps.title: Use an OpenShell policy for a destination allowlist
body: With backend "openshell", set plugins.entries.openshell.config.policy to the absolute path of an OpenShell policy YAML on the Gateway host that permits only the destinations the agent needs; Docker network keys do not apply to that backend.

steps.title: Allowlist host-exec egress
body: `openclaw config set secrets.egressProxy.allowedHosts '["api.openai.com"]' --strict-json` with the egress proxy enabled; an empty array is lockdown (only secret-bound and bypass hosts). Cooperating clients only — raw sockets can bypass it.

steps.title: Block web_fetch destinations
body: Set tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy.blockedHostnames for hosts and wildcard subdomains to deny and keep dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork false; private and internal targets stay blocked unless named in allowedHostnames.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: OpenClaw's own sandbox network is on or off. A domain-level allowlist lives either in OpenShell, a separate runtime the OpenShell backend delegates to, or in the egress proxy, which only cooperating clients on Gateway-hosted exec honour (the vendor says raw sockets bypass it). The Gateway's own model, channel and web_fetch traffic is not destination-allowlisted, the sandboxed browser uses its own bridge network, and an unsandboxed exec backend is bounded only by the host. proxy.proxyUrl routing is only as strong as the operator proxy's policy.

original.mechanism: Sandbox containers default to network none; secrets.egressProxy.allowedHosts is an exact-hostname traffic allowlist for Gateway-hosted exec; web_fetch and browser SSRF policies block private ranges with allowedHostnames / blockedHostnames; proxy.proxyUrl routes all runtime HTTP/WebSocket traffic through an operator-run forward proxy (the proxy itself is external)

steps.title: Keep the sandbox offline
body: Leave agents.defaults.sandbox.docker.network at its default "none"; "host" is blocked and container namespace joins need a dangerously* break-glass key.

steps.title: Allowlist exec egress
body: `openclaw config set secrets.egressProxy.allowedHosts '["api.openai.com"]' --strict-json` with the egress proxy enabled; an empty array is lockdown (only secret-bound and bypass hosts). Cooperating clients only — raw sockets can bypass it.

steps.title: Pin web_fetch destinations
body: Set tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy.allowedHostnames and blockedHostnames and keep dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork false; private and internal hostnames are blocked by default with DNS pinning.

steps.title: Route everything through your proxy
body: Set proxy.proxyUrl (or OPENCLAW_PROXY_URL) and validate with `openclaw proxy validate --proxy-url <url>`; the proxy's destination policy is the real boundary and OpenClaw ships none.

original.note: Sandboxed exec is bounded by the container network and the egress proxy allowlist; the gateway process's own model and channel calls follow proxy.proxyUrl but are not destination-filtered, and a local (unsandboxed) exec backend is bounded only by the host.

controls.mechanism: ClawHub security audits of published skill and plugin releases, with a blocked release refused at install; `openclaw security audit --deep` code-safety scans of installed plugins and skills (plugins.code_safety, skills.code_safety); security.installPolicy runs the user's own scanner before an install commits. Packages the agent installs and local model weights are not scanned.

steps.title: Read the release audit before installing
body: Community ClawHub installs print the release's audit outcome and details link; a blocking outcome or disabled download is refused, and a Review outcome only informs.

steps.title: Scan what is installed
body: Run `openclaw security audit --deep`, which adds the plugin and skill code-safety scans to the ordinary audit.

steps.title: Put your scanner in the install path
body: Configure security.installPolicy (enabled, targets ["skill", "plugin"], exec.command) so your scanner returns allow, warn or block; neither --force nor the acknowledgement overrides block.

steps.title: Avoid unscanned skills
body: Do not use `--force-install`, which installs a GitHub-backed skill before ClawHub's scan completes, and treat skills-sh, git and local installs as unscanned.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: the project's registry scans what it hosts and the CLI can scan installed extension code, but the boundary is ClawHub releases and this Gateway's extension roots. Official packages and bundled plugins skip the release-trust check, npm, git and local installs are not scanned by ClawHub, the code scans are static and bounded, and the Python, npm or other packages the agent installs through exec, like any local model weights the user points models.providers at, reach the host unscanned. Admission scanning at a package mirror or artifact repository is the external control.

original.note: Models are remote provider APIs or local servers (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp) the user points models.providers at; nothing inspects model files. Scan any local GGUF or other weights with an external tool before configuring them, including the local embedding option for memory.search.provider. Rated none rather than not applicable because the product's optional local model and local embedding paths load weights the operator supplies, and nothing in the product scans them.
